papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the Coulomb drag transresistivity in double-layer two-dimensional electron gases (2DEGs) within the quantum Hall regime near a filling factor of ν = 1/2. The study investigates the temperature and magnetic field dependencies of transresistivity, focusing on the impact of Fermi-liquid interactions between quasiparticles. The central finding is that Fermi-liquid interactions can significantly influence the transresistivity, explaining its observed independence of interlayer spacing for experimentally relevant values. The author derives an expression for the transresistivity, incorporating Fermi-liquid effects, and compares the results with experimental data. The model predicts a nearly quadratic enhancement of transresistivity with deviations from ν = 1/2, consistent with experiments. The study highlights the role of Fermi-liquid interactions in reducing the compressibility of the composite fermion (CF) liquid, thereby increasing the screening length and explaining the insensitivity of transresistivity to interlayer spacing. A key limitation is the reliance on approximations and the scope conditions of the model, particularly at low temperatures. The work is significant because it offers a theoretical framework to understand the behavior of Coulomb drag in double-layer systems, providing insights into the role of many-body interactions in quantum Hall physics and offering a possible explanation for experimental observations.

Research Context
Prior research on Coulomb drag in double-layer 2DEGs has shown a temperature dependence of transresistivity proportional to T^(4/3) at ν = 1/2, attributed to ballistic contributions. Experiments revealed a quadratic enhancement of transresistivity with deviations from ν = 1/2, with curvature dependent on temperature but insensitive to the sign of the deviation or interlayer distance. Existing theoretical models, such as those based on composite fermion (CF) approaches, lacked a complete explanation for the observed behavior, particularly the insensitivity to interlayer spacing. The current work addresses this gap by incorporating Fermi-liquid interactions into the theoretical framework, which were not fully considered in previous studies. This allows for a more comprehensive understanding of the experimental results.

Research Question Hypothesis
The primary research question is: How do Fermi-liquid interactions affect the transresistivity in double-layer 2DEGs near ν = 1/2, and can these interactions explain the experimentally observed behavior, including the insensitivity of transresistivity to interlayer spacing? The central hypothesis is that Fermi-liquid interactions between quasiparticles in the 2DEGs significantly influence the transresistivity, leading to its observed characteristics. The author predicts that incorporating these interactions will result in a model that accurately describes the temperature and magnetic field dependencies of transresistivity, including its quadratic enhancement with deviations from ν = 1/2 and its insensitivity to interlayer spacing. The alternative hypothesis is that other factors, not considered in the model, are responsible for the observed behavior. The study aims to validate the hypothesis by comparing the theoretical predictions with experimental data, specifically the magnetic field and temperature dependence of the transresistivity and its relationship to the interlayer spacing.

Methodological Details
The study employs a theoretical approach, deriving an expression for the Coulomb drag transresistivity in double-layer 2DEGs. The analysis starts from a well-known expression relating transresistivity to the density-density components of the polarization in the layers. The author uses the Composite Fermion (CF) approach, adopting the Random Phase Approximation (RPA). The polarizability matrix is calculated, and the density-density response function is derived. The CF conductivity components are calculated at filling factors slightly away from 1/2. The Boltzmann transport equation is used to derive the CF conductivity components. The model incorporates Fermi-liquid interactions by renormalizing the polarizability. The screened interlayer potential is taken from a previous work. The transresistivity is then calculated, and the results are compared with experimental data. The study focuses on the ballistic contribution to the transresistivity, using approximations applicable in a nonlocal and high-frequency regime. The analysis involves several mathematical steps, including Fourier series expansions and the introduction of new variables. The model uses the compressibility of the ν = 1/2 state, which is renormalized due to Fermi-liquid interactions. The study does not include details on experimental setups, as it is a theoretical work. The author does not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections, as it is a theoretical study.

Procedures Architectures
The study does not involve the design or implementation of physical architectures or experimental procedures. Instead, it utilizes a theoretical framework based on established concepts in condensed matter physics. The core procedure involves deriving an expression for the transresistivity, starting from the known formula relating transresistivity to density-density components of the polarization in the layers. The model adopts the Composite Fermion (CF) approach and the Random Phase Approximation (RPA). The author calculates the polarizability matrix and the density-density response function. The CF conductivity components are calculated using the Boltzmann transport equation. The model incorporates Fermi-liquid interactions by renormalizing the polarizability. The screened interlayer potential is taken from a previous work. The transresistivity is calculated, and the results are compared with experimental data. The model uses the compressibility of the ν = 1/2 state, which is renormalized due to Fermi-liquid interactions. The model uses several equations and approximations, including the expansion of the CF velocity components in Fourier series and the use of asymptotic expressions for the CF conductivity components. The model does not specify any particular software or hardware.

Key Results
The study derives an expression for the transresistivity ρD, which is separated into two terms: ρD0, the transresistivity at ν = 1/2, and δρD, a correction arising from a non-zero effective magnetic field. The expression for ρD0 coincides with a known result: ρD0 = (h/e^2) * (Γ(7/3)ζ(4/3)/3√3) * (T/T0)^(4/3). The leading term of the correction δρD at low temperatures (T/T0) ≪ 1 is given by δρD = (2/3)ρD0 * (1/(kF R)) * (1 + (3/8) * (1/(kF R))) + a2 * (h/e^2) * (2T/T0)^(2/3) * (∆ν)^2, where kF is the Fermi wave vector, R is the CF cyclotron radius, and ∆ν = ν - 1/2. The derived expression predicts a nearly quadratic enhancement of transresistivity with ∆ν, consistent with experimental observations. The analysis shows that the magnetic field dependence of the transresistivity near ν = 1/2 matches that observed in experiments (Figure 1). The ratio ρD/ρD0 can be presented in the form ρD/ρD0 = 4β(∆ν)^2 + 1, where β is a coefficient proportional to the curvature of the plot of Eq. (22). The temperature dependence of β^(-1) also agrees with experimental results (Figure 2). The model provides a possible explanation for the insensitivity of the drag to the interlayer spacing. The Fermi liquid interaction provides a significant reduction of the compressibility of the CF liquid, and a consequent enhancement in the screening length in single layers. The results show a reasonably good agreement between the theoretical predictions and the experimental results, using A0 = 15 and A1 = 3 (m* = 4mb).

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that Fermi-liquid interactions play a crucial role in the behavior of Coulomb drag in double-layer 2DEGs near ν = 1/2. The model's ability to reproduce the experimental results, particularly the quadratic dependence on ∆ν and the insensitivity to interlayer spacing, supports the hypothesis that these interactions are a key factor. The study implies that the Fermi-liquid interactions significantly reduce the compressibility of the CF liquid, enhancing the screening length within the layers. This enhanced screening, in turn, explains why the transresistivity is less sensitive to the distance between the layers. The work provides a theoretical basis for understanding the experimental observations and offers insights into the role of many-body interactions in quantum Hall systems. The results suggest that the experimental data can be used to estimate the strength of Fermi-liquid interactions in the CF system near ν = 1/2, which is important for further studies.

Contradictions Limitations
The study relies on several approximations, including the RPA and the use of asymptotic expressions for the CF conductivity components. The model's validity is limited by the conditions ωτ ≫ 1 and ql ≫ 1, which define the ballistic regime. The results are not applicable in the limit T → 0. The model's accuracy depends on the choice of parameters, such as the Fermi-liquid coefficients A0 and A1, which are estimated. The study does not address the limitations of the RPA or the potential impact of other factors not included in the model. The model does not fully explain the observed asymmetry in the plot of Eq. (22) relative to ∆ν = 0. The study does not discuss the potential influence of disorder or other effects that could affect the transresistivity. The paper does not provide details on the experimental setup or the specific materials used in the experiments, which limits the ability to fully assess the model's applicability. The author acknowledges that the condition α > 1 could be satisfied for small values of the compressibility of the ν = 1/2 state, but this is not fully demonstrated.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the scaled drag resistivity versus ∆ν at T = 0.6 and compares the theoretical results with experimental data. The figure's axes are scaled drag resistivity and ∆ν. Figure 2 shows the temperature dependence of the coefficient β^(-1) for different interlayer distances and compares them with experimental curvature data. The figure's axes are β^(-1) and temperature. These figures are critical for validating the model's predictions against experimental observations.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the theoretical demonstration that Fermi-liquid interactions can explain the behavior of Coulomb drag in double-layer 2DEGs near ν = 1/2, specifically the quadratic enhancement of transresistivity with deviations from ν = 1/2 and the insensitivity to interlayer spacing.

(2) The strongest evidence supporting the claims is the good agreement between the theoretical predictions and experimental results, particularly the qualitative match of the magnetic field and temperature dependence of the transresistivity, as shown in Figures 1 and 2, which validates the model.

(3) The primary limitation is the reliance on approximations and the scope conditions of the model, especially at low temperatures. A forward path includes refining the model by considering other factors, such as disorder and other effects that could affect the transresistivity, and comparing the results with further experimental data.

arXiv:0704.0228v1  [gr-qc]  2 Apr 2007

Einstein vs Maxwell: Is gravitation a curvature of space,
a ﬁeld in ﬂat space, or both?
Theo M. Nieuwenhuizen
Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of Amsterdam, Valckenierstraat 65, 1018 XE Amsterdam, The Netherlands
PACS 04.20.Cv – Fundamental problems and general formalism
PACS 04.20.Fy – Canonical formalism, Lagrangians, and variational principles
PACS 98.80.Bp – Origin and formation of the Universe
Abstract. - Starting with a ﬁeld theoretic approach in Minkowski space, the gravitational energy
momentum tensor is derived from the Einstein equations in a straightforward manner. This allows
to present them as acceleration tensor = const. × total energy momentum tensor. For ﬂat space
cosmology the gravitational energy is negative and cancels the material energy. In the relativistic
theory of gravitation a bimetric coupling between the Riemann and Minkowski metrics breaks
general coordinate invariance.
The case of a positive cosmological constant is considered.
A
singularity free version of the Schwarzschild black hole is solved analytically. In the interior the
components of the metric tensor quickly die out, but do not change sign, leaving the role of time
as usual. For cosmology the ΛCDM model is covered, while there appears a form of inﬂation at
early times. Here both the total energy and the zero point energy vanish.
It is said that in introducing the general theory of rela-
tivity (GTR), Einstein made the step that Lorentz and
Poincar´e had failed to make: to go from ﬂat space to

Executive Summary
This paper explores the nature of gravitation, contrasting Einstein's theory of general relativity (GTR) with a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space, and its extension, the relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG). The author derives the gravitational energy-momentum tensor from the Einstein equations, presenting them as an acceleration tensor proportional to the total energy-momentum tensor. For flat space cosmology, gravitational energy is negative and cancels material energy. The RTG, which incorporates bimetric coupling between Riemann and Minkowski metrics, breaks general coordinate invariance. The paper considers a positive cosmological constant and presents an analytical, singularity-free solution for the Schwarzschild black hole's interior. In this solution, the metric tensor components decay rapidly but do not change sign, preserving the role of time. For cosmology, the RTG covers the ΛCDM model and exhibits inflation at early times, with both total and zero-point energy vanishing. The study reveals that the field-theoretic approach is equivalent to a curved space description. The RTG, however, views gravitation as a field in flat space, aligning with Maxwell's perspective. A key finding is the regularization of the Schwarzschild black hole interior within the RTG framework, where time maintains its standard role, and escape is theoretically possible. The primary limitation is the focus on theoretical models without empirical validation. Future work includes exploring realistic equations of state for black holes, classical tunneling of its radiation, and aspects of inflation and inhomogeneous cosmology.

Research Context
The paper addresses the fundamental question of whether gravitation is best described as a curvature of spacetime (Einstein's view) or as a field in flat space (Maxwell's view). The standard model of general relativity faces challenges in defining a local energy-momentum density. Prior work by Babak and Grishchuk derived the proper energy-momentum tensor of gravitation using a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space. Nathan Rosen's bimetric theory, involving both Minkowski and Riemann metrics, provides another relevant context. These approaches offer alternatives to GTR's reliance on general coordinate invariance. The paper builds on these foundations by exploring the implications of these different perspectives, particularly in the context of black holes and cosmology. The lack of a clear understanding of gravitational energy and the limitations of GTR in describing black hole interiors and early universe inflation motivate this research.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether gravitation is fundamentally a curvature of space, a field in flat space, or a combination of both. The paper explores this question by examining the mathematical and physical consequences of different theoretical frameworks. The primary hypothesis is that a field-theoretic approach, particularly the RTG, can provide a more complete and potentially more tractable description of gravitation, especially in extreme environments like black holes and the early universe. The paper predicts that the RTG will offer a singularity-free solution for the Schwarzschild black hole interior, preserving the standard role of time. It also predicts that the RTG will align with the ΛCDM model in cosmology and exhibit an inflationary phase at early times. The study aims to support these hypotheses by deriving and analyzing the mathematical properties of the RTG and comparing its predictions with those of GTR. The alternative hypothesis is that GTR remains the most accurate and complete description, and the RTG will encounter inconsistencies or fail to provide significant advantages. The outcomes that would support the primary hypothesis include a well-behaved black hole interior, consistency with cosmological observations, and a natural explanation for inflation. Refutation would involve inconsistencies within the RTG framework or discrepancies with observed phenomena.

Methodological Details
The paper employs a theoretical methodology, deriving and analyzing equations within the framework of general relativity and the relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG). The study begins with a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space, utilizing the metric tensor and the acceleration tensor. The Einstein equations are then re-expressed in terms of the total energy-momentum tensor. The analysis proceeds by considering the Friedman-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric for cosmology. The paper then transitions to the RTG, which introduces bimetric coupling and breaks general coordinate invariance. The Schwarzschild black hole is analyzed within the RTG framework. The analysis involves solving equations derived from the Einstein equations with a positive cosmological constant, and the harmonic condition. The paper uses mathematical derivations and analytical solutions to explore the behavior of the metric tensor components and the motion of test particles. The study does not involve empirical data collection or experimental procedures. The analysis relies on the manipulation of equations and the interpretation of their solutions. The paper does not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. The study's ethical considerations are not explicitly addressed. The paper uses the following definitions: Minkowski metric (γµν), Riemann metric tensor (gµν), acceleration tensor (Aµν), total energy momentum tensor (Θµν), FLRW metric (ds²), Schwarzschild black hole, and the RTG. The paper does not specify the software used.

Procedures Architectures
The paper's core procedure involves deriving and analyzing equations within the context of general relativity and the relativistic theory of gravitation (RTG). The analysis begins with the Einstein equations, which are reformulated using a field-theoretic approach in Minkowski space. The key component is the derivation of the acceleration tensor (Aµν) and the total energy-momentum tensor (Θµν). The RTG framework introduces bimetric coupling, using both the Minkowski metric (γµν) and the Riemann metric (gµν). The Schwarzschild black hole solution is derived and analyzed within the RTG framework. The paper presents a parametric solution for the metric components (U, V, W) inside the black hole. The equations are solved to determine the behavior of the metric components and the motion of test particles. The architecture involves the interaction of the Minkowski and Riemann metrics within the RTG. The paper introduces a small parameter, η, related to the cosmological constant, to analyze the black hole solution. The paper also discusses the implications of the harmonic constraint, which reduces the gauge invariance of GTR. The new element is the application of the RTG to the Schwarzschild black hole, providing a singularity-free solution. The paper uses equations (1) through (26) to describe the mathematical framework and the key results. The paper does not specify the hardware used.

Key Results
The paper presents several key results. First, the Einstein equations can be expressed in terms of an acceleration tensor proportional to the total energy-momentum tensor (Equation 6). For flat space cosmology, the gravitational energy density is negative and cancels the matter energy density, resulting in zero total energy. In the RTG, the choice of a positive cosmological constant allows for a singularity-free solution for the Schwarzschild black hole interior. The metric components U and V remain positive inside the horizon, preserving the role of time (Figure 1). The paper provides an analytical solution for the metric components U, V, and W inside the black hole, which coincides with the Schwarzschild solution for ξ ≫ 1. The width of the transition layer, or 't Hooft's brick wall, is estimated to be ℓ⋆ = ηrh. The paper also analyzes the motion of test particles within the RTG framework. In cosmology, the RTG recovers the ΛCDM model (Equation 26). The paper finds that the gravitational energy precisely compensates for other energy contributions at all times, and the vacuum energy vanishes. The solution for the black hole interior shows that the components of the metric tensor quickly die out, but do not change sign. The paper does not report any baseline comparisons or effect sizes.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the field-theoretic approach to gravitation, particularly the RTG, offers a viable alternative to GTR, especially in extreme gravitational environments. The regularization of the Schwarzschild black hole interior within the RTG framework implies that the singularity problem might be resolved, and the standard role of time is preserved. The recovery of the ΛCDM model in cosmology supports the RTG's consistency with observed phenomena. The vanishing of total energy in flat space cosmology and the compensation of gravitational and material energy suggest a deeper connection between gravity and energy. The results support the interpretation that curvature is a geometric description of the gravitational field in flat space. The findings imply that the quantum version of RTG, if it exists, will involve the quantization of fields, but not of space. The paper suggests that the RTG aligns with Maxwell's view of gravitation as a field in flat space. The results shift the understanding of black holes and cosmology by providing a potentially more complete and consistent theoretical framework.

Contradictions Limitations
The primary limitation of the paper is its purely theoretical nature, lacking empirical validation. The absence of experimental or observational evidence to support the RTG's predictions is a significant constraint. The paper relies on mathematical derivations and analytical solutions, without addressing potential inconsistencies or limitations within the RTG framework itself. The paper does not discuss the potential for subgroup effects or the external validity of the theoretical models. The paper does not discuss the potential for inconsistencies with prior literature, except to highlight the differences between the RTG and GTR. The paper's focus on theoretical models limits its applicability to real-world scenarios. The paper does not mention the random seed, train/test split, or demographics. The analysis of the Schwarzschild black hole is limited to a specific theoretical framework, and the implications of the findings depend on the validity of the RTG. The paper's conclusions are based on mathematical derivations and analytical solutions, which may not fully capture the complexities of the physical world.

(2) The strongest evidence is the analytical solution for the metric components inside the black hole, which, as shown in Figure 1, remains positive, demonstrating the absence of a singularity and the preservation of time. (3) The primary limitation is the lack of empirical validation. Future work should focus on testing the RTG's predictions against observational data and exploring its implications for other gravitational phenomena, such as the behavior of matter falling into black holes.

arXiv:0704.0301v1  [cs.CC]  3 Apr 2007
Differential recursion and
differentially algebraic functions∗
Akitoshi Kawamura
Department of Computer Science
University of Toronto
Moore introduced a class of real-valued “recursive” functions by analogy with
Kleene’s formulation of the standard recursive functions. While his concise def-
inition inspired a new line of research on analog computation, it contains some
technical inaccuracies. Focusing on his “primitive recursive” functions, we pin
down what is problematic and discuss possible attempts to remove the ambiguity
regarding the behavior of the diﬀerential recursion operator on partial functions.
It turns out that in any case the purported relation to diﬀerentially algebraic
functions, and hence to Shannon’s model of analog computation, fails.
1. Introduction
There are several diﬀerent kinds of theoretical models that talk about “computability” and
“complexity” of real functions. Computable Analysis [19] and some other equivalent models
use approximation in one way or another to bring real numbers into the framework of the
standard Computability Theory that deals with discrete data in discrete time. Another well-
known model is the Blum–Shub–Smale model [1] in which continuous quantities are treated
as an entity in themselves but the machine still works with discrete clock ticks.
A third approach is analog computation in which not only are the data real-valued, but
also the transition takes place in continuous time [15].
One of the oldest and the best-
studied models of such computation is Shannon’s General Purpose Analog Computer [18]
that models the Diﬀerential Analyzer [3], a computing device built and put to use during
the thirties through the ﬁfties. The GPAC, after some reﬁnements [8, 12, 16], was shown
capable of generating (in a sense) all and only the diﬀerentially algebraic functions. We will
explore this class in Section 2 and show that it can be characterized in many diﬀerent ways.
Little is known about how such analog models relate to the standard (digital) computabil-
ity. Moore [13] addressed this question for his new function classes that also try to express

the power of GPAC-like computation. In imitation of Kleene’s characterization of the usual
recursive functions, these classes are deﬁned as the closures under certain operators that
are supposedly real-number versions of primitive recursion and minimization. He makes the
following claims, among others, that relate his classes of real primitive recursive and real re-
cursive functions to analog and digital computation, respectively [13, Propositions 9 and 13].
Claim 1. Real primitive recursive functions are diﬀerentially algebraic.1
Claim 2. Each (partial) recursive function on the nonnegative integers (in the standard
sense) is a restriction of some real recursive function.
Despite its impact on the subsequent study on the classes and their variants [2, 4, 5, 8, 14],
his work lacked formality in some ways, as already pointed out [6, 7]. In fact, the deﬁnition of
the classes suﬀers from ambiguity. In Section 3 of this paper, we reformulate Moore’s theory
up to the real primitive recursive functions in a mathematically sound way. With the aid of
the preparation in Section 2, we show that, even though our formulation of the class seems
the most restrictive possible, Claim 1 fails. In section 4, we discuss some issues about classes
other than the real primitive recursive functions, including Claim 2.
Throughout the paper, we write N, Z, R for the sets of nonnegative integers (including
0), integers and real numbers, respectively.
Partial functions
In this paper, a function f :⊆Rm →Rn may be partial, as opposed to
total; that is, the set dom f of x ∈Rm for which the value f x ∈Rn is deﬁned is allowed to
be a proper subset of Rm. By the restriction of f to a set J ⊆Rm we mean the function g
with dom g = J ∩dom f such that gx = f x for every x ∈dom g. When dom f is open, f
is said to be (real) analytic if for every a = (a0, . . . , am−1) ∈dom f there are an open set

2. Differentially algebraic functions
We show some facts about single- and multi-place diﬀerentially algebraic functions.
Theorem 3. Let m, n and i < m be nonnegative integers and f :⊆Rm →Rn be an analytic
function with open domain. Let (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv) be the following statements:

Let (iR), (iiR) and (iiiR) be the statements obtained by replacing Z by R in (i), (ii) and (iii),
respectively. Then (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (iR), (iiR) and (iiiR) are equivalent.
Proof. The implications (i) ⇒(ii) ⇒(iii) ⇒(iv) and (i) ⇒(iR) ⇒(iiR) ⇒(iiiR) are obvious.
It has been known that (iiiR) ⇒(iii), see Theorem 16. To see (iv) ⇒(i), consider, for each Zn-
coeﬃcient polynomial P, the set JP of all x ∈J satisfying (2). Since by (iv) these countably
many closed sets JP cover the open set J, one of them must have nonempty interior by Baire
Category Theorem 14. This JP must then equal J by the Identity Theorem 15.
Deﬁnition 4. Let m and n be nonnegative integers. An analytic function f :⊆Rm →Rn is
diﬀerentially algebraic2 if for each i < m it satisﬁes one (or all) of the clauses in Theorem 3.
Note that f need not be the unique solution of (2). For example, every function (with
open domain) that is constant on each connected component of its domain is diﬀerentially
algebraic because of the single set of equations Deif x = 0.
The clauses (ii)–(iv) show that being diﬀerentially algebraic is a “local” property.
When dom f is connected, (i) reduces to the following statement:
(i′) there is a Zn-coeﬃcient nonzero polynomial P such that we have (2) for all x ∈dom f.
Hence, the clause (iii) shows that, as long as dom f is connected, our deﬁnition is equivalent
to that of many authors, including Moore [13], who ﬁrst state the deﬁnition for m = 1 by (i′)
and then extend it to m > 1 by saying that a function is diﬀerentially algebraic when it is so
as a unary function of each argument when all other arguments are held ﬁxed.3 We proved
Theorem 3 in order to use (i) to present a counterexample to Claim 1 later.

4.2. Linear differential recursion
We have seen that many of the problems in Moore’s original work were caused by failure to
deal with partial functions properly. Some authors avoid this trouble by studying only oper-

Claim 1 has been the main rationale for calling variants of Moore’s classes a model of analog
computation. Now that we have lost it, an important challenge is the following.
Open Problem. Find a subclass of our real primitive recursive functions, preferably with an
equally simple deﬁnition, that has a close relationship to the diﬀerentially algebraic functions.
Another direction would be to reformulate further the rest of Moore’s work, as well as other
authors’ works that also suﬀer from the same kind of ambiguity. For example, it may be
interesting to work out Mycka and Costa’s class arising from the operator of taking limits [14].

Executive Summary
This paper revisits Moore's work on real-valued recursive functions, which aimed to model analog computation, and demonstrates that a key claim relating real primitive recursive functions to differentially algebraic functions is incorrect. Moore's definition of these function classes, inspired by Kleene's work on standard recursive functions, contained ambiguities, particularly regarding partial functions. The author clarifies these definitions, especially the differential recursion operator, and proves that real primitive recursive functions, as defined with a more restrictive domain, are not necessarily differentially algebraic. This refutes Moore's claim that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic and, by extension, related to Shannon's model of analog computation. The paper also discusses the implications of this finding, including the need for a new approach to relate real primitive recursive functions to differentially algebraic functions and the challenges in defining real recursive functions with the minimization operator. The main contribution is the formalization of Moore's theory and the demonstration that the purported connection between real primitive recursive functions and differentially algebraic functions fails. The primary limitation is the loss of the direct link to differentially algebraic functions, which necessitates further research to find a suitable subclass. The results suggest that the original claims about the relationship between Moore's function classes and analog computation need to be reevaluated, and the paper proposes open problems for future research.

Research Context
The paper addresses the gap in understanding the relationship between analog and digital computation, specifically concerning Moore's classes of real-valued recursive functions. Moore's work aimed to create a framework for analog computation, inspired by Kleene's characterization of standard recursive functions. Prior approaches include Computable Analysis and the Blum-Shub-Smale model, which use approximation or treat continuous quantities as entities. Shannon's General Purpose Analog Computer (GPAC) is a well-studied model of analog computation. Moore's work, however, lacked formality and suffered from ambiguities, particularly in the handling of partial functions. The closest prior approaches are Moore's initial work and subsequent studies on variants of his classes. The main limitation of these prior approaches is the lack of a rigorous mathematical foundation, which leads to ambiguous definitions and erroneous claims, specifically concerning the relationship between real primitive recursive functions and differentially algebraic functions.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether Moore's claim that real primitive recursive functions are differentially algebraic holds true. The primary hypothesis, implicitly tested, is that real primitive recursive functions, as defined by Moore, are differentially algebraic. An alternative hypothesis is that the class of real primitive recursive functions is not a subset of the class of differentially algebraic functions. The paper investigates this by formalizing Moore's definitions, particularly the differential recursion operator, and examining the properties of real primitive recursive functions. The study differs from prior work by providing a mathematically sound formulation of Moore's theory, which addresses the ambiguities in the original definition, especially regarding partial functions. The outcomes that would support the primary hypothesis would be the demonstration that all real primitive recursive functions satisfy the defining properties of differentially algebraic functions. The paper refutes the primary hypothesis by showing that real primitive recursive functions are not necessarily differentially algebraic, using the Gamma function as a counterexample.

Methodological Details
The paper employs a theoretical methodology, focusing on formal definitions and mathematical proofs. The study does not involve empirical data or experiments. The primary materials are the definitions and theorems from mathematical analysis and computability theory, particularly those related to real-valued functions, differential equations, and differential algebra. The key concepts include real primitive recursive functions, differentially algebraic functions, the differential recursion operator, and the minimization operator. The study uses the definitions of juxtaposition, composition, and differential recursion operators to define real primitive recursive functions. The definition of the differential recursion operator is carefully reformulated to address ambiguities in Moore's original work, particularly concerning the domain of the resulting functions. The paper uses the characterization of differentially algebraic functions to prove that real primitive recursive functions are not necessarily differentially algebraic. The proof relies on the properties of the Gamma function, which is shown to be real primitive recursive but not differentially algebraic. The paper also discusses the implications of using different versions of the differential recursion operator, such as Campagnolo's drC, and their impact on the properties of the resulting function classes. There is no mention of preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections, as the study is theoretical. The study adheres to standard mathematical practices for proofs and definitions, ensuring the reproducibility of the results.

The paper does not describe any specific procedures or architectures in the context of computational models. The focus is on the mathematical definitions and properties of function classes. The study defines the real primitive recursive functions using three operators: juxtaposition, composition, and differential recursion. The juxtaposition operator, denoted as `jx`, combines functions by concatenating their outputs. The composition operator, denoted as `cm`, applies one function to the output of another. The differential recursion operator, denoted as `dr`, is the most complex, defining functions through integral equations. The paper provides a detailed definition of `dr`, including the concept of a unique solution to an integral equation. The paper also discusses an alternative differential recursion operator, `drC`, proposed by Campagnolo, which relaxes some conditions on the domain of the integrand. The paper does not contain any key figures or tables that are central to its claims. The paper uses Figure 1 to illustrate the concept of unique solutions in the context of partial functions. Figure 2 illustrates the function with a singularity.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the rigorous formalization of Moore's theory of real-valued recursive functions and the demonstration that a key claim relating real primitive recursive functions to differentially algebraic functions is incorrect. (2) The strongest evidence supporting the claims is the proof that the Gamma function, which is real primitive recursive, is not differentially algebraic, contradicting Moore's claim (Section 3.4). (3) The primary limitation is the loss of the direct link between real primitive recursive functions and differentially algebraic functions, which necessitates further research to find a suitable subclass or alternative approaches to model analog computation.

Enhanced sensitivity to variation of me/mp in molecular spectra
D. DeMille,1 S. Sainis,1 J. Sage,1 T. Bergeman,2 S. Kotochigova,3 and E. Tiesinga4
1Department of Physics, Yale University, New Haven, CT 06520, USA
2Department of Physics and Astronomy, SUNY, Stony Brook, NY 11794, USA
3Physics Department, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA 19122, USA
4Joint Quantum Institute and Atomic Physics Division,
National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD 20899
(Dated: February 16, 2013)
We propose new experiments with high sensitivity to a possible spatial or temporal variation of
the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ ≡me/mp. We consider a nearly-degenerate pair of molecular
vibrational levels, where each state is associated with a diﬀerent electronic potential. The change
in the splitting between such levels, with respect to a change in µ, can be large both on an absolute
scale and relative to the splitting. We demonstrate the existence of such pairs of levels in Cs2.
The narrow spectral lines achievable with ultracold Cs2 in these long-lived levels make this system
promising for future searches for small variations in µ.
PACS numbers: 06.20.Jr,33.80.Ps,33.20.Wr,33.20.Bx
The notion that the fundamental constants of nature
may actually vary has recently generated intense inter-
est [1, 2]. Theoretical motivation comes from a variety
of string-inspired models; these can include space-time
with extra dimensions of variable geometry, and/or light
scalar ﬁelds whose variable amplitude couples to ordinary
matter. Both eﬀects can change the apparent values of
constants. Such ﬁelds are potential candidates (dubbed
“quintessence”) to explain the observed dark energy that
dominates the universe.
Sensitive probes for possible
variation of fundamental constants are among the few
ways to verify or constrain models such as these.
On quite general principles, measurements can only
detect variation in dimensionless constants [2]. To date,
most attention has focused on possible variation of the
ﬁne structure constant α. However, variations in α are
no more likely than in any other fundamental dimen-
sionless parameter.
In fact, it has been argued that
within the context of grand uniﬁed theories, variation
in the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ ≡me/mp should
be larger than the variation in α by a factor of ∼30 [2].
As a result, study of µ is a potentially more sensitive
method to observe any variation of constants.
The most sensitive tests for variation in µ have come
from examining molecular spectra from cosmologically
distant sources, at redshifts corresponding to ∼1010 years
ago [3]. Comparisons of spectral lines in these objects
to the same lines measured now in the laboratory, yield
stringent bounds at the level ∼10−15/year on the time
variation of µ.
However, systematic errors associated
with these measurements can be signiﬁcant, and are diﬃ-
cult to eliminate due to the uncertainty in the structure,
environment, and dynamics of the sources.
We propose a new type of laboratory experiment to
search for variation of µ with high sensitivity. We show
that the energy of molecular vibrational levels can be
highly sensitive to changes in µ.
In addition, pairs of
closely-spaced levels can be used to enhance the sensitiv-
ity relative to the level splitting. We show spectroscopic
data verifying such a near-degeneracy in the ground vi-
bronic levels of Cs2. We argue that the splitting between
pairs of levels in Cs2 could be measured precisely enough
to sense a fractional change ∆µ/µ ≲10−17.
The sensitivity of our proposed measurement is gov-
erned by a few key parameters. Most important is the
absolute change ∂µΩof the energy splitting Ωwith re-
spect to a fractional change ∆µ/µ: ∂µΩ≡∂Ω/∂(lnµ).
(ℏ= c = 1 throughout.) Ωcan be measured with statis-
tical uncertainty δΩ= Γ/S, where Γ is the linewidth of
the transition and S is the signal-to-noise. Hence, ∆µ/µ
can be detected with statistical uncertainty δ(∆µ/µ) =
δΩ/∂µΩ= (Γ/∂µΩ)S−1, and the ratio ∂µΩ/Γ provides a
primary ﬁgure of merit for any such measurement. How-
ever, the relative change of the splitting, ∂µΩ/Ω, is also
of importance, for two reasons. First, since ultimately Ω
must be measured with respect to some reference clock
(with fractional uncertainty δΩc/Ωc), it is impossible to
determine Ωto better than δΩmin = Ω(δΩc/Ωc). In addi-
tion, many systematic eﬀects are proportional to Ω(e.g.
Doppler shifts).
Hence, ∂µΩ/Ωprovides an important
secondary ﬁgure of merit.

µ changes, with the assumption that both me and α
remain constant.

cal atomic transitions, which also depend parametrically
only on Ry and α.) We approximate the vibrational en-

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a novel experimental approach to detect potential variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio, µ = me/mp, by exploiting the sensitivity of molecular vibrational levels to changes in µ. The authors focus on Cs2 molecules, specifically examining the near-degeneracy between vibrational levels associated with different electronic potentials. The study demonstrates the existence of such level pairs in Cs2, which can amplify the sensitivity to changes in µ. The authors utilize two-color photoassociation spectroscopy to determine the positions of deeply bound a3Σ+u levels in Cs2. The key finding is the identification of a near-degeneracy between the a3Σ+u (va = 37) and X1Σ+g (vX = 138) levels, which is crucial for enhancing sensitivity. They estimate that a fractional change of ∆µ/µ ≲ 10−17 could be detected in approximately one day of integration. This work is significant because it provides a new method for probing fundamental physics by searching for variations in fundamental constants, potentially offering a more sensitive approach than existing methods. The primary limitation is the need for further experimental data to confirm the near-degeneracies and refine the sensitivity estimates.

Research Context
The search for variations in fundamental constants, such as the fine-structure constant α and the electron-to-proton mass ratio µ, is motivated by theoretical models, including those inspired by string theory and quintessence. Prior research has primarily focused on variations in α, with less attention given to µ, despite theoretical predictions suggesting that variations in µ could be more pronounced. Existing methods, such as examining molecular spectra from distant sources, face challenges related to systematic errors. This work addresses the need for a new laboratory experiment to search for variations in µ with high sensitivity, overcoming the limitations of previous approaches by utilizing molecular spectra in ultracold Cs2.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: Can the sensitivity to variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio, µ, be enhanced by exploiting the properties of molecular spectra? The authors hypothesize that the energy of molecular vibrational levels can be highly sensitive to changes in µ, and that the sensitivity can be further amplified by utilizing nearly-degenerate pairs of vibrational levels associated with different electronic potentials. They predict that the splitting between such levels in Cs2 can be measured with sufficient precision to detect a fractional change of ∆µ/µ ≲ 10−17. This approach differs from previous work by focusing on laboratory-based experiments using ultracold molecules, which offer the potential for improved control and reduced systematic errors compared to astrophysical observations. The successful identification of near-degenerate levels in Cs2 and the demonstration of their sensitivity to changes in µ would support the hypothesis. Conversely, if no suitable level pairs were found or if the sensitivity was significantly lower than predicted, the hypothesis would be challenged.

Methodological Details
The study employs a theoretical and experimental approach to investigate the sensitivity of molecular spectra to variations in µ. The experimental design involves two-color photoassociation (PA) spectroscopy to probe the vibrational levels of Cs2 molecules. The sample of ultracold Cs atoms (T ∼ 100 µK) is cooled and confined in a dark SPOT magneto-optic trap. A uniform magnetic field is applied, and atoms are optically pumped into the 6s1/2 F = mF = 4 state. A CW laser (PA laser) excites the atoms into a bound state of the (2)0−g potential, which then decays to a manifold of a3Σ+u vibrational levels. A second CW (probe) laser is used to search for resonances between the a3Σ+u levels and the (2)0−g level excited by the PA laser. The probe laser frequency is scanned while monitoring the ion yield to detect resonant dips in the signal. The binding energy of the a3Σ+u level is determined from the difference between the frequencies of the resonant probe and PA lasers. The data analysis involves fitting the potentials to all known levels in both the a3Σ+u and X1Σ+g states, taking into account the SO2 interaction. The potentials were modeled using the "Hannover" analytic form where data was insufficient. The experimental procedure includes the use of a CW laser for photoassociation and a pulsed laser for ionization. The analysis includes a global fit of the potentials to experimental data. The study does not mention pre-registration or multiple-comparison corrections. The study was conducted with ultracold atoms, and the experimental setup included a magneto-optic trap and lasers.

Procedures Architectures
The experimental setup utilizes a magneto-optic trap (MOT) to cool and confine Cs atoms. The MOT is a standard configuration, using laser cooling and magnetic fields to trap the atoms. The atoms are then optically pumped into a specific hyperfine state (6s1/2 F = mF = 4). Two continuous-wave (CW) lasers are used: a photoassociation (PA) laser and a probe laser. The PA laser excites the atoms into a bound state of the (2)0−g potential. The probe laser scans across the spectrum to detect resonances with the a3Σ+u vibrational levels. A pulsed laser is used for ionization. The PA laser is tuned to excite only J' = 2 levels in the (2)0−g state. The probe laser polarization is controlled to select specific transitions. The experiment uses a two-color photoassociation scheme, where the first laser (PA laser) creates molecules, and the second laser (probe laser) probes the molecular levels. The analysis involves a global fit of the a3Σ+u and X1Σ+g potentials, using the "Hannover" analytic form where data is limited. The system's architecture involves the interaction of the PA laser, probe laser, and the Cs atoms. The output of the experiment is the ion yield as a function of the probe laser frequency.

Key Results
The study demonstrates the existence of near-degenerate vibrational levels in Cs2, specifically the a3Σ+u (va = 37) and X1Σ+g (vX = 138) levels. Figure 1 shows the energy sensitivity versus binding energy for the X1Σ+g and a3Σ+u states of Cs2. Figure 2 shows data indicating a degeneracy between the deeply bound a3Σ+u (va = 37) and X1Σ+g (vX = 138) levels in Cs2. The authors observed multiple sublevels for several a3Σ+u vibrational levels with |Eb(v)|∼400−1500 GHz. The root mean square deviation was approximately 90 MHz for HF/rotational/SO2-induced sublevel splittings, and approximately 200 MHz for absolute binding energies. The authors estimate that a fractional change of ∆µ/µ ≲ 10−17 could be achieved in approximately one day of integration. The authors predict a magnetic dipole transition between the observed level a|(1, 7)6, 4, 10⟩ and X|(0, 6)6, 4, 10⟩, at Ω ≈ 6.3 GHz, with transition amplitude M ≈ 0.1 µB. They also predict an E1 transition between the observed level a|(1, 7)8, 2, 10⟩ and X|(0, 7)7, 3, 10⟩ at Ω ≈ 9.8 GHz, with M ≈ 1.5 × 10−4 ea0 ≈ 0.04 µB. The study found that the energy sensitivity ∂µE(X)vX increases monotonically with |Eb|, throughout the region of a state levels.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that molecular spectroscopy, particularly in systems like Cs2, can be a sensitive probe for variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio. The near-degeneracy of vibrational levels enhances the sensitivity, providing a mechanism to amplify the effects of changes in µ. The results support the theoretical expectation that variations in µ could be detectable and potentially more significant than variations in the fine-structure constant. The study implies that laboratory-based experiments can offer a viable alternative to astrophysical observations for probing fundamental constants. The proposed approach could lead to a deeper understanding of fundamental physics and potentially constrain models of dark energy and extra dimensions.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is the need for further experimental data to confirm the near-degeneracies and refine the sensitivity estimates. The paper does not provide details on the specific systematic errors that might affect the measurements. The study does not mention the random seed used for the experiment. The external validity of the findings is limited by the specific choice of Cs2 molecules. The study's conclusions rely on the assumption that the fine-structure constant α and the electron mass me remain constant, which could be a source of uncertainty. The paper does not discuss potential conflicts with prior literature in detail. The sensitivity estimate is based on a conservative assumption of the signal-to-noise ratio and measurement time, which could be improved in future experiments.

The figure plots ion signals vs. probe laser frequency, demonstrating the spectral features associated with the near-degeneracy. These figures are crucial for understanding the sensitivity of the method and the experimental results.

(2) The strongest evidence supporting the claims is the identification of a near-degeneracy between the a3Σ+u (va = 37) and X1Σ+g (vX = 138) levels in Cs2, as demonstrated in Figure 2, along with the estimated sensitivity of δ(∆µ/µ) ∼ 10−17 in approximately one day of integration.

papers.fulltext:
Estimating the size of the solution space of metabolic net-
works
Alfredo Braunstein1,2, Roberto Mulet2, Andrea Pagnani3
1ISI Foundation Viale Settimio Severo 65, Villa Gualino, I-10133 Torino, Italy
2“Henri-Poincar´e-Group” of Complex Systems and Department of Theoretical Physics, Physics Faculty, University of Havana, La
Habana, CP 10400, Cuba
3Politecnico di Torino, Corso Duca degli Abruzzi 34, I-10129, Torino, Italy
Email: Alfredo Braunstein - alfredo.braunstein@polito.it; Roberto Mulet∗- mulet@ﬁsica.uh.cu; Andrea Pagnani∗- pagnani@isi.it;
∗Corresponding author
Abstract
Background: Cellular metabolism is one of the most investigated system of biological interactions. While the
topological nature of individual reactions and pathways in the network is quite well understood there is still a lack
of comprehension regarding the global functional behavior of the system. To get some insight in this direction, in
the last few years powerful theoretical methods such as extreme pathways calculation and ﬂux-balance analysis
(FBA) have been introduced. These methods strongly rely on the hypothesis that the organism maximizes an
objective function. However only under very speciﬁc biological conditions (e.g. maximization of biomass for E-Coli
in reach nutrient medium) the cell seems to obey such optimization law. A more reﬁned analysis not assuming
extremization remains an elusive task for large metabolic systems due to algorithmic constraints.
Results: In this work we propose a novel algorithmic strategy that allows for an eﬃcient characterization of
the whole set of stable ﬂuxes compatible with the metabolic constraints. Using a technique derived from the
ﬁelds of statistical physics and information theory we designed a stochastic algorithm to estimate the size of the
aﬃne space containing all possible steady-state ﬂux distributions of metabolic networks. The algorithm, based
on the well-known Bethe approximation, allows the computation in polynomial time of the volume of a non
full-dimensional convex polytope in high dimensions. We show results for toy models that compare very well with
the results of exact algorithms. The result of our algorithm match closely the prediction of Monte Carlo based
estimations of the ﬂux distributions of the Red Blood Cell metabolic network. It is then used to analyze the
statistical properties of the average ﬂuxes of the reactions in the E-Coli metabolic network and ﬁnally to test the
eﬀect of gene knock-outs on the size of the solution space of the E-Coli central metabolism.
Conclusions: We propose a novel eﬃcient algorithmic strategy to estimate the size and shape of the aﬃne space
of a non full-dimensional convex polytope in high dimensions. The method is shown to obtain, quantitatively and
qualitatively compatible results compared with known algorithms (where this comparison is possible) being still
eﬃcient on the analysis of large biological systems, where all other known strategies experience an explosion in
algorithmic time.

Background
Cellular metabolism is a complex biological problem.
It can be viewed as a chemical engine that trans-
forms available raw materials into energy or into the
building blocks needed for the biological function of
the cells. In more speciﬁc terms a metabolic net-
work is indeed a processing system transforming in-
put metabolites (nutrients), into output metabolites
(amino acids, lipids, sugars etc.) according to very
strict molecular proportions, often referred as stoi-
chiometric coeﬃcients of the reactions.
Although the general topological properties of
these networks are well characterized, see for exam-
ple [1–3], and non-trivial pathways are well known
for many species [4] the cooperative role of these
pathways is hard to comprehend. In fact, the large
sizes of these networks, usually containing hundreds
of metabolites and even more reactions, makes the
comprehension of the principles that govern their
global function a challenging task. Therefore, a nec-
essary step to achieve this goal is the use of mathe-
matical models and the development of novel statis-
tical techniques to characterize and simulate these
networks.
For example, it is well known that under evo-
lutionary pressure, prokaryotes cells like E-Coli be-
have optimizing their growth performance [5]. Flux
Balance Analysis (FBA) provides a powerful tool to
predict, from the whole space of phenotipic states,
which one will these cells acquire. In few words one
may say that FBA maximizes a linear function (usu-
ally the growth rate of the cell) subject to biochemi-
cal and thermodynamic constraints [6]. On the other
hand, cells with genetically engineered knockouts or
bacterial strains that were not exposed to evolution
pressures, need not to optimize their growth. In fact,
the method of minimization metabolic adjustment
(MOMA) [7] has shown that knockout metabolic
ﬂuxes undergo a minimal redistribution with respect
to the ﬂux conﬁguration of the wild type.
Yet,
in more general situations, the results are unpre-
dictable, therefore, a tool to characterize the shape
and volume of the whole space of possible phenotipic
solutions must be welcome.
Unfortunately,
this
characterization
has
re-
mained an elusive task. As far as we know the at-
tempts to obtain such a characterization were always
based on the Monte Carlo sampling of the steady-
state ﬂux space [8]. But unfortunately, it appeared
that this kind of sampling is a very expensive calcu-
lation and is unsuitable for very large networks. To
address this problem we propose, using a technique
derived from the ﬁelds of statistical physics and in-
formation theory, an algorithm that may eﬃciently
characterize the whole set of stable ﬂuxes compati-
bles with the stoichiometric constraints.
Mathematical Model
As already mentioned, a metabolic network is an
engine that converts metabolites into other metabo-
lites through a series of intra-cellular intermediate
steps. The fundamental equation characterizing all
functional states of a reconstructed biochemical re-
action network is a mass conservation law that im-
poses simple linear constraints between the incoming
and outcoming ﬂuxes at any chemical reaction. It is
call the dynamic mass balance equation:

where ρ is the vector of the M metabolite concen-

erned by the M ×N stoichiometric linear operator ˆS
(usually named stoichiometric matrix) encoding the
coeﬃcient of the M intra-cellular relations among
the N ﬂuxes.
As long as just steady-state cellular properties
are concerned one can assume that a variation in
the concentration of metabolites in a cell can be ig-
nored and considered as constant. Therefore in case
of ﬁxed external conditions one can assume metabo-
lites (quasi) stationarity and consequently the lhs of

problem of ﬁnding the metabolic ﬂuxes compatible

Without loss of generality we can assume that the

Results and Discussion
Performance on low dimensional systems
In this section we will analyze the performance of
our algorithm against an exact algorithm on low di-
mensional polytopes. Among the diﬀerent packages
available in the Internet, we have chosen LRS [9], a
program based on the reverse search algorithm pre-
sented by Avis and Fukuda in [10] that can compute
the volume of non-full dimensional polytopes. Actu-
ally, it computes the volume of the lexicographically
smallest representation of the polytope, that for the
benchmark used below, coincides with the conven-
tional volume estimated by our algorithm.
We have devised a speciﬁc benchmark generating
random diluted stoichiometric matrices at a given
ratio α = M/N and ﬁxed number of terms diﬀerent
from zero K in each of the reactions. All ﬂuxes were
constrained inside the hypercube 0 ≤νi ≤1. As a
general strategy we have calculated several random
instances of the problem and measured the volume
(entropy) of the polytope using the LRS and BP al-
gorithm. In particular, we have ﬁrst generated 1000
realizations of random stoichiometric matrices with
N = 12, M = 4. Note that N = 12 is around the
maximum that allows simulations with LRS in rea-
sonable time (around one hour per instance). For
each polytope then we have computed the two en-
tropies SLRS and SBP with both algorithms, ﬁx-
ing the same maximum value for the discretization
qmax = 1024 for all ﬂuxes.
In Figure 1.2 we show how the quality of the
BP measure is aﬀected by the discretization, by
displaying the histogram of the relative diﬀerences
δS = SBP −SLRS
SLRS
with an increasing number of bins
per variable qmax = 16, 64, 256, 1024. One can see
how a ﬁner binning of messages improves the qual-
ity of the approximation, seeminlgy converging to a
3

single distribution of errors. It is expected that for
larger N the histograms would shrink: upon increas-
ing the number of ﬂuxes, loops become larger and
the overall topology of the graph becomes more lo-
cally tree-like, validating the hypothesis behind the
Bethe approximation. Unfortunately, the huge in-
crease of computer time experimented in the calcu-
lation of the volumes using LRS made impossible to
test systems large enough to make any reasonable
scaling analysis.
Finally we address the issue of the computational
complexity of the algorithm which is a crucial one if
one is interested in approaching real world metabolic
networks whose size typically is at least 50 times the
size of the largest network that can be analyzed with
exact algorithms. In Figure 1.1 we display the run-
ning time of both LRS and BP as a function of the
number of ﬂuxes N. Interesting, LRS outperforms
BP up to sizes N ∼12 where the running time of
LRS explodes exponentially while BP maintains a
modest almost-linear behavior.
Distribution of ﬂuxes in Red Blood Cell
The algorithm was used to obtain the distribution
of ﬂux values for each of the reactions of the Red
Blood Cell metabolism. The maximum allowed val-
ues for the ﬂuxes, as well as the corresponding sto-
ichiometric matrix were extracted directly from [8].
The network contained 46 reactions and 34 metabo-
lites.
Our distributions appear in Figure 1.3 and
as can be checked by direct comparison they are
almost identical to those obtained with the Monte
Carlo method in with the Figure 5 in [8]. However,
while the Monte Carlo method appears to be quite
expensive in computational resources (the authors
of [8] reported one week of computer computation
in a Dell Dimension 8200 to obtain their distribu-
tions) our algorithm converged to the same results
in a couple of minutes of computation on a similar
machine.
Analysis of gene knock-out in E-Coli
Then, we analyze the distribution function of the av-
erage ﬂuxes of the metabolic network of the E-Coli.
The network used contains, in its original format,
1035 reactions and 626 metabolites, [11]. From this
network we eliminated all those reactions with frac-
tional stoichiometric indexes, since our algorithm in
its present form is unable to deal with them, and all
those metabolites with connectivity larger than 40.
These metabolites are cofactors of the metabolism
and their elimination helps to sparse the matrix im-
proving the convergence of the algorithm. Finally
we checked for inconsistencies (i.e. metabolites that
after the previous transformations are only produced
or consumed), and we obtain a matrix with 1005 re-
actions and 560 metabolites. We ran our algorithm
on this network and computed the average ﬂuxes in
each reaction. The probability distribution function
(pdf) of these average values appears in Figure 1.4.
As can be clearly seen the distribution is large and
may be ﬁtted with a power law with exponent close
to 1, a result that compares very well with previous
simulations [12, 13] in real networks and with the
approach followed by Bianconi and Zecchina [14].
Moreover, it most be mentioned that a more careful
analysis of the data may suggest that the distribu-
tion of averages ﬂuxes has a richer structure.
In
Figure 1.5 is presented the integrated distribution
function of the average ﬂuxes of the reactions and a
clear jump appears for ν ≈0.5, and smaller ones for
ν ≈0.4 and µ ≈0.6. Whether these jumps are just
due to normal statistical ﬂuctuations (and are cor-
rectly smeared out in the usual binning process done
to plot the pdf in log-log scale) or reﬂect relevant bi-
ological or structural information of the network is
not yet known.
Finally, we concentrated our eﬀorts in the study
the E-Coli central metabolism [11]. To simplify the
analysis of the results, all cofactors were removed
with the exception of ATP and ADP that have been
thus considered as output and input ﬂuxes respec-
tively.
Under these conditions, the network has
40 metabolites, 74 internal reactions and 10 exter-
nal ﬂuxes that were considered irreversible following
their nominal directions. The maximum ﬂuxes of all
the reactions were considered equal to 1.
We then studied the inﬂuence of knockouts on
the volume of the solution space. In each simulation
the values of the maximum ﬂux was kept constant
and equal to 1 for all the reactions but the one with
a knockout. For each knockout we assumed a reduc-
tion of the maximum permitted ﬂux qmax equal to
the 0.25 of the original value. We assumed that each
reaction is knockout independently, this, despite the
fact that it is known that some reactions are associ-
ated with the same enzyme.
The distribution of entropy change (∆S = SKO−
S0) of the solution space for the diﬀerent reaction
knock-outs turns out to show two possibilities: while
4

most of the reactions have ∆S > −3 and show little
and similar impact in the size of the solution space
a relevant fraction of them, has ∆S < −3 but with
a very uniform distribution. To understand if there
is any connection between these reactions with large
∆S and the structure of the network, we show in
Figure 1.6 the changes in S for the diﬀerent reaction
knock-outs. In the x−axis we plot the reactions nu-
merated and the lines indicate the values of ∆S for
each reaction. We annotate also these reactions with
∆S < −3. Most of them are associated with the
glycolysis pathway, being more speciﬁc, with those
reactions of the glycolysis process that show little
redundancy in the topology of the network. Other
reactions, like FUM, ACONT, SUC and SUCCD1i
appear in the Krebb cycle and again show little path-
way redundancy in the network.
Finally in Figure 1.7 we display the correlations
between the changes in the entropy for diﬀerent re-
action knock-outs and the most probable values ν∗
and the average values ¯ν of the ﬂuxes in the wild
network. As can be seen, two kinds of regimes are
divided by a clear threshold at ν ∼0.6 : A ﬁrst one,
for small ﬂuxes, that show consistent and slowly in-
creasing correlations between ν and ∆S, and a sec-
ond one for large ﬂuxes, where the correlations in-
crease rapidly but with large ﬂuctuations. The pres-
ence of this threshold can be understood noting that
reactions belonging to the linear (glycolysis) an cir-
cular (Krebb cycle) pathways are, in the wild cell,
fast-ﬂux reactions, with average values for the ﬂuxes
larger than 0.5. Therefore once they are knock-out,
the metabolic capacities of the network are highly
aﬀected.
Conclusions
We proposed a novel algorithm to estimate the
size and shape of the aﬃne space of a non full-
dimensional convex polytope in high dimensions.
The algorithm was tested in speciﬁc benchmark, i.e.
random diluted stoichiometric matrices at a given
ratio α = M/N and ﬁxed number of terms diﬀer-
ent from zero K, in each of the reactions, with re-
sults that compare very well with those of exact al-
gorithms. Moreover, we show that while the run-
ning time of exact algorithms increases more than
exponentially for already moderate sizes, our algo-
rithm keeps a polynomial behavior for sizes as large
as N = 120.
The program was run on the Red
Blood Cell metabolism, showing with less compu-
tational eﬀort, results that compare very well with
those previously obtained using Monte Carlo meth-
ods. Then, we calculate the distribution of the av-
erage values of the ﬂuxes in the metabolism of the
E-Coli and present results that are consistent with
those of the literature.
Finally, our program was
used to study the E-Coli central metabolism, and
we show that, as expected, reactions with little re-
dundancy are the ones with more impact in the size
of the space of the metabolic solutions. Speciﬁcally,
most of the reactions associated with the transfor-
mation of glucose in pyruvate, belong to this set, as
well as some reactions in the citric cycle. In addition
we show strong correlations between the characteris-
tics of the ﬂux distributions of the wild type network
and the changes in size of the space of solutions after
reaction knock-outs.
Let us conclude by noting that in principle the
presented approach can be extended to deal with
constraints whose functional form is more general
than linear, provided that the number of variables
involved in each of the constraints remains small, as
in the case of inequalities enforcing the second low
of thermodynamics for the considered reactions [15].
Work is in progress in this direction.
Methods
Volume computation
From a computational point of view, the problem of
the exact computation of the volume of a polytope
with current methods requires the enumeration of
all its vertexes. The vertex enumeration problem is
#P-hard [16,17], but even the problem of computing
the volume, given the set of all vertexes is a big com-
putational challenge.
Various algorithms exist for
calculating the exact volume of a polytope from its
vertexes (for a review see [18]), and many software
packages are available in the Internet.
Computa-
tional limitations restrict however exact algorithmic
strategies to cope with polytopes in relatively few di-
mensions (e.g N −M around 10 or so). To overcome
such severe limitations we will introduce a very eﬃ-
cient approximate computational strategy that will
allow us to compute the volume and the shape of the
space of solutions for real-world metabolic networks.
Although the coeﬃcient λ could be explicitely
calculated, it turns out that as far as only relative
volume quantities are concerned, as in the case of the
