papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a novel algorithmic strategy, based on the Bethe approximation, to efficiently estimate the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks. The method computes the volume of a non-full dimensional convex polytope in high dimensions, representing the space of possible steady-state flux distributions. The algorithm's performance was evaluated on toy models and compared to an exact algorithm (LRS), showing comparable results. It was then applied to the Red Blood Cell metabolic network, matching Monte Carlo-based estimations of flux distributions but with significantly reduced computational time (minutes vs. one week). The method was also used to analyze the statistical properties of average fluxes in the E-Coli metabolic network, with results consistent with prior literature. Finally, the algorithm was used to study the effect of gene knock-outs on the solution space of the E-Coli central metabolism, revealing that reactions with little pathway redundancy have a more significant impact on the solution space size. The primary novelty lies in the efficient estimation of the solution space volume, enabling analysis of large metabolic networks where other methods are computationally prohibitive. This work is important because it provides a tool to characterize the phenotypic solutions of metabolic networks, which is crucial for understanding cellular behavior, especially in scenarios where cells do not necessarily optimize growth. A limitation is that the method, in its present form, is unable to deal with reactions with fractional stoichiometric indexes.

Research Context
Understanding the global functional behavior of metabolic networks is challenging due to their size and complexity. Existing methods like Flux Balance Analysis (FBA) rely on the assumption of cellular optimization, which may not always hold. Monte Carlo sampling has been used to characterize the solution space, but it is computationally expensive and unsuitable for large networks. This work addresses the need for an efficient method to characterize the shape and volume of the solution space of metabolic networks, particularly in scenarios where cells are not under evolutionary pressure to optimize growth. Prior approaches, such as FBA and MOMA, have limitations in predicting results in general situations, thus a tool to characterize the shape and volume of the whole space of possible phenotypic solutions is needed.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to efficiently estimate the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks. The primary hypothesis is that a stochastic algorithm, based on the Bethe approximation, can efficiently compute the volume of the solution space, allowing for analysis of large metabolic networks. This hypothesis is supported if the algorithm's results match those of existing methods (like Monte Carlo simulations) on smaller networks while being computationally more efficient. The study also investigates the statistical properties of average fluxes in the E-Coli metabolic network and the effect of gene knock-outs on the solution space. The alternative hypothesis is that the Bethe approximation will not provide accurate estimations or will not be computationally efficient for large networks. The study differs from prior work by providing an efficient method to characterize the whole set of stable fluxes compatible with the metabolic constraints, which is not based on the assumption of cellular optimization.

Methodological Details
The study employs a stochastic algorithm based on the Bethe approximation to estimate the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks. The algorithm computes the volume of a non-full dimensional convex polytope in high dimensions, representing the space of possible steady-state flux distributions. The study design involves applying the algorithm to different metabolic networks and comparing its performance to existing methods. The Red Blood Cell metabolic network (46 reactions, 34 metabolites) and the E-Coli metabolic network (1005 reactions, 560 metabolites, and the E-Coli central metabolism with 74 internal reactions and 40 metabolites) were used. The algorithm's performance was compared to an exact algorithm (LRS) on low-dimensional systems. The study uses the LRS algorithm based on the reverse search algorithm presented by Avis and Fukuda. The volume of the polytope was estimated using the LRS and the Belief Propagation (BP) algorithm. The performance of the BP measure was affected by the discretization, by displaying the histogram of the relative diﬀerences δS = SBP −SLRS/SLRS with an increasing number of bins per variable qmax = 16, 64, 256, 1024. The metric used was the volume of the solution space. The study also analyzed the distribution of average fluxes and the impact of gene knock-outs on the solution space. The study used the maximum ﬂuxes of all the reactions were considered equal to 1. For each knockout, a reduction of the maximum permitted ﬂux qmax equal to the 0.25 of the original value was assumed. The algorithm was implemented in a standard laptop. No preregistration or ethics review information is provided.

Procedures Architectures
The core of the methodology is a stochastic algorithm based on the Bethe approximation, used to compute the volume of the solution space. The algorithm is implemented using the Belief Propagation (BP) algorithm. The metabolic problem is cast into a constraint satisfaction framework where the M stoichiometric relations impose a constraint onto a subset of the metabolic ﬂuxes. The algorithm exchanges messages between variable nodes (representing fluxes) and factor nodes (representing mass conservation). The algorithm involves two types of messages: µi→a(ν), the probability that ﬂux i takes value ν in the absence of reaction a, and ma→i(ν), the non-normalized probability that the balance in reaction a is fulﬁlled given that ﬂux i takes value ν. These messages are updated iteratively until convergence. The algorithm uses a recursion to speed up the computation of the messages. The algorithm was tested on random diluted stoichiometric matrices, the Red Blood Cell metabolism, and the E-Coli metabolism. The algorithm was implemented in C++. The algorithm's performance was compared to an exact algorithm (LRS). The algorithm was run on a standard laptop. The main novelty is the application of the Bethe approximation to efficiently estimate the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks, allowing for the analysis of large networks.

Key Results
The algorithm's performance was evaluated on low-dimensional systems and compared to an exact algorithm (LRS). The running time of LRS explodes exponentially while the proposed algorithm maintains a modest almost-linear behavior (Figure 1.1). The algorithm's results closely matched the predictions of Monte Carlo-based estimations of flux distributions in the Red Blood Cell metabolic network (Figure 1.3), but with a significantly shorter computation time (minutes vs. one week). The distribution of average fluxes in the E-Coli metabolic network was analyzed, and the results were consistent with those in the literature (Figure 1.4). The distribution of average fluxes was fitted with a power law with exponent close to 1. The study of gene knock-outs in the E-Coli central metabolism revealed that reactions with little pathway redundancy have a more significant impact on the size of the solution space (Figure 1.6). Reactions in the glycolysis and Krebs cycle pathways showed the most impact. Strong correlations were found between the characteristics of the flux distributions of the wild type network and the changes in size of the space of solutions after reaction knock-outs (Figure 1.7). A clear threshold at ν ∼0.6 was found. The histogram of the relative diﬀerences δS = SBP −SLRS/SLRS with an increasing number of bins per variable qmax = 16, 64, 256, 1024, showed that a ﬁner binning of messages improves the quality of the approximation.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the proposed algorithm provides an efficient and accurate method for estimating the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks. The results support the idea that the Bethe approximation can be effectively applied to this problem. The analysis of the E-Coli metabolic network and the impact of gene knock-outs provide insights into the structure and function of metabolic networks. The study shows that reactions with little pathway redundancy are critical for maintaining the size of the solution space. The correlations between flux distributions and the impact of knock-outs highlight the importance of flux distributions in understanding the behavior of metabolic networks. The results suggest that the algorithm can be used to analyze the effects of perturbations on metabolic networks.

Contradictions Limitations
The algorithm's inability to handle reactions with fractional stoichiometric indexes is a limitation. The study does not provide details on the specific hardware or software versions used, which could affect reproducibility. The study does not mention the random seed used, which could affect reproducibility. The study does not provide information about the statistical significance of the results. The study does not provide information on the demographics of the datasets. The study does not provide information on the multiple-comparison corrections. The study does not address the external validity of the findings. The study does not explicitly discuss the limitations of the Bethe approximation in the context of metabolic networks. The study's focus on steady-state cellular properties may limit the generalizability of the findings to dynamic metabolic processes.

Figure 1.4 shows the probability distribution function (pdf) of the average values of the ﬂuxes in the metabolism of the E-Coli. Figure 1.6 shows the changes in entropy for the diﬀerent reaction knock-outs. Figure 1.7 displays the correlations between the changes in the entropy for diﬀerent reaction knock-outs and the most probable values ν∗ and the average values ¯ν of the ﬂuxes in the wild network.

Three Takeaways
The core novel contribution is an efficient algorithm to estimate the size and shape of the solution space of metabolic networks, based on the Bethe approximation. The strongest evidence is that the algorithm's results closely matched the predictions of Monte Carlo-based estimations of flux distributions in the Red Blood Cell metabolic network, but with a significantly shorter computation time (minutes vs. one week). The primary limitation is that the method, in its present form, is unable to deal with reactions with fractional stoichiometric indexes. A forward path would be to extend the approach to deal with constraints whose functional form is more general than linear.

Uniﬁcation of the phonon mode behaviour in semiconductor alloys
O. Pag`es,∗M. Kassem, A. Chaﬁ, A. Nassour, S. Doyen and A. V. Postnikov
Laboratoire de Physique des Milieux Denses,
Universit´e Paul Verlaine – Metz,
1 Bd. Arago, F-57078 Metz, France
This work concludes a series of systematic re-examinations of the Raman/Infrared spectra of
representative semiconductor alloys in the traditionally admitted classiﬁcation of phonon mode
behaviour, i.e.
In1−xGaxAs (1-bond→1-mode), In1−xGaxP (modiﬁed 2-mode) and presently
ZnTe1−xSex (2-bond→1-mode), based on a crude description of the alloy disorder at the macro-
scopic scale in terms of the virtual crystal approximation (VCA). Here we show that the latter
alloy obeys the same phonon mode behaviour as the former two, thereby a universal one, of a
percolation type (1-bond→2-mode). The ‘VCA→Percolation’ change of paradigm confers to vi-
brational spectroscopies the attractive privilege to provide natural insight into the alloy disorder
at the unusual mesoscopic scale, with potential interest for the study of the long scale (self)
organization in alloys, in general.
The key issue regarding mixtures is how to handle the
substitutional disorder. For natural mixtures, of a forbid-
ding complexity at the microscopic scale, a percolation-
based approach was developed at the mesoscopic scale.1
The central notion is the volume fraction of each con-
stituent. Singularities in the physical properties are ex-
pected at the percolation thresholds, at which composi-
tions the minor constituents coalesce into a continuum.
Surprisingly, for those ideally-disordered mixtures that
are usual semiconductor (SC) AB1−xCx alloys (atoms in
substitution on a regular lattice), made of the two in-
terpenetrating A and (B,C) cfc sublattices, the virtual
crystal approximation (VCA) seems suﬃcient, in ﬁrst
approximation. With this, each atom A is surrounded
by four virtual B1−xCx atoms, i.e. the crystal is viewed
at the macroscopic scale as a continuum (Fig. 1a). The
physical properties are accordingly averaged. No singu-
larity is expected in their dependence on x.
Here, we focus on the bond force constant (K) in
SC alloys. K is sensitive to the bond distortion (bond
length plus bond angles) required to accommodate the
mismatch in the A-B and A-C bond lengths, and as
such provides an integrated insight into the substitutional
disorder.(a)
K is routinely probed by Raman and In-
frared (IR) spectroscopies, via the frequency of the trans-
verse optical (TO) phonon.(b) The VCA for K leads to
a 1-bond→1-mode TO behaviour, as accounted for by
the modiﬁed-random-element-isodisplacement (MREI)
model.2 Only one adjustable parameter is needed per
bond, i.e. the frequency of the impurity mode ωimp –
see Methods. The MREI-VCA supports a classiﬁcation
of the TO-Raman/IR data in terms of 2-mode (pure
1-bond→1-mode) (i),
mixed-mode (2-bond→1-mode)

phase vibrations of the A and (B,C) sublattices, perpendicular
to the direction of propagation.
(ii) and dominant-plus-minor mixed-modes (modiﬁed-2-

In1−xGaxAs, ZnTe1−xSex and In1−xGaxP, respectively
(ref. 3).

From the Elliott–CPA cri-

The ωimp values were estimated by relying on thorough

direct comparison with the Raman spectra we take Zn-

(−0.32, 7.20, 176–206 cm−1), respectively.(g) The result-

the Zn-Se and Zn-Te oscillators are so close. Therefore
the individual LOZn−Te, LOSe
Zn−Se and LOTe
Zn−Se modes
(not shown) do ⃗E-couple strongly, with the result that

This ex-

certainly the origin of the MREI-VCA classiﬁcation of
ZnTeSe. Residual LOint. and LO−modes, in the sense of

modes.

the sum of close TOZn−Te and TOSe

modes exhibit antagonist strength variations when the
composition changes, and have similar heights at ∼70%
Se, consistently with experimental observations.21 An ad-
ditional minor LO-TO inverted oscillator within the main

signed as the LOint. –TOTe

(ref. 6).
Then it vanishes in the di-

(ref. 13).
In
brief, all the ‘anomalous’ features in the Raman/IR spec-
tra of ZnTeSe ﬁnd a natural assignment in terms of al-
lowed modes within the percolation picture, on a quan-
titative basis. Actually, there is a quasi-perfect analogy
between the phonon mode behaviours of ZnTeSe and In-
GaP (ref. 9).
To secure a basis of our discussion on TO modes we
provide independent ab initio insight into the TO density
of states (TO-DOS) at the zone-center (ZC), that com-
pares directly to the Raman signal, in a fully-relaxed 32-
atom supercell (volume and internal coordinates) at the
representative composition x∼0.5. The Se and Te atoms
are equally distributed over all substituting planes, as ex-
pected in a random alloy. We apply the plane-wave pseu-
dopotential method within the density functional the-
ory and the local density approximation (LDA), and a
linear response technique.22 The ZC TO-DOS obtained
per atom for uniformly-damped Zn, Se and Te oscillators
(∼10 cm−1) are displayed in the inset of Fig. 3, together
with the supercell. As expected, three equidistant oscil-
lators spaced by ∼10 cm−1, with similar strengths, i.e. a
ZnTe-like below two ZnSe-like ones (refer to the arrows
in the inset of Fig. 3), show up. A slight overall blue-
shift of the ZC TO-DOS with respect to the correspond-
ing Raman lineshape (∼20 cm−1) is due to a well-known
overbinding in LDA. We have checked that the interplay
between the frequencies and strengths of the three oscil-
lators in the ZC TO-DOS and the phenomenological TO
Raman lineshapes are consistent over the whole compo-
sition domain.
Percolation vs. Elliott-CPA and MREI-VCA
The percolation schemes for InGaAs, InGaP and
ZnTeSe are schematically reproduced in Fig. 4.
Only
the TO branches are shown, for clarity, while simplifying
the continuum regimes to straight lines – see Methods.
There is an obvious analogy between the three schemes,
indicating that the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA
classiﬁcation has, in fact, no raison d’ˆetre.
Still, the percolation schemes must be consistent with
the latter classiﬁcation, which we discuss now. In both
InGaAs and InGaP, the impurity modes stay out of the
parent TO-LO bands, so that the Ga- and In-related TO-
LO bands in the alloy (shaded areas in Figs 4a and 4b)
do not overlap. In contrast the Zn-Se and Zn-Te TO-LO
bands do overlap in ZnTeSe (refer to the over-shaded area
in Fig. 4c). This is consistent with the Elliott-CPA classi-
ﬁcation of InGa(As,P) and ZnTeSe as types (i) and (ii),
respectively.
The percolation schemes are also consis-
tent with the MREI-VCA classiﬁcation. It is just a mat-
ter of regrouping close individual/double TO branches as
shown by ovals in Fig. 4. The usual terminology of indi-
FIG. 4 Simpliﬁed 1-bond→2-mode TO (thick lines) percola-
tion schemes of InGaAs (a), InGaP (b) and ZnTeSe (c). The
generic fraction of bonds corresponding to each TO branch is
indicated in part (b). The bond-related optical bands simply
obtained by linear convergence of the parent TO and LO fre-
quencies onto the related impurity frequencies are shown as
shaded areas.
vidual modes [(i), Fig. 4a], dominant-plus-minor modes
[(iii), Fig. 4b] and mixed-mode [(ii), Fig. 4c] comes out
naturally.
A probable reason why diﬀerences in the detail of the
phonon mode behaviours of InGaAs, InGaP and ZnTeSe
were previously mistaken for diﬀerences in the principles
of the phonon mode behaviours lies in an implicit, but
wrong, assumption that the TO and LO modes behave
similarly in an alloy. In particular, in the LO symmetry a
strong ⃗E-coupling occurs between the like LO modes that
come from the same double-branch, because these refer to
the same bond species and as such have close frequencies.
The result is that the actual 1-bond→2-mode behaviour
visible in the TO symmetry, supporting a description of
the phonon mode behaviour at the mesoscopic scale on a
percolation basis, is literally rubbed out in the LO sym-
metry. What is left is an apparent 1-bond→1-mode LO
behaviour, encouraging a more crude description at the
macroscopic scale according to the MREI-VCA. Due to
this TO vs. LO duality, any attempt to explain the TO
and LO modes in an alloy on the same intuitive basis
is damned to fail. Simplicity arises by focusing on TO
modes; LO modes follow.
In brief, we show that ZnTeSe obeys the 1-bond→2-
phonon percolation model, as InGaAs and InGaP do.
We propose a three-oscillator [1 Zn-Te, 2 Zn-Se] ver-
sion, supported by existing EXAFS data and home-made
ab initio phonon calculations. This leads to uniﬁcation
of the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classiﬁcation
into a single class covered by the percolation model. It
emerges that even those ideally-disordered systems that
are the usual SC alloys can not escape a description of
some of their very basic physical properties via a percola-
tion concept. As such, they do not diﬀer fundamentally
from other mixtures, contrarily to a broadly accepted as-
sumption. On the practical side, this work reveals that

5
vibrational spectroscopies provide natural insight (non
destructive and contactless) into the alloy disorder at the
unusual mesoscopic scale, which is hardly achieved oth-
erwise. This oﬀers an attractive perspective for the study
of the long scale (self-) organization in alloys, be it local
ordering9 or anti-clustering.23
The authors acknowledge support from the IFCPAR
(N◦3204-1) and the CINES (N◦pli2623).
Methods
MREI-VCA (TO) model: The VCA for a bond-related
property, such as K, comes to a picture where the
bond is immersed into a continuum whose properties
are smoothly x-dependent (Fig. 1a).
The bonds of
like species are all equivalent, thereby contributing to
a unique TO-Raman/IR mode. The intensity scales as
the corresponding fraction of bonds, and when x changes
the mode shifts smoothly between the parent and impu-
rity limits. No singularity is expected. A short (long)
impurity bond is tensed (compressed) in a matrix with
a large (small) lattice constant, which reduces (enlarges)
K, with concomitant impact on ωimp [see note (a)]. Gen-
erally ωimp remains close to the parent TO-frequency,
because each bond tends to keep its natural bond length
in an alloy.
So, the trend in a ‘TO-frequency vs.
x’
plot is that the A-B and A-C TO branches remain quasi-
parallel, with slight, but ﬁnite, slopes.
TO-based MREI-VCA classiﬁcation: Two main types of
TO behaviour proceed from the MREI-VCA: (i) If the
parent TO frequencies are much distinct, the alloy ex-
hibits well-separated A-B and A-C TO branches, corre-
sponding to a typical 1-bond→1-mode behaviour. (ii) If
the parent TO frequencies are close enough, the A-B and
A-C TO branches merge into an apparent 2-bond→1-
mode behaviour with a unique (A-B, A-C)-mixed TO
mode that has quasi-stable strength, and shifts regularly
between the parent TO modes. There seems to exist an
intermediary-type behaviour, referred to as (iii), with
two (A-B, A-C)-mixed TO modes, i.e. a dominant one
of type (ii), plus a minor one that does not allow to fully
discard type (i). While the MREI-VCA model fully ac-
counts for types (i) and (ii), it can not account for type
(iii), even qualitatively.
Percolation (TO) model: This distinguishes between vi-
brations of like bonds within the naturally-formed B-rich
and C-rich regions (Fig. 1b), the result of diﬀerent lo-
cal bond distortions.
In a ‘TO-frequency vs.
x’ plot,
this results in a splitting of each MREI-like TO branch
into a symmetrical double-branch, attached at its two
ends to the parent and impurity modes. The strength of
each ‘sub-mode’ scales as the corresponding B-rich (x)
or C-rich region (1-x). Singularities in the TO-frequency
occur at the bond percolation thresholds (PT’s), where
the minor A-B (xB=0.19) or A-C (xC=0.81) bonds be-
come connected throughout the crystal. Below the PT,
the minor region consists of a dispersion of ﬁnite clus-
ters with similar structures, which generates invariance
in the TO-frequency. Above the PT, the ﬁnite clusters
coalesce into a continuum whose local composition turns
smoothly x-dependent, as does the TO-frequency.
A
rescaled-MREI approach applies where the continuum,
viewed as a pseudo-alloy, takes an apparent composition
varying from 0 to 1 over its domain of existence (refer to
y, z in Fig. 1b).
Ab initio protocol for a self-consistent percolation model:
For straightforward data-independent (Raman/IR) in-
sight into ωimp. and ∆in any zincblende alloy we pro-
pose here a simple protocol based on ab initio bond
length/phonon calculations in prototype fully-relaxed su-
percells at the dilute limits. We use 64-atom supercells,
that are well-converged in size for such purpose.24 The
calculations are performed by using the computer code
Siesta within the LDA (ref. 25).
To access ωimp. we use a supercell containing a sin-
gle impurity (∼3% imp.). This is the ultimate conﬁg-
uration that refers to an impurity in the region rich of
the other substituting species. We search for the impu-
rity bond length, and we estimate ωimp. via γ as usual
(see main text).
A direct calculation of the impurity
frequency ωcalc.
imp. does not help here, due to the eﬀective
overbinding in LDA.
To access ∆we use a supercell containing two neigh-
bouring substitutional impurities.
This pair forms the
germ of the impurity-rich region, i.e. the ultimate con-
ﬁguration that refers to an impurity staying in its own
environment. We search for the frequency of the phonon
mode along the chain of the two impurity bonds, referred
to as ωcalc.
pair , and ∆is estimated as
  ωcalc.
imp. −ωcalc.
pair
  . The
systematic error due to LDA is thus eliminated.
We have checked that the theoretical and experimental
(ωimp, ∆) values for random InGaAs, InGaP and ZnTeSe,
and also (Zn,Be)-chalcogenides that exhibit a unusually
large contrast in the bond properties, agree within ∼5%.
This validates the ab initio protocol. Together with it,
our phenomenological percolation model forms a self-
consistent model for the calculation of the 1-bond→2-
mode Raman/IR behaviour in any zincblende alloy. This
can be viewed as a sophistication to the mesoscopic scale
of the traditional 1-bond→1-mode MREI model, that op-
erates at the macroscopic scale.
papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper challenges the traditional understanding of phonon mode behavior in semiconductor alloys, specifically those with substitutional disorder. The study demonstrates that seemingly disparate alloy systems, such as InGaAs, InGaP, and ZnTeSe, actually exhibit a universal phonon mode behavior of a percolation-type (1-bond→2-mode). This contrasts with the virtual crystal approximation (VCA), which leads to a 1-bond→1-mode behavior. The authors propose a shift from the VCA's macroscopic perspective to a mesoscopic, percolation-based model to better understand alloy disorder. The research is supported by ab initio simulations of the phonon density of states at the zone-center of representative supercells and a simple ab initio protocol is proposed to estimate the parameters of the percolation model. The key finding is the unification of the phonon mode behavior across different alloy systems, suggesting a more fundamental understanding of vibrational spectra in these materials. The study's novelty lies in its mesoscopic perspective on alloy disorder, offering a new framework for interpreting vibrational spectroscopy data. The main limitation is the reliance on a simplified model and the need for further validation across a wider range of alloy compositions and systems.

Research Context
The traditional approach to understanding vibrational spectra in semiconductor alloys relies on the virtual crystal approximation (VCA), which simplifies the alloy disorder at a macroscopic scale. The VCA, however, struggles to accurately classify and explain the phonon mode behavior in certain alloy systems, particularly those exhibiting mixed-mode or 2-bond→1-mode behavior. Prior work, such as the modified-random-element-isodisplacement (MREI) model and the Elliott-CPA criterion, have been used to classify the TO-Raman/IR data. These approaches, however, have limitations, particularly in explaining the behavior of alloys like InGaP. This work addresses the gap by proposing a percolation-based model that accounts for the mesoscopic scale of alloy disorder, offering a more nuanced understanding of phonon behavior.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether different semiconductor alloys, traditionally classified with different phonon mode behaviors, can be unified under a single, universal model. The primary hypothesis is that alloys like InGaAs (1-bond→1-mode), InGaP (modified 2-mode), and ZnTeSe (2-bond→1-mode) share a common phonon mode behavior, specifically a percolation-type (1-bond→2-mode). The alternative hypothesis is that the observed differences in phonon behavior are fundamental and cannot be explained by a unified model. The study aims to support the primary hypothesis by demonstrating the applicability of a percolation model to ZnTeSe, which would unify its behavior with that of InGaAs and InGaP. This approach differs from prior work by shifting from a macroscopic to a mesoscopic perspective, focusing on the topology of the substituting species rather than averaging properties.

Methodological Details
The study employs a combination of theoretical modeling and ab initio calculations. The core methodology involves the development and application of a percolation model to describe the phonon mode behavior in semiconductor alloys. The model is applied to three representative systems: InGaAs, InGaP, and ZnTeSe. The study uses the virtual crystal approximation (VCA) and the modified-random-element-isodisplacement (MREI) model as baselines for comparison. The ab initio calculations are performed using the plane-wave pseudopotential method within the density functional theory and the local density approximation (LDA). The calculations are performed using the computer code Siesta. The study focuses on the transverse optical (TO) modes, which are probed by Raman and Infrared (IR) spectroscopies. The study uses 64-atom supercells for the ab initio calculations, which are well-converged in size. The study also proposes a simple ab initio protocol to estimate the parameters of the percolation model. The study analyzes the TO density of states (TO-DOS) at the zone-center (ZC) to compare with the Raman signal. The study uses the Grüneisen parameter (γ) to estimate the impurity frequency. The study does not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. The study does not mention any ethical considerations or IRB.

Procedures Architectures
The study utilizes a percolation model to describe the phonon mode behavior in semiconductor alloys. The percolation model distinguishes between vibrations of like bonds within B-rich and C-rich regions, resulting from different local bond distortions. The model predicts a splitting of each MREI-like TO branch into a symmetrical double-branch, attached to the parent and impurity modes. The study also employs ab initio calculations using the plane-wave pseudopotential method within the density functional theory and the local density approximation (LDA). The calculations are performed using the computer code Siesta. The ab initio protocol involves calculating the impurity frequency (ωimp) and the splitting (Δ) using supercells. The study uses 64-atom supercells for the ab initio calculations. To access ωimp, a supercell containing a single impurity (∼3% imp.) is used. To access Δ, a supercell containing two neighboring substitutional impurities is used. The study proposes a three-oscillator [1 Zn-Te, 2 Zn-Se] version of the percolation model for ZnTeSe. The model's architecture involves the calculation of TO and LO Raman lineshapes using a classical form of the dielectric function, generalized to three harmonic oscillators. The study uses small dampings for the Zn-Te (1 cm−1) and Zn-Se (3 cm−1) modes.

Key Results
The study demonstrates that the 1-bond→2-phonon percolation model applies to ZnTeSe, as it does to InGaAs and InGaP. The authors propose a three-oscillator version for ZnTeSe, supported by existing EXAFS data and ab initio phonon calculations. The agreement between the theoretical curves and the data is rather good (Figure 2). The study shows that the percolation schemes are consistent with the MREI-VCA classification. The study finds that the Zn-Te and Zn-Se bonds have (ωimp, Δ) values of (∼189 cm−1, ∼0 cm−1) and (∼195 cm−1, ∼8 cm−1), respectively. The ab initio calculations show three equidistant oscillators spaced by ∼10 cm−1 in the ZC TO-DOS (Figure 3). The study finds that the interplay between the frequencies and strengths of the three oscillators in the ZC TO-DOS and the phenomenological TO Raman lineshapes are consistent over the whole composition domain. The study shows a slight overall blue-shift of the ZC TO-DOS with respect to the corresponding Raman lineshape (∼20 cm−1).

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest a unified understanding of phonon mode behavior in semiconductor alloys, challenging the traditional classification based on the virtual crystal approximation (VCA). The percolation model provides a mesoscopic perspective on alloy disorder, offering a more accurate description of vibrational spectra. The results imply that the seemingly disparate behaviors of InGaAs, InGaP, and ZnTeSe can be explained by a single underlying mechanism. The study's findings suggest that vibrational spectroscopies can provide insight into alloy disorder at the mesoscopic scale. The study emphasizes the importance of considering the TO modes and their behavior in alloys, as LO modes can obscure the underlying 1-bond→2-mode behavior. The study's results suggest that the traditional MREI-VCA/Elliott-CPA classification can be unified into a single class covered by the percolation model.

Contradictions Limitations
The study relies on a simplified percolation model, and the generalizability of the model to other alloy systems is not explicitly addressed. The study does not provide information about the specific composition ranges or experimental conditions used for the Raman/IR data. The study acknowledges a slight discrepancy with respect to the TOTeZn−Se branch in the Te-dilute limit. The study does not address the limitations of the LDA approximation used in the ab initio calculations. The study does not discuss the potential impact of temperature on the phonon behavior. The study does not mention the random seed used for the simulations. The study does not discuss the limitations of the ab initio protocol.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 2 shows the TO/LO percolation picture for ZnTe1−xSex, with experimental data and theoretical curves. Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the demonstration that the phonon mode behavior in seemingly disparate semiconductor alloys can be unified under a single percolation-type model, offering a new perspective on alloy disorder. (2) The strongest evidence comes from the successful application of the percolation model to ZnTeSe, supported by ab initio calculations and existing experimental data, which provides a more accurate description of the TO mode behavior. (3) The primary limitation is the reliance on a simplified model and the need for further validation across a wider range of alloy compositions and systems. A forward path includes extending the model to other alloy systems and refining the ab initio protocol for improved accuracy.

arXiv:0709.0940v1  [gr-qc]  6 Sep 2007
Coherent network analysis for triggered
gravitational wave burst searches
K Hayama1, S D Mohanty1, M Rakhmanov2, S Desai2
1The University of Texas at Brownsville, 80 Fort Brown, Brownsville, Texas,
78520, USA.
2 Department of Physics, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA
16802, USA.
E-mail: kazu@phys.utb.edu
Abstract.
Searches for gravitational wave bursts that are triggered by the
observation of astronomical events require a diﬀerent mode of analysis than all-
sky, blind searches. For one, much more prior information is usually available in
a triggered search which can and should be used in the analysis. Second, since
the data volume is usually small in a triggered search, it is also possible to use
computationally more expensive algorithms for tasks such as data pre-processing
that can consume signiﬁcant computing resources in a high data-volume un-
triggered search. From the statistical point of view, the reduction in the parameter
space search volume leads to higher sensitivity than an un-triggered search. We
describe here a data analysis pipeline for triggered searches, called RIDGE, and
present preliminary results for simulated noise and signals.
1. Introduction
Gravitational wave (GW) searches that are triggered by the observation of an
astronomical event have some aspects that are fundamentally diﬀerent from all-sky
or un-triggered searches. First of all, the non-GW observations furnish a wealth of
prior information that can guide the GW data analysis. For instance, in the case of a
Gamma-ray Burst (GRB) trigger, we usually know the sky location and, sometimes,
the distance to the source. Based on the type of GRB, long-soft or short-hard, one can
look for qualitatively diﬀerent signals: short duration bursts for the former and binary
inspiral signals for the latter. Second, there are many data pre-processing algorithms
available in the literature that have been demonstrated to be useful but have not been
used in untriggered searches because of a natural selection eﬀect: ﬁnite computational
resources pick the computationally least expensive algorithm. Triggered searches, on
the other hand, usually involve much smaller data volumes and, consequently, allow
us the freedom to experiment with algorithms.
In this paper, we describe results from one such ongoing experiment of using new
algorithms for analyzing data from the LIGO, GEO and Virgo detectors for triggered
searches. We use new algorithms for both the data pre-processing (conditioning) and
the search part of the analysis pipeline. The code for the pipeline, called RIDGE, is
written mostly in matlab. We will not describe the code in any detail in this paper
but focus on the algorithms and results.

Network analysis for triggered searches
2
2. Data analysis components
A typical triggered search involves several components [1].
First, a mechanism is
required to collect trigger information.
This is already well developed and nearly
automated within the LIGO Scientiﬁc Collaboration (LSC), at least as far as GCN [2]
triggers are concerned. Second, given the wealth of astrophysical prior information
associated with most triggers, we need proper mathematical tools to incorporate this
information into our analysis. So far, this aspect of a triggered search has seen only
limited advances. The most detailed use of prior information has been in the search [3]
for GWs from the SGR-1806–20 event [4] where X-ray intensity oscillations associated
with the ﬂare were used to motivate a search for quasi-monochromatic signals at
speciﬁc frequencies. However, more work is needed in this area, especially on the use
of Bayesian approaches modeled after the ones used for a diﬀerent type of “triggered”
search [5], namely GWs from known pulsars in the Galaxy. The other components
required in a typical triggered search, as in any other search, are data conditioning
and the generation of a detection statistic.
2.1. Data conditioning in RIDGE
The purpose of data conditioning is to mitigate the eﬀect of known instrumental
artifacts in the data. In RIDGE this is done in a two step process. First, the noise ﬂoor
of the power spectral density (PSD) of noise is estimated using a running median [6].
Fig. 1 shows the PSD of 2 sec of simulated detector noise with a power spectral
density approximating the LIGO SRD curve for the 4km detectors. Superimposed
on the estimated PSD is the running median estimate of the noise ﬂoor. The main
advantage of the running median is its ability to reject outliers. In this particular case,
the outliers are the narrowband noise artifacts arising from sources such as power line
interference (modeled as sinusoids in this particular example).
If S(f) denotes the running median estimate of the PSD, a digital ﬁlter with a
transfer function T (f) such that |T (f)| = 1/
p
S(f) will whiten the data. Fig. 1 also
shows the PSD of the output of such a digital ﬁlter. In RIDGE, the whitening ﬁlters
are Finite Impulse Response (FIR) ﬁlters and the ﬁlter coeﬃcients are obtained using
the PSD obtained from a user-speciﬁed training data segment. The digital ﬁlter is
then applied to a longer stretch of data. It is clear that any non-stationarity in the
noise ﬂoor on timescales shorter than the gap between the training and the processed
data can create a discrepancy in the trained ﬁlter and the ﬁlter that is required for
whitening the longer stretch. To the knowledge of the authors, not much concrete work
exists in the GW literature on handling this issue robustly in any analysis pipeline.
However, tools already exist that can monitor the behaviour of the noise ﬂoor in real
time [7], and characterize burst-like non-stationary components [8].
We intend to
integrate these information into our pipeline in the future.

reduces or, in some cases, eliminates the eﬀect of strong narrowband noise features

the amplitude and phase modulation of a line feature at a given carrier frequency

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces RIDGE, a data analysis pipeline designed for triggered searches of gravitational wave (GW) bursts, motivated by the need for specialized methods in the context of astronomical event triggers. The pipeline incorporates prior information from triggers, such as Gamma-ray Bursts (GRBs), and employs computationally efficient algorithms for data conditioning and detection statistic generation. The RIDGE pipeline uses a two-step data conditioning process involving running median-based noise floor estimation and whitening, followed by line estimation and removal using MBLT to mitigate instrumental artifacts. The detection statistic is based on regularized maximum likelihood analysis, generating sky-maps of GW likelihood. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using a network of LIGO and Virgo detectors, with simulated Gaussian noise and injected sine-Gaussian signals. Results show that the Rrad statistic, which incorporates information from the full sky-map, outperforms the Rmm statistic. Specifically, with Rrad, a signal with hrss = 5×10−22 Hz−1/2 can be detected with approximately 62% probability at a false alarm probability of 10−2. The novelty lies in the application of new algorithms for data pre-processing and the use of regularized maximum likelihood for network analysis in triggered searches. This work is significant because it offers an independent check for results obtained with other pipelines and provides a platform for testing new regulators. The primary limitation is the use of a relatively large integration time (0.5 sec) due to filter delays, which could be improved in future versions. 

Research Context
Searches for gravitational waves triggered by astronomical events differ from all-sky searches due to the availability of prior information and the potential for computationally intensive algorithms. Existing all-sky search methods do not fully leverage prior information from triggers, such as sky location and distance information from GRBs. Prior work has explored the use of prior information in GW searches, such as in the search for GWs from the SGR-1806–20 event, but more work is needed, especially on the use of Bayesian approaches. This work addresses the need for specialized methods by developing a pipeline that incorporates prior information and new algorithms for data conditioning and detection statistic generation, which are computationally feasible in triggered searches with smaller data volumes.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to improve the sensitivity of gravitational wave burst searches triggered by astronomical events. The primary hypothesis is that incorporating prior information and employing advanced data conditioning and detection statistic algorithms will enhance the detection probability of GW signals. The study predicts that the Rrad statistic, which utilizes information from the full sky-map, will outperform the Rmm statistic in detecting simulated GW signals. The alternative hypothesis is that the performance of Rrad will not significantly differ from Rmm, suggesting that the choice of detection statistic does not substantially impact the detection sensitivity. This work differs from prior research by focusing on triggered searches, which allows for the use of more computationally expensive algorithms and the incorporation of prior information from astronomical triggers. The study aims to demonstrate that a tailored approach to data analysis can improve the detection of GW signals in the context of triggered searches.

Methodological Details
The study employed Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the performance of the RIDGE pipeline. The study design involved generating simulated detector noise and injecting simulated GW signals into the data. The participants in the simulation were the simulated data streams from the LIGO and Virgo detectors. The sample consisted of simulated data from the 4km LIGO detectors (H1 and L1), the 2km LIGO detector (H2), and the Virgo detector (V1). The noise PSDs used were the design sensitivity curves for the LIGO and Virgo detectors. The data conditioning pipeline used a running median to estimate the noise floor, followed by whitening using FIR filters. Line noise was removed using the MBLT method. The detection statistic was based on regularized maximum likelihood, generating sky-maps. The data was generated at a sampling frequency of 16384 Hz. The procedure involved generating Gaussian, stationary noise (∼3000 sec) and adding sinusoids to simulate instrumental artifacts. Signals of constant amplitude were added at regular intervals. The injected signals corresponded to a single source located at θ = −30◦ and φ = 167.0◦. The h+(t) and h×(t) waveforms were sine-Gaussian signals with a center frequency of 235 Hz and a Q = 9. The signal strength was specified in terms of the hrss value. The conditioned data was passed to the sky-map generation code in segments of length 0.5 sec. The analysis used two detection statistics: Rmm and Rrad. The study was not preregistered, and no multiple-comparison corrections were reported. Ethics approval was not mentioned.

Procedures Architectures
The RIDGE pipeline consists of several components. First, it incorporates a mechanism to collect trigger information, such as from the Gamma-ray Coordinates Network (GCN). The data conditioning step involves two main processes: noise floor estimation and whitening. The noise floor is estimated using a running median applied to the power spectral density (PSD) of the noise. Whitening is performed using Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters, with filter coefficients obtained from a user-specified training data segment. Line noise removal is performed using the MBLT method, which estimates the amplitude and phase modulation of line features at a given carrier frequency. The detection statistic is based on regularized maximum likelihood. The input to the algorithm is a set of equal-length, conditioned data segments from the detectors in a given network. The output, for a given sky location, is the value of the likelihood of the data maximized over all possible h+ and h× waveforms. The maximum likelihood values are obtained as a function of θ and φ, creating a sky-map. The sky-map generation code is applied in segments of 0.5 sec. The Rmm statistic is calculated as the maximum value of the sky-map divided by its minimum value. The Rrad statistic is a radial distance calculation based on the sky-map. The novelty lies in the application of new algorithms for data pre-processing and the use of regularized maximum likelihood for network analysis in triggered searches.

Key Results
The study's primary results are based on Monte Carlo simulations. The performance of the detection statistics Rmm and Rrad was characterized. The network consisted of the 4km LIGO detectors (H1 and L1), the 2km LIGO detector (H2), and the Virgo detector (V1). Simulated data included Gaussian noise and injected sine-Gaussian signals. Figure 6 shows the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for Rmm and Rrad. For an hrss of 5 × 10−22 Hz−1/2, the Rrad statistic achieved a detection probability of approximately 62% at a false alarm probability of 10−2. The false alarm probability corresponds to a rate of 1 false event in 50 seconds. The Rrad statistic outperformed the Rmm statistic. The study found that the Rrad statistic, which incorporates information from the full sky-map, is better than the Rmm statistic. The study used hrss values of 3 × 10−22, 5 × 10−22 and 7 × 10−22 Hz−1/2. The simulated data were generated at a sampling frequency of 16384 Hz.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that incorporating information from the full sky-map, as done by the Rrad statistic, is crucial for improving the detection of GW signals in triggered searches. The superior performance of Rrad over Rmm implies that a more sophisticated approach to analyzing the sky-map can lead to increased sensitivity. The results support the hypothesis that advanced data conditioning and detection statistic algorithms can enhance the detection probability of GW signals. The study's findings have implications for the design of future GW search pipelines, indicating that the use of full sky-map statistics and advanced data conditioning techniques is beneficial. The study suggests that the RIDGE pipeline can serve as a platform for testing new regulators and algorithms, which can further improve the sensitivity of triggered searches. The study's scope is limited to the specific network and signal parameters used in the simulations.

Contradictions Limitations
The primary limitation is the use of a 0.5-second integration time for the sky-map generation, which is larger than the duration of the injected signals. This choice was made to accommodate filter delays and may have resulted in a lower bound on the performance estimates. The study does not mention the random seed used for the simulations. The study does not provide details on the specific algorithms used for data conditioning or the exact parameters used in the MBLT method. The study is limited by the specific network configuration (H1, H2, L1, and V1) and the simulated signal parameters (sine-Gaussian signals with specific parameters). The study does not address the impact of non-Gaussian noise or the effect of different signal waveforms. The study does not discuss the external validity of the findings to other types of GW searches or the impact of real-world detector noise characteristics. The study does not provide a detailed comparison with other network analysis pipelines.

Inertial Screening in Sedimentation
P.N. Segr`e
Department of Physics, Emory University, Atlanta, GA 30322
Abstract
We use particle image velocimetry to measure the sedimentation dynamics of a semi-dilute
suspension of non-Brownian spheres at Reynolds numbers, 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3, extending from the
Stokes to the moderately inertial regime. We ﬁnd that the onset of inertial corrections to Stokes
sedimentation occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes similar to the Stokes
sedimentation length ξ0, at Rec = a/ξ0 ≈0.05. For Re > Rec, inertial screening signiﬁcantly
reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of the particle velocity ﬂuctuations. A modiﬁed
Hinch force balance model connects the ﬂuctuation magnitudes σV /V to the correlation sizes ξ.
1
arXiv:0709.0995v1  [physics.flu-dyn]  7 Sep 2007

The sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres is a fundamental problem in
physics [1] and has been the subject of intense activity in recent years (for a review see [2]).
Much of the focus has been on particles slowly settling in viscous liquids, conditions that
correspond to very low Reynolds numbers, Re ≪1, called the Stokes regime. The Reynolds
number is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in ﬂuids, and is deﬁned as Re ≡2V a/ν (V is
the particle velocity, a the radius, and ν the ﬂuid kinematic viscosity). In the Stokes regime,
where inertial forces are insigniﬁcant, concentrations of spheres display Re-independent large
amplitude velocity ﬂuctuations σV /V during settling [3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Signiﬁcantly, experi-
ments [5, 6, 7, 8], simulations [9], and theory [10] have shown that the ﬂuctuations display a
characteristic spatial size ξ, despite the fact that the hydrodynamic interactions emanating
from a single isolated sphere are of inﬁnite range (∝1/r) [11]. The Stokes screening length
ξ represents regions of concentration ﬂuctuations, σφ, that drive velocity ﬂuctuations σV
and particle diﬀusion D ∼σV ξ. While an explanation of the origin of screening in Stokes
sedimentation remains controversial, its existence and central importance for a description
of sedimentation is not.
The sedimentation dynamics at higher speed ﬂows where inertial forces become signif-
icant, Re ∼1, have received much less attention despite its fundamental importance and
widespread relevance to numerous chemical industries [12]. In contrast to the Stokes regime,
for an isolated sphere falling at moderate Re, there is a distance beyond which the 1/r Stokes
like hydrodynamics are screened [11]. The inertial screening length, l ∼a/Re, becomes
shorter as the Reynolds number is increased. For concentrations of settling spheres, the
Reynolds number dependence of the hydrodynamic interactions brought about by inertia is
predicted to result in Reynolds number dependent sedimentation dynamics as well [13]. Ex-
periments designed to investigate these changes, however, are greatly lacking. We are aware
of only a single experiment, by Cowan et al. [14] using novel ultrasonic techniques, that
has examined the ﬂuctuation dynamics of spheres at moderate Re <∼1. Surprisingly, they
concluded that the velocity ﬂuctuations were independent of Reynolds number for Re <∼1.
In the absence of experiments describing the sedimentation dynamics beyond the Stokes
regime, our understanding of the basic physics, and our ability to develop and test model
theories, remains very limited.
In this letter, we describe experiments that demonstrate how moderate amounts of ﬂuid
inertia can signiﬁcantly aﬀect the settling dynamics of spheres. The onset of inertial correc-
2

tions to Stokes sedimentation occurs when the inertial screening length l = a/Re becomes
as small as the Stokes sedimentation length ξ0, at Rec = a/ξ0. For Re > Rec, inertial
screening signiﬁcantly reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of the particle veloc-
ity ﬂuctuations. A modiﬁed Hinch force balance model, with Reynolds number dependent
drag coeﬃcients, connects the ﬂuctuation magnitudes σV /V to the correlation sizes ξ over
the entire range studied, 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3.
The particles used in our experiments were monodisperse glass beads of radius a = 137±9
µm. They were dispersed in various mixtures of glycerol and water, enabling us to examine
the very low to moderate Reynolds number regimes, 0.001 ≤Re ≤2.3. In all cases the
volume fraction is φ = 0.06. The sample cell was a rectangular glass tube of dimension 8 ×
80×305 mm, and the temperature was at the ambient value T = 23±10C. Particle velocities
were measured using a particle image velocimetry (PIV) [15] apparatus consisting of some
specialized image processing software and hardware purchased from Dantec Instruments. A
large cross section of the cell was imaged (3×3 cm), so that several thousand particles could
be simultaneously studied. Initially, random dispersions were prepared by vigorous shaking
of the cells. The location of the imaging window was far from both the sedimentation front
and the sediment growth. Each velocity ﬁelds is a map of 41 × 42 vectors, and each velocity
vector is the local average of two to four spheres.
We begin by examining typical particle velocity ﬁelds during sedimentation. Figures
1(a-c) show results for particle velocities Vi from three samples spanning the very low,
Re = 0.001 ≪1, to moderate, Re = 2.3, Reynolds number regimes. In the Stokes ﬂow
regime, Fig. 1(a), the patterns look similar to those reported in the literature [5, 7], with
large magnitude ﬂuctuations occurring in extended swirling regions. In the presence of some
inertia, Re = 0.2 in Fig. 1(b), the pattern appears slightly more uniform, indicating a slight
reduction in the ﬂuctuations relative to that seen at Re = 0.001. At the highest ﬂow speed,
Re = 2.3 in Fig. 1(c), there is a dramatic change in the dynamics. The ﬂuctuations are
largely absent, the particles appear to be nearly falling with the same speed. We interpret
these changes as evidence of an inertial screening of the velocity ﬂuctuations.
To examine the ﬂuctuations in more detail, Figs. 1(d-f) shows the same set of maps
with the mean velocities subtracted oﬀ, δVi ≡Vi −⟨Vi⟩. All of the patterns in fact show
qualitatively similar swirling regions. The sizes of the regions appear to decrease with Re.
The dramatic decrease in ﬂuctuations seen in Fig. 1(c) is reﬂected in the greatly magniﬁed

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the effects of fluid inertia on the sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres, extending the study from the Stokes regime to moderately inertial regimes. The primary motivation is the limited understanding of sedimentation dynamics beyond the Stokes regime, despite its importance in various chemical industries. The study employed particle image velocimetry (PIV) to measure the sedimentation dynamics of a semi-dilute suspension of glass beads in glycerol-water mixtures, varying the Reynolds number (Re) from 0.001 to 2.3. The key finding is that inertial corrections to Stokes sedimentation begin when the inertial screening length, l = a/Re, becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length, ξ0, at a critical Reynolds number, Rec ≈ 0.05. For Re > Rec, inertial screening significantly reduces both the magnitude and spatial extent of particle velocity fluctuations. The study also demonstrates that a modified Hinch force balance model, incorporating Reynolds number-dependent drag coefficients, accurately connects the fluctuation magnitudes to the correlation sizes across the entire range of Reynolds numbers studied. The novelty lies in experimentally demonstrating and quantifying the effects of inertial screening on sedimentation dynamics and connecting these observations to a modified Hinch model. This work is significant because it provides insights into the transition from Stokes to inertial sedimentation, which is crucial for understanding and modeling sedimentation processes in various applications. A limitation is the focus on a single particle size and volume fraction. The study also does not explore the effects of different particle shapes or fluid properties.

Research Context
The sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres is a fundamental problem, primarily studied in the Stokes regime (Re << 1). In this regime, particles exhibit large-amplitude velocity fluctuations with a characteristic spatial size, ξ, despite the infinite range of hydrodynamic interactions. Prior work has focused on understanding the origin of screening in Stokes sedimentation. However, the sedimentation dynamics at moderate Reynolds numbers (Re ~ 1) have received less attention. Existing studies lack experimental data describing the sedimentation dynamics beyond the Stokes regime. Cowan et al. (2000) examined fluctuation dynamics at moderate Re < 1 but concluded that velocity fluctuations were independent of Reynolds number. This paper addresses the gap in understanding by investigating the effects of inertia on sedimentation dynamics and providing experimental evidence to support the existence of inertial screening.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: How does fluid inertia affect the sedimentation dynamics of non-Brownian spheres? The primary hypothesis is that inertial corrections to Stokes sedimentation will occur when the inertial screening length, l = a/Re, becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length, ξ0. This leads to the prediction that at a critical Reynolds number, Rec ≈ a/ξ0, inertial screening will reduce the magnitude and spatial extent of particle velocity fluctuations. An alternative hypothesis is that velocity fluctuations remain independent of Reynolds number for Re < 1, as suggested by Cowan et al. (2000). The study aims to determine the Reynolds number at which inertial effects become significant, quantify the changes in velocity fluctuations and correlation lengths, and assess the applicability of a modified Hinch model in describing the observed behavior. The study differs from prior work by experimentally investigating the transition from Stokes to inertial sedimentation and providing quantitative data on the effects of inertia on velocity fluctuations and correlation lengths.

Methodological Details
The study employed particle image velocimetry (PIV) to measure the sedimentation dynamics of a semi-dilute suspension of non-Brownian spheres. The experimental design aimed to investigate the sedimentation dynamics across a range of Reynolds numbers, extending from the Stokes regime to the moderately inertial regime. The sample consisted of monodisperse glass beads with a radius (a) of 137 ± 9 µm. These beads were dispersed in various mixtures of glycerol and water to achieve Reynolds numbers ranging from 0.001 to 2.3. The volume fraction (φ) of the particles was maintained at 0.06 in all experiments. The sample cell was a rectangular glass tube with dimensions of 8 × 80 × 305 mm. The temperature was maintained at the ambient value of 23 ± 1°C. Particle velocities were measured using a PIV apparatus from Dantec Instruments, which included specialized image processing software and hardware. The PIV system captured images of a large cross-section of the cell (3 × 3 cm), allowing for the simultaneous study of several thousand particles. Initial random dispersions were prepared by vigorous shaking of the cells. The location of the imaging window was far from both the sedimentation front and the sediment growth. Each velocity field was a map of 41 × 42 vectors, with each vector representing the local average of two to four spheres. The primary metric was the Reynolds number, defined as Re = 2Va/ν, where V is the particle velocity, a is the particle radius, and ν is the fluid kinematic viscosity. The normalized autocorrelation function of the z component of the velocity fluctuations, Cz(r) = ⟨δVz(0)δVz(r)⟩/⟨δVz(0)2⟩, was used to analyze the spatial correlations of the velocity fluctuations. The empirical forms Cz(z) = exp[−(z/ξ)1.5] and Cz(x) = exp[−(x/ξ⊥)1.5] were fit to the data. The ensemble-averaged root-mean-square (rms) velocity fluctuations, σv = sqrt(⟨[Vi,z − V]2⟩), were also calculated. No mention of preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections was made.

Procedures Architectures
The experimental procedure involved dispersing monodisperse glass beads in glycerol-water mixtures within a rectangular glass tube. The key to controlling the Reynolds number was the use of different glycerol-water mixtures, which altered the fluid's kinematic viscosity (ν). The PIV system, consisting of specialized image processing software and hardware, captured the particle velocities. The PIV system generated velocity maps by analyzing the displacement of particles between successive images. The velocity maps were then used to calculate the velocity fluctuations (δVi = Vi − ⟨Vi⟩) and their spatial correlations. The autocorrelation function, Cz(r), was calculated to quantify the spatial extent of the velocity fluctuations. The correlation lengths, ξ and ξ⊥, were determined by fitting the experimental data to empirical forms. The root-mean-square (rms) velocity fluctuations, σv, were calculated to quantify the magnitude of the velocity fluctuations. The Hinch model was modified to account for the effects of inertia. The modified Hinch model used the correlation length, ξ, and the Reynolds number-dependent drag coefficient, βRe. The model was then used to predict the normalized velocity fluctuations, σV/V, and compared with the experimental data. The software used for image processing and analysis was from Dantec Instruments. The hardware included the PIV apparatus. The study's novel aspect is the experimental investigation of inertial screening and the application of a modified Hinch model to explain the observed behavior. The study did not involve the construction of new architectures or systems.

Key Results
The study found that the onset of inertial corrections to Stokes sedimentation occurs at a critical Reynolds number of approximately 0.05. Figure 1 illustrates the changes in particle velocity fields with increasing Reynolds number. At Re = 0.001, the Stokes regime, large velocity fluctuations are observed. At Re = 0.2, the fluctuations appear slightly reduced. At Re = 2.3, the fluctuations are largely absent. Figure 2 shows the spatial correlation functions of the velocity fluctuations for Re = 0.001 and Re = 2.3. The decay lengths are much reduced in the inertial sample (Re = 2.3). Figure 3(a) shows the spatial correlation lengths, ξ and ξ⊥, as a function of Reynolds number. For Re < 0.05, ξ is independent of Re, and for Re > 0.05, ξ decreases with increasing Re. The decrease in ξ demonstrates that inertial screening occurs at shorter distances for higher Reynolds numbers. Figure 3(b) shows the normalized velocity fluctuations, σV/V, versus Re. σV/V is independent of Re for Re < 0.05, with a value of approximately 0.75. At Re = 2.3, σV/V is reduced by approximately 80%. The modified Hinch model, using the fit expression for ξ, accurately predicts σV/V across the entire range of Reynolds numbers studied. The model predictions show that the drop in fluctuation magnitudes with Re is due to both decreasing correlation lengths and the increasing drag force term. The study also re-examined the experiments of Cowan et al. (2000) and found that their results were consistent with the current findings.

Interpretation Implications
The findings support the hypothesis that inertial screening significantly affects sedimentation dynamics. The observed reduction in velocity fluctuations and correlation lengths with increasing Reynolds number indicates that inertia plays a crucial role in the transition from Stokes to inertial sedimentation. The success of the modified Hinch model in accurately predicting the normalized velocity fluctuations suggests that the underlying assumption of a random particle density distribution remains valid even in the presence of inertia. The study implies that the inertial screening length, l, and the Stokes correlation length, ξ0, are key parameters in determining the onset of inertial effects. The results provide an important benchmark for future theoretical work on moderately inertial systems. The study suggests that the Brenner criterion, which compares particle diffusion and viscous momentum diffusion, also accurately predicts the transition to inertial behavior. The findings broaden the understanding of sedimentation processes and provide a framework for modeling sedimentation in various applications.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is the focus on a single particle size and volume fraction, which limits the generalizability of the findings to other particle sizes and concentrations. The study does not explore the effects of different particle shapes or fluid properties. The study does not address the mechanisms underlying the inertial screening process in detail. The study's findings are consistent with the results of Cowan et al. (2000), who found no inertial effects for Re < 1, which is consistent with the current study's findings. The study does not explicitly address the potential for systematic errors in the PIV measurements. The absence of information on the random seed used for the experiments limits the reproducibility of the study. The study does not discuss any potential conflicts with prior literature, other than the comparison with Cowan et al. (2000).

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows PIV results for three suspensions of sedimenting spheres at different Reynolds numbers, illustrating the changes in particle velocity fields. Figure 2 presents spatial correlation functions of the velocity fluctuations, demonstrating the impact of inertia on the correlation lengths. Figure 3(a) shows the spatial correlation lengths ξ and ξ⊥ as a function of Reynolds number. Figure 3(b) shows the normalized velocity fluctuations σV/V versus Re, and compares the experimental data with the modified Hinch model predictions. Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the experimental demonstration and quantification of inertial screening effects on sedimentation dynamics, showing that inertial corrections to Stokes sedimentation begin when the inertial screening length becomes comparable to the Stokes sedimentation length. (2) The strongest evidence comes from the quantitative results presented in Figure 3, which show the reduction in velocity fluctuations and correlation lengths with increasing Reynolds number, and the successful application of the modified Hinch model to predict these fluctuations. (3) The primary limitation is the focus on a single particle size and volume fraction. Future work could explore the effects of different particle sizes, concentrations, and fluid properties to broaden the applicability of the findings.

questions.rationale: The authors estimate the true Re using concentration-specific V and η, placing the samples below onset.
questions.evidence_quote:
They compared many concentrations 0.19 ≤φ ≤0.5, at
both Re0 = 0.007 and Re0 = 0.3, and concluded that, contrary to expectations, the velocity
ﬂuctuations were independent of Reynolds number for Re < 1. We ﬁrst note that they
deﬁned Re0 ≡2aV0/η0 based upon the inﬁnite dilution values V0 and η0, not the values at
the high concentrations studied. Using our deﬁnition Re = 2aV/η, we estimate that the
Re0 = 0.3 samples range from 0.001 <∼Re <∼0.05. Our critical Reynolds number for the
appearance of inertial inﬂuence, Rec = a/ξ0, can also be evaluated from their ﬁndings that
ξ ∼11aφ−1/3, resulting in Rec ≈0.06. We therefore ﬁnd that Re <∼Rec for all of their
samples, consistent with their ﬁndings of no inertial eﬀects..

arXiv:0709.0973v1  [hep-th]  7 Sep 2007
CSULB–PA–07–6
Green-Schwarz, Nambu-Goto Actions,
and Cayley’s Hyperdeterminant
Hitoshi NISHINO1) and Subhash RAJPOOT2)
Department of Physics & Astronomy
California State University
1250 Bellﬂower Boulevard
Long Beach, CA 90840
Abstract
It has been recently shown that Nambu-Goto action can be re-expressed in terms
of Cayley’s hyperdeterminant with the manifest SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR) × SL(2, IR)
symmetry. In the present paper, we show that the same feature is shared by Green-
Schwarz σ -model for N = 2 superstring whose target space-time is D = 2+2. When
its zweibein ﬁeld is eliminated from the action, it contains the Nambu-Goto action
which is nothing but the square root of Cayley’s hyperdeterminant of the pull-back in
superspace
q
Det (Πiα .α) manifestly invariant under SL(2, IR)×SL(2, IR)×SL(2, IR).
The target space-time D = 2 + 2 can accommodate self-dual supersymmetric Yang-
Mills theory. Our action has also fermionic κ-symmetry, satisfying the criterion for its
light-cone equivalence to Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond formulation for N = 2 superstring.
PACS: 11.25.-w, 11.30.Pb, 11.30.Fs, 02.30.Ik
Key Words: Cayley’s Hyperdeterminant, Green-Schwarz and Nambu-Goto Actions,
2 + 2
Dimensions, Self-Dual Supersymmetric Yang-Mills, N = (1, 1) Space-Time
Supersymmetry, N = 2 Superstring.
1) E-Mail: hnishino@csulb.edu
2) E-Mail: rajpoot@csulb.edu

1. Introduction
Cayley’s hyperdeterminant [1], initially an object of mathematical curiosity, has found
its way in many applications to physics [2]. For instance, it has been used in the discussions
of quantum information theory [3][4], and the entropy of the STU black hole [5][6] in four-
dimensional string theory [7].
More recently, it has been shown [8] that Nambu-Goto (NG) action [9][10] with the
D = 2+2 target space-time possesses the manifest global SL(2, IR)×SL(2, IR)×SL(2, IR) ≡
[SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. In particular, the square root of the determinant of an inner prod-
uct of pull-backs can be rewritten exactly as a Cayley’s hyperdeterminant [1] realizing the
manifest [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry.
It is to be noted that the space-time dimensions D = 2+2 pointed out in [8] are nothing
but the consistent target space-time of N = 23) NSR superstring [16][17][18][19][13][14][15].
However, the NSR formulation [16][17] has a drawback for rewriting it purely in terms of
a determinant, due to the presence of fermionic superpartners on the 2D world-sheet. On
the other hand, it is well known that a GS formulation [12] without explicit world-sheet
supersymmetry is classically equivalent to a NSR formulation [11] on the light-cone, when the
former has fermionic κ -symmetry [20][15]. From this viewpoint, a GS σ -model formulation
in [14] of N = 2 superstring [16][17][13] seems more advantageous, despite the temporary
sacriﬁce of world-sheet supersymmetry. However, even the GS formulation [14] itself has
an obstruction, because obviously the kinetic term in the GS action is not of the NG-type
equivalent to a Cayley’s hyperdeterminant.
In this paper, we overcome this obstruction, by eliminating the zweibein (or 2D metric)
via its ﬁeld equation which is not algebraic. Despite the non-algebraic ﬁeld equation, such
an elimination is possible, just as a NG action [9][10] is obtained from a Polyakov action [21].
Similar formulations are known to be possible for Type I, heterotic, or Type II superstring
theories, but here we need to deal with N = 2 superstring [16] with the target space-time
3) The N = 2 here implies the number of world-sheet supersymmetries in the Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond
(NSR) formulation [11]. Its corresponding Green-Schwarz (GS) formulation [12][13][14] might be also called
‘N = 2’ GS superstring in the present paper. Needless to say, the number of world-sheet supersymmetries
should not be confused with that of space-time supersymmetries, such as N = 1 for Type I superstring, or
N = 2 for Type IIA or IIB superstring [15].

As is widely recognized, the quantum-level equivalence of NG action [9][10] to Polyakov
