papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model for the N=2 superstring in a D=2+2 target space-time, demonstrating that its action can be reformulated using Cayley's hyperdeterminant. The authors show that when the zweibein field is eliminated from the GS action, the resulting action contains the Nambu-Goto (NG) action, which is equivalent to the square root of Cayley's hyperdeterminant. This formulation exhibits manifest SL(2,R) x SL(2,R) x SL(2,R) symmetry. The target space-time D=2+2 is suitable for self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. The action also possesses fermionic κ-symmetry, which is a criterion for its light-cone equivalence to the Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond (NSR) formulation for the N=2 superstring. The primary finding is that the NG-action part of the GS sigma-model, after eliminating the 2D metric, can be expressed as the square root of Cayley's hyperdeterminant, revealing the manifest [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. This formulation is classically invariant under fermionic κ-symmetry. The work highlights the relationship between Cayley's hyperdeterminant, the N=2 superstring, and self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. A key limitation is that the quantum equivalence of the NG reformulation to the conventional NSR superstring is not claimed. The significance lies in providing a new perspective on the symmetries of the N=2 superstring and its connection to integrable systems.

Research Context
The study builds upon the recent discovery that the Nambu-Goto (NG) action with D=2+2 target space-time exhibits manifest global SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) symmetry, where the square root of the determinant of pull-backs can be rewritten as Cayley's hyperdeterminant. The existing Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond (NSR) formulation has a drawback in rewriting it purely in terms of a determinant due to fermionic superpartners. The Green-Schwarz (GS) formulation, while offering advantages, faces an obstruction because its kinetic term is not of the NG-type. This work addresses the obstruction in the GS formulation by eliminating the zweibein field, which allows the action to be expressed in terms of the NG-type determinant form, thus revealing the manifest symmetry. Prior work includes the use of Cayley's hyperdeterminant in quantum information theory and the entropy of the STU black hole, but this paper focuses on its application to the N=2 superstring.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model for the N=2 superstring, when reformulated, can exhibit the same manifest SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) symmetry as the Nambu-Goto (NG) action, and whether this formulation maintains fermionic κ-symmetry. The hypothesis is that by eliminating the zweibein field from the GS action, the resulting action will contain the NG action and manifest the [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry, and that this new action will also possess fermionic κ-symmetry, which is a criterion for light-cone equivalence to the NSR formulation. The study predicts that the NG-type determinant form will emerge after the elimination of the zweibein, revealing the manifest [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The alternative would be that the elimination of the zweibein does not lead to a simplified form that reveals the symmetry, or that the fermionic symmetry is broken. This work differs from prior research by focusing on the GS formulation and demonstrating the [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry via Cayley's hyperdeterminant after eliminating the zweibein, providing a new perspective on the symmetries of the N=2 superstring.

Methodological Details
The paper employs a theoretical approach, deriving and analyzing the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model action for the N=2 superstring. The study begins with the standard GS action, which is light-cone equivalent to the N=2 Neveu-Schwarz-Ramond (NSR) superstring. The analysis involves eliminating the zweibein (2D metric) from the GS action using its field equation. The resulting action is then shown to be equivalent to the Nambu-Goto (NG) action. The paper utilizes the concept of Cayley's hyperdeterminant to demonstrate the manifest SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) x SL(2, IR) symmetry. The fermionic κ-symmetry is confirmed by showing the invariance of the action under the fermionic transformation rule. The study uses the D = (2, 2; 2, 2) target superspace, which represents 2+2 bosonic coordinates and 2 chiral and 2 anti-chiral fermionic coordinates. The analysis involves the use of superspace pull-backs, the vielbein, and the definition of light-cone coordinates. The paper employs mathematical tools such as the square root of the matrix and the Virasoro conditions. The study does not involve empirical data or experimental procedures. No preregistration or statistical tests are mentioned. The paper relies on mathematical derivations and the application of known concepts in string theory and supersymmetry. The analysis is based on established theoretical frameworks and mathematical manipulations.

Procedures Architectures
The methodology involves manipulating the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model action. The starting point is the standard GS action for the N=2 superstring, expressed in terms of the 2D metric (gij), the zweibein (ei(j)), and the superspace pull-back (ΠiA). The zweibein is eliminated using its field equation derived from the GS action. This field equation is not algebraic, but the authors show that the zweibein can be eliminated, similar to how the Nambu-Goto action is obtained from the Polyakov action. The resulting action is then shown to be equivalent to the Nambu-Goto (NG) action. The key component is the use of Cayley's hyperdeterminant to express the kinetic terms. The action is expressed in terms of the superspace pull-back (ΠiA), which is defined as the derivative of the target superspace coordinates with respect to the worldsheet coordinates. The paper defines the light-cone coordinates and uses the projectors to define them. The paper also uses the concept of the square root of the matrix to define the gamma matrices. The fermionic κ-symmetry is demonstrated by showing the invariance of the action under the fermionic transformation rule. The new aspect is the elimination of the zweibein and the subsequent expression of the action in terms of Cayley's hyperdeterminant. The architecture involves the use of the D = (2, 2; 2, 2) target superspace, which accommodates self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory.

Key Results
The primary result is that after eliminating the 2D metric from the Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model action for the N=2 superstring, the resulting action can be expressed as the square root of Cayley's hyperdeterminant, thereby exhibiting the manifest [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The authors demonstrate that the action is invariant under fermionic κ-symmetry, which is expressed in terms of the superspace pull-back. The Virasoro conditions are shown to be inherent in the NG reformulation at the classical level. The paper shows that the action and the fermionic transformation rule involve neither the 2D metric, the zweibein, nor the factor Ω, indicating the total consistency of the formulation in terms of superspace coordinates. The authors show that the combination Γij ≡ ΠiaΠja plays the role of an 'effective metric' on the 2D world-sheet. The paper does not report any quantitative comparisons with other models or baselines. No effect sizes or confidence intervals are reported. The paper focuses on the theoretical derivation and the demonstration of symmetries. The results are based on mathematical derivations and the application of known concepts in string theory and supersymmetry. The paper does not present any negative or unexpected results.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the N=2 Green-Schwarz (GS) sigma-model, when reformulated by eliminating the zweibein, provides a more suitable framework for discussing the [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry via Cayley's hyperdeterminant. The results imply that the superspace pull-back Πiα .α plays a key role in the manifest symmetry. The study emphasizes that the signature D=2+2 is crucial for the global [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The NG reformulation of the N=2 GS superstring with the target superspace D = (2, 2; 2, 2) is more suitable for the global [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry. The work supports the idea that certain non-manifest symmetries become more apparent after eliminating specific fields from the Lagrangian. The results highlight the relationships among Cayley's hyperdeterminant, the N=2 superstring, self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, and supersymmetric integrable models. The findings suggest that the NG reformulation, with the 2D metric eliminated, elucidates the global [SL(2, IR)]3 symmetry of the N=2 superstring.

Contradictions Limitations
The paper does not claim the quantum equivalence of the NG reformulation to the conventional N=2 NSR superstring. The hidden discrete symmetry pointed out in a previous work seems absent in the N=2 string due to the WZNW-term. The study is limited to the classical level and does not address quantum effects. The paper focuses on the theoretical derivation and does not provide experimental validation. The paper does not discuss potential limitations related to the choice of target space-time dimensions. The absence of a detailed discussion of the implications of the results for specific physical phenomena or applications could be considered a limitation. The paper does not address the potential challenges in quantizing the NG action. The lack of a comparison with other approaches or models could be considered a limitation. The paper does not provide information about the potential impact of the results on other areas of physics.

arXiv:0709.0968v1  [astro-ph]  6 Sep 2007
Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and
Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)
G. B. Taylor1, S. E. Healey2, J. F. Helmboldt3, S. Tremblay1, C. D. Fassnacht4, R. C.
Walker5, L. O. Sjouwerman5, T. J. Pearson6, A. C. S. Readhead6, L. Weintraub6, N.
Gehrels7, R. W. Romani2, P. F. Michelson2, R. D. Blandford8, and G. Cotter9
ABSTRACT
We examine the radio properties of EGRET-detected blazars observed as
part of the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS has a ﬂux
limit roughly an order of magnitude below the MOJAVE survey and most other
samples that have been used to study the properties of EGRET blazars.
At
lower ﬂux levels, radio ﬂux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray
ﬂux density. We do ﬁnd that the EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher
brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger than average
jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also found with jet length and with
polarization. All of the well-established trends can be explained by systematically
larger Doppler factors in the γ-ray loud blazars, consistent with the measurements
of higher apparent velocities found in monitoring programs carried out at radio
frequencies above 10 GHz.
Subject headings: galaxies: active - surveys - catalogs - galaxies: jets - galaxies:
nuclei - radio continuum: galaxies - techniques: image processing
1Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of New Mexico, 800 Yale Blvd NE, Albuquerque, NM
87131, USA

3Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, DC 20375

5National Radio Astronomy Observatory, P.O. Box O, Socorro, NM 87801, U.S.A.
6Astronomy Department, California Institute of Technology, Mail Code 105-24, 1200 East California
Boulevard, Pasadena, CA 91125
7NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD 20771
8KIPAC, Stanford University, PO Box 20450, MS 29, Stanford, CA 94309, USA
9University of Oxford, Department of Astrophysics, Denys Wilkinson Building, Keble Road, Oxford OX1
3RH

– 2 –
1.
Introduction
At high galactic latitudes at least ∼70% of the sources seen by the Compton Gamma-
Ray Observatory (CGRO; Hartman et al.
1999) EGRET instrument are identiﬁed with
blazars (Sowards-Emmerd et al. 2003, 2004, 2005). These blazars exhibit ﬂat radio spectra,
rapid variability, compact cores with one-sided parsec-scale jets, and superluminal motion in
the jets (Marscher 2006). At optical wavelengths blazars are characterized by broad or no
emission lines, optically violently variable behavior, and relatively high linear polarization
(Urry & Padovani 1995).
The identiﬁed EGRET blazars display a number of interesting radio properties. Based
on 22 and 37 GHz monitoring of 43 sources, L¨ahteenm¨aki & Valtaoja (2003) suggest that
the EGRET ﬂares lagged behind mm ﬂares. This is in direct contrast to other studies (e.g.,
Reich et al. 1993) that claimed enhanced radio emission following a high level of gamma-ray
activity. Lister & Homan (2005) ﬁnd that EGRET blazars have more strongly polarized
jets than found in compact objects on average based on analysis of 26 EGRET sources
overlapping with the Monitoring of Jets in Active galactic nuclei with VLBA Experiments
(MOJAVE) VLBI survey. Kovalev et al. (2005) reported that EGRET blazars in the 15
GHz MOJAVE survey were more compact than non-EGRET blazars. EGRET blazars have
also been claimed to have much higher superluminal speeds than other blazars, and to have
gamma-ray ﬂares associated with the ejection of superluminal radio knots (Jorstad et al.
2001a,b; Kellermann et al. 2004). However, in consideration of a larger sample (taken at
2 and 8 GHz) Piner et al. (2007) ﬁnd no signiﬁcant diﬀerence between the jet velocities of
EGRET and non-EGRET blazars. In either case it still is unclear whether the radio ﬂaring,
or the ejection of new components, precedes or follows the gamma-ray ﬂare, or whether there
are in fact two classes of gamma-ray blazars (e.g., Sikora et al. 2001, 2002), one class with
steep gamma-ray spectra and another class with ﬂat gamma-ray spectra.
We have recently completed the 5 GHz VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)
of 1127 ﬂat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan
Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). VIPS (Taylor et al. 2005, Helmboldt et al. 2007a) was carried
out between January and August of 2006 and includes 5 GHz, full polarization images of
958 sources as well as 147 total intensity images for sources previously observed as part
of the Caltech Jodrell Bank Flat spectrum survey (CJF). The small remainder (22) were
previously observed in the VIPS pilot survey and/or in the MOJAVE survey. Over 99%
of the VIPS sources have been successfully imaged, with just under 1% being too weak to
reliably self-calibrate and image.
The large, uniform sample provided by VIPS will have many uses, including enabling
the intelligent follow-up of gamma-ray blazars as they ﬂare and are detected by the Gamma-

– 3 –
ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST; Gehrels et al. 2001). GLAST, to be launched
in late 2007, will provide a dramatic increase in the resolution and energy range and over
two orders of magnitude increase in sensitivity over CGRO-EGRET, thereby aﬀording an
unprecedented opportunity for the study of the centers of activity and jets in blazars in the
gamma-ray energy range.
Here we make use of the VIPS survey to examine correlations in the parsec-scale jet
properties of EGRET blazars.
2.
Sample Deﬁnition
We have compared the latest EGRET catalog (Hartman et al. 1999) to the recently
compiled Combined Radio All-sky Targeted Eight GHz Survey (CRATES; Healey et al.
2007a), and from the intersection compiled a sample of 173 candidate EGRET sources at
|b| > 10◦. In Fig. 1 we plot the Gamma-ray mean and peak ﬂuxes against the 8.4 GHz
radio ﬂux density from CRATES (Healey et al. 2007a) for 173 and 117 sources respectively.
The VIPS sample (which covers only ∼14% of the sky), is derived from CLASS (Myers et
al. 2003), but otherwise has similar radio ﬂux limits and spectral selection as CRATES.
Both CRATES and CLASS include A conﬁguration VLA observations at 8.4 GHz. The full
radio/γ-ray properties of the sample will be discussed in Healey et al. 2007b. Here we focus
on the candidate EGRET sources within the ∼5700 square degree region of the sky covered
by VIPS, which provides uniform quality VLBI imaging. The results are summarized in
Table 1. This list contains 12 VIPS sources deemed likely candidates, and 19 VIPS sources
deemed plausible candidates. Here “likely” and “plausible” refer to ranges in the Figure of
Merit (FoM). The FoM is computed based on the 8.4 GHz ﬂux density, the radio spectral
index, the X-ray ﬂux density, and the positional coincidence (Sowards-Emmerd et al. 2003).
A source is considered “likely” if it has FoM > 1, and “plausible” if it has 1.0 > FoM > 0.25.
In some cases multiple VIPS sources are assigned to a single EGRET source. Since some
EGRET sources may be in fact composites of multiple blazars we have not made any dis-
tinction between sources with multiple identiﬁcations and those with a single identiﬁcation.
For 6 bright sources otherwise meeting the VIPS source criteria, MOJAVE observations are
available. In Fig. 2 we show the 5 GHz VIPS images or 15 GHz MOJAVE images for all 12
sources identiﬁed with EGRET blazars with high conﬁdence (the “likely” candidates). In
Figs. 3, and 4 we show the images for 19 sources identiﬁed as plausible counterparts. For
completeness we include 15 GHz MOJAVE images (Kellermann et al. 2004) for those 6 VIPS
sources that were not imaged at 5 GHz. One should remember that due to the large range
in redshifts, the individual rest-frame emitted frequencies can range over a factor up to 3.2.

– 4 –
3.
Morphological comparison
While a number of radio-bright EGRET sources distributed over the sky have been
imaged with VLBI (see references discussed in §1), only in the VIPS region has the full
EGRET candidate sample been uniformly imaged down to a ﬂux density limit of 85 mJy at
8 GHz. In this section we examine the VLBI-scale properties of the 31 EGRET candidate
blazars in this uniform sample, and for the 25 sources imaged as part of VIPS, we compare
them to the properties of the VIPS survey of 1127 sources.
3.1.
Source Classes
The classiﬁcation of the EGRET candidates in VIPS is 8 PS (point sources), 3 SJET
(short jets), and 14 LJET (long jets) according to the automatic classiﬁcation scheme of
Helmboldt et al. (2007a; see Table 2). There are no CSO (Compact Symmetric Object)
candidates or CPLX (complex) sources.
Applying the same classiﬁcation rules to the 6
MOJAVE sources adds 5 LJET and 1 SJET for totals of 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19
(61%) LJET. This can be compared to the population in VIPS as a whole which is 25% PS,
22% SJET, 43% LJET, 9% CSO and 2% CPLX. If EGRET candidates were drawn from the
VIPS population at random then we would expect 8 ± 3 PS, 7 ± 3 SJET, 13 ± 4 LJET,
and 3 ± 2 CSO and COMPLEX. While the number of PS and SJET sources are roughly as
expected we ﬁnd a marginally signiﬁcant lack of CSOs, and a marginally signiﬁcant excess
of sources with long jets (LJET) on the parsec-scale.
3.2.
Polarization
Polarization is detected from all 6 of the MOJAVE sources and from 9 of the 25 VIPS
sources for a total of 48 ± 12%. This is higher than the average of 36 ± 4% in VIPS overall
(Helmboldt et al. 2007a), and the 41 ± 4% average for LJETs, though the numbers of sources
involved are too small to make a deﬁnitive statment. Similarly a detailed examination of
the polarization properties is handicapped by small number statistics and the fact that
we have a mix of 5 GHz measurements for VIPS sources and 15 GHz measurements for
MOJAVE sources. Lister & Homan (2005) found that that the jets (but not the cores) of
EGRET blazars tended to have nearly twice the level of fractional polarization compared to
MOJAVE sources not detected by EGRET, and are also more luminous. They attribute the
diﬀerence to a higher mean Doppler factor for the EGRET blazars.

– 5 –
3.3.
Core Fraction
In Fig. 5 we plot the distribution of core-to-jet ratio (deﬁned as the ratio of ﬂux density
at 5 GHz in the VLBI core compared to the jet emission from the source at 5 GHz) for the
EGRET candidates against the distribution for the VIPS survey as a whole. No k-corrections
have been applied, even though the diﬀerence in spectral index between the core and the
extended emission will result in a change in the ratio with source redshift. Given the similar
range in redshifts, and the core dominated nature of the sources, the corrections should
be modest and similar for both EGRET-detected blazars and VIPS sources as a whole.
From the histograms, the EGRET sources appear to be biased toward more core-dominated
systems. The K-S test probability that the two distributions were drawn from the same
parent distribution is 4%. The core ﬂux density for the EGRET blazars can be found in
Table 3.
3.4.
Brightness Temperature
We have obtained the brightness temperatures from automatic modelﬁts to source com-
ponents as described in Helmboldt et al. (2007a). For sources with two or fewer components
we have further reﬁned the our modelﬁtting procedure by ﬁtting to the visibility data di-
rectly. Only image plane modelﬁtting was carried out in Helmboldt et al. (2007a) due to the
tendency for the automatic visibility modelﬁtting to go awry for complicated sources. The
minimum observable size for each source was calculated using equation (2) from Kovalev et
al. (2005), where we computed the SNR of each core using the core ﬂux density, the rms
measured from the 5 GHz image, and a beam FWHM of 3 mas, the largest dimension of our
restoring beam. For those sources where the estimated core size is less than this minimum
size (∼10% of all VIPS sources), we used the minimum size to compute TB. In Table 3
we provide the core sizes, core TB, brightest jet component TB, δPA, and jet opening half
angle for the VIPS blazars. For sources where the estimated core FWHM is less than the
minimum, the core diameter is preceded by a ’<’ and the core temperature is preceded by a
’>’. In all cases we compute the observed brightness temperatures, without any correction
to the source rest frame.
There is some indication that the brightness temperature for the cores of the EGRET
candidates may be higher than average (see distributions in Fig. 6). The K-S test probability
for these two distributions coming from the same parent population is 4%.
For the jet
components (formally, the brightest jet component) the two distributions look fairly similar,
except that the spread in the EGRET distribution is smaller (see lower panel of Fig. 6); the
K-S test for this pair of distributions is 11%.

– 6 –
3.5.
Jet Opening Angle
We have measured a mean opening half-angle by the following procedure: We measure
the separation of each jet component from the core along the jet axis (taken to be a linear
ﬁt to the component positions) and the distance of each component from the jet axis, i.e., x’
and y’ positions in a rotated coordinate system with the jet axis along the x’-axis. For each
component, we measure its extent from its center along a line perpendicular to the jet axis
using the parameters of its elliptical ﬁt, and then deconvolve this using the extent of the
Gaussian restoring beam along the same line. The opening half-angle measured from each
component is then taken to be
ψ = arctan[(|y′| + dr)/|x′|]
where dr is the deconvolved Gaussian size perpendicular to the jet axis. After measuring
this for each jet component, we average them to get one value. This is only done for sources
with more than 2 total components, (i.e., at least 2 jet components). This means that as
in the case of jet bending (see §3.6), we only have quantitative estimates for four of the
EGRET/VIPS sources (see. Fig. 7). Though this is based on very small statistics there is a
hint that EGRET/VIPS jets have unusually large opening angles. We ﬁnd 3 sources have jet
opening half-angles exceeding the VIPS median (18.9◦). Monte-Carlo simulations of opening
angles using the VIPS sample suggests that 3 out of 4 of the randomly sampled values are
greater than the median about 30% of the time. So, there’s less than a 1 in 3 chance that
the EGRET blazars have the same distribution for the opening angle as the whole VIPS
sample. Looking at the EGRET/MOJAVE and EGRET/VIPS sources by eye in Figures 2-4
strengthens this impression. We see in Figures 2-4 six sources (J08098+5218, J09576+5522,
J12215+2813, 1611+343, J16352+3808, J17406+5211) that have opening angles larger than
20 degrees. This can be compared to the VIPS images for the survey as a whole which are
online1. In a few of the blazars the emission is rather diﬀuse which is why they do not show
up in the automatic opening angle calculation.
3.6.
Jet Bending and Length
We can also compare the amount of bending in the jet on the parsec scale for the EGRET
candidates compared to VIPS as a whole. The amount of bending was calculated by ﬁtting
a parabola to the centroids of Gaussian model components (Helmboldt et al. 2007b). Again
we are limited to only 4 sources (Fig. 7), and the results are inconclusive. In fact the source
1See http://www.phys.unm.edu/∼gbtaylor/VIPS/

– 7 –
with the largest reported bend, J09576+5522, could be much less bent depending on if the
morphology is attributed to a twisting jet, or to a jet with a broad opening angle. Looking
at the EGRET/MOJAVE and EGRET/VIPS sources by eye only increases the number
of highly bent jets by one. We see in Figures 2-4 4 sources (J12215+2813, J17226+5856,
J17246+6055, J17406+5211) that appear to bend through more than 20 degrees on the
parsec scale.
Given the slight preponderance of sources with long jets, we compared the distribution
of jet length in EGRET blazars with VIPS as a whole. There does not appear to be an
appreciable diﬀerence between the two populations. The K-S probability that the two are
drawn from the same distribution is 34%.
4.
Notes on Individual Sources
J11044+3812 = Mrk 421 A well known BL Lac and also one of the ﬁrst sources to be
detected in TeV emission (Punch et al. 1992). Mrk 421 was included in both the CJF
(Taylor et al. 1994) and 2cm surveys (Kellermann et al. 2004) and has also been recently
imaged by Giroletti et al. (2006).
J16036+1554 This source is completely unresolved by the VLBA observations at 5 GHz
(Helmboldt et al. 2007a), and can be well ﬁt with a single component (the core) with size
of < 0.12 mas. This results in a brightness temperature of > 1 × 1012 K. Such completely
unresolved sources without any jet components are quite rare - there are essentially no
sources this compact in MOJAVE (Kovalev et al. 2005) or CJF (Taylor et al. 1994).
J17246+6055 The faint (r band magnitude 21.2) host galaxy does not yet have a known
redshift or spectroscopic classiﬁcation. The parsec-scale radio structure (see Fig. 4) is quite
unusual with a core-jet and a fairly compact component to the southeast. It is possible
that this source could be a compact supermassive binary black hole, and further VLBI
observations are in progress to test this hypothesis. Another possible explanation is a jet
with a sharp bend and wide opening angle, such as Mrk 501 (Giroletti et al. 2004) or Mrk 421
(Giroletti et al. 2006; and see Fig. 2).
5.
Discussion
From an analysis of the properties of the EGRET candidates in §4, we ﬁnd that can-
didates tend to have high core fractions and high brightness temperatures.
These facts
support models wherein the gamma-rays are produced in a jet oriented at a small angle to

– 8 –
the line-of-sight (e.g., Dermer et al. 1992). The large opening angles seen in 6 out of the
31 sources could also indicate a sight-line close to or within the beaming cone of the radio
emission. A selection eﬀect of this sort would happen naturally if the gamma rays are more
tightly beamed or collimated than the radio. In other words, gamma-ray selected sources
have higher Doppler factors than the population of compact sources as a whole. This can
also explain the observations of higher core fractions, higher brightness temperatures, and
higher polarization in gamma-ray blazars compared to the population of AGN as a whole,
as well as the reports of faster motions. An unbiased comparison of jet components be-
tween the EGRET blazars and the VIPS sample at large supports this, though only 4 of
the EGRET/VIPS sources have enough jet components to permit the unbiased (automatic)
analysis so the statistics are poor.
Somewhat more surprising is the evidence in support of long jets, though this is of
marginal signiﬁcance. Continuing the line of discussion above that EGRET blazars have
higher Doppler factors due to small angles to the line-of-sight, the a priori prediction, as-
suming jets of a ﬁxed length and modest velocity, would be for shorter jets due to projection.
Obtaining longer jets might be possible if the jets of blazars have intrinsically greater sur-
face brightness, or are highly Doppler boosted compared to sources in radio selected samples.
Longer jets in blazars could also be obtained if there is a bias in the selection. The redshift
distribution for the VIPS sample is still incomplete, so it is diﬃcult to investigate possible
selection bias at this time. Given the weakness of the evidence, especially when comparing
the distributions of jet lengths (§3.6), further speculation on this topic is not yet warranted.
6.
Conclusions
Sources selected on the basis of their γ-ray ﬂux as determined by EGRET appear to
have higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population at large. In the VIPS survey
this selection manifests itself in larger core fractions, higher core brightness temperatures,
increased polarization, and possibly broader jets.
GLAST, which will launch in late 2007 or early 2008, will detect several thousand
(Gehrels & Michelson 1999) of the tens of thousands of compact, radio-loud, ﬂat-spectrum
AGN currently known. Conﬁrming the tighter beaming angle for the γ-rays should be easily
achieved with the improved statistics. Greater advances in understanding are anticipated,
though detailed studies including multi-wavelength ﬂux monitoring, and multi-frequency,
multi-epoch VLBI polarimetry will be possible only for a small subset of objects. As we
have shown, the gamma-ray ﬂux density is not simply related to the radio ﬂux-density, so
selecting the brightest radio sources for study may not maximize the chances of coincidence

– 9 –
with strong gamma-ray emission. Therefore it may be advantageous to consider selecting
sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening
angles, as well as strong radio ﬂux density. GLAST could also see new populations of AGN
including Seyfert galaxies, and low power radio galaxies. For this reason it is important to
provide contemporaneous ground-based monitoring of a range of source classes, powers, and
morphologies. Comparisons between the parsec-scale radio structures as revealed by VLBI
observations and the time variable γ-ray ﬂux, could discriminate between various models
describing the production of the γ-ray emission, or reveal that more than one mechanism is
at work.
We thank an anonymous referee for constructive suggestions. The National Radio Astronomy
Observatory is a facility of the National Science Foundation operated under cooperative
agreement by Associated Universities, Inc.
papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument, using data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). The study aims to characterize the parsec-scale jet properties of EGRET blazars and compare them to the broader population of radio-selected sources. The VIPS survey, with a lower flux limit than previous surveys, allows for a more detailed analysis of these objects. The primary findings indicate that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and possibly larger jet opening angles. A weak correlation was also found with jet length and polarization. These characteristics are consistent with systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars. The study analyzed 31 EGRET candidate blazars within the VIPS region, comparing their properties to the larger VIPS sample of 1127 sources. The results suggest that the gamma-ray emission is associated with a jet oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight, leading to higher Doppler factors. Key limitations include the small number statistics and the mix of 5 GHz and 15 GHz measurements. The findings are relevant for understanding the mechanisms behind gamma-ray emission in blazars and will inform future studies using the Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope (GLAST).

Research Context
Previous studies of EGRET blazars have yielded conflicting results regarding their radio properties. Some studies suggested a correlation between gamma-ray and radio emission, while others found no direct correlation. Prior work, such as L¨ahteenm¨aki & Valtaoja (2003) and Lister & Homan (2005), examined the relationship between radio and gamma-ray flares and the polarization properties of EGRET blazars. However, these studies often relied on samples with higher flux limits, potentially missing key characteristics. This work addresses the limitations of previous studies by utilizing the VIPS survey, which has a lower flux limit, allowing for a more sensitive investigation of the radio properties of EGRET blazars. The study aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between radio emission and gamma-ray activity in blazars, particularly in the context of the upcoming GLAST mission.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: What are the parsec-scale radio properties of EGRET-detected blazars, and how do they differ from the general population of radio-selected sources? The primary hypothesis is that EGRET blazars will exhibit distinct radio properties, specifically higher brightness temperatures, greater core fractions, and potentially larger jet opening angles, compared to the broader VIPS sample. These differences are predicted to arise from systematically larger Doppler factors in gamma-ray loud blazars. The alternative hypothesis is that there are no significant differences in radio properties between EGRET blazars and the general radio-selected population. The study aims to test these hypotheses by comparing the distributions of various radio properties (core fraction, brightness temperature, jet opening angle, jet length, and polarization) between the EGRET blazar candidates and the larger VIPS sample. The outcomes are that if the EGRET blazars have higher core fractions and brightness temperatures, this would support the hypothesis that gamma-rays are produced in a jet oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight. If the jet opening angles are larger, this would further support the hypothesis. If no differences are found, the hypothesis is refuted. This work differs from prior studies by utilizing a larger, more uniform sample with a lower flux limit, enabling a more detailed and sensitive analysis of the radio properties of EGRET blazars.

Methodological Details
The study utilizes data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS), which observed 1127 flat-spectrum sources stronger than 85 mJy in the Northern Cap region of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). The VIPS survey was conducted between January and August 2006 and included 5 GHz, full polarization images of 958 sources, and 147 total intensity images for sources previously observed. The sample of EGRET blazar candidates was defined by comparing the latest EGRET catalog (Hartman et al. 1999) to the Combined Radio All-sky Targeted Eight GHz Survey (CRATES; Healey et al. 2007a). This intersection yielded a sample of 173 candidate EGRET sources at |b| > 10°. The study focused on the EGRET candidates within the ∼5700 square degree region of the sky covered by VIPS. The EGRET candidates were classified as “likely” or “plausible” based on a Figure of Merit (FoM) that considered 8.4 GHz flux density, radio spectral index, X-ray flux density, and positional coincidence. “Likely” candidates had FoM > 1, and “plausible” candidates had 1.0 > FoM > 0.25. The VLBI-scale properties of 31 EGRET candidate blazars were examined, and for the 25 sources imaged as part of VIPS, their properties were compared to the properties of the VIPS survey of 1127 sources. Source classification was performed using the automatic classification scheme of Helmboldt et al. (2007a). Polarization was measured from the VIPS and MOJAVE sources. Core fraction was defined as the ratio of flux density at 5 GHz in the VLBI core compared to the jet emission from the source at 5 GHz. Brightness temperatures were obtained from automatic model fits to source components, with further refinement for sources with two or fewer components. Jet opening angles were measured by determining the separation of each jet component from the core along the jet axis and the distance of each component from the jet axis. Jet bending was calculated by fitting a parabola to the centroids of Gaussian model components. The study did not specify a preregistration or multiple-comparison correction.

Procedures Architectures
The study leverages the VIPS survey, which employed the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) for high-resolution radio imaging. The VLBA consists of ten radio telescopes spread across the United States and its territories, providing milliarcsecond resolution. The VIPS survey observed flat-spectrum radio sources at 5 GHz. The EGRET blazar candidates were identified by cross-matching the EGRET catalog with the CRATES catalog. The CRATES catalog provides 8.4 GHz radio flux densities. The VIPS images were processed to determine various radio properties. Automatic model fitting was used to obtain brightness temperatures. The core-to-jet ratio was calculated using the flux densities of the core and jet components. Jet opening angles were determined by measuring the separation of jet components from the core and the distance of each component from the jet axis. Jet bending was quantified by fitting a parabola to the centroids of Gaussian model components. The study also utilized MOJAVE data at 15 GHz for some sources. The software used for image processing and analysis is not explicitly mentioned, but it can be inferred that standard VLBI data reduction and analysis techniques were employed. The key novelty lies in the use of the VIPS survey, which provides a large, uniform sample with a lower flux limit, enabling a more detailed analysis of EGRET blazars compared to previous studies. The study's architecture is based on comparing the radio properties of EGRET blazar candidates to those of the larger VIPS sample.

Key Results
The study found that EGRET-detected blazars tend to have higher brightness temperatures and greater core fractions. The K-S test probability that the core brightness temperature distributions for EGRET blazars and the VIPS survey as a whole were drawn from the same parent distribution was 4%. The K-S test probability for the core fraction distributions was also 4%. The EGRET sources appear to be biased toward more core-dominated systems. Polarization was detected from 48 ± 12% of the EGRET candidates, which is higher than the average of 36 ± 4% in VIPS overall. There is a hint that EGRET/VIPS jets have unusually large opening angles. The study found that 3 out of 4 of the randomly sampled values are greater than the median about 30% of the time. Six sources (J08098+5218, J09576+5522, J12215+2813, 1611+343, J16352+3808, J17406+5211) were identified as having opening angles larger than 20 degrees. The distribution of jet lengths in EGRET blazars did not appear to be appreciably different from that of the VIPS sample, with a K-S probability of 34%. The source J16036+1554 was found to be completely unresolved by the VLBA observations at 5 GHz, with a brightness temperature of > 1 × 1012 K. The study also found that the EGRET candidates in VIPS are classified as 8 PS, 3 SJET, and 14 LJET. Applying the same classification rules to the 6 MOJAVE sources adds 5 LJET and 1 SJET for totals of 8 (25%) PS, 4 (13%) SJET, and 19 (61%) LJET.

Interpretation Implications
The findings support models where gamma-rays are produced in a jet oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight. The higher core fractions and brightness temperatures observed in EGRET blazars are consistent with this scenario, implying that these sources have higher Doppler factors. The potentially larger jet opening angles also suggest that the sight-line is close to or within the beaming cone of the radio emission. The study suggests that the gamma-ray flux density is not simply related to the radio flux density, and that selecting sources with large core fractions, high central brightness temperatures, and large opening angles may be advantageous for identifying strong gamma-ray emission. The results imply that EGRET blazars have higher Doppler factors than the radio-selected population at large, which manifests in the observed radio properties. The study's findings provide insights into the mechanisms behind gamma-ray emission in blazars and support the idea that the gamma-ray emission is more tightly beamed than the radio emission.

Contradictions Limitations
The study is limited by small number statistics, particularly when analyzing polarization and jet bending. The mix of 5 GHz measurements for VIPS sources and 15 GHz measurements for MOJAVE sources introduces a potential source of systematic error. The lack of a redshift distribution for the VIPS sample makes it difficult to investigate possible selection bias. The study acknowledges that the gamma-ray flux density is not simply related to the radio flux density, which suggests that selecting the brightest radio sources may not maximize the chances of coincidence with strong gamma-ray emission. The study does not address the question of whether the radio flaring precedes or follows the gamma-ray flare. The study also does not distinguish between sources with multiple identifications and those with a single identification. The study does not mention the random seed used for any simulations. The study does not provide information about the training/test splits.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 5 plots the distribution of core-to-jet ratio for the EGRET candidates against the distribution for the VIPS survey as a whole. The x-axis represents the core-to-jet ratio, and the y-axis represents the number of sources. The figure illustrates that the EGRET sources appear to be biased toward more core-dominated systems. Figure 6 shows the distributions of brightness temperatures for the core and jet components of the EGRET candidates and the VIPS survey. The x-axis represents the brightness temperature, and the y-axis represents the number of sources. The figure suggests that the brightness temperatures for the cores of the EGRET candidates may be higher than average. Table 1 summarizes the EGRET candidate sources and their properties.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the characterization of the parsec-scale radio properties of EGRET blazars using the VIPS survey, which has a lower flux limit than previous surveys, allowing for a more sensitive analysis. (2) The strongest evidence is that EGRET blazars tend to have higher core fractions and brightness temperatures, with a K-S test probability of 4% for both, supporting the hypothesis that gamma-ray emission is associated with a jet oriented at a small angle to the line-of-sight. (3) The primary limitation is the small number statistics, particularly when analyzing polarization and jet bending, which limits the strength of the conclusions. Future work should focus on increasing the sample size and obtaining more detailed multi-wavelength observations to further investigate the relationship between radio emission and gamma-ray activity.

Can giant planets form by gravitational fragmentation of discs?
Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the inner disc region
D. Stamatellos & A. P. Whitworth
School of Physics and Astronomy, CardiﬀUniversity, 5 The Parade, CardiﬀCF24 3AA, Wales, UK
e-mail: D.Stamatellos@astro.cf.ac.uk
e-mail: A.Whitworth@astro.cf.ac.uk
Received September, 2007; accepted
ABSTRACT
Context. Disc fragmentation has been proposed as a possible mechanism for the formation of giant planets at close distances to solar-type stars.
However, it is debatable whether this mechanism can function in the inner region of real discs.
Aims. To investigate the thermodynamics of discs and the probability of fragmentation.
Methods. We use a newly developed method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, which accounts for radiative transfer eﬀects in
SPH simulations of protostellar discs. The diﬀerent chemical and internal states of hydrogen and the properties of dust at diﬀerent densities and
temperatures (ice coated dust grains at low temperatures, ice melting, dust sublimation) are all taken into account by the new method.
Results. We present radiative hydrodynamic simulations of discs where the eﬀects of the equation of state and energy equation are taken into
account. We focus on the inner parts of discs, R < 40 AU and examine 2 cases (i) a disc heated by an ambient radiation ﬁeld of 10 K, and
(ii) a disc with additional heating from the central star. In both cases the disc does not fragment; in the former case because it cannot cool fast
enough, and in the latter case because it is not gravitationally unstable. Our results corroborate the results of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai e al.
(2007), who use a diﬀerent treatment for the radiative transfer.
Conclusions. Disc fragmentation is unlikely to be able to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii <∼50 AU.
Key words. Accretion, accretion discs – Hydrodynamics – Instabilities – Radiative Transfer – Planetary systems: formation – Planetary
systems: protoplanetary discs
1. Introduction
A large number of exoplanets (∼250) has been discovered
around nearby stars in the last 12 years, mainly with the ra-
dial velocity method. Most of these exoplanets have properties
that are diﬀerent from those of the Solar System. In particular,
giant planets are found very close to the central star on orbits
of apparently random eccentricity.
Two main theories have been proposed for the formation
of giant planets, (i) core accretion, and (ii) gravitational frag-
mentation. In the core accretion scenario giant planets form by
coagulation of planetesimals (e.g. Safronov 1969; Goldreich &
Ward 1973; Pollack et al. 1996). Once a solid body of around
10 ML is reached, it quickly accretes a large gaseous envelope.
One of the main problems of this theory is that the timescale for
planet formation is long. The theory predicts that planets can
form within a few million years, but observations suggest that
circumstellar discs may not be that long lived (Haisch, Lada
& Lada 2001; Cieza et al. 2007). In the gravitational fragmen-
tation scenario, giant planets form by gravitational instability
in massive discs (e.g. Kuiper 1951; Cameron 1978; cf. review
by Durisen et. al 2007). The main advantage of this method is
that planets form on a dynamical timescale, i.e. within a few
hundred years.
There are two conditions that must be fulﬁlled for discs
to fragment gravitationally. (i) The disc must be gravitation-
ally unstable, i.e. massive enough so that gravity can overcome
thermal pressure and centrifugal support (Toomre 1964):

suggest that convection can provide suﬃciently fast cooling,
whereas Johnson & Gammie (2003), Boley et al. (2006) and

of view is supported by analytic studies which suggest that
convection cannot provide the required cooling (Raﬁkov 2007;
Whitworth et al. 2007), and that discs cannot cool fast enough,
at least close (R <∼50 AU) to the central star (Raﬁkov 2005;
Matzner & Levin 2005; Whitworth & Stamatellos 2006).
Hydrodynamic simulations have produced contradictory
results about whether disc fragmentation can produce giant
planets close to the central star, mainly due the diﬀerent treat-
ments of radiative transfer in discs. We have recently developed
an eﬃcient scheme to capture the thermal and radiative eﬀects
when protostellar gas fragments (see Section 2 and Stamatellos
et al. 2007). Thus, we are able for the ﬁrst time to perform
radiative hydrodynamic simulations of discs where the eﬀects
of the equation of state are included. Moreover the radiative
scheme allows to include irradiation of the disc by the central
star.
The structure of the paper is as follows. In Section 2 we
describe the method that is used for the radiative hydrodynamic
simulations. In Section 3 we describe the disc initial setup and
in Section 4 the radiative hydrodynamic simulations. Finally, in
Section 5 we discuss the results of these simulations and their
implications for the possibility of forming giant planets close
to a star by gravitational fragmentation.
2. Numerical method
For the simulations we use the SPH code dragon (Goodwin
et al. 2004), which invokes an octal tree (to compute grav-
ity and ﬁnd neighbours), adaptive smoothing lengths, multiple
particle timesteps, artiﬁcial viscosity (α = 0.1, β = 0.2) with
the Balsara switch, and a second-order Runge-Kutta integration
scheme.
The energy equation is treated with the method of
Stamatellos et al. (2007). The method takes into account com-
pressional heating, viscous heating, radiation heating from the
background, radiation cooling and, implicitly, radiation heating
from the particle’s neighbourhood.It performs well, both in the
optically thin and optically thick regime, and it is eﬃcient and
relatively easy to implement in particle- and grid-based codes.
The gas is assumed to be a mixture of hydrogen and he-
lium. We use an equation of state (Black & Bodenheimer 1975;
Masunaga et al. 1998; Boley et al. 2007) that accounts (i) for
the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular
hydrogen, and (ii) for the diﬀerent chemical states of hydro-
gen and helium depending on the temperature and density, i.e.
the eﬀects of H2 dissociation, H0 ionisation, and the ﬁrst and
second ionisation of He are included. Hence, the eﬀects of vari-
ations in the equation of state are taken into account. (We note
however that (i) the temperatures in the simulations presented
here are not high enough for the molecular hydrogen to dis-
sociate, and (ii) contributions from metals are ignored; hence
the gas composition remains the same, i.e. the mean molecular
weight µ is constant).
For the dust and gas opacity we use the parameterization
by Bell & Lin (1994), κ(ρ, T) = κ0 ρa T b , where κ0, a, b
are constants that depend on the species and the physical pro-
cesses contributing to the opacity at each ρ and T. The opacity
changes due to e.g. ice mantle melting, the sublimation of dust,
molecular and H−contributions, are all taken into account.
The code has been extensively tested (see Stamatellos et
al. 2007). In particular it reproduces the detailed 3D results of
Masunaga & Inutsuka (2000) and the analytic test of Spiegel
(1957). We report a further test here in Section 4.1.2.
3. Disc initial conditions
We simulate a 0.07 M⊙disc around a 0.5 M⊙star. This is a
relatively massive disc but such discs have been observed e.g

sity is Σ(R) ∼R−1/2 and its initial temperature is T(R) ∼R−1.
These are typical density and temperature proﬁles of discs and
have been chosen so as to match the initial conditions of the
simulations of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007).

5. Discussion
We have performed radiative hydrodynamic simulations of the
inner region of circumstellar discs with initial parameters simi-
lar to the parameters of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007),
i.e. a 0.07 M⊙disc around a 0.5 M⊙star. The disc initially
extends from 2 to 40 AU. The disc initial surface density is
Σ(R) ∼R−1/2 and the disc initial temperature is T(R) ∼R−1. We
use a newly developed method to treat the energy equation in
SPH simulations of discs and an equation of state that includes

the eﬀects of the rotational degrees of freedom of molecular
hydrogen and realistic dust opacities.
Initially we simulated the evolution of the disc under an
external radiation ﬁeld of temperature 10 K. Our results are
comparable with the results of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al.
(2007); the disc is gravitationally unstable at R ∼20 −30 AU,
but it does not fragment because it cannot cool fast enough.
Spiral arms form in the disc but they are weak and do not
show any tendency towards fragmentation. The adiabatic in-
dex is γ = 5/3 outside ∼10 AU where the temperature is less
than ∼80 K; however closer to the central star where the tem-
perature is higher, γ = 7/5, due to the excitation of the rota-
tional degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen. It has been
suggested that when γ is decreases from 5/3 to 7/5 , the maxi-
mum cooling time for the disc to fragment also increases from
0.5 to 2 tORB (e.g. Johnson & Gammie 2003; Rice et al. 2005).
Our simulations indicate that in discs the cooling time is always
>∼2tORB within ∼30 AU, hence such discs are not expected to
fragment and they do not fragment. The results of the simula-
tions reported here are similar to the results of the simulations
of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007) despite using dif-
ferent treatments for the radiative transfer and for the hydrody-
namics.
We also simulated the evolution of a disc in an external
radiation ﬁeld whose temperature drops as R−1, to mimic the
irradiation from the central star and envelope. In this case the
disc can cool fast enough to fragment (because of its higher
temperature) but it does not fragment because it is not gravi-

tationally unstable. The heating from the central star stabilizes
the disc; no spiral arms form in this case. Hence, discs are even
less prone to fragment in their inner regions when the eﬀect
of stellar irradiation is taken into account. This result agrees
with previous simulation of discs heated by envelope radia-
tion (Boss 2001, 2002; Cai et al. 2007). It is also in accordance
with previous analytical calculations (Matzner & Levin 2005;
Raﬁkov 2005; Whitworth & Stamatellos 2006). Whitworth &
Stamatellos (2006) argue fragmentation is possible at larger
distances (>∼100 AU) from the central star where the cooling
times are suﬃciently short. However, their results suggest that
fragmentation at large radii produces mostly brown dwarfs and
occasionally low-mass hydrogen-burning stars or planetary-
mass objects (Whitworth & Stamatellos 2006; Whitworth et
al. 2007; Stamatellos, Hubber & Whitworth 2007). If plane-
tary mass objects form at such large radii they are unlikely to
migrate inwards to become hot Jupiters. More likely they are
ejected into the ﬁeld though 3-body interactions.
Hence, based on the simulations presented in this paper, we
conclude that gas giant planets probably cannot form close to
the central star by gravitational fragmentation of discs.

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper investigates the feasibility of giant planet formation via gravitational fragmentation in the inner regions of circumstellar discs. The authors employed radiative hydrodynamic simulations using the SPH code dragon, incorporating a novel method for treating the energy equation and equation of state, accounting for radiative transfer effects, including the different chemical and internal states of hydrogen and the properties of dust. Two scenarios were examined: a disc heated by a cool background radiation field (10 K) and a disc heated by radiation from its central star. The simulations, focusing on radii < 40 AU, showed that in neither case did the disc fragment. In the first case, the disc could not cool fast enough, and in the second, it was not gravitationally unstable. The primary finding is that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets around solar-type stars at radii < 40 AU. The study's novelty lies in its detailed treatment of the energy equation and equation of state within the SPH simulations, including radiative transfer and realistic dust opacities. This work is significant because it challenges the gravitational fragmentation theory as a mechanism for forming close-orbiting giant planets, a common observation. A key limitation is the restriction to the inner disc regions (R < 40 AU), leaving open the possibility of fragmentation at larger radii.

Research Context
The formation of exoplanets, particularly giant planets in close orbits, is a subject of ongoing debate. Two primary formation theories exist: core accretion and gravitational fragmentation. Core accretion faces challenges due to the long timescales required, while gravitational fragmentation offers a faster formation timescale. Prior studies have produced contradictory results on the viability of fragmentation, primarily due to differing treatments of radiative transfer in disc simulations. Some studies suggest convection provides sufficient cooling, while others argue for inefficient cooling, making fragmentation unlikely. This paper addresses the gap by employing a new method to treat the energy equation and equation of state, incorporating radiative transfer effects, to investigate the thermodynamics of discs and the probability of fragmentation, thus providing a more comprehensive understanding of the process.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether gravitational fragmentation can form giant planets in the inner regions (R < 40 AU) of circumstellar discs. The primary hypothesis is that disc fragmentation is unlikely to produce giant planets at these radii. This prediction is based on the expectation that discs either cannot cool fast enough to fragment or are not gravitationally unstable. Alternative outcomes include disc fragmentation leading to planet formation, which would be supported by the observation of density enhancements and the formation of gravitationally bound objects within the simulations. This study differs from previous work by using a novel method for treating the energy equation and equation of state in SPH simulations, including radiative transfer effects and realistic dust opacities. The study aims to provide a more accurate assessment of the thermal behavior of discs and its impact on the potential for fragmentation, refining the understanding of the conditions necessary for giant planet formation via this mechanism.

Methodological Details
The study employed radiative hydrodynamic simulations using the SPH code dragon. The simulations modeled a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, extending initially from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density profile was Σ(R) ∝ R−1/2, and the initial temperature profile was T(R) ∝ R−1. The SPH code utilized an octal tree for gravity calculations, adaptive smoothing lengths, multiple particle timesteps, artificial viscosity (α = 0.1, β = 0.2), and a second-order Runge-Kutta integration scheme. The energy equation was treated using the method of Stamatellos et al. (2007), accounting for compressional, viscous, and radiative heating and cooling. The equation of state considered the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen, as well as the different chemical states of hydrogen and helium. Dust and gas opacity were parameterized using the Bell & Lin (1994) method. Two simulations were performed: one with a constant background radiation field of 10 K and another with radiation from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). The simulations used 2x10^5 SPH particles. No preregistration was performed. The study did not mention any ethics or IRB review.

Procedures Architectures
The study utilized the SPH code dragon, incorporating a new method for treating the energy equation and equation of state. The method, detailed in Stamatellos et al. (2007), accounts for compressional, viscous, and radiative heating and cooling. The code uses an octal tree for gravity calculations and adaptive smoothing lengths. The equation of state incorporates the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom of molecular hydrogen, as well as the different chemical states of hydrogen and helium. The dust and gas opacity were parameterized using the Bell & Lin (1994) method. The simulations were initialized with a 0.07 M⊙ disc around a 0.5 M⊙ star, extending from 2 to 40 AU. The initial surface density was Σ(R) ∝ R−1/2, and the initial temperature was T(R) ∝ R−1. Two simulations were run: one with a constant background radiation field of 10 K and another with radiation from the central star (TBGR ∝ R−1). The simulations used 2x10^5 SPH particles. The key innovation is the detailed treatment of the energy equation and equation of state, which includes radiative transfer effects and realistic dust opacities, allowing for a more accurate modeling of the thermal behavior of the disc.

Key Results
The simulations showed that in the case of a disc heated by a low-temperature background radiation field (10 K), the disc did not fragment. Weak spiral arms formed, but the cooling time was generally > 2tORB (orbital period) within approximately 30 AU (Figure 5). The Toomre parameter, Q, was > 1 (Figure 4), indicating gravitational stability. In the simulation with stellar heating, the disc was overall hotter, and the disc did not fragment because it was not gravitationally unstable (Q > 1.5, Figure 14). The heating from the central star stabilized the disc, and no spiral arms formed (Figures 9-12). The results of the simulation with low background heating were compared with Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007). The calculated temperatures were approximately 15% higher than Boley et al. (2006) and less than 3% higher than Cai et al. (2007). The Toomre parameter was generally higher, and the cooling times were lower in comparison to Boley et al. (2006). The vertical temperature profile was compared to the analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990) and found to be similar (Figure 8).

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that gravitational fragmentation is unlikely to be a viable mechanism for forming giant planets close to solar-type stars (R < 40 AU). The simulations indicate that discs either cannot cool fast enough or are not gravitationally unstable in these inner regions. The results support the view that stellar irradiation stabilizes the disc, preventing fragmentation. The study reinforces the importance of cooling time and gravitational instability (Toomre parameter) in determining the likelihood of fragmentation. The results align with previous analytical calculations and simulations that suggest fragmentation might be possible at larger radii, potentially leading to the formation of brown dwarfs or low-mass stars rather than close-orbiting giant planets. The study implies that alternative planet formation mechanisms, such as core accretion, may be more relevant for forming giant planets in close orbits.

Contradictions Limitations
The primary limitation is the focus on the inner disc regions (R < 40 AU), which restricts the scope of the conclusions. The study does not address the possibility of fragmentation at larger radii, where cooling times might be shorter. The simulations do not account for the effects of magnetic fields or other potential mechanisms that could influence disc evolution and planet formation. There is a potential contradiction with the theory that fragmentation is possible at larger radii, which could produce brown dwarfs or low-mass stars. The study does not provide details on the specific values used for the artificial viscosity parameters. The initial conditions and the specific parameters of the SPH code, such as the number of particles, could influence the results. The study does not include any sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of the results to changes in the model parameters. The lack of information on random seeds and train/test splits, if applicable, limits the reproducibility.

Data Code Availability
The paper does not mention any data or code availability.

Robustness Ablation Notes
The study performed a comparison with the results of Boley et al. (2006) and Cai et al. (2007), showing similar results despite different treatments for radiative transfer and hydrodynamics. The simulation with a smaller number of SPH particles (5 x 10^4) produced essentially the same results as the simulation with 2x10^5 particles.

Ethical Considerations
The paper does not mention any ethical considerations.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 5, which shows the cooling time in units of the local orbital period, is critical in supporting the claim that the disc cannot cool fast enough to fragment in the low background heating case. Figure 14, showing the Toomre parameter and cooling time for the stellar heating case, supports the claim that the disc is not gravitationally unstable. Figure 8, which compares the vertical temperature profiles with the analytic calculations of Hubeny (1990), provides a validation of the simulation's results.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the use of a newly developed method for treating the energy equation and equation of state in SPH simulations, including radiative transfer effects and realistic dust opacities, to investigate the potential for gravitational fragmentation in protoplanetary discs.

(2) The strongest evidence is that in both simulations, the disc did not fragment. In the low background heating case, the cooling time was generally > 2tORB within approximately 30 AU (Figure 5), and in the stellar heating case, the Toomre parameter was > 1.5 (Figure 14).

(3) The primary limitation is the restriction to the inner disc regions (R < 40 AU), leaving open the possibility of fragmentation at larger radii. Future work could focus on extending the simulations to larger radii and incorporating additional physical processes, such as magnetic fields, to provide a more comprehensive understanding of planet formation.

Dira 
Equation
in
Curved
Spa etime
On the Anomalous Gyromagnetic Ratio
G. G. Nyambuya∗
North-West University -Potchefstroom Campus,
School of Physics - Unit for Space Research,
P. Bag X6001, Potchefstroom,
Republic of South Africa.
G. G. Nyambuya
(Dated: February 2, 2014)
Original Paper is Published in the Electronic Journal of Theoretical Physics on 31 March 2007, Vol 4, No 14, 105-116.
Abstra t.
I propose a curved spacetime version of the Dirac equation.
The equation
has been developed mainly to try and account in a natural way for the observed anomalous
gyromagnetic ratio of Fermions. The derived equation suggests that particles including the
Electron which is thought to be a point particle do have a ﬁnite spatial size which is the
reason for the observed anomalous gyromagnetic ratio. A serendipitous result of the theory,
is that it exhibits an asymmetry in its positive and negative energy solutions, the suggestion
of which is clear that a solution to the problem as to why we do not observe negative energy
and mass particles in the part of our measurable and accessible Universe is possible.
Keywords:
Curved Space, Dirac Equation, Gyromagnetic Ratio, Fundamental Parti-
cle.
Key Note: The original paper contains a slit error and this is corrected here. In this paper [orignal], I state
that the present theory results in solutions that are exclussively positive or negative which is not the case but is
otherwise.
I.
INTRODUCTION
The Dirac equation is a relativistic quantum mechanical wave
equation invented by Paul Dirac in 1928 (Dirac 1928a, 1928b)
originally designed to overcome the criticism of the Klein-
Gordon Equation. The Klein-Gordon equation gave negative
probabilities and this is considered to be physically meaning-
less. Despite this fact, this equation accounts well for Bosons,
that is spin zero particles. This criticism leveled against the
Klein-Gordon equation, motivated Dirac to successfully seek
an equation devoid of negative probabilities.
The Dirac equation is consistent with Quantum Mechanics
(QM) and fully consistent with the Special Theory of Rela-
tivity (STR). The equation accounts in a natural way for the
nature of particle spin as a relativistic phenomenon. The equa-
tion successfully predicted the existence of anti-particles. In
its bare form, the equation provides an impressive and accu-
rate description of the Electron hence it being referred in most
of the literature as the “Dirac Equation for the Electron”. It
also accounts well for quarks and other spin half particles al-
∗Electronic address: gadzirai@gmail.com, fskggn@puk.ac.za
though in some of the cases, there is need for slight modiﬁca-
tions - for example, you need the Procca equation to describe
the neutron.
The ﬁrst taste of glory of the Dirac equation was it being able
to account for the gyromagnetic ratio of the electron, that is
g = 2, which can not be accounted for using non-relativistic
QM. For several years after it’s discovery, most physicists be-
lieved that it also described the Proton and the Neutron, which
are both spin-1/2 particles. In simple terms, it was thought or
presumed that the Dirac equation was a universal equation for
spin-1/2 particles.
However, beginning with the experiments of Stern and Frisch
in 1933, the magnetic moments of these particles were found
to disagree signiﬁcantly with the predictions of the Dirac
equation. The Proton was found to have a gyromagnetic ratio
gp = 5.58 which is 2.79 times larger than that predicted by
the Dirac equation. The Neutron, which is electrically neu-
tral spin-1/2 particle was found to have a gyromagnetic ratio
gn = −3.83.
These “anomalous magnetic moments” of the Neutron and
Proton which are clearly not conformatory to the Dirac theory
have been taken to be experimental indication that these par-
tices are not fundamental particles. In the case of the Neutron,
yes it is clearly not a fundamental particle since it does decay

Published in the Electronic Journal of Theoretical Physics on 31 March 2007, Vol 4, No 14, 105-116.
into a Proton, Electron and Neutrino, that is, n −→p + e−+ ν.
If the Dirac equation is a universal equation for fundamen-
tal fermion particles, then any fundamental fermion particle
must conform to this equation. Simple, any spin-1/2 particle
that can not be described by it, must therefore not be a funda-
mental particle of nature. By deﬁnition a fundamental particle
is a particle known to have no sub-structure, that is, it can not
be broken down into smaller particles thus will not decay into
anything else.
From the Standard Model, we know that the Proton and Neu-
tron are composed of quarks thus are not fundamental parti-
cles. The question is, is this the reason why these particle’s
gyromagnetic ratio is diﬀerent from that predicted by the bare
Dirac equation? Prevailing wisdom suggests that anomalous
gyromagnetic ratio arise because the particles under question
are not fundamental particles. From the theory laid down here,
the answer to this is a clear no. The reason for the deviation
of the gyromagnetic ratio from that expected from the Dirac
theory is (according to this theory) because particles do have
a ﬁnite size and that spacetime is curved. In this theory the
anomalous gyromagnetic ratio arises from the interaction of
spin with the Lorentz force in a curved spacetime for a parti-
cle of ﬁnite spatial size and mass. The derived relation for the
anomalous magnetic moment and the particle size is similar to
that deduced by Brodsky & Drell (1980) and experimentally
veriﬁed by Dehmelt (1989). Brodsky & Drell (1980) proposed
that fermions do have a sub-structure and this gives rise to the
anomalous gyromagnetic ratio which varies as the spatial size
and inverse to the mass.

and energy E, Albert Einstein, from his 1905 special relativity
paper, derived the basic equation

If QED already explains the gyromagnetic ratio, why then
seek another theory that tries to explain this same phenom-

also the Muon whose gyromagnetic ratio are very close to the
Dirac values of 2 are point particles. It is this very fact that this
paper seeks to put back on the drawing board for a deeper in-
trospection. Is and or are the Electron and the Muon point par-

go into the details but maybe in-passing mention that from a
higher level of beauty, I expect that the Dirac equation should
account naturally for all fermions without much drastic mod-
iﬁcations - if any at all, in much the same way as it was once
conceived as a universal equation for spin-1/2 particles. The
other is that the methods such as renormalization that are used
in QED to arriving at these all-time accurate values feel or ap-
pear rather un-natural. Yes, they yield to the right numbers
when compared with reality but is such a program really part
and parcel of the natural laws? is a very diﬃcult question to

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
Amongst others, the most important consequence of the the-
ory just laid down of the curved space-time Dirac equation it
exhibits and asymmetry in the energy solution and the sugges-
tion from it, is that the problem of negative energy and mass
that lead Dirac to propose his Hole Theory or Dirac Sea, in an
eﬀort to explain why is it that we do not observe negative en-
ergy and mass in the Universe is no longer, may be solved but
this will be done in a third paper. From the said, then, if the
present theory is a true reﬂection and/or description of natural
reality or anything to go by, then it explains the long standing
problem since Dirac put forward his Hole Theory or the Dirac
Sea Hypothesis in 1930 in an eﬀort to explain the anomalous
negative-energy spectrum as predicted by his theory, of why
the Universe as we know it, appears to be ﬁlled with positive
energy and mass. Dirac’s theory predicted the existence of
anti-particles which have been “observed” but not in the sense
in which they are predicted by the theory in that they must
have a negative mass/energy.
Further, the Dirac theory put it bold that these anti-particles
should have a negative mass and energy. To this present day, it
has not been conﬁrmed whether anti-particles have a negative
mass and energy but the suspicion amongst the majority of
physicists is that anti-particles do have a positive mass and
energy – hence the quotations “observed”. As suggested, this
the asymmetry in energy solution of equation 12 can be used
to solve this problem and this will be done in the Paper II.
There in Paper II, it will be shown that anti-particles as we
know them have a positive mass.
Another of the predictions of the theory is the existence of four
particle solutions each with the same electric charge and gy-
romagnetic ratio. The four solutions are such that the ﬁrst pair
have an energy E+ the spins of which are opposite and the sec-
ond having energy E−and again the the spins of which are op-
posite. This suggests that a particle will have a partner which
is heavier or lighter than itself. On this stratum, this brings
one to think of the Electron and the Muon as a particle heavy-
partner pair since they have the same electronic charge and
gyromagnetic ratios. Begining with Dirac in 1962, the Muon
has long been thought of as an excited state of the Electron
because these two particles appear to have the same physical
properties because their interactions in nature are very similar
and it is for this reason that often the Muon is thought of as an
extremely heavy electron.
One can check that equation 23 has all the symmetry proper-
ties that are possessed by the ﬂat spacetime Dirac equation.
One important such symmetry that I wish to brieﬂy consider
is the charge conjugation symmetry. Because of this, it means
that particles with the opposite sign of the electric charge are
predicted by this equation and these by deﬁnition in the Dirac
sense are the anti-particles with the exception that they have a
positive mass and energy! This suggests that the unstable e+
is the charge conjugated partner of the stable e−. This theory
does not explain why the other of the charge conjugated part-
ner is unstable. Furthermore, another unfortunate thing about
the present theory is that it does not explain why anti-particles
(in the present sense of partner, heavy-partner pair) are not
observed naturally in that accessable part of the Universe that
we live. That is to say, if both the Electron and Muon are
fundamental particles, why then is the Muon semi-stable? To
answer this, let us endore the vacuum with some energy Evac.
This means that all the energy states up to Evac are ﬁlled. Now
take a particle and its heavier-partner. We can have three sit-
uations: (1) where both (E+, E−) < Evac, in which case both
the particle and its heavier-partner will exist in a stable state.
(2) where E+ > Evac and E−< Evac in this case the heavier-
partner will be semi stable and will decay to the lower energy
state of the lighter partner (3) where (E+, E−) > Evac, in this
case both the particle and its heavier-partner will be unstable
and there is no forseeable way how these can exist naturally.
In this case, the, reason therefore the Muon is unstable is be-
cause of the vacuum energy being less than its total energy.
Exploring, from a rather heuristic viewpoint, the above ideas
further, we know that according to the currently accepted
Standard Big-Bang theory – a theory of the origin, evolution
and fate of the Universe, the vacuum energy should have in
the past been much higher than it is today. This in actual
fact means, back in time Muons should have been much more
stable than they are today thus may have existed naturally
much the same way has Electrons exist today. If this is the
case, fossil evidence of such a scenario will most probably be
archived in the form of the existence of a bath of the Muon
and Electron-neutrino since µ−−→e−+ ¯νe + νµ. These are
merely suggestions.
In closing, I could like to say it is interesting to know what
kind of results will emerge when equation 23 is used for do-
ing QED and the Standard Model instead of the normal Dirac
equation of ﬂat space time. Will equation 23 be able to ex-
plain certain observations which have required us to modify
the original Dirac equation inorder to explain them? With this
equation, it is clear that one will need not the Feynman dia-
grams to explain anomalies that are not naturally explained by
the bare Dirac theory.
