Executive Summary
This paper proposes three new curved spacetime versions of the Dirac equation to address the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio of fermions. The author suggests that particles, including the electron, possess a finite spatial size, which accounts for the observed anomaly. The derived equations exhibit an asymmetry in their positive and negative energy solutions, potentially offering a solution to the mass asymmetry between the electron and muon. The theory also suggests an explanation for the three-stage mass hierarchy of leptons. The core of the work involves modifying the Dirac equation to account for curved spacetime, leading to a new equation (Equation 23). This equation predicts four particle solutions, potentially explaining the electron and muon mass difference. The author derives a modified gyromagnetic ratio formula (Equation 36) that incorporates particle size. The theory suggests that the observed anomalous gyromagnetic ratio arises from the interaction of spin with the Lorentz force in a curved spacetime for a particle of finite spatial size and mass. The author suggests that the asymmetry in energy solutions may solve the problem of negative energy and mass particles. A key limitation is the lack of experimental verification and the reliance on theoretical derivations. The paper's significance lies in its attempt to reconcile the Dirac equation with observed phenomena like the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio and mass hierarchies, potentially offering a new perspective on fundamental particles and spacetime.

Research Context
The Dirac equation, a cornerstone of relativistic quantum mechanics, accurately describes the electron's properties, including its gyromagnetic ratio (g=2). However, experimental measurements reveal an anomalous gyromagnetic ratio for the electron and other spin-1/2 particles, deviating from the Dirac equation's prediction. This discrepancy has led to modifications of the Dirac equation and the development of Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) to account for these anomalies. QED, while highly accurate, relies on methods like renormalization, which the author views as unnatural. The author seeks an alternative explanation for the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio by considering the effects of curved spacetime, motivated by the General Theory of Relativity, which posits that matter curves spacetime. Prior approaches, such as QED, treat particles as point-like, whereas this work proposes that particles have a finite size.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: Can a curved spacetime version of the Dirac equation account for the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio of fermions and other observed phenomena, such as the mass hierarchy of leptons? The primary hypothesis is that incorporating curved spacetime into the Dirac equation will naturally explain the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio without requiring modifications to the original equation. The author predicts that the new equation will exhibit an asymmetry in its positive and negative energy solutions, potentially resolving the issue of negative energy solutions in the Dirac equation. The author also hypothesizes that the theory will provide an explanation for the mass differences between leptons, specifically the electron and muon, by predicting the existence of four particle solutions. The approach differs from previous work, such as QED, by not treating particles as point-like and by incorporating the effects of curved spacetime directly into the Dirac equation. The success of the theory would be indicated by the derivation of a gyromagnetic ratio consistent with experimental observations and an explanation for the mass hierarchy of leptons. Failure would be indicated by the inability of the curved spacetime Dirac equation to account for these phenomena.

Methodological Details
This study employs a theoretical approach, deriving new equations based on established principles of relativistic quantum mechanics and general relativity. The methodology involves modifying the Dirac equation to incorporate the effects of curved spacetime. The starting point is the Einstein equation (Equation 10), which describes the relationship between energy, momentum, and the metric of spacetime. The author then derives a curved spacetime version of the Klein-Gordon equation (Equation 16) and, subsequently, a corresponding Dirac equation (Equation 23). The derivation involves the use of gamma-bar matrices (Equation 20) and the application of standard quantum mechanical procedures. The author examines the solutions of the derived equation, particularly focusing on the implications for the gyromagnetic ratio. The study does not involve experimental data collection or computational simulations. The analysis relies on mathematical derivations and theoretical arguments. The paper references prior work by Dirac (1928a, 1928b), Zee (2003), Brodsky & Drell (1980), and Dehmelt (1989). The study is purely theoretical; no specific software or hardware is mentioned. There is no mention of preregistration, ethics review, or multiple-comparison corrections. The study does not include any information on the sample size or demographics, as it is a theoretical paper.

Procedures Architectures
The core procedure involves modifying the Dirac equation to account for curved spacetime. The author begins with the standard Dirac equation in flat spacetime (Equation 4) and considers its equivalent in curved spacetime. The author uses the Einstein equation (Equation 10) as a starting point, which relates energy, momentum, and the metric of spacetime. The author then derives the curved spacetime Klein-Gordon equation (Equation 16), which leads to the derivation of the curved spacetime Dirac equation (Equation 23). This equation incorporates the gamma-bar matrices (Equation 20) and is the central equation of the paper. The author then analyzes the solutions of this equation, specifically focusing on the implications for the gyromagnetic ratio. The author derives a modified equation for the gyromagnetic ratio (Equation 36). The new aspect of the work is the introduction of the gamma-bar matrices and the derivation of the curved spacetime Dirac equation. The architecture involves the mathematical manipulation of equations, starting from the Einstein equation and the standard Dirac equation, and culminating in the new curved spacetime Dirac equation. The process involves mathematical derivations and the application of quantum mechanical principles.

Key Results
The primary result is the derivation of a new curved spacetime Dirac equation (Equation 23). This equation predicts four particle solutions, potentially explaining the electron and muon mass difference. The author derives a modified gyromagnetic ratio formula (Equation 36): a = (√2(1 ± λc/Rp) − 1), where 'a' is the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio, λc is the Compton wavelength, and Rp is the particle radius. The author finds that the curved spacetime Dirac equation exhibits an asymmetry in its positive and negative energy solutions (Equation 14), which may solve the problem of negative energy and mass particles. The author notes that the new equation has the same symmetry properties as the flat spacetime Dirac equation, including charge conjugation symmetry. The author states that the derived equation automatically tells us that the gyromagnetic ratio of the electron is 2, as in the original Dirac equation. The author also states that the theory suggests that a particle will have a heavier or lighter partner, which could explain the relationship between the electron and muon. The author does not provide any quantitative comparisons with experimental data for the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio, but references Brodsky & Drell (1980), who proposed a similar relation |g − 2| = Rp/λc.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that incorporating curved spacetime into the Dirac equation can provide a natural explanation for the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio of fermions. The asymmetry in the energy solutions of the derived equation may resolve the issue of negative energy solutions. The theory implies that particles have a finite spatial size, which is a departure from the point-particle assumption of QED. The existence of four particle solutions suggests a potential explanation for the mass hierarchy of leptons, particularly the electron and muon. The theory implies that anti-particles may have a positive mass and energy. The results shift the understanding of fundamental particles by suggesting that spacetime curvature plays a role in their properties. The proposed mechanism is the interaction of spin with the Lorentz force in a curved spacetime for a particle of finite spatial size and mass. The scope conditions are that the theory applies to fundamental fermions and that spacetime curvature is significant at the particle level.

Contradictions Limitations
A key limitation is the lack of experimental verification of the derived equations. The theory is based on theoretical derivations and does not provide any empirical evidence. The paper does not address the stability of the heavier-partner particles. The theory does not explain why anti-particles are not observed naturally in the accessible part of the universe. The paper does not provide details on the specific form of the curved spacetime metric used in the derivations. The paper acknowledges that the theory does not offer a complete explanation for all observed phenomena, such as the instability of certain particles. The theory relies on the assumption that particles have a finite spatial size. The lack of experimental validation poses a significant threat to the validity of the claims. The absence of specific details regarding the curved spacetime metric and the lack of quantitative comparisons with experimental data limit the ability to assess the theory's accuracy.

Resonant magnetic x-ray diﬀraction experiments on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice TbB4 were
carried out under strong pulsed magnetic ﬁelds up to 29 T. TbB4 exhibits a multi-step magnetization
process above 16 T when magnetic ﬁelds are applied along the c-axis. This magnetization curve is,
however, hardly predicted, because TbB4 has an XY -type ground state. We observed the intensity
of the 100 magnetic reﬂection as a function of magnetic ﬁeld and found that the magnetization
plateau phases are accompanied by large XY components of magnetic moments. A simple spin
model is deduced from the data and the magnetization is calculated using this model. Finally we
propose that frustration is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization.
PACS numbers: 75.25.+z,75.30.Kz,78.70.Ck
When one applies pressure to a substance, the volume
will be reduced at all times depending on its compress-
ibility. In contrast to such natural behavior, several mag-
netic materials exhibit magnetization plateaus, where the
magnetization keeps a constant value at a ﬁnite range
of magnetic ﬁelds even below the saturation ﬁeld. This
“zero compressibility” is simply ascribed to the fact that
Sz is a good quantum number, while a variety of mech-
anisms give rise to plateaus in the magnetization curve.
The easy-axis magnetization of an Ising antiferromag-
net is most comprehensible.
An example is the one-
third magnetization plateau of CoCl2·2H2O shown in
Fig. 1(a) [1]; a combination of a ﬁnite number of Ising
spins produces step-like magnetization. The multi-step
magnetization curves of PrCo2Si2 [2] and CeSb [3] are
also classiﬁed into this category. The plateau phases are
described by a complex seaquence of up- and down-spins.
Magnetization plateaus are observed not only for Ising
spins but also for Heisenberg spins. Isolated (or weakly
interacting) dimers are a trivial case. Cs3Cr2Cl9 (S= 3
2
dimers) and Ba3Mn2O8 (S=1 dimers) exhibit three-step
and two-step magnetization curves, respectively [4, 5]. In
the orthogonally connected S= 1
2 dimers SrCu2(BO3)2,
superstructures of excited triplet dimers are stabilized
and one-eighth, one-fourth, and one-third magnetization
plateaus are observed [6, 7].
Geometrically frustrated Heisenberg antiferromagnets
also frequently exhibit a magnetization plateau.
One-
third and one-half plateaus are observed in triangular-
and
pyrochlore-lattice
antiferromagnets,
respectively
(Fig. 1(b)). Although for these lattices the ﬁeld range
of the plateau phase is zero if only the nearest-neighbor
interaction is taken into account, in real magnets addi-
tional mechanisms stabilize the plateau phase. A four-
spin exchange coupling, quantum ﬂuctuations, single-ion
anisotropy, and magnetoelastic coupling have been sug-
gested for C6Eu [8], RbFe(MoO4)2 [9], GdPd2Al3 [10],

and CdCr2O4 [11], respectively. A crucial point is that
all plateau phases have a collinear magnetic structure.
No ordered magnetic moment perpendicular to the mag-
netic ﬁeld exists in the plateau phases.
Recently, a multi-step magnetization curve was ob-
served in TbB4. Intriguingly, several experimental evi-
dences indicate that TbB4 resembles none of the above-
mentioned magnets. In the rest of this letter, we show
that TbB4 indeed belongs to another rare class of mag-
nets, characterized by ordered perpendicular components
in the plateau phase. To our best knowledge, CsFeCl3 is
considered to be the only example [12]. In these mag-
nets, frustration plays a central role in their multi-step
magnetization process.
The rare-earth tetra-boride RB4 crystallizes into a
tetragonal structure (space group: P4/mbm). The net-
work of the rare-earth ions is equivalent to the frustrated
Shastry-Sutherland (SS) lattice [13].
Several pieces of
work thus have been carried out from a viewpoint of frus-
tration between rare-earth quadrupole moments [14, 15].
Somewhat confusingly, in the strict sense, classical con-
tinuous spins on the SS lattice are not frustrated, because
the ground state is a unique helical or N´eel structure and

2
has no degeneracy [13]. However, for helical stuructures,
each antiferromagnetic bond is not antiparallel and thus
local pair exchange energy is not minimized. Each spin is
not satisﬁed and still feels “frustration”. We will revisit
this point later.
In TbB4, there are two transition points TN1=44 K
and TN1=22 K. The total angular momentum of the Tb
ion is large (J=6) and hence the Tb spin is approximated
by a classical spin. The magnetic structure between TN1
and TN2 revealed by neutron powder diﬀraction experi-
ments is shown in Fig. 2(a) [16]. The magnetic moments
are conﬁned in the basal ab-plane. Additional in-plane
anisotropy orients the moments parallel to the diagonal
line. The nearest-neighbor interaction J1 is antiferromag-
netic. The next-nearest-neighbor interaction J2 is prob-
ably antiferromagnetic, and J1 and J2 form a frustrated
SS lattice. In RB4, the further-neighbor antiferromag-
netic interaction J3 is taken into account and stabilizes
the observed magnetic structure. In this structure, the J2
bond is not satisﬁed. A Dzialoshinsky-Moriya type inter-
action is also expected because only the positive chirality
state is selected. Below TN2, the magnetic moments ro-
tate in the ab-plane and a collinear-like antiferromagnetic
structure is realized. This transition is accompanied by
a structural change, probably in order to gain antiferro-
magnetic exchange energy at the cost of elastic energy.
When a magnetic ﬁeld is applied to such XY -type
magnets along the z(c)-axis, one may anticipate a linear
magnetization process, because the magnetic moments
simply slant toward the magnetic ﬁeld. On the contrary,
the magnetization process of TbB4 parallel to the c-axis
exhibits multi-step metamagnetic behavior between 16
and 28 T as shown in Fig. 2(b) [17]. The number of the
steps is reported to be 9, and the one-half magnetization
plateau is most prominent. Although the metamagnetic
behavior suggests that there are low-lying Ising excited
states just above the XY ground state, the origin of the
multiple successive transitions is not easily understood.
Diﬀraction experiments are the most powerful tool
for investigating an ordered regular array of atoms and
magnetic moments.
Recently, x-ray diﬀraction experi-
ments under strong pulsed magnetic ﬁelds have been in-
tensively developed at several places utilizing brilliant
third-generation synchrotron x-rays [18, 19, 20].
Now
a structural phase transition above 30 T can be readily
observed using these state-of-the-art technologies. How
about magnetic phase transitions? X-rays do have mag-
netic scattering cross-sections.
Although these values
are usually very small, when one tunes the x-ray energy
through an absorption edge of an element, the magnetic
scattering cross section of the element becomes large. In
the hard x-ray regime, where conventional x-ray diﬀrac-
tion experiments can be performed, this eﬀect, known
as resonance enhancement, is particularly large for rare-
earth elements [21].

The ﬁeld strength was also monitored as a

The sample surface was locally heated by irradiation of

From
this result, we understand that the plateau phases include
the (1,0,0) component in their magnetic structures.
The second important outcome is obtained from the
characteristic polarization dependence of RMXD. The
scattering amplitude is proportional to m·(ǫi×ǫf), where

Many states are degenerate at Hc1/2 when E=∞. When E
is ﬁnite, the one-third plateau phase, for instance, reduces its
energy, while the one-half plateau phase does not.
Hence, when a defect is introduced, the magnetic struc-
ture around the defect relaxes and gains exchange energy.
This does not happen in magnetic lattices without frus-
tration, because all exchange energies have already been
minimized.
In the one-third plateau phase, the magnetic moments
are rearranged and reduce the total energy as shown in
the ﬁgure.
In contrast, the resultant magnetic lattice
of the one-half plateau phase is not frustrated, as il-
lustrated by collinear in-plane components. Hence the
critical ﬁeld of the one-third plateau phase Hc1/3 is in-
evitably smaller than the critical ﬁeld of the one-half
plateau phase Hc1/2 (see Fig. 4(c)). For magnetic sys-
tems with short-range interactions, it is expected that
small commensurate unit cells are more stable than large
or incommensurate cells. Thus it is plausible that a ﬁ-
nite number of selected magnetization steps appear in
the magnetization curve through this mechanism. Inci-
dentally, interactions further than J3 must be included
to account for the splitting at Hc1.
The proposed spin model (very hard XY ground state,
excited Ising spins and no cross-term between them) is
very much simpliﬁed.
However, we believe that this
model captures basic features of the real TbB4.
We
would also like to emphasize that the spin models for
TbB4 and CsFeCl3 are quite diﬀerent. Nevertheless, the
basic scenario that frustration lifts the degeneracy at a
metamagnetic transition is common for both magnets.
We can state that frustration-driven successive metam-
agnetic transitions are a general mechanism.
In conclusion, we have investigated the multi-step mag-
netization process of TbB4 using RMXD. The magnetic
intensity observed in the plateau phases unambiguously
illustrates that large XY -components of the magnetic
moments coexist with aligned Z-components.
A sim-
ple spin model reproduces the one-half magnetization
plateau, and it is found that the frustrated nature of the
SS lattice lifts the degeneracy at the critical ﬁelds and
creates the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior.
Paradoxically, frustration is not only an origin of degen-
erate states, but also breaks degeneracy.
Finally, we stress that integration of two advanced
experimental techniques, RMXD using brilliant third-
generation synchrotron radiation and excellent pulsed-
magnetic-ﬁeld techniques, enables us to explore magnetic
structures at high magnetic ﬁelds close to 30 T. Although
this is still a challenging experiment, the technique will be
widely applied in the near future to the high-ﬁeld phases
of many interesting magnets.

Executive Summary
This paper investigates the multi-step magnetization process in the Shastry-Sutherland lattice compound TbB4 using resonant magnetic X-ray diffraction (RMXD) under strong pulsed magnetic fields. The study reveals that TbB4 exhibits a multi-step magnetization process above 16 T when the magnetic field is applied along the c-axis. The key finding is the presence of large XY components of magnetic moments in the magnetization plateau phases, which is atypical compared to conventional magnetization plateaus. The researchers used RMXD at the Tb LIII absorption edge to probe the magnetic structure under high magnetic fields up to 29 T. A simple spin model was developed to calculate the magnetization curve, and it successfully reproduced the one-half magnetization plateau. The authors propose that frustration within the Shastry-Sutherland lattice is the driving force behind the observed multi-step magnetization behavior. This work is significant because it provides insights into the interplay of frustration and metamagnetic transitions in a rare-earth compound. The primary limitation is the simplified spin model, which does not account for all interactions. The study's findings suggest that frustration can break degeneracy at metamagnetic transitions, leading to complex magnetization behavior.

Research Context
Magnetization plateaus, where magnetization remains constant over a range of magnetic fields, are observed in various magnetic materials. These plateaus are typically associated with collinear magnetic structures. Previous research has explored plateaus in Ising and Heisenberg spin systems, including geometrically frustrated antiferromagnets. However, the multi-step magnetization behavior observed in TbB4, with its XY-type ground state, is not easily explained by existing models. The study addresses the gap in understanding the origin of multi-step magnetization curves in materials with XY-type ground states, particularly those exhibiting frustration. Prior work on magnetization plateaus primarily focuses on collinear magnetic structures, while this work investigates a system with non-collinear components.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: What is the mechanism behind the multi-step magnetization process observed in TbB4? The primary hypothesis is that frustration in the Shastry-Sutherland lattice of TbB4 drives the multi-step magnetization behavior. This hypothesis is supported by the observation of large XY components of magnetic moments in the plateau phases, which is not typical for conventional magnetization plateaus. The alternative hypothesis is that the multi-step magnetization is caused by other mechanisms, such as single-ion anisotropy or magnetoelastic coupling. The study aims to determine whether frustration, as opposed to other factors, is the key to understanding the observed multi-step magnetization. The study differs from prior work by focusing on a system with an XY-type ground state and exploring the role of frustration in driving metamagnetic transitions, rather than focusing on collinear structures.

Methodological Details
The study employed resonant magnetic X-ray diffraction (RMXD) experiments on TbB4 single crystals. The experiments were conducted at the undulator beamline BL22XU at SPring-8. The x-ray energy was tuned to the Tb LIII absorption edge (7.514 keV) to enhance the magnetic scattering cross-section. Magnetic fields up to 29 T were generated using a small pulsed magnet with a pulse duration of approximately 0.6 ms. The sample was cooled using a closed-cycle refrigerator to 18 K. The scattering plane was horizontal, and the a* axis was in the plane. The magnetic field was applied along the c-axis. The 100 magnetic reflection was monitored as a function of the magnetic field. A high-counting-rate avalanche photodiode detector was used to measure the diffraction intensity with a typical resolution of 10 µs. The field strength was also monitored as a function of time. The temperature dependence of the magnetic peak intensity was measured to estimate the sample temperature. The data presented are an average of 30 field scans. The single crystals of TbB4 were grown by the floating zone method. The study did not specify any pre-registration or multiple-comparison corrections.

Procedures Architectures
The experimental setup utilized resonant magnetic X-ray diffraction (RMXD) at the SPring-8 synchrotron facility. The core component was the pulsed magnet, designed to generate magnetic fields up to 29 T. The magnet had a split-pair configuration with windows for incoming and outgoing X-rays. The sample, TbB4 single crystal, was mounted on the cold head of a closed-cycle refrigerator, allowing for temperature control at 18 K. The X-ray energy was tuned to the Tb LIII absorption edge (7.514 keV) to enhance the magnetic scattering. The detector was an avalanche photodiode, providing high-speed data acquisition. Data acquisition involved measuring the diffracted intensity as a function of time, with a resolution of 10 µs. The data acquisition system was synchronized with the pulsed magnetic field. The study also involved the development of a simple spin model. The model assumed an XY-spin ground state with in-plane anisotropy and excited Ising spins with an energy gap. The model considered a 4-spin unit cell with periodic boundary conditions. The model's parameters included exchange interactions (J1, J2, J3), in-plane anisotropy (E), and energy gap (D). The model was used to calculate the magnetization curve, which was then compared to the experimental data.

Key Results
The RMXD experiments revealed that the 100 reflection intensity remained significant in the magnetization plateau phases above 16 T (Figure 3(c)). The intensity decreased with increasing magnetic fields above 16 T and kept a constant value between 20 and 24 T, where the one-half magnetization plateau was observed (Figure 3(c)). The observed large (1,0,0) component in the plateau phases consisted of the ab-plane components. The calculated magnetization curve using the spin model reproduced the one-half magnetization plateau (Figure 4(a)). The model used parameters J1=2, J2=1, J3=2, and D=1. The diffracted intensity of this structure was approximately one-quarter of the ground state intensity, consistent with the observed intensity. The study showed that the one-half magnetization plateau is clearly reproduced and the corresponding magnetic structure is shown in the inset of Figure 4(a). The intensity of the 100 reflection as a function of temperature is shown in Figure 3(b). The incident energy dependence of the 100 reflection is shown in Figure 3(a).

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the multi-step magnetization process in TbB4 is driven by frustration within the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. The presence of large XY components of magnetic moments in the plateau phases, as revealed by RMXD, indicates a departure from the typical collinear magnetic structures observed in conventional magnetization plateaus. The spin model, which successfully reproduced the one-half magnetization plateau, supports the idea that the interplay between XY-type spins, Ising-like spins, and frustration is crucial. The study implies that frustration can lift the degeneracy at critical fields, leading to the observed multi-step metamagnetic behavior. The results broaden the understanding of how frustration can influence the magnetic properties of materials and provide a mechanism for generating complex magnetization curves.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is the simplified spin model, which does not account for all possible interactions within the TbB4 lattice. The model assumes a very hard XY ground state and excited Ising spins, which may not fully capture the complexity of the real material. The study does not address the effects of temperature variations beyond 18 K. The absence of details on the exact parameters used in the calculations, such as the specific values of the exchange interactions, is also a limitation. The study does not discuss the potential influence of other factors, such as single-ion anisotropy or magnetoelastic coupling, on the magnetization process. The study does not provide information about the crystal quality or any potential defects that might affect the results. The study does not mention the random seed used in the calculations. The study does not provide information about the demographics of the sample.

The π-π' channel is proportional to sin 2θ.", "contradicting_evidence": "", "implications": "This result indicates that the plateau phases include the (1,0,0) component in their magnetic structures."}]

Key Figures Tables
Figure 2(b) shows the magnetization process of TbB4, illustrating the multi-step behavior. Figure 3(c) presents the field dependence of the 100 reflection, highlighting the presence of the one-half magnetization plateau. Figure 4(a) displays the calculated magnetization curve from the spin model, reproducing the one-half plateau. These figures are critical for understanding the experimental results and the model's validation. The x-axis of Figure 2(b) is the magnetic field in Tesla, and the y-axis is the magnetization in units of µB/f.u. Figure 3(c) shows the counts per 10µs on the y-axis and the magnetic field in Tesla on the x-axis. Figure 4(a) shows the magnetization on the y-axis and the magnetic field in units of gµBH on the x-axis.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the identification of a multi-step magnetization process in TbB4, characterized by large XY components of magnetic moments in the plateau phases, which is driven by frustration in the Shastry-Sutherland lattice. (2) The strongest evidence supporting this claim is the observation of the one-half magnetization plateau in the RMXD experiments, along with the successful reproduction of this plateau using a simple spin model. (3) The primary limitation is the simplified spin model, and future work could involve more sophisticated models to fully capture the complexity of the TbB4 system, or explore the effects of temperature variations.

source.source_title: Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by scanning   tunneling microscopy

papers.fulltext:
Mapping of functionalized regions on carbon nanotubes by 
scanning tunneling microscopy 
P. Nemes – Incze*,†, Z. Kónya‡, I. Kiricsi‡, Á. Pekker§, Z.E. Horváth†, K. Kamarás§, L.P. 
Biró† 
Abstract 
Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) gives us the opportunity to map the surface of functionalized 
carbon nanotubes in an energy resolved manner and with atomic precision. But this potential is largely 
untapped, mainly due to sample stability issues which inhibit reliable measurements. Here we present 
a simple and straightforward solution that makes away with this difficulty, by incorporating the 
functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNT) into a few layer graphene – nanotube 
composite. This enabled us to measure energy resolved tunneling conductance maps on the nanotubes, 
which shed light on the level of doping, charge transfer between tube and functional groups and the 
dependence of defect creation or functionalization on crystallographic orientation. 
Keywords: functionalization, carbon nanotubes, few layer graphene, STM, CITS, STS 
In the decades following their discovery, the chemistry of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has grown into a 
mature field of research1,2,3. Sidewall functionalization of CNTs has turned out to be a versatile tool to 
change their electronic properties1,4,5,6,7 and the ways in which the tubes interact with their 
environment8,9,10,11. This broadens considerably their applicability, from sensors and medical 
uses2,10,12,13 to composite materials8. In all such cases we need a clear picture of the changes 
                                                          
*  Corresponding author email: nemes@mfa.kfki.hu 
†  Research Institute for Technical Physics and Materials Science, H-1525, PO. Box 49 Budapest, Hungary 
‡  Department of Applied and Environmental Chemistry, University of Szeged, Rerrich Béla sqr. 1, H-6720 
Szeged, Hungary 
§  Research Institute for Solid State Physics and Optics, Hungarian Academy of Sciences, H-1525, PO Box 49 
Budapest, Hungary 

functionalization induces in the nanotube, like: surface topography, band structure, doping, etc. to be 
able to refine these applications and to better understand the physical and chemical processes involved 
in functionalization. Changes to the nanotube electronic structure are usually investigated via 
spectroscopic methods, which are a global probe of CNT properties6. Complementary to these 
methods are scanning probe methods, namely scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and atomic force 
microscopy (AFM), which provide spatially resolved information down to the atomic scale. STM is 
one of the most important tools in nanoscale science and has been the source of landmark findings in 
the study of carbon nanotubes. Using STM, Wildöer et al. gave a first account of the relation between 
CNT wrapping direction and their predicted band structure14, while Lemay et al. were able to map 
individual wavefunctions of CNTs15. These breakthroughs were possible because the tunneling current 
in STM can be measured simultaneously as a function of both energy and location on the sample. One 
way to achieve this is by using the so called Current Imaging Tunneling Spectroscopy or CITS mode, 
during which in each pixel of the CITS image the scanning STM tip acquires a tunneling current vs. 
voltage (STS) curve and stores it together with the topographic information. Using CITS image we can 
obtain local tunneling conductance maps of the sample by plotting the derivative of the current (dI/dV) 
as a function of the tip – sample bias voltage value. Among other examples, it has been applied in 
mapping the local photovoltaic performance of organic solar cells16 and to map the charge 
inhomogeneity of SiO2 supported graphene17. However, the full potential of STM as a tool in mapping 
the electronic properties of functionalized CNTs has not been achieved yet. Direct STM and CITS 
measurements could yield more insight into the extent and nature of sidewall functionalization as 
opposed to other methods of visualizing functionalized sites18. One key bottleneck in achieving this is 
sample stability. 
In the case of STM, as with any high resolution microscopy tool, good mechanical stability of the 
sample is of paramount importance to obtain reliable measurements. Because of the presence of 
functional groups on the tube surface the contact area with the substrate decreases and this leads to a 
weakening of the overall force (ex. van der Waals) which anchors the tubes to the support. The metal 
tip of the STM can exert considerable forces, mainly electrostatic in nature, on the tubes19,20 and it can 

move the CNTs in the fast scan direction and can effectively “clean out” the scan area of the tubes we 
would want to investigate (Fig. 1). This is illustrated in Fig. 1b, where we show an AFM image of a 
20x20 µm2 area which was previously scanned by STM. After only 3 passes over the same area, 
practically all of the CNTs have been brushed to the sides. The inset in Fig. 1 shows how, during 
scanning of the STM tip, a nanotube can move to the side, then after a few scan lines the tube moves 
back to its original position. We can also find evidence of such tube movement in the literature18,21,22,23. 
While this problem seems to be less critical in the case of lightly functionalized tubes24 and/or if the 
measurement is performed in UHV25,26,27,28 it makes imaging such CNTs a challenge. One way around 
this problem is to immobilize the nanotubes, for example by binding the tubes to the substrate via 
strong chemical bonds. The work of Zhang et al. is a good example of this22, where they have used Au 
– S chemistry to anchor the thiol or thiophene terminated functional groups on the nanotubes to the Au 
substrate, effectively immobilizing them. While fruitful, this method is not applicable in all cases 
because of the need to have chemical binding between the nanotubes and substrate. Furthermore, the 
chemical bond may perturb the tube electronic structure22. Here we present a method to immobilize 
CNTs on a graphitic support, which provides a sample that is stable enough to allow reproducible 
CITS measurements and is a well studied CNT – support system. 
 

Figure 1. (a) Successive STM images (top and bottom) of a region on HOPG containing functionalized CNTs show that 
CNTs can be swept away by the STM tip. Extensive movement of the CNTs can be observed on the top image. The nanotube 
movement is also evident in the inset, where a single CNT shifts position during scanning and shifts back to its original 
position after a few scan lines. (b) Tapping mode AFM image of functionalized CNTs on a HOPG surface measured in a 
region where the STM tip was previously scanned (Fig. 1a). The AFM image is taken after the 3rd STM scan. STM scanning 
was performed using 300 pA current setpoint and 100 mV bias voltage. The fast scan direction is horizontal. 
Results and Discussion 
Multiwalled CNTs used in this study have been prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene 
over alumina supported Co/Fe catalyst29. The functionalization of the nanotubes was done in a three 
step process reported elsewhere30. Briefly, in the first step the pristine CNTs were treated in 
H2SO4/HNO3 (3:1) mixture for 24 h at room temperature. Such a treatment attaches –OH and –COOH 
groups to the CNT outer wall, which were transformed into –COCl groups in a second step involving 
stirring overnight in SOCl2. In a final step the as obtained sample was stirred in diaminopropane for 
24h. The diaminopropane can connect the functional groups on the nanotubes, which results in 
covalently interconnected MWCNTs as illustrated in Fig. 2a and the TEM image shown in Fig. 3c. 
Functionalization increases the tube surface defect concentration, as observed in the Raman spectra 
through an increase in the D peak intensity relative to the G peak (ID/IG)31 (Fig. 2b). Attenuated Total 
Reflection – IR (ATR – IR) spectra of the pristine sample shows some signs of OH groups, which may 
be due to isopropanol residues in the CNT suspension or may be the sign of mild oxidation of the 
pristine sample. The spectra of the functionalized samples shows a peak corresponding to the -NH 
group. However, the presence of carboxyl can still be recognized, which indicates that the conversion 
of –COCl groups into amide was not complete. Such cross-linked carbon nanotubes are an interesting 
avenue in improving the mechanical and electrical transport properties of nanotube networks32,33 and 
functionalization schemes similar to our own have been studied6,34. Here we report for the first time 
atomic resolution STM and CITS measurements on such CNTs. 

 
Figure 2. (a) MWCNTs interconnected by diaminopropane. (b) Raman spectra of the starting CNT material and of the 
functionalized sample. The spectra are normalized to the G peak intensity. (c) ATR-IR spectra shows peaks corresponding to 
–OH and –COOH groups in both the pristine and functionalized samples and a signature of –NH in the functionalized 
sample. 
 
Figure 3. (a) Illustration of the CNT – FLG composite and the STM measurement. (b) STM image of a functionalized CNT 
sticking out from beneath a FLG layer, also seen in Fig. 4d. (c) and (d) TEM images of the functionalized CNTs. The surface 
of the tubes is irregular and some tubes are interconnected as seen in (c). 

The immobilization of the functionalized CNTs is done by sandwiching them between few layer 
graphite (FLG) flakes in a CNT – FLG composite, i.e. a buckypaper (Fig 3a, b). The nano-composite 
has regions on its surface where functionalized CNTs stick out from beneath a FLG layer we show an 
STM image of such a region in Fig. 3b. In places like this, the movement of the nanotube is restricted 
by the clamping FLG layer and provides a good sample for stable and reproducible STM and CITS 
measurements. This particular composite is advantageous, because graphite and MWCNTs have 
nearly the same work function35, thus no significant doping by the substrate is expected. 
 
Figure 4. (a), (d) STM images and (b), (e) tunneling conductance maps of functionalized nanotubes extending from below a 
FLG clamping layer (conductance units are in nano Siemens). Figure (a) shows a bundle of 3 nanotubes, which are possibly 
cross linked by functional groups. The tunneling conductance maps are displayed at -160 mV bias voltage. In (c) and (f) we 
show dI/dV spectra from the regions marked by arrows of the same color in (b) and (e) respectively. The spectra are 
displaced vertically for ease of comparison. 

STM images of a bundle of three functionalized nanotubes and a single tube can be seen in Fig. 4a and 
Fig. 4d, while in Fig. 4 b,e we present a map of the simultaneously acquired local tunneling 
conductance on these tubes. We obtained this map from the CITS image by taking the first derivative 
of the STS curves and displaying the conductance value at -160 mV bias voltage. We can observe on 
the same image the different conductance of the graphite support and of the nanotubes. Such dI/dV 
tunneling conductance maps are qualitatively proportional to the nanotube local density of states 
(LDOS). At a first glance the dI/dV map on the nanotube surface shows regions of high and low 
conductance. Comparing the dI/dV curves from such selected regions we can see some similarities and 
some differences in the spectra. The curves from the high conductance regions (red arrow and curve) 
and the substrate (black arrow and curve) are similar and have a typical graphitic shape, with 
monotonically increasing conductance that is symmetrical with respect to the LDOS minimum. 
Measuring a graphitic dI/dV signal on multiwalled CNTs is a reasonable expectation, because at the 
large tube diameters in this sample (~15 nm) the Van Hove singularities are very close together and 
get smoothed out due to the spread of the Fermi function at 300K and due to disorder effects36. The 
minimum of LDOS, which occurs because of the vanishing electron states at the K points, is shifted 
slightly to positive tip – sample bias voltages. This means that the chemical potential is shifted away 
from its equilibrium position, i.e. that the sample is p-doped. It has been shown that nitric and sulfuric 
acid can have a strong, p doping effect on CNTs37,38. In our case, acid molecules adsorbed on the 
nanotube surface are a result of the purification treatment. These molecules donate a positive charge to 
the carbon lattice, which becomes delocalized over the π electron system. Additional causes for the p 
doping may be the result of measuring under ambient conditions, during which oxygen or oxygen 
containing adsorbents can be present on the composite buckypaper (water from ambient, isopropanol 
from the CNT suspension)39. These processes lead to a “global” p doping of the nanotubes and has 
been measured previously by optical reflectivity and thermopower measurements 37,38. But the true 
power of CITS measurements comes from the local information it provides. Thus, examining the 
conductance maps further we can see regions with lower conductance than the support or other regions 
on the tubes (green arrow and curve). dI/dV curves in these regions have a much less well defined 
minimum and are highly asymmetrical in places. We attributed these types of curves to defective 

and/or intensely functionalized regions of the CNTs, where the low conductance values arise from the 
destruction of the sp2 π electron lattice40. During functionalization the sp2 carbon atoms change to sp3, 
thus reducing the number of delocalized π electrons. In the case of monovalent functional groups, such 
as in our case, theory predicts the existence of well defined impurity states near the Fermi level4, but 
we were unable to find the signature of such states in the dI/dV curves taken above functionalized 
sites, contrary to other systems we have studied41. Again, this is a sign that in these regions the surface 
cannot be treated as graphitic, the functionalization does not perturb but rather completely alter the 
graphite lattice. This conclusion is also supported by the TEM images, where we can see that the 
graphitic layers of the tubes are damaged. 
 
Figure 5. STM images of two sections of a functionalized CNT shown in Fig 4d. Zoomed in, lattice resolved images were 
obtained in the regions marked by blue squares. Tunneling conductance maps were obtained simultaneously and are 
displayed at -225 mV bias voltage. Functionalized regions show up as protrusions on the nanotube surface and as low 

conductance areas in the conductance maps. Red lines mark the zigzag direction on the atomic resolution image. The 
functionalized regions follow the zigzag direction. The superstructure patterns on the atomic lattice are a sign of defect 
scattering (marked by circle). 
The STM topography of these tubes also shows a rough surface, which is typical of highly defective 
and functionalized CNTs, where the functional groups usually appear as protrusions on the nanotube 
surface22,24. Figure 5a,b show two distinct STM topography images of a functionalized CNT. 
Comparing the conductance maps with the topography, we can observe that the low conductance 
regions show a degree of correlation with the protrusions on the surface. Especially in Fig. 5a, bands 
of protrusions can be observed, along with bands of low conductance in the corresponding dI/dV map. 
Furthermore, it was not possible to obtain atomic resolution images on the low conductance regions, 
only on the regions with high conductance. Alongside the graphitic dI/dV curves, this suggests that the 
regions with high conductance are mostly free of defects and functional groups. Here the atomic lattice 
shows a typical superstructure pattern, a hallmark of electron scattering between two non equivalent K 
points in the Brillouin zone24,28,42. As these superstructure patterns can extend to a few nanometers 
from the defect site producing them42 it is fair to say that they are due to scattering taking place on the 
defects created by functionalization. If we compare the atomic resolution images with the 
functionalized bands, we find that these follow the zigzag direction along the nanotube circumference. 
To date, only a few such STM studies are available which show the correlation between 
crystallographic direction and functionalization, for example on fluorinated CNTs28. These 
measurements provide experimental evidence that oxidation reactions on CNTs can prefer a specific 
crystallographic direction, as it was presumed in recent experiments which involved the unzipping of 
carbon nanotubes to graphene nanoribbons43. Although the acid treatment in our case is much milder 
than in the case of CNT43 and graphene oxidation44, our results suggest that in the specific case 
discussed here, which involves nitric-sulfuric acid oxidation, this direction is the zigzag direction. 

 
Figure 6. Tunneling conductance maps of the nanotube region seen in Fig. 5b, with selected dI/dV curves. The bias voltages 
at which the maps were plotted are marked by dashed lines. Atomic resolution was achieved in the region marked by the red 
arrow. The low conductance regions show similar dI/dV curves as the ones seen in Fig 4 (green). (The dI/dV maps are 75x75 
nm in size). Lower right: map of the dI/dV minimum in the same region as the conductance map the bias voltage value for 
the dI/dV minimum is displayed on a color scale. Colored arrows show the positions where the respective dI/dV curves were 
taken. 

Now, let us examine the dI/dV maps of one nanotube in more detail. In Fig. 6 we show six plots of the 
tunneling conductance map of the tube shown in Fig. 5b at different tip – sample bias voltages. These 
voltages have been selected in such a way, as to be symmetrical relative to the dI/dV minimum. We 
can distinguish three regions based on these maps. One region is where atomic resolution could be 
achieved (marked by a red arrow). Maps of such regions have symmetrical conductance values with 
respect to the minimum of dI/dV or in other words to the LDOS minimum. Such behavior is graphitic 
in nature, due to the symmetry in energy of the nanotube bands around the K points. As we have seen 
before, another region is where the overall conductance is low and no atomic resolution can be 
achieved. We have attributed these changes to heavily functionalized regions (marked with a green 
arrow). Further inspection of the maps reveals a third region, where the dI/dV maps are asymmetrical, 
here the tunneling conductance is higher for positive tip – sample bias voltages (blue arrow). The 
origin of this asymmetry is not clear, but it may be due to impurity states at functionalized or defect 
sites4,41. Another feature of this dI/dV curve is that its minimum is shifted towards a more negative 
sample voltage, making this region less p-doped. We can expect such behavior if there is charge 
transfer between the nanotube and attached molecules or radicals, which leads to a local Coulomb 
potential and therefore to a shift in energy of the nanotube bands. In Fig. 6 we plot a map of the LDOS 
minimum on the nanotube by displaying the bias voltage value for the dI/dV minimum on a color 
scale. From this map we can see that the mostly functional group free regions are heavily p-doped, 
with a Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV. This is the global doping level of the sample, and as we 
discussed earlier it arises due to acid molecule adsorption and additionally it is expected if we have 
functionalization by electron acceptors such as carboxyl groups or other oxygen containing 
complexes45. The map of LDOS minimum correlates nicely with the conductance map showing the 
places of asymmetric dI/dV curves attributed to functionalized sites (blue arrows in Fig. 6). We have 
to mention that the interpretation of this map is not straightforward in the low conductance regions, 
where the sp2 carbon lattice is heavily damaged and the electronic structure of the surface is unknown. 
Conclusions 

The CNT immobilization technique presented here is widely applicable to any type of functionalized 
nanotube and provides a well studied CNT – support system, i.e. CNT on graphite. We have shown for 
the first time that acid oxidation and subsequent functionalization has a preference of advancing along 
the zigzag crystallographic direction on large diameter multiwalled CNTs. Our measurements 
illustrate clearly the kind of advantage energy resolved maps can give, namely to spot sample features 
that are not apparent from STM topography maps and provides a local functionalization state and 
doping. Furthermore, this measurement technique allows certain ‘in situ’ studies that could not be 
performed otherwise, for example to examine the topography and energy resolved behavior of 
functionalized CNTs, while being exposed to different gas or vapor environments10. This may lead to a 
better understanding of the adsorption processes and the electronic structure variations involved in gas 
sensing with functionalized nanotube networks. 
Methods 
The composite presented here is a buckypaper obtained by mixing the functionalized CNTs with 
commercially available exfoliated graphite in isopropyl alcohol by ultrasonic stirring. The as obtained 
suspension was filtered through a polycarbonate membrane filter (200 nm pore size) and left to dry. 
Pieces from this buckypaper were cut out and placed on the STM sample holder, electrical contact to 
the buckypaper was made by carbon colloid paste. 
A Multimode III SPM (Veeco) was operated in the CITS mode to acquire the STM images. The STS 
data was extracted from the raw CITS files and processed separately using Scilab (www.scilab.org) for 
easy manipulation and extraction of individual STS curves. All the STM images and STS curves 
presented here were obtained using the same Pt/Ir STM probe. Tips were mechanically cut from Pt/Ir 
(80:20) wire and were use for characterization only if they produced reproducible STS spectra and 
atomic resolution on graphite. Atomic resolution images on the nanotubes were acquired using 500 pA 
tunneling current and 100 mV tip – sample bias voltage. STM topography and CITS images were 
acquired using 300 pA tunneling current and 300 mV bias voltage. 

TEM measurements were done using a Philips CM20 microscope operated at 200 keV.
papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a method for stabilizing functionalized multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) for scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) and current imaging tunneling spectroscopy (CITS) measurements. The authors incorporated functionalized MWCNTs into a few-layer graphene (FLG)-nanotube composite to mitigate sample instability issues that have hindered the application of STM to functionalized nanotubes. This approach enabled energy-resolved tunneling conductance mapping, revealing information on doping levels, charge transfer between the nanotubes and functional groups, and the influence of crystallographic orientation on defect creation and functionalization. The study found that acid oxidation and subsequent functionalization preferentially occurs along the zigzag crystallographic direction in large-diameter MWCNTs. Key findings include the observation of p-doping in the nanotubes and the identification of regions with low conductance attributed to defective and/or intensely functionalized areas. The study's novelty lies in the use of a CNT-FLG composite to stabilize functionalized nanotubes for STM/CITS, allowing for atomic-resolution imaging and energy-resolved mapping. This work is significant because it provides a method to study the electronic properties of functionalized CNTs at the nanoscale, which is crucial for their applications in sensors, composite materials, and other areas. A major limitation is the unknown electronic structure of the surface in heavily functionalized regions, where the sp2 carbon lattice is damaged.

Research Context
The study addresses the challenge of imaging functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNTs) with scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). Prior research has established the potential of STM and CITS for mapping the electronic properties of CNTs, but sample instability, due to the presence of functional groups weakening the contact with the substrate, has limited the technique's application. Previous methods to immobilize nanotubes, such as chemical bonding, have limitations, including potential perturbation of the tube's electronic structure. This work builds on prior studies that have used STM to study CNTs and the relation between CNT wrapping direction and band structure, and mapping individual wavefunctions of CNTs. The study aims to overcome the limitations of previous approaches by developing a stable platform for STM/CITS measurements on functionalized CNTs.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to map the surface of functionalized carbon nanotubes with atomic precision using STM, overcoming the sample instability issues that have hindered this application. The primary hypothesis is that incorporating functionalized MWCNTs into a FLG-nanotube composite will stabilize the nanotubes sufficiently to allow for reproducible STM and CITS measurements. The study predicts that this method will enable the acquisition of energy-resolved tunneling conductance maps, revealing information on the level of doping, charge transfer between the tube and functional groups, and the dependence of defect creation or functionalization on crystallographic orientation. The alternative hypothesis is that the composite will not sufficiently stabilize the nanotubes, resulting in unstable measurements and an inability to obtain clear conductance maps. Another alternative is that the composite will alter the electronic properties of the nanotubes, making it difficult to interpret the results. The study differs from prior work by using a CNT-FLG composite to stabilize the nanotubes, which allows for STM/CITS measurements without the need for chemical bonding that could perturb the tube's electronic structure.

Methodological Details
The study employed STM and CITS to investigate functionalized MWCNTs. The MWCNTs were prepared by chemical vapor deposition of acetylene over an alumina-supported Co/Fe catalyst. Functionalization involved a three-step process: treatment in H2SO4/HNO3 mixture, followed by stirring in SOCl2, and finally, stirring in diaminopropane. This process attached –OH and –COOH groups, which were transformed into –COCl groups, and then cross-linked with diaminopropane. The functionalized MWCNTs were incorporated into a buckypaper composite with exfoliated graphite in isopropyl alcohol, which was then filtered through a polycarbonate membrane. STM imaging was performed using a Multimode III SPM (Veeco) in CITS mode. The STS data was extracted from the raw CITS files and processed using Scilab. The STM images and STS curves were obtained using a Pt/Ir STM probe. Atomic resolution images on the nanotubes were acquired using a 500 pA tunneling current and 100 mV tip – sample bias voltage. STM topography and CITS images were acquired using a 300 pA tunneling current and 300 mV bias voltage. TEM measurements were performed using a Philips CM20 microscope operated at 200 keV. The study did not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. Ethical considerations, including IRB approval and informed consent, were not reported.

Procedures Architectures
The study utilized a CNT-FLG composite to stabilize functionalized MWCNTs for STM and CITS measurements. The functionalized MWCNTs were mixed with exfoliated graphite in isopropyl alcohol and ultrasonically stirred to create a suspension. This suspension was then filtered through a polycarbonate membrane to form a buckypaper. The buckypaper was cut into pieces and placed on the STM sample holder, with electrical contact made using carbon colloid paste. The STM measurements were performed using a Multimode III SPM (Veeco) in CITS mode. The STM probe was a mechanically cut Pt/Ir (80:20) wire. The STM tip was characterized by obtaining reproducible STS spectra and atomic resolution on graphite. The CITS mode allowed for the simultaneous acquisition of STM images and STS curves. The STS data, representing the tunneling current as a function of voltage, was extracted from the raw CITS files and processed using Scilab. The STM images and STS curves were obtained using the same Pt/Ir STM probe. The study used a three-step functionalization process, including acid treatment, SOCl2 treatment, and diaminopropane treatment. The novelty of the approach lies in the use of a CNT-FLG composite to provide a stable platform for STM/CITS measurements on functionalized CNTs, which is not found in the literature.

Key Results
The study successfully obtained STM and CITS measurements on functionalized MWCNTs using the CNT-FLG composite. The STM images revealed a rough surface topography, with functional groups appearing as protrusions. The dI/dV maps showed regions of high and low conductance. The high conductance regions exhibited graphitic-like behavior, while the low conductance regions were attributed to defective and/or intensely functionalized areas. The dI/dV curves from these regions had a much less well-defined minimum and were highly asymmetrical. The study found that the nanotubes were p-doped, with a Fermi level shift of around 0.25 eV in the mostly functional group-free regions. The map of the LDOS minimum correlated with the conductance map, showing the places of asymmetric dI/dV curves attributed to functionalized sites. The study also found that the functionalized regions followed the zigzag direction along the nanotube circumference. The Raman spectra showed an increase in the D peak intensity relative to the G peak (ID/IG), indicating an increase in the tube surface defect concentration. The ATR-IR spectra showed peaks corresponding to –OH and –COOH groups in both the pristine and functionalized samples and a signature of –NH in the functionalized sample. The study did not report any baseline comparisons or effect sizes. The p-doping was attributed to acid molecule adsorption and functionalization by electron acceptors. The study did not report any unexpected or negative results.

Interpretation Implications
The findings support the hypothesis that the CNT-FLG composite provides a stable platform for STM/CITS measurements on functionalized MWCNTs. The observation of different conductance regions on the dI/dV maps suggests that the functionalization process alters the electronic structure of the nanotubes. The p-doping observed in the nanotubes is attributed to acid molecule adsorption and the presence of electron-accepting functional groups. The preferential functionalization along the zigzag direction implies that oxidation reactions on CNTs can favor a specific crystallographic direction. The study provides experimental evidence that oxidation reactions on CNTs can prefer a specific crystallographic direction. The results suggest that the functionalization process leads to a destruction of the sp2 π electron lattice in the functionalized regions. The study's findings contribute to a better understanding of the electronic properties of functionalized CNTs and their potential applications in sensing and composite materials.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is the unknown electronic structure of the surface in heavily functionalized regions, where the sp2 carbon lattice is heavily damaged and the electronic structure of the surface is unknown. The interpretation of the LDOS minimum map is not straightforward in the low conductance regions. The study does not provide information on the sample's homogeneity, which could affect the interpretation of the results. The study does not report the random seed used for the experiment or the train/test split. The study does not mention the demographics of the sample. The study's conclusions are limited to the specific functionalization process and the type of MWCNTs used. The study acknowledges that the acid treatment is milder than in other studies. The study does not address the potential impact of the STM tip on the functionalized nanotubes. The study does not discuss the external validity of the findings.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 4 presents STM images and tunneling conductance maps of functionalized nanotubes, illustrating the different conductance of the graphite support and the nanotubes. Figure 5 shows zoomed-in, lattice-resolved images and tunneling conductance maps of a functionalized CNT, demonstrating the correlation between functionalized regions and low conductance areas. These figures are critical for visualizing the results and supporting the main claims of the study.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the development of a CNT-FLG composite that enables stable STM and CITS measurements on functionalized MWCNTs, overcoming the limitations of previous methods. (2) The strongest evidence comes from the successful acquisition of STM and CITS measurements, which revealed the preferential functionalization along the zigzag direction and the p-doping in the nanotubes, as shown in Figures 4, 5, and 6. (3) The primary limitation is the unknown electronic structure of the surface in heavily functionalized regions, which presents an open problem for future research, and further investigation is needed to fully understand the impact of functionalization on the electronic properties of CNTs.

2. The Model
In this section we discuss how equation (1.1) can be derived to describe the propagation
of a ﬁnite amplitude transverse wave in a nonlocally elastic medium. Before stating
our derivation, we need to introduce the concept of nonlocal elasticity.
One of the
major drawbacks in the conventional theory of elasticity is that it does not include any
intrinsic length scale and consequently does not take into account the long range forces
that become increasingly important at small scales. As a result, the conventional theory
of elasticity is incapable of predicting, for instance, (i) the dispersive nature of harmonic
waves in crystal lattices and (ii) the boundedness of the stress ﬁeld near the tip of a
crack. In order to overcome such deﬁciencies various generalizations of the conventional
theory of elasticity have been proposed. One such generalization is the theory of nonlocal
elasticity which has been developed by Kr¨oner [4], Eringen and Edelen [5], Kunin [6],
Rogula [7], Eringen [8, 9] over the last several decades (For more recent studies on the
subject of generalized theories of elasticity, see, for instance, [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]
and references therein). What distinguishes the theory of nonlocal elasticity from the
conventional theory of elasticity is that the stress at a point depends on the strain ﬁeld
at every point in the body. Although there has been a considerable amount of research
done on small scale eﬀects within the context of the theory of nonlocal elasticity, they
are mostly restricted to linear models. Recently, in [1, 2, 3] various Cauchy problems
based on a one-dimensional nonlinear model of nonlocal elasticity have been studied.
Here, we show how the approach in those studies is extended to the dynamic anti-plane
shearing problem of nonlinear nonlocal elasticity.

of the medium by its rectangular Cartesian coordinates in a reference conﬁguration:
X = (X1, X2, X3).
We assume that the reference conﬁguration is unstressed.
Let
x(X, t) = (x1(X, t), x2(X, t), x3(X, t)) denote the position of the same point at time t.
Then the displacement and the deformation gradient are given by u(X, t) = x(X, t)−X
and A(X, t) = Grad x(X, t), respectively.
We suppose that a (local) strain energy
density function F(A) per unit volume of the undeformed reference conﬁguration exists,
i.e., the material is (locally) hyperelastic and that it sustains a nontrivial anti-plane shear
motion. In the conventional theory of elasticity, a constitutive equation of the form
σ = σ(A) ≡∂F(A)/∂A holds for a hyperelastic material (see equation (4.3.7) of [16]),
where σ is the nominal stress tensor (note that some authors use its transpose referred
to as the ﬁrst Piola-Kirchhoﬀstress tensor). In the theory of nonlocal elasticity the
(nonlocal) stress tensor S is related to the (local) stress tensor σ through the constitutive

Executive Summary
This paper investigates the Cauchy problem for a class of two-dimensional, nonlinear, nonlocal wave equations that model anti-plane shear motions in nonlocal elasticity. The nonlocality is represented by a convolution integral. The study establishes conditions for the global existence and finite-time blow-up of solutions, depending on the initial data's smoothness and the properties of the convolution kernel. The core approach extends techniques used for one-dimensional nonlocal Boussinesq-type wave equations. The main findings include local well-posedness results under specific conditions on the Sobolev space and the kernel's regularity. Global existence is proven under a positivity condition on the nonlinear function and sufficient smoothness of the initial data. A finite-time blow-up result is also established. The novelty lies in extending existing techniques to a two-dimensional wave equation within the context of nonlocal elasticity. This work is significant because it contributes to the understanding of wave propagation in materials where long-range forces are important, particularly at small scales. A key limitation is the reliance on specific conditions for global existence and blow-up, which may not always be met in real-world scenarios.

Research Context
Conventional elasticity theory lacks an intrinsic length scale, failing to account for long-range forces significant at small scales. This limitation hinders the accurate prediction of phenomena like dispersive wave behavior in crystal lattices and stress field boundedness near crack tips. Nonlocal elasticity theory addresses these shortcomings by incorporating long-range interactions, where stress at a point depends on the strain field at every point in the body. Prior research, such as in [1, 2, 3], has explored one-dimensional nonlinear models of nonlocal elasticity. This paper extends these techniques to a two-dimensional wave equation, contributing to the understanding of anti-plane shear motions in nonlocally elastic media. This work builds upon and extends previous research by applying established techniques to a more complex, two-dimensional setting.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: Under what conditions does the Cauchy problem for a class of two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equations, modeling anti-plane shear motions, have global solutions or exhibit finite-time blow-up? The paper implicitly tests several hypotheses. First, it hypothesizes that the local Cauchy problem is well-posed for initial data in suitable Sobolev spaces. This is supported by establishing local existence and uniqueness theorems (Theorems 3.7 and 3.8). Second, it hypothesizes that, under certain conditions on the nonlinearity and initial data, global solutions exist. This is supported by Theorem 4.3, which proves global existence under specific conditions. Third, it hypothesizes that, under different conditions on the nonlinearity and initial energy, solutions will blow up in finite time. This is supported by Theorem 5.2, which provides conditions for finite-time blow-up. These hypotheses are tested by analyzing the properties of solutions to the Cauchy problem, specifically their existence, uniqueness, and long-time behavior. The study differs from prior work by extending techniques from one-dimensional models to a two-dimensional setting and exploring the interplay between the convolution kernel, initial data, and the nonlinear function in determining solution behavior.

Methodological Details
The study employs analytical methods to investigate the Cauchy problem for a two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation. The primary study design involves analyzing the equation's properties to establish well-posedness, global existence, and finite-time blow-up. The participants are not explicitly defined, as the study focuses on the mathematical properties of the equation rather than on physical experiments or observations. The materials consist of the two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation (1.1) and the associated initial conditions (1.2). The equation models anti-plane shear motions in nonlocal elasticity. The data are the initial conditions, specifically the initial displacement,  ϕ(x, y), and initial velocity, ψ(x, y). The software used is not specified. The procedure involves transforming the initial value problem into a system of Banach space-valued ordinary differential equations, analyzing the properties of the operator K, and applying mathematical tools such as Sobolev embedding theorems, Gronwall's lemma, and energy conservation principles. The analysis involves establishing local well-posedness, proving global existence under certain conditions, and demonstrating finite-time blow-up under other conditions. The analysis uses the Fourier transform and inverse Fourier transform. The norm used for the Hs Sobolev space is defined as ∥u∥2s = ∫R2(1 + |ξ|2)s|bu(ξ)|2dξ. The L∞ norm is denoted as ∥u∥∞. The inner product of u and v in L2(R2) is denoted as ⟨u, v⟩. The study does not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. Ethical considerations are not applicable as the study is theoretical.

Procedures Architectures
The paper focuses on the mathematical analysis of a two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation, rather than on a specific architecture or computational procedure. The equation (1.1) models anti-plane shear motions in nonlocal elasticity and is the central object of study. The equation is defined as wtt = (β ∗ ∂F/∂wx)x + (β ∗ ∂F/∂wy)y, where w = w(x, y, t) represents the out-of-plane displacement, F is a nonlinear function of |∇w|2, and β is a convolution kernel. The kernel's Fourier transform, bβ(ξ), is assumed to be nonnegative and satisfy a growth condition (1.3): 0 ≤ bβ(ξ) ≤ C(1 + |ξ|2)−r/2, where C is a positive constant and r ≥ 2. The initial conditions are w(x, y, 0) = ϕ(x, y) and wt(x, y, 0) = ψ(x, y). The paper transforms the initial value problem into a system of ordinary differential equations in Banach spaces. The Banach space Xs is defined as Xs = {w ∈ Hs(R2); wx, wy ∈ L∞(R2)}, with the norm ∥w∥s,∞ = ∥w∥s + ∥wx∥∞ + ∥wy∥∞. The operator K is defined as Kw = (β ∗ ∂F/∂wx)x + (β ∗ ∂F/∂wy)y. The analysis involves the use of the Fourier transform and inverse Fourier transform. The linear operator R is defined as Rpu = F−1((bβ(ξ))−p/2bu(ξ)), where F−1 denotes the inverse Fourier transform. The core novelty lies in the application of these mathematical tools and techniques to analyze the two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation, extending the approaches used for one-dimensional Boussinesq-type wave equations. The paper does not describe any specific hardware or software versions.

Key Results
The paper establishes several key results regarding the Cauchy problem for the two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation. Theorem 3.7 proves local well-posedness for initial data in Hs(R2) with s > 2 and r ≥ 2. Theorem 3.8 improves this result, showing local well-posedness for s ≥ 1 and r > 3. Theorem 4.3 demonstrates global existence under the conditions s ≥ 1, r > 4, Rψ ∈ L2(R2), and F(|∇ϕ|2) ∈ L1(R2), along with a positivity condition on F. Theorem 5.2 establishes finite-time blow-up under the conditions Rϕ, Rψ ∈ L2(R2), F(|∇ϕ|2) ∈ L1(R2), a condition on F′, and a negative initial energy. The paper uses the Sobolev Embedding Theorem (Lemma 3.1) which states that if s > n/2 + k, then Hs(Rn) ⊂ Ck(Rn) ∩ L∞(Rn). Lemma 3.5 states that if s ≥ 1 and F ∈ C[s]+1(R), then for any w ∈ Xs, ∂F/∂wx(|∇w|2) ∈ Hs−1 and ∂F/∂wy(|∇w|2) ∈ Hs−1. Lemma 3.9 states that there is a global solution of the Cauchy problem (1.1)-(1.2) if and only if for any T > 0, lim supt→T−(∥wx(t)∥∞ + ∥wy(t)∥∞) < ∞. The paper does not provide any comparisons with other methods or datasets.

Interpretation Implications
The findings provide insights into the behavior of solutions to the Cauchy problem for a class of two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equations. The local well-posedness results (Theorems 3.7 and 3.8) indicate that the problem is well-defined and has unique solutions for a short time interval under certain regularity conditions on the initial data and the convolution kernel. The global existence theorem (Theorem 4.3) implies that, under specific conditions on the nonlinearity and initial data, solutions can exist for all time. The finite-time blow-up theorem (Theorem 5.2) suggests that, under different conditions, solutions can develop singularities in finite time. The results highlight the importance of the convolution kernel's properties, the initial data's smoothness, and the nonlinearity's characteristics in determining the long-time behavior of solutions. The findings contribute to the theoretical understanding of wave propagation in nonlocally elastic materials, offering a mathematical framework for analyzing the dynamics of these systems. The results suggest that the interplay between the nonlocal effects, the initial conditions, and the nonlinearity can lead to a variety of solution behaviors, including global existence and finite-time blow-up.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is its focus on specific conditions for global existence and blow-up, which may not always be met in real-world scenarios. The results are dependent on the assumptions made about the convolution kernel, the initial data, and the nonlinearity. The analysis is purely theoretical, and the results' applicability to physical systems depends on the validity of the model and the accuracy of the assumptions. The paper does not address the question of how the results might change if the assumptions are relaxed. The absence of numerical simulations or experimental validation limits the ability to assess the model's predictive power. The paper does not discuss any internal inconsistencies. The study does not address the impact of different kernel functions or the sensitivity of the results to changes in the parameters.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the extension of techniques used for one-dimensional nonlinear nonlocal Boussinesq-type wave equations to the analysis of a two-dimensional nonlocal nonlinear wave equation governing anti-plane shear motions. (2) The strongest evidence comes from the theorems that demonstrate local well-posedness, global existence, and finite-time blow-up, with specific conditions on the Sobolev space, the kernel's regularity, and the initial data. For example, Theorem 3.7 proves local well-posedness for s > 2 and r ≥ 2. Blow-up and global existence for a general class of nonlocal
nonlinear coupled wave equations
N. Duruk1, H. A. Erbay2∗, A. Erkip1
1 Faculty of Engineering and Natural Sciences, Sabanci University, Tuzla 34956, Istanbul, Turkey
2 Department of Mathematics, Isik University, Sile 34980, Istanbul, Turkey
Abstract
We study the initial-value problem for a general class of nonlinear nonlocal coupled
wave equations. The problem involves convolution operators with kernel functions whose
Fourier transforms are nonnegative. Some well-known examples of nonlinear wave equa-
tions, such as coupled Boussinesq-type equations arising in elasticity and in quasi-continuum
approximation of dense lattices, follow from the present model for suitable choices of the
kernel functions. We establish local existence and suﬃcient conditions for ﬁnite time
blow-up and as well as global existence of solutions of the problem.
Keywords:
Nonlocal Cauchy problem, Boussinesq equation, Global existence, Blow-up,
Nonlocal elasticity.
2000 MSC: 74H20, 74J30, 74B20

chain of particles with elastic couplings [12], for water waves with surface tension [13]
