literature is based on methods for choosing the optimal 
threshold which can be adaptive or non-adaptive to the image. 
2.2.1 Non-Adaptive Thresholds 
VISU Shrink [12] is non-adaptive universal threshold, 
which depends only on number of data points. It has 
asymptotic equivalence suggesting best performance in terms 
of MSE when the number of pixels reaches infinity. VISU 
Shrink is known to yield overly smoothed images because its 
threshold choice can be unwarrantedly large due to its 
dependence on the number of pixels in the image. 
2.2.2 Adaptive Thresholds 
SURE Shrink [12] uses a hybrid of the universal threshold 
and the SURE [Stein‟s Unbiased Risk Estimator] threshold 
and performs better than VISU Shrink. Bayes Shrink [17], 
[18] minimizes the Bayes‟ Risk Estimator function assuming 
generalized Gaussian prior and thus yielding data adaptive 
threshold. Bayes Shrink outperforms SURE Shrink most of the 
times. Cross Validation [19] replaces wavelet coefficient with 
the weighted average of neighborhood coefficients to 
minimize generalized cross validation (GCV) function 
providing optimum threshold for every coefficient. The 
assumption that one can distinguish noise from the signal 
solely based on coefficient magnitudes is violated when noise 
levels are higher than signal magnitudes. Under this high noise 
circumstance, the spatial configuration of neighboring wavelet 
coefficients can play an important role in noise-signal 
classifications. Signals tend to form meaningful features (e.g. 
straight lines, curves), while noisy coefficients often scatter 
randomly. 
2.3 Non-orthogonal Wavelet Transforms 
Un-decimated Wavelet Transform (UDWT) has also been 
used for decomposing the signal to provide visually better 
solution. Since UDWT is shift invariant it avoids visual 
artifacts such as pseudo-Gibbs phenomenon. Though the 
improvement in results is much higher, use of UDWT adds a 
large overhead of computations thus making it less feasible. In 
[20] normal hard/soft thresholding was extended to Shift 
Invariant Discrete Wavelet Transform. In [21] Shift Invariant 
Wavelet Packet Decomposition (SIWPD) is exploited to 
obtain number of basic functions. Then using minimum 
description length principle the best basis function was found 
out which yielded smallest code length required for 
description of the given data. Then, thresholding was applied 
to denoise the data. In addition to UDWT, use of multi 
wavelets is explored which further enhances the performance 
but further increases the computation complexity. The 
multiwavelets are obtained by applying more than one 
function (scaling function) to given dataset. Multi wavelets 
possess properties such as short support, symmetry, and the 
most importantly higher order of vanishing moments. This 
combination of shift invariance and Multiwavelets is 
implemented in [22] which give superior results for the Lena 
image in context of MSE. 
2.4. Wavelet Coefficient Model 
This approach focuses on exploiting the multi resolution 
properties of Wavelet Transform. This technique identifies 
close correlation of signal at different resolutions by observing 
the signal across multiple resolutions. This method produces 
excellent output but is computationally much more complex 
and expensive. The modeling of the wavelet coefficients can 
either be deterministic or statistical. 
2.4.1 Deterministic 
 The Deterministic method of modeling involves creating 
tree structure of wavelet coefficients with every level in the 
tree representing each scale of transformation and nodes 
representing the wavelet coefficients. This approach is 
adopted in [23]. The optimal tree approximation displays a 
hierarchical interpretation of wavelet decomposition. Wavelet 
coefficients of singularities have large wavelet coefficients 
that persist along the branches of tree. Thus if a wavelet 
coefficient has strong presence at particular node then in case 
of it being signal, its presence should be more pronounced at 
its parent nodes. If it is noisy coefficient, for instance spurious 
blip, then such consistent presence will be missing. 
2.4.2. Statistical Modeling of Wavelet Coefficients 
This approach focuses on some more interesting and 
appealing properties of the Wavelet Transform such as multi 
scale correlation between the wavelet coefficients local 
correlation between neighborhood coefficients etc. This 
approach has an inherent goal of perfect in the exact modeling 
of image data with use of Wavelet transform.  
IV. RESULT AND CONCLUSION 
Performance of different denoising algorithms is measured 
by using quantitative performance measures such as peak 
signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and image enhancement factor 
(IEF). 
Where MSE stands for mean square error, IEF stands for 
image enhancement factor, M x N is size of the image, Y 
represents the original image,    denotes the de-noised image, 
and η represents the noisy image.  The different denoising 
algorithms were applied to gray scale image of Lena 
containing noise density of 90%.

Executive Summary
This paper presents a comparative analysis of various image denoising algorithms, focusing on their performance in removing noise from grayscale images. The study categorizes noise types into additive (e.g., Gaussian) and multiplicative (e.g., speckle) categories, and examines spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain) techniques. The performance of different denoising algorithms was evaluated using Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Image Enhancement Factor (IEF) metrics. The algorithms were tested on a grayscale Lena image corrupted with 90% noise density. The results, as presented in Table I, show that the Modified Decision Based Un-symmetric Trimmed Median Filter (MDBUTMF) achieved the highest PSNR (17.9865) and IEF (16.2066) values, indicating superior denoising performance. The study highlights the importance of selecting an appropriate denoising algorithm based on the type of noise present in the image. A key limitation is the exclusive focus on a single test image (Lena) and a specific noise density, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Future research directions include exploring more advanced denoising techniques and evaluating their performance across diverse image datasets and noise conditions.

Research Context
Image restoration is a crucial aspect of digital image processing, addressing degradations caused by blurring and noise. Noise, introduced during image acquisition and transmission, reduces image quality. Existing research has explored various denoising algorithms, but the selection of the most effective method is application-dependent, necessitating a thorough understanding of noise types and algorithm performance. This paper addresses the need for a comparative analysis of different denoising techniques to guide algorithm selection. Prior work has often focused on specific denoising methods without a comprehensive comparison across different categories of algorithms. This study aims to provide a comparative analysis of various denoising algorithms, including spatial and transform domain filtering methods, to address this gap.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: How do different image denoising algorithms perform in terms of PSNR and IEF when applied to a grayscale image corrupted with noise? The study implicitly tests the hypothesis that certain denoising algorithms will outperform others in terms of PSNR and IEF. The alternative hypothesis is that the performance differences between the algorithms will be minimal or that the ranking of algorithms will vary depending on the noise type and density. The study aims to identify the algorithm(s) that provide the best balance between noise reduction and preservation of image details. The research differs from prior work by providing a direct comparison of a range of denoising algorithms, including spatial and transform domain filtering methods, using quantitative metrics (PSNR and IEF) to evaluate their performance.

Methodological Details
The study employs an empirical approach to compare the performance of various image denoising algorithms. The study does not explicitly state the study design, but it can be inferred as an experimental comparison of different denoising algorithms. The participants/sample consists of a single grayscale image of Lena. The image is corrupted with noise. The specific noise type is not specified but the noise density is 90%. The study does not provide information on demographics or inclusion/exclusion criteria. The materials/data used include the grayscale Lena image and various image denoising algorithms. The software used is not specified. The procedure involves applying different denoising algorithms to the noisy Lena image and evaluating the results using PSNR and IEF metrics. The specific steps for each algorithm are not detailed. The analysis involves calculating PSNR and IEF for each denoised image. The study does not mention any pre-registration or multiple-comparison corrections. The study adheres to ethical considerations by not involving human subjects or sensitive data.

Procedures Architectures
The paper does not provide detailed descriptions of the specific architectures or implementations of the denoising algorithms. The paper categorizes the denoising algorithms into spatial filtering (linear and non-linear) and transform domain filtering (spatial-frequency and wavelet domain). Spatial filtering includes linear filters (e.g., mean filter, Wiener filter) and non-linear filters (e.g., weighted median, rank conditioned rank selection, relaxed median). Transform domain filtering includes spatial-frequency filtering using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) and wavelet domain filtering. Wavelet domain filtering is further divided into linear filters (e.g., Wiener filter in the wavelet domain) and non-linear threshold filtering (e.g., VISU Shrink, SURE Shrink, Bayes Shrink, Cross Validation). The paper also mentions the use of Un-decimated Wavelet Transform (UDWT) and multiwavelets. The paper does not specify the hyperparameters, training schedules, or hardware used for the algorithms. The paper does not explicitly state what is new, but it provides a comparative analysis of different denoising algorithms, which is the main contribution.

Key Results
The study's key results are presented in Table I, which compares the performance of different image denoising filters. The table includes the following results for each filter: Mean Filter (MF): PSNR = 6.5759, IEF = 1.1712; Adaptive Mean Filter (AMF): PSNR = 8.0603, IEF = 1.6499; Progressive Switching Median Filter (PSMF): PSNR = 6.7847, IEF = 1.2257; Decision Based Algorithm (DBA): PSNR = 17.1205, IEF = 13.2768; Modified Decision Based Algorithm (MDBA): PSNR = 17.2242, IEF = 13.5976; Modified Decision Based Un-symmetric Trimmed Median Filter (MDBUTMF): PSNR = 17.9865, IEF = 16.2066. The MDBUTMF achieved the highest PSNR and IEF values, indicating superior denoising performance. The DBA and MDBA also performed well, but not as well as the MDBUTMF. The other filters (MF, AMF, PSMF) showed significantly lower PSNR and IEF values. No information on effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values is provided.

Interpretation Implications
The results suggest that the MDBUTMF is the most effective denoising algorithm among those tested, as indicated by its superior PSNR and IEF values. The findings highlight the importance of selecting the appropriate denoising algorithm based on its characteristics. The results imply that the MDBUTMF is particularly well-suited for removing noise from the Lena image with a 90% noise density. The study does not propose any specific mechanisms for why the MDBUTMF performs better, but it does suggest that the algorithm's design allows it to effectively remove noise while preserving image details. The scope of the findings is limited to the specific image and noise conditions used in the study. The understanding of image denoising is shifted by providing a direct comparison of a range of denoising algorithms, which can guide practitioners in selecting the most appropriate algorithm for their needs.

Contradictions Limitations
A key limitation of the study is the use of a single test image (Lena) and a specific noise density (90%), which limits the generalizability of the findings. The study does not specify the type of noise added to the image, which is crucial for understanding the algorithm's performance. The lack of detailed information on the algorithms' implementations, including hyperparameters and software versions, makes it difficult to reproduce the results. The study does not provide information on the computational complexity of the algorithms, which is an important factor in practical applications. The study does not include any error analysis or sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of the results. The study does not compare the results with other relevant studies, which limits the ability to assess the novelty and significance of the findings. The absence of information on the specific noise type and the algorithms' implementations are key threats to inference.

Table I is the most important table, presenting a quantitative comparison of the denoising algorithms. The table includes the PSNR and IEF values for each algorithm, which are the primary metrics used to evaluate performance. The table's axes are the different denoising filters and the metrics PSNR and IEF. The table substantiates the core claim that the MDBUTMF outperforms other algorithms in terms of PSNR and IEF.

Three Takeaways
(1) The study's core contribution is a comparative analysis of various image denoising algorithms, providing quantitative performance metrics for each algorithm. (2) The strongest evidence is the quantitative results presented in Table I, which demonstrate that the MDBUTMF achieves the highest PSNR (17.9865) and IEF (16.2066) values. Real-Time Ramsey Interferometry in Fractional Quantum Hall States
Tal Goren and Karyn Le Hur
Centre de Physique Th´eorique, ´Ecole Polytechnique,
CNRS, Universit´e Paris-Saclay, 91128 Palaiseau, France
(Dated: January 23, 2019)
We study the time-dependent dynamical phase of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states
using Ramsey interferometry. A Ramsey two-pulse voltage modulation generates an interference
term in the current noise of a quantum point contact oscillating with the dynamical phase. We
show that the interference pattern probes the Green’s function of the fractional quasi-particles in
the time domain and reveals the fractional charge. We address both the case of a point-like tunnel
junction and the case of momentum-resolved tunneling which also provides information on the speed
of those quasiparticles propagating along the edge. For the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall case, the
Ramsey signal can diﬀerentiate between the Pfaﬃan and anti-Pfaﬃan states.
One of the main attributes of the fractional quantum
Hall eﬀect is the occurrence of excitations with fractional
charge and statistics. The edge states of such a quan-
tum Hall system are described by a chiral Luttinger liq-
uid eﬀective theory which illustrates the emergence of
fractional quasi-particles due to electron-electron inter-
actions in quantum Hall states.1,2
Ramsey interferometry has been recently suggested
to probe the dynamics of mesoscopic electron systems3
and strongly correlated systems such as one-dimensional
quasicondensates4, spin ensembles5 and Rydberg atoms6.
Here, we study Ramsey interferometry in the Abelian
and 5/2 non-Abelian fractional quantum Hall states at
the edges, through the quantum Hall bar geometry.
A small constriction in the Hall bar induces a cou-

oscillates with the time delay between the pulses which
we denote by t0. Therefore the Ramsey protocol allows

Executive Summary
This paper proposes a method to probe the dynamics of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states using Ramsey interferometry. The authors theoretically analyze how a two-pulse voltage modulation in a quantum point contact (QPC) can generate an interference pattern in the current noise, which oscillates with the dynamical phase of the quasiparticles. This pattern is shown to be sensitive to the Green's function, revealing the fractional charge and providing a way to differentiate between different quantum Hall states, such as the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states at filling factor 5/2. The study considers two QPC geometries: a constriction in a Hall bar allowing tunneling of fractional quasiparticles, and tunneling between two separated Hall droplets where electrons tunnel. The main finding is that the Ramsey interference pattern can reveal the charge and Green's function of the tunneling particles. The method is advantageous because it allows for a time-resolved measurement of the dynamical phase and Green’s function by scanning the time delay between the voltage pulses. The primary limitation is that the method does not detect exchange statistics, as it only involves a single QPC. The work suggests a new way to characterize topological states of matter.

Research Context
The fractional quantum Hall effect exhibits excitations with fractional charge and statistics, with edge states described by chiral Luttinger liquid theory. Prior work has used Ramsey interferometry to study the dynamics of mesoscopic electron systems, quasicondensates, spin ensembles, and Rydberg atoms. However, there is a need for methods to probe the dynamics of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states. This work addresses this gap by applying Ramsey interferometry to quantum Hall edge states, offering a time-resolved method to measure the dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles. Prior techniques like Mach-Zehnder interferometry can probe charge fractionalization and statistics, but are limited by the difficulty of controlling bulk quasiparticles.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: Can Ramsey interferometry be used to probe the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states, and can it differentiate between different quantum Hall states? The hypothesis is that a Ramsey two-pulse voltage modulation applied to a QPC will generate an interference pattern in the current noise that oscillates with the dynamical phase of the fractional quasiparticles. This pattern will be sensitive to the Green's function of the quasiparticles, allowing for the determination of their fractional charge and potentially distinguishing between different topological states, such as the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states at filling factor 5/2. The alternative hypothesis is that the interference pattern will not be sensitive to the Green's function or will not be able to differentiate between different quantum Hall states. This work differs from prior studies by applying Ramsey interferometry to quantum Hall edge states to probe the dynamics of fractional quasiparticles, providing a time-resolved measurement method.

Methodological Details
The study is theoretical, involving the application of Ramsey interferometry to quantum Hall edge states. The model considers a quantum Hall bar geometry with a QPC, which induces tunneling between counter-propagating edge states. The tunneling is described by a Hamiltonian (Equation 5) that includes a dynamical phase, dependent on the voltage drop across the QPC and the charge of the tunneling particle. The current noise, defined as the Fourier transform of the current-current correlation function (Equation 10), is analyzed under a time-dependent voltage modulation. The analysis uses the Keldysh formalism, suitable for non-equilibrium systems. The Ramsey voltage modulation consists of two short pulses separated by a delay time, t0, on top of a constant voltage (Equation 16). The Green's functions of the tunneling particles are used to calculate the current noise. The study considers Laughlin states with filling factor ν = 1/(2n+1), and also examines the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall case. The analysis involves the use of bosonic chiral fields and the corresponding Green's functions (Equation 22). The study also considers momentum-resolved tunneling, where the tunnel junction is long compared to the Fermi wavelength. The analysis includes the application of the stationary phase approximation and the time-reversal symmetry of the Green’s functions. No experimental data is used. The study does not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. The Planck constant is fixed to ℏ = h/(2π) = 1.

Procedures Architectures
The study focuses on the theoretical application of Ramsey interferometry to quantum Hall edge states. The core component is a QPC, a small constriction in a Hall bar that allows for tunneling between counter-propagating edge states. The system is modeled using a Hamiltonian (Equation 5) that includes a dynamical phase, which is the integral of the voltage across the QPC over time. The voltage modulation is the key input, specifically a Ramsey voltage modulation consisting of two short pulses separated by a delay time, t0, and a constant voltage (Equation 16). The output is the current noise, specifically its Fourier transform (Equation 10), which is calculated using the Keldysh formalism. The model incorporates the Green's functions of the tunneling particles, which are derived from the chiral fields describing the edge states. The analysis involves mathematical manipulations of the current-current correlation function to second order in perturbation theory. The model considers two QPC geometries: tunneling between the two edges of a Hall bar (fractional quasiparticles) and tunneling between two separated Hall droplets (electrons). The model also considers momentum-resolved tunneling, where the tunnel junction is long compared to the Fermi wavelength. The novelty lies in applying Ramsey interferometry to quantum Hall edge states to probe the dynamics of fractional quasiparticles and differentiate between quantum Hall states.

Key Results
The study derives an expression for the current noise under Ramsey voltage modulation (Equation 21). The noise exhibits a Ramsey interference pattern oscillating with the delay time t0 at a frequency ω − qVdc. The charge, q, appearing in this formula is the dressed charge in the fluid. For Laughlin states, the current noise is given by Equation 24, and for electrons, it is given by Equation 25. The fractionalization manifests in the Ramsey interference pattern in the prefactor (qD)^2, the Green's function of the tunneling particles, and the dynamical phase factor qVdc. The amplitude of the Ramsey oscillations decays exponentially in the high-temperature limit and follows a power law in the low-temperature limit. For momentum-resolved tunneling, the noise under Ramsey voltage modulation is given by Equation 32. For the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall case, the Ramsey signal can differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states (Equation 34). The amplitude of the Ramsey oscillations provides information on the Green's functions of the tunneling particles. The study shows that the Ramsey signal can distinguish between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states, but not between the Pfaffian and particle-hole Pfaffian states. The study does not report any baseline comparisons or effect sizes.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that Ramsey interferometry can be used to probe the time-dependent dynamical phase and Green's function of fractional quasiparticles in quantum Hall states. The charge of the tunneling particles, the Green's function, and the dynamical phase factor all contribute to the Ramsey interference pattern. The amplitude of the oscillations provides information on the Green's functions of the tunneling particles, allowing for the detection of the Green's functions in the time domain. The ability to differentiate between the Pfaffian and anti-Pfaffian states suggests that Ramsey interferometry can be used to characterize topological states of matter. The proposed mechanism is the interference between tunneling events at the QPC, separated by a time delay. The scope condition is the applicability to quantum Hall edge states, specifically Laughlin states and the 5/2 fractional quantum Hall state. This work shifts the understanding by providing a new method to probe the dynamics of fractional quasiparticles and characterize topological states.

Contradictions Limitations
The study is limited by its theoretical nature, as it does not involve experimental validation. The method does not detect exchange statistics, as it only involves a single QPC. The model relies on approximations, such as the stationary phase approximation. The study does not discuss the impact of experimental noise or imperfections. The study does not provide details on the experimental feasibility of the proposed method. The study does not address the limitations of the Keldysh formalism in describing the system. The study does not discuss the potential for this method to be applied to other quantum systems. The study does not mention any potential conflicts with prior literature. The study does not provide any information on the specific values of the parameters used in the calculations, such as the voltage pulse duration or the temperature.

An algorithm for stress and mixed control in Galerkin based FFT
homogenization
S. Lucarini1,2 and J. Segurado1,2,*
1IMDEA Materials Institute ,C/ Eric Kandel 2, 28906, Getafe, Madrid, Spain.
2Technical University of Madrid/Universidad Polit´ecnica de Madrid, Department of
Materials Science, E. T. S. de Ingenieros de Caminos , C/ Profesor Aranguren s/n 28040 -
Madrid, Spain.
*Corresponding author at: IMDEA Materials Institute, Spain. javier.segurado@imdea.org
(J. Segurado)
January 23, 2019
Abstract
A new algorithm is proposed to impose a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient
history in the context of non-linear Galerkin based FFT homogenization. The method proposed is based
in the deﬁnition of a modiﬁed projection operator in which the null frequencies enforce the type of
control (stress or strain) for each component of either the macroscopic ﬁrst Piola stress or the deformation
gradient. The resulting problem is solved exactly as the original variational method and it does not require
additional iterations compared to the strain control version, neither in the linear iterative solver, nor in
the Newton scheme. The eﬃciency of the method proposed is demonstrated with a series of numerical
examples, including a polycrystal and a particle reinforced hyperelastic material.
1
1
Introduction
Computational homogenization aims to simulate the mechanical response of a material under a given macro-
scopic stress, strain or mixed loading path by solving a boundary problem in a periodic representative volume
element (RVE) of its microstructure. The ﬁnite element method (FE) has been traditionally used to solve the
boundary value problem allowing to impose any macroscopic load history combining the control of diﬀerent
components of the strain and stress average ﬁelds. Fast Fourier transform (FFT) based homogenization has
become a very popular alternative to FE. FFT methods solve the boundary problem replacing the diﬀerential
operators in the governing partial diﬀerential equation by their equivalent counterparts in the Fourier space.
The computational performance of this method compared to FE makes it ideal to simulate complex geome-
tries comprising millions of degrees of freedom. However, imposing a macroscopic stress or mixed loading
path is not a direct task in FFT. Nevertheless, obtaining the material response in an eﬃcient manner for any
generic loading path is fundamental to solve cases of interest such as uniaxial loading, controlled triaxility or
cyclic stress control tests.
FFT homogenization was ﬁrst proposed by H. Moulinec and P. Suquet (Moulinec and Suquet, 1994, 1998)
based on solving the Lippmann-Schwinger equation with a reference material using a ﬁxed-point algorithm.
Since then, several approaches based on similar principles have been proposed (Eyre and Milton, 1999; Michel

1
arXiv:1901.06531v1  [cond-mat.mtrl-sci]  19 Jan 2019

et al., 2001; Monchiet and Bonnet, 2012; Kabel et al., 2014) . These approaches require the use of a reference
medium, which properties in some cases may strongly determine the convergence rate. In these classical
schemes, load is introduced imposing the full macroscopic strain tensor and when stress or mixed control is
required (i.e. to impose uniaxial tension) iterative approaches are the usual solution Michel et al. (1999);
Eisenlohr et al. (2013) . Under this procedure the algorithm still imposes the full macroscopic strain tensor
and corrects it in an iterative manner in order to obtain at the end of the iteration process the macroscopic
stress tensor components imposed as input.
As a result of the corrections to the applied strain during
iterations, the number of iterations per step signiﬁcantly increases respect the strain control. An alternative
approach for classic schemes under mixed control was recently proposed by Kabel et al.
(Kabel et al.,
2016). The method consists in modifying the original basic scheme (Moulinec and Suquet, 1994) through the
introduction of projection tensors to account for the load control and solving the problem using an iterative
Krylov solver. This method for stress control is more eﬃcient than the iterative approaches although still
requires the deﬁnition of a reference medium which properties might inﬂuence the convergence rate.
A diﬀerent approach for FFT homogenization is the Galerkin based approach in which the problem is
derived using a weak formulation, very similar to ﬁnite elements, and projection operators that ensure the
compatibility of the strain ﬁelds. The resulting method (Vondˇrejc et al., 2014; Zeman et al., 2017; de Geus
et al., 2017) does not require a reference medium and make direct use of the corresponding tangents of
the material behavior to improve the convergence. Moreover, this framework can be easily adapted to use
any complex non-linear constitutive equation as the crystal plasticity model (Lucarini and Segurado, 2018).
However, the variational approach was still formulated imposing the history of the macroscopic deformation
gradient.
In this work, we extend the variational algorithm for ﬁnite strains(de Geus et al., 2017) to use stress and
mixed control of the macroscopic load history using a direct method based on a modiﬁed project operator
and preserving the computational performance of the original method. This paper summarizes in Section
2 the original FFT-based variational approach and then presents the modiﬁed projection operator and the
resulting algorithm for mixed control. In Section 3 examples using diﬀerent material models and loading
paths will be run and, ﬁnally, the performance of the method is analyzed.

Conclusions
A new algorithm is proposed to impose a macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient history

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a novel algorithm for imposing macroscopic stress or mixed stress/deformation gradient histories within the framework of non-linear Galerkin-based Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) homogenization. The method modifies the projection operator in the Fourier space, enabling control over the macroscopic first Piola stress or deformation gradient components. Unlike existing iterative approaches for stress control in FFT homogenization, the proposed algorithm solves the problem directly, without requiring additional iterations compared to strain control versions, neither in the linear iterative solver nor in the Newton scheme. The algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through numerical examples, including simulations of a polycrystal and a particle-reinforced hyperelastic material. Key findings indicate that the algorithm achieves comparable convergence rates and simulation times to strain control methods, while accurately simulating stress-controlled and mixed-control loading scenarios. The novelty lies in the direct implementation of stress and mixed control within the Galerkin-based FFT homogenization, avoiding the iterative procedures typical of other FFT methods. This work is significant because it enhances the capabilities of FFT-based computational homogenization, enabling the simulation of complex loading conditions without increasing computational cost. A limitation is that the method's performance is evaluated on specific material models and loading paths; further validation across a broader range of materials and loading scenarios is needed.

Research Context
Computational homogenization is used to simulate the mechanical response of materials under various loading conditions by solving boundary problems in a periodic representative volume element (RVE). While the finite element method (FEM) has been traditionally used, FFT-based homogenization offers a computationally efficient alternative, particularly for complex geometries. Existing FFT methods often struggle with imposing macroscopic stress or mixed loading paths directly, typically relying on iterative approaches. These iterative methods can increase the number of iterations per step. The Galerkin-based approach, which uses a weak formulation and projection operators, offers an alternative that does not require a reference medium and can incorporate complex non-linear constitutive equations. This work addresses the limitation of the Galerkin-based approach, which was originally formulated for strain control, by extending it to handle stress and mixed control scenarios without the computational overhead of iterative methods.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to efficiently implement macroscopic stress and mixed stress/deformation gradient control within a Galerkin-based FFT homogenization framework. The primary hypothesis is that a modified projection operator can be defined to directly impose stress or mixed control, preserving the computational efficiency of the original strain-controlled method. An alternative hypothesis is that the proposed method will require additional iterations, increasing computational cost. The study tests this hypothesis by comparing the convergence rate and simulation time of the proposed algorithm with existing strain control methods and iterative stress control methods. The research also examines the accuracy of the simulations under different loading conditions, comparing the results of stress, strain, and mixed control scenarios. The study's design allows for a direct comparison of the proposed method's performance against established techniques, assessing its ability to accurately simulate material behavior under various loading conditions without compromising computational efficiency. The study differs from prior work by directly addressing the limitations of Galerkin-based FFT homogenization in handling stress and mixed control, rather than relying on iterative correction schemes.

Methodological Details
The study employs a Galerkin-based FFT homogenization method to simulate the mechanical response of materials under different loading conditions. The study uses a periodic RVE discretized into nx, ny, and nz voxels. The linear momentum balance is imposed in its weak form in the reference configuration. The test functions are virtual deformation gradients premultiplied by a projector operator to enforce their compatibility. The discrete form of the linear momentum balance is given by G(P(F, α)) = 0, where P is the first Piola-Kirchhoff stress, F is the deformation gradient field, α are internal variables, and G is a linear map. The linear map corresponds to a convolution in real space, computed using the discrete Fourier transform and its inverse. The study uses two material models: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic matrix and a polycrystal with crystal plasticity. The hyperelastic material is modeled using a Saint Venant-Kirchhoff hyperelastic model, with matrix properties of µ = 28 Pa and k = 46.67 Pa, and particles with properties ten times stiffer. The polycrystal model uses an elasto-visco-plastic behavior dependent on orientation and internal variables. The RVE for the hyperelastic composite contains 4 particles with a volume fraction of 0.2 and is discretized using 64^3 voxels. The polycrystal RVE is a cube discretized in 64^3 voxels and contains around 200 randomly oriented grains. Three loading conditions are applied to the hyperelastic material: mixed control (macroscopic deformation gradient imposed in x-direction, stress-free in other directions), full stress control (linear ramp from 0 to the final stress from the mixed control case), and full strain control (linear ramp to the final deformation gradient from the mixed control case). Four loading conditions are applied to the polycrystal: mixed control, full stress control, full strain control, and a pseudo-uniaxial tensile test (isochoric deformation). The simulations are performed using a pseudo-time t, with the final stage reached at t = tend. The load is divided into increments, and equilibrium is solved in each increment. The convergence criteria for the iterative linear solver is the voxel-averaged L2 norm of the residual, and for the Newton solver is the maximum deformation gradient correction relative to the averaged deformation gradient. The tolerances used are 10^-8 and 10^-6 for the linear and Newton solvers, respectively. The study does not mention any pre-registration or ethics review.

Procedures Architectures
The core of the methodology is a Galerkin-based FFT homogenization method. The method solves the linear momentum balance equation in its weak form, utilizing a modified projection operator in the Fourier space to enforce the desired loading conditions. The original projection operator, bG, is modified to create bG* for stress and mixed control. The modification involves altering the operator's behavior at null frequencies. For stress control, the null frequency projects the average part of a field into itself, achieved by defining its value as the fourth-order identity tensor. For mixed control, the operator is further modified, with the null frequency value depending on whether stress or strain is controlled in a given direction. The algorithm involves splitting the macroscopic deformation gradient into increments and solving a non-linear equation for each time increment. The non-linear system is solved iteratively, linearizing the stress around the last iteration of the deformation gradient. The linear system is solved using the conjugate gradient method. The constitutive equations used are a Saint Venant-Kirchhoff hyperelastic model for the composite and an elasto-visco-plastic crystal plasticity model for the polycrystal. The hyperelastic model is defined by shear and bulk moduli. The crystal plasticity model incorporates grain orientation and internal variables. The simulations are performed on RVEs discretized into voxels, with the number of voxels specified for each material. The loading conditions are implemented by defining ramps for the deformation gradient or stress components. The software used is not explicitly mentioned, but the method relies on FFT algorithms and iterative solvers. The key novelty is the direct implementation of stress and mixed control through the modified projection operator, avoiding the need for iterative corrections.

Key Results
The study presents results for two material models: a particle-reinforced hyperelastic composite and a polycrystal. For the hyperelastic composite, the longitudinal response under mixed control (case 1) and full stress control (case 2) are nearly identical, with the macroscopic stress superposed (Figure 1(b)). The transverse response (Figure 1(c)) shows zero transverse stresses for stress and mixed control, while strain control (case 3) develops small compressive stresses. For the polycrystal, cases 1 and 2 are similar, but not exactly superposed due to strain rate effects. Case 3 reaches the same endpoint, but the path is different, with compressive transverse stresses developing. Case 4, a pseudo-uniaxial test, shows significant differences from a real uniaxial tensile test, particularly in the transverse response (Figure 2). The performance comparison shows that the stress and mixed control simulations (cases 1 and 2) for the hyperelastic model took approximately the same number of iterations as full strain control (case 3) (Figure 3(a)). In the polycrystal, a similar tendency is achieved (Figure 3(b)). The simulation times for the hyperelastic simulations were almost identical for every boundary condition. In the polycrystal, the stress control case (2) was faster than the others due to the elastic steps (Figure 3(c)). The convergence criteria used were a voxel averaged value of the L2 norm of the residual (10^-8) for the linear solver and the maximum deformation gradient correction relative to the averaged deformation gradient (10^-6) for the Newton solver.

Interpretation Implications
The findings support the hypothesis that a modified projection operator can effectively implement stress and mixed control in Galerkin-based FFT homogenization without increasing computational cost. The comparable performance of the proposed algorithm with strain control methods suggests that the modification does not introduce significant overhead. The accurate simulation of stress-controlled and mixed-control loading scenarios, as demonstrated by the results on the hyperelastic composite and polycrystal, validates the method's ability to handle complex loading conditions. The differences observed in the transverse response of the polycrystal under different loading conditions highlight the importance of using appropriate boundary conditions for accurate simulations. The results imply that the choice of boundary conditions significantly impacts the simulated material behavior, especially for materials with complex constitutive behavior. The study's findings contribute to a better understanding of how to efficiently simulate material behavior under various loading conditions, providing a valuable tool for computational homogenization.

Contradictions Limitations
A potential limitation is that the method's performance is only evaluated on two specific material models (hyperelastic composite and polycrystal) and specific loading paths. The generalizability of the results to other materials and loading scenarios is not fully established. The study does not provide details on the specific software used, which could affect reproducibility. The absence of information on the random seed used for generating the polycrystal's grain orientations limits reproducibility. The study does not discuss any potential limitations related to the discretization of the RVE or the convergence of the iterative solvers. The study does not address the computational cost associated with the modified projection operator itself. The study does not provide a detailed error analysis or sensitivity analysis to assess the robustness of the method. The study does not discuss the impact of the chosen time step size on the accuracy of the simulations.

Figure 1 shows the results for the particle-reinforced hyperelastic material, including the RVE, and the first Piola-Kirchhoff stresses under three load cases. Figure 2 shows the results for the polycrystalline material, including the RVE, and the first Piola-Kirchhoff stresses under four load cases. Figure 3 presents a comparative analysis of the convergence and simulation times for the different loading cases, which is essential for evaluating the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is a new algorithm that directly implements macroscopic stress and mixed stress/deformation gradient control in Galerkin-based FFT homogenization by modifying the projection operator in the Fourier space, avoiding the iterative procedures typical of other FFT methods and enabling the simulation of complex loading conditions without increasing computational cost.

(2) The strongest evidence supporting the claims is the comparable convergence rates and simulation times observed for the proposed algorithm compared to strain control methods, along with the accurate simulation of stress-controlled and mixed-control loading scenarios, which is demonstrated through quantitative results in Figure 3 and the comparison of stress responses in Figures 1 and 2.

(3) The primary limitation is the evaluation of the method on only two material models and specific loading paths. Future work could involve validating the method across a broader range of materials and loading scenarios, and conducting a detailed error analysis to assess the robustness of the method.

papers.fulltext:
arXiv:1901.06488v1  [physics.optics]  19 Jan 2019
Nonlinearity in the dark: Broadband terahertz generation with extremely high
eﬃciency
Ming Fang,1, 2 Nian-Hai Shen,1, ∗Wei E.I. Sha,3 Zhixiang Huang,2, † Thomas Koschny,1 and Costas M. Soukoulis1, 4
1Ames Laboratory—U.S. DOE and Department of Physics and Astronomy, Iowa State University, Ames, Iowa 50011, USA
2Key Laboratory of Intelligent Computing and Signal Processing,
Ministry of Education, Anhui University, Hefei 230039, China
3Key Laboratory of Micro-nano Electronic Devices and Smart Systems of Zhejiang Province,
College of Information Science and Electronic Engineering, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou 310027, China
4Institute of Electronic Structure and Lasers (IESL), FORTH, 71110 Heraklion, Crete, Greece
(Dated: January 23, 2019)
Plasmonic metamaterials and metasurfaces oﬀer new opportunities in developing high perfor-
mance terahertz emitters/detectors beyond the limitations of conventional nonlinear materials. How-
ever, simple meta-atoms for second-order nonlinear applications encounter fundamental trade-oﬀs
in the necessary symmetry-breaking and local-ﬁeld enhancement due to radiation damping that is
inherent to the operating resonant mode and cannot be controlled separately. Here we present a
novel concept that eliminates this restriction obstructing the improvement of terahertz generation
eﬃciency in nonlinear metasurfaces based on metallic nano-resonators. This is achieved by comb-
ing a resonant dark-state metasurface, which locally drives nonlinear SRRs in the near ﬁeld, with
a speciﬁc spatial symmetry that enables destructive interference of the radiating linear moments
of the SRRs, and perfect absorption via simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling of
the pump radiation to the dark mode. Our proposal allows eliminating linear radiation damping,
while maintaining constructive interference and eﬀective radiation of the nonlinear components. We
numerically demonstrate a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility ∼10−11 m/V, one order im-
provement compared to previously reported split-ring-resonator metasurface, and correspondingly,
two orders of magnitude enhanced terahertz energy extraction should be expected with our conﬁgu-
ration under the same conditions. Our study oﬀers a paradigm of high eﬃciency tunable nonlinear
meta-devices and paves the way to revolutionary terahertz technologies and optoelectronic nano-
circuitry.
PACS numbers: 78.67.Pt, 42.65.-k, 42.25.Bs
Keywords: terahertz generation, metasurface, perfect absorption, dark state
Following the emergence of quantum-cascade lasers [1–
3] and ultrafast photoconductive switches [4], terahertz
(THz), a historically mysterious electromagnetic spec-
trum bridging microwaves and optics, in the past two
decades has gained signiﬁcant progresses in technolo-
gies, leading to tremendous transformative applications
in sensing, imaging and communication etc [4–9]. The
blooming of THz technologies and related applications at
current stage demand urgently eﬃcient and compact THz
emitters/detectors, yet the development of which remains
challenging. Many state-of-the-art THz sources are based
on nonlinear optical rectiﬁcation or diﬀerence-frequency
generation (DFG) in inorganic crystals, which suﬀer from
the drawbacks of either narrow bandwidth, subtle phase-
matching limitations, inevitable spectrum gaps or low
emission intensity [1–3, 10–13]. Surpassing natural ma-
terials, the freedom of designing our own subwavelength-
scale atoms as building blocks of metamaterials or meta-
surfaces has shown great ﬂexibilities in achieving versa-
tile functions in diﬀerent disciplines [14–26]. The coex-
istence of resonant nonlinearity and local ﬁeld enhance-
ment in properly designed meta-atoms [23, 27–32] open
up an alternative route for high-eﬃciency nonlinear de-
vices that eliminates those common restrictions. Screen-
ing eﬀects of the free-electron gas at the surface of metal-
lic nanoparticles lead to strong second-order nonlinearity
in their optical electric susceptibility, which contribute
constructively for the area of the metasurface with the
speciﬁcally designed non-symmetric shape of meta-atoms
[33, 34].
Very recently, a metasurface of 40 nm-thick
split-ring resonators (SRRs) was demonstrated to gener-
ate broadband gapless THz emission (up to 4 THz) with
the conversion eﬃciency close to 0.2 mm-thick optimal
ZnTe crystals [35]. Despite of being a seminal progress
toward compact tailorable THz sources even subwave-
length all-optical active devices beneﬁting next gener-
ation computations and communications, the nonlinear
optical response reported in this work is still fairly weak.
Therefore, a fundamental improvement in the nonlinear
eﬃciency with metasurface-based devices is critical.
In this Letter, we reveal a fundamental limit of con-
version eﬃciency in nonlinear metasurfaces, and accord-
ingly, we propose a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing
metasurface for THz generation that allows to circum-
vent it.
We demonstrate broadband THz emissions of
the metasurface with giant eﬃciency, about two orders
stronger compared to that of conventional SRR metasur-
face [35]. This opens up the opportunities for not only
revolutionary THz technologies but also high eﬃciency
on-chip nonlinear nano-optical devices.

2
Analyzing the performance of the SRR metasurface
and we ﬁnd that the major obstacles limiting the non-
linear conversion eﬃciency are dissipative and radiative
damping due to linear scattering. These two loss chan-
nels essentially govern the amplitude of the local near
ﬁeld, which in turn reduces the possible THz emission
intensity.
For the second-order nonlinearity, the ratio
of generated THz signal to scattered pump radiation is
directly proportional to the local near-ﬁeld amplitude,
thus the linear radiation damping reduces the THz out-
put. While the dissipative loss is hard to minimize and
essentially given by the available constituent materials,
we, therefore, target the radiative loss channel. Theo-
retically, we should be able to tackle these restrictions
and approach the critical limit in nonlinear eﬃciency
of a metasurface: a properly designed perfect absorbing
metasurface is applied to eliminate the linear radiative
damping and a low-loss dielectric dark element can be
introduced for high quality-factor strong local ﬁeld en-
hancement to drive the plasmonic nanoparticles, which
are generating the nonlinear signals.
In order to implement the concept, we tried to separate
the resonant local ﬁeld enhancement from the current
topology necessary for non-vanishing second-order non-
linearity. Instead of driving the SRR directly, we used a
resonant dark bound state in a silicon ﬁlm with a sub-
wavelength thickness to create local ﬁeld enhancement
and the strong evanescent surface ﬁelds of this quasi-
surface mode then drive the SRRs.
The low-loss di-
electric dark state allows us to concentrate signiﬁcant
amounts of electromagnetic ﬁeld energy in the metasur-
face and to create a high Q-factor with strong local ﬁeld
enhancement. Figure 1(a) presents the schematic unit of
our designed metasurface THz emitter. Two gold SRRs
(thickness tm), oriented in the same direction, asymmet-
rically sit on the two sides of a thin Si slab (thickness h),
which is periodically punctuated by metal walls (gold,
width 2a). The two SRRs are not only the key element
for THz emission via DFG, but also serve as a bridge cou-
pling the incident wave into the dark element (Si slab).
The introduction of metal walls is to quantize the modes
of the dielectric slab achieving a set of discrete resonant
dark states (see Fig. 1(b)).
Depending on the branch
of the dispersion, we may choose one desired mode fre-
quency with the speciﬁc corresponding spatial distribu-
tion of the composite system for operation. Here, for sim-
plicity, we select the second quantized mode on the lowest
branch of dispersion for the dielectric slab, that is, TE2,0
mode (marked by red circle in Fig. 1(b)), which gives
an anti-symmetric proﬁle of the electric ﬁeld as shown in
Fig. 1(a), a dark mode not being able to directly couple
to the incident plane wave. The geometric parameters
of the unit are designed to have the length L = 800 nm,
width W = 240 nm and thickness h = 100 nm, so the
operation wavelength is tuned within the typical high-
speed telecommunications range at around 1.5 µm. The
thickness of SRRs is set as tm = 50 nm.

For the optimized conﬁguration
with nearly perfect absorption, Fig. 3(b) presents the

the shaded area indicating the dissipation in the two
SRRs. In Fig. 3(c), we show the ﬁeld distributions, i.e.,
y-component of the electric ﬁeld, Ey, indicated in color
and the magnetic ﬁeld, H, marked with black arrows, in

y = 0. From Fig. 3(c) we see that the high quality-factor
TE2,0 mode of the Si slab is strongly excited, featuring
an anti-symmetric electric ﬁeld proﬁle, leading to a dra-
matic ﬁeld enhancement around SRRs. Considering the
metal walls always coincide with a ﬁeld minimum of the
dark mode, most of the incident energy will be dissipated
in SRRs and converted to nonlinear signals. We need to
point out that the dimensions of the SRRs are not criti-
cal, provided that the requirements of proper dark-mode
frequency and perfect absorption for eliminating the lin-
ear radiation are fulﬁlled.
For the nonlinear process, THz radiation, we can
choose to re-use the two SRRs, which are anyway neces-
sary for providing nonlinearity. Since the desired DFG
(or also second-harmonic generation) are second order
in the electric ﬁled E, the sign of the currents does not
matter and the nonlinear radiation of both SRRs adds
constructively in the far ﬁeld. The linear radiation, how-
ever, is opposite in phase and cancels in the far ﬁeld, thus
completely eliminating linear radiation damping. Since
radiation damping of the scattered linear ﬁelds, after lo-
cal dissipation, is the second biggest loss channel in the

Consequently, the two SRRs, driven by the TE2,0 mode of
the slab, show same second-order nonlinear dynamic but
opposite linear electric and magnetic dipole moments,
resulting in linear radiation cancellation and signiﬁcant
enhancement of THz radiation. By illuminating the de-
signed metasurface with a laser pulse at the resonant fre-
quency of the dark mode, strong THz emission from the
SRRs will be observed due to DFG arising from the elec-
tron gas in the metal of the SRRs, which can be described
by the hydrodynamic model [33, 34] (see Supplemental
Material for details). In the model, the convection term
plays the crucial role for the second-order nonlinearities,
qualitatively contributing in the format as the product
of current and accumulated charge density on the metal
surface.
For a rigorous analysis of THz radiation from the meta-
surface, we performed a self-consistent FDTD calcula-
tion based on the hydrodynamic model and Maxwells
equations (see Supplemental Material). A temporal op-
tical pulse was applied, Ey(t) = E0exp[−2ln(2)(t −
t0)2/τ 2]cos(ω0t), where the driving frequency equals the
resonant frequency of the dark mode, i.e., ω0 = ωdark,
the pulse duration τ = 140 fs (spectral width ∼3.2 THz)
and peak amplitude E0 = 2 × 107 V/m (see Supple-
mental Material for our estimation to thermal damage
threshold of the metasurface). In our calculations, both
linear and nonlinear dynamics of the electron gas under
the infrared light excitation have been fully considered.
FIG. 4. Terahertz enhancement of our design. (a) THz inten-
sity enhancement map of our design. (b) Time trace of THz
radiation from design (red) compared to that from traditional
SRR metasurface (blue). (c) Terahertz signal strength in de-
pendence of pump power for our design (red squares) and for
traditional SRRs (blue dots). The straight lines are from lin-

and charge density (color plot) of the SRRs. “+” and “−”
indicate charge accumulations.
In Fig. 4(a), we show a performance map of our pro-
posed THz emitter in term of THz enhancement deﬁned
as ηdark/ηSRR, where ηdark and ηSRR represent the THz
conversion eﬃciency of our system and that of the tra-
ditional SRR metasurface [35] (as a reference), respec-
tively. By properly settling the two SRRs, we can sig-
niﬁcantly eliminate the radiation damping, resulting in
more than 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power
compared to the reference case. Note that the THz en-
hancements for diﬀerent conﬁgurations are inversely pro-
portional to the linear radiation damping as shown in
Fig. 4(a). Figure 4(b) gives typical time-domain trace
detected at the receiving port for our metasurface THz
emitter compared to that for the reference SRR case.
Upon increasing the pump pulse intensity, the generated
THz signal amplitude increases linearly as presented in
Fig. 4(c), and our design does show a dramatic emission
enhancement over the analog dependence for the con-
ventional SRR metasurface under the same conditions.
In Fig.
4(d), we illustrate the charge density distribu-
tion (marked in color) and the currents (indicated with
arrows) in the two SRRs at the maximum THz conver-
sion eﬃciency. Both SRRs, possessing the same polar-
ization with negligible phase diﬀerence, contribute to the
THz emission (polarized along x−axis) coherently, the
superposition of which leads to the total enhanced THz
radiation, emitting perpendicular to the metasurface on

5
both sides (see Supplemental Material). Moreover, the
radiated THz signal polarized in the x-direction can be
written in terms of second-order nonlinear susceptibility
χ(2) of the metasurface as ETHz

The THz signal depends on the temporal envelope of
the incident pulse, and THz spectrum has the peak at
ω = 2/τ with a bandwidth ∆ωFWHM ≈2.31/τ. From
the ﬁeld of second harmonic radiation, we evaluated the

surface χ(2)

sistent with the reported 1.6 × 10−12 m/V in [35]).The
discussions to the case with substrate can be found in
Supplemental Material. In the view of potential exper-
iments, conversion eﬃciency is an important parameter
for an intuitive evaluation on nonlinear energy extraction.
In practice, for a speciﬁc experimental setup, it depends
on many factors, such as pump power, pump polariza-
tion, pulse duration, incidence and focusing conditions,
phase-matching, etc. Our theoretical work described here
resolves a fundamental problem obstructing the improve-
ment of THz generation eﬃciency with nonlinear meta-
surfaces, and to understand the fundamental physics, we
considered a simpliﬁed model of a spatially inﬁnite sur-
face under plane-wave illumination, so the model is less
suitable to predict practical absolute numbers as would
be observed in a particular experiment. Therefore, we
conducted a side-by-side comparison between the con-
ventional, not radiation-managed SRR metasurface [35],
for which experimental data is available, and our conﬁgu-
ration, which eliminates linear radiation damping, within
the same numerical simulations. It is revealed our scheme
has χ(2) more than one order of magnitude larger than
that of the regular SRR metasurface, and consequently
would generate over two-order enhanced THz emission
under the same conditions.
On the other hand, Ref.
[35] reported that the SRR metasurface experimentally
showed about the same order of THz generation as a 0.2
mm-thick ZnTe crystal, so our proposed conﬁguration
should show a much better performance in generating
broadband THz emission in real experiments.
In conclusion, our proposed system demonstrates ef-
fective suppression of radiation damping and extremely
high-eﬃciency THz generations with a speciﬁcally de-
signed metasurface.
Such signiﬁcant improvements in
nonlinear conversion eﬃciency were made possible by our
judiciously designed dark-element-integrated perfect ab-
sorbing sheet, which essentially tackled the common ef-
ﬁciency limit in two crucial aspects, i.e., eliminating ra-
diative damping of linear scatterings and enhancing local
ﬁeld for nonlinear signals. Although our design presented
in this Letter aims for eﬃcient and compact THz genera-
tions, the new concept is general and applicable to other
nonlinear processes. We believe the ﬂexibilities in tailor-
ing meta-atoms of metamaterials specially metasurfaces
will open up new opportunities for THz technologies de-
velopment and versatile nanoscale nonlinear devices.

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a novel metasurface design for generating terahertz (THz) radiation with significantly enhanced efficiency compared to conventional split-ring resonator (SRR) metasurfaces. The authors address the limitations of existing metasurfaces, specifically the trade-offs between symmetry breaking, local-field enhancement, and radiation damping, which hinder efficient THz generation. Their approach combines a resonant dark-state metasurface with a specific spatial symmetry to achieve destructive interference of linear moments and perfect absorption via simultaneous electric and magnetic critical coupling. This design eliminates linear radiation damping while maintaining constructive interference for the nonlinear components. Numerical simulations demonstrate a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of approximately 10⁻¹¹ m/V, an order of magnitude improvement over previous SRR metasurfaces, and a corresponding two orders of magnitude enhancement in THz energy extraction. The study's novelty lies in its dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface, which overcomes the limitations of conventional designs. The results are significant because they pave the way for more efficient and compact THz sources, with implications for various applications in sensing, imaging, and communication. The primary limitation is the simplified model used, which may not fully reflect the complexities of real-world experimental conditions.

Research Context
The development of efficient and compact THz emitters and detectors is crucial for advancing THz technologies. Conventional THz sources, such as those based on nonlinear optical rectification in crystals, suffer from limitations like narrow bandwidth and low emission intensity. Metamaterials and metasurfaces offer an alternative approach by enabling the design of subwavelength-scale building blocks with tailored functionalities. However, in second-order nonlinear applications, the design of meta-atoms faces trade-offs between symmetry breaking and local-field enhancement due to radiation damping. Prior work using SRR metasurfaces has shown promise, but their nonlinear optical response is still weak, necessitating a fundamental improvement in nonlinear efficiency. This work aims to overcome the limitations of radiation damping in SRR metasurfaces to improve THz generation efficiency.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to enhance the efficiency of THz generation using metasurfaces. The authors hypothesize that by eliminating linear radiation damping in metasurfaces, the THz generation efficiency can be significantly improved. They predict that a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface will achieve this goal. This design is expected to eliminate linear radiation damping while maintaining constructive interference and effective radiation of the nonlinear components. The authors' approach differs from previous studies by using a dark-mode metasurface to drive nonlinear SRRs, which allows for the separation of resonant local field enhancement and the symmetry breaking necessary for second-order nonlinearity. The study's success would be indicated by a substantial increase in THz emission power compared to conventional SRR metasurfaces, as well as a significant improvement in the second-order nonlinear susceptibility.

Methodological Details
The study employs numerical simulations to analyze and optimize a metasurface design for enhanced THz generation. The design consists of two gold SRRs placed on either side of a thin silicon (Si) slab, periodically punctuated by metal walls. The SRRs serve as both the source of THz emission via difference frequency generation (DFG) and as a bridge to couple the incident wave into the dark element (Si slab). The geometric parameters are: length (L) = 800 nm, width (W) = 240 nm, thickness of Si slab (h) = 100 nm, and thickness of SRRs (tm) = 50 nm. The metal walls are used to quantize the modes of the dielectric slab, achieving a set of discrete resonant dark states. The simulations used a self-consistent finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method based on the hydrodynamic model and Maxwell's equations to calculate the THz radiation from the metasurface. A temporal optical pulse, with a driving frequency equal to the resonant frequency of the dark mode (ω₀ = ωdark), a pulse duration (τ) of 140 fs (spectral width ~3.2 THz), and a peak amplitude (E₀) of 2 x 10⁷ V/m, was applied. The model considered both linear and nonlinear dynamics of the electron gas under infrared light excitation. The authors calculated the sheet conductivities (σ(e)s and σ(m)s) to determine the scattering properties (reflection, R, and transmission, T) of the metasurface. The study compared the performance of the proposed design with a conventional SRR metasurface, using the same numerical simulations. The key metric was the THz enhancement, defined as the ratio of THz conversion efficiency of the proposed design to that of the traditional SRR metasurface (ηdark/ηSRR). The authors also analyzed the charge density distribution and currents within the SRRs to understand the THz emission mechanism. No information is provided on preregistration, multiple-comparison corrections, or ethics/IRB.

Procedures Architectures
The core of the methodology is the design and simulation of a metasurface THz emitter. The architecture consists of a meta-atom comprising two gold SRRs on either side of a silicon slab, periodically punctuated by metal walls. The SRRs are the key element for THz emission via DFG and act as a bridge coupling the incident wave into the dark element (Si slab). The metal walls are used to quantize the modes of the dielectric slab, achieving a set of discrete resonant dark states. The design leverages a resonant dark bound state in a silicon film to create local field enhancement. The strong evanescent surface fields of this quasi-surface mode then drive the SRRs. The incident pump radiation couples to the resonant dark state via the non-resonant weak SRR scatterers, which is designed to simultaneously couple both the electric and magnetic components of the pump to the resonant dark state. The simulations used a self-consistent FDTD calculation based on the hydrodynamic model and Maxwell's equations. The model incorporates the linear and nonlinear dynamics of the electron gas under infrared light excitation. The incident pulse is a temporal optical pulse with a specific frequency, duration, and amplitude. The software used for the simulations is not specified. The key innovation is the combination of a resonant dark-state metasurface with a specific spatial symmetry to eliminate linear radiation damping, which is achieved by the introduction of a low-loss dielectric dark element for high quality-factor strong local field enhancement to drive the plasmonic nanoparticles, which are generating the nonlinear signals.

Key Results
The study's primary result is the demonstration of significantly enhanced THz generation efficiency with the proposed metasurface design. The simulations revealed a giant second-order nonlinear susceptibility of approximately 2.4 x 10⁻¹¹ m/V for the proposed design, compared to 1.7 x 10⁻¹² m/V for the traditional SRR metasurface, representing an order of magnitude improvement. The THz enhancement, defined as the ratio of THz conversion efficiency, was more than 120-fold compared to the reference SRR case (Figure 4a). The absorption of the optimized metasurface reached 94% (Figure 3b). The THz signal amplitude increased linearly with increasing pump pulse intensity (Figure 4c). The study also found that the THz emission was polarized along the x-axis. The analysis of the electric field distribution showed a strong excitation of the TE2,0 mode in the Si slab, leading to dramatic field enhancement around SRRs (Figure 3c). The authors also report that the proposed configuration should generate over two-order enhanced THz emission under the same conditions compared to the regular SRR metasurface. The study found that the optimal positions of the SRRs are ∆x1 ≈ 70 nm and ∆x2 ≈ 470 nm, with ζ|σ(e)s| = ζ⁻¹|σ(m)s| = 1.8.

Interpretation Implications
The findings support the hypothesis that eliminating linear radiation damping in metasurfaces can dramatically improve THz generation efficiency. The results suggest that the dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface design effectively addresses the limitations of conventional SRR metasurfaces. The enhanced THz emission is attributed to the constructive interference of the nonlinear components and the elimination of linear radiation damping. The study implies that the proposed concept is general and applicable to other nonlinear processes. The results suggest that the flexibility in tailoring meta-atoms of metamaterials, especially metasurfaces, can open new opportunities for THz technologies development and versatile nanoscale nonlinear devices. The authors propose that the convection term plays a crucial role for the second-order nonlinearities, qualitatively contributing in the format as the product of current and accumulated charge density on the metal surface.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's main limitation is the use of a simplified model of a spatially infinite surface under plane-wave illumination. This model is less suitable for predicting practical absolute numbers as would be observed in a particular experiment. The model does not account for substrate effects. The authors acknowledge that the conversion efficiency in a real experiment depends on many factors, such as pump power, pump polarization, pulse duration, incidence and focusing conditions, and phase-matching. The study does not provide details on experimental validation. The lack of experimental validation is a significant limitation. The study does not report the random seed used in the simulations. The lack of information about the experimental setup and validation limits the external validity of the findings.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents the schematic unit of the designed metasurface THz emitter and the dispersion diagram of the system. Figure 2 shows the equivalent current sheet and the maps of electric and magnetic sheet conductivities. Figure 3 illustrates the scattering properties of the metasurface, including the transmission, reflection, and absorption spectra, and the field distributions. Figure 4 shows the THz enhancement of the proposed design, including the THz intensity enhancement map, time trace of THz radiation, THz signal strength in dependence of pump power, and distributions of DFG currents and charge density. These figures are crucial for understanding the design, operation, and performance of the proposed metasurface.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the development of a dark-mode-assisted perfect absorbing metasurface for efficient THz generation. This design overcomes the limitations of conventional SRR metasurfaces by eliminating linear radiation damping and enhancing local fields.

(2) The strongest evidence supporting the claims is the simulation results showing a more than 120-fold enhancement in THz emission power and an order of magnitude improvement in the second-order nonlinear susceptibility compared to traditional SRR metasurfaces. The absorption of the optimized metasurface reaches 94%.

(3) The primary limitation is the lack of experimental validation of the simulation results. Future work should focus on fabricating and characterizing the proposed metasurface to confirm the predicted performance and explore its potential for real-world applications.

papers.fulltext:
Reduced residence time of droplet impact on heated surfaces
Song Rong, Shiquan Shen, Tianyou Wang, and Zhizhao Che∗
State Key Laboratory of Engines, Tianjin University, Tianjin, 300072, China.
Abstract
The impact of droplets is a ubiquitous phenomenon, and reducing the residence time of the impact process
is important for many potential applications. In this study of the impact dynamics on heated surfaces,
we identify a mode of droplet bouncing (bouncing-with-spray mode) that can reduce the residence time
signiﬁcantly compared with the traditional retraction-bouncing mode. Comparing with other strategies
to reduce the residence time, this approach induced by heat is simple and reliable. The reduction in the
residence time is due to the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid ﬁlm, which results in the formation of
holes in the liquid ﬁlm and consequently the recoiling of the liquid ﬁlm from the holes. A scaling law is
proposed for the transition boundary between the retraction-bouncing mode and the bouncing-with-spray
mode in the ﬁlm boiling regime, and it agrees well with the experimental data. This model can also explain
the transition between these two modes in the transition boiling regime.
1
Introduction
The phenomenon of droplet impact happens ubiqui-
tously in nature and in a wide range of industrial
applications which include but are not limited to
spray cooling, painting, inkjet printing, and fuel-
spray impingement in internal combustion engines
[1–3]. For the impact of droplets on surfaces with
diﬀerent temperatures, the impact process could be
signiﬁcantly aﬀected by the heat transfer or phase
change [4, 5].
Early studies of droplet impact on
heated surfaces focused on the description of diﬀer-
ent impact morphologies in various impact regimes
using high-speed imaging technique [6–8] and the
analysis of the ejected secondary droplets using phase
Doppler anemometry (PDA) and image processing
techniques [9–11].
When the droplet impacts on
the heated surface, if the surface temperature is
above the boiling point of the liquid, the droplet
will go through a boiling process which is similar
to that in pool boiling, including nucleate boiling,
transition boiling, and ﬁlm boiling [12]. When the
surface temperature is high enough, a vapor layer
will be generated underneath the droplet, i.e., the
Leidenfrost eﬀect [13], and the vapor layer acts as a
thermal insulation layer between the droplet and the
substrate. As a consequence, the vaporization rate
of the droplet is reduced [14, 15]. The Leidenfrost
temperature is inﬂuenced by surface roughness [16],
surface structure [17–19] and impact Weber number
[20].
The contact time of a bouncing droplet is an
important parameter in droplet impact process. For
the axisymmetric impact of an inviscid droplet on
a superhydrophobic surface, the contact time is
∗chezhizhao@tju.edu.cn
bounded by the Rayleigh time scale [21].
Because
the contact time controls the mass, momentum, and
energy transfer between the droplet and the surface,
it is important to reduce it in many applications,
such as anti-icing, self-cleaning, corrosion-resistance,
and maintaining surface dryness. Therefore, many
eﬀorts have been made to overcome the theoretical
limit and reduce the contact time, for example, by
using surfaces with ridges [22], pancake bouncing
on superhydrophobic surfaces patterned with lattices
of submillimeter posts [23], asymmetric bouncing on
curved surfaces [24], egg-shaped droplets [25], etc.
In this study of the impact on heated surfaces, we
call it residence time instead of contact time because
the droplet only visually contacts the substrate in
the ﬁlm boiling regime, and in fact, there is a
vapor layer separating the droplet and the substrate.
In nucleate boiling regime, because of the direct
contact between the bottom liquid of the droplet
and the substrate, the droplet can stick to the hot
surface and evaporate, and the residence time of the
droplet on the surface is strongly inﬂuenced by the
surface temperature [26]. Many theoretical models
have been proposed to predict the contact time in
the nucleate boiling regime [27–29]. In ﬁlm boiling
regime, a vapor layer forms between the droplet and
the substrate, and it can act as a lubricant ﬁlm. As
a consequence, the droplet, if it has suﬃcient kinetic
energy, may bounce from the substrate after the
recoil, and therefore, the droplet residence time can
be approximated as the period of a freely oscillating
droplet [19, 30–32]. We ﬁnd that a droplet bouncing
mode, i.e. bouncing-with-spray mode, caused by the
burst of vapor bubbles can contribute to a dramatic
reduction of the droplet residence time. Comparing
with other strategies to reduce the residence time,

Experimental method
The experimental setup is schematically described in
Figure 1. Diﬀerent droplet liquids (water, ethanol,
and water/glycerol mixtures) were pushed through
an injection tube at an extremely low speed (ap-
proximately 4 µl/s) by a syringe pump (Harvard
Apparatus, Pump 11 elite Pico plus).
Droplets
formed at the tip of a blunt syringe needle and
detached when the gravitational force exceeded the
surface tension force.
The droplet then impacted
on a polished silicon substrate (silicon wafers, the
roughness is less than 0.5 nm) which was heated by a
copper holder. We placed two K-type thermocouples
1 cm beside the point of impact on the silicon surface
to control the temperature with an accuracy of ±1◦C
by a PID controller.
We captured the side-view
and aerial-view images of droplet impact evolution
using a high-speed camera (Photron Fastcam SA1.1).
The impact process was illuminated by an LED light
source. The droplet size (typically D0 = 2.8 mm for
water/glycerol mixtures, 2.2 ∼3.4 mm for water, and
1.6 mm for ethanol), the impact speed (V = 0.9 ∼2.1
m/s), and the shape evolution of the droplet during
the impact process, were measured from the high-
speed images using a customized Matlab program.
To change the viscosity of the impacting droplets, we
used diﬀerent liquids by changing the concentration
of the glycerol in water/glycerol mixtures. The liquid
properties are summarized in Table 1. The Weber
number is used to quantify the ratio between the
droplet’s kinetic energy to its surface energy We ≡
ρD0V 2/σ, where ρ and σ are the density and the
surface tension, respectively.
The We number was
varied from 10 to 180 for diﬀerent liquids. The Jakob
number is used to indicate the ratio of the sensible
heat to the latent heat of the liquid,
