3.1
Impact morphology and droplet
residence time
Diﬀerent impact morphologies were observed when
varying the substrate temperature and the droplet
speed and diﬀerent kinds of liquids in three boiling
regimes, namely nucleate boiling, transition boil-
ing, and ﬁlm boiling.
Figure 2 shows the impact
morphologies by taking water as a representative.
These diﬀerent morphologies result in a dramatic
diﬀerence in the residence time of the droplet on
the substrate. Here, the residence time is deﬁned as
the interval between the moments that the droplet
visually contacts the substrate and that it visually
detaches the substrate.
In the nucleate boiling regime, because of the
direct contact between the bottom of the droplet and
the heated surface, the liquid can boil so quickly that
vapor bubbles form immediately upon impact, then
rise through the droplet and break up at the free
surface [33]. As shown in Figure 2a, the jet ejection
due to the breakup of bubbles is followed by the
inward surface wave propagation and the formation
of tiny droplets created by the disintegration of the
jets. After droplet spreading, the bottom liquid still
sticks to the surface.
In the transition boiling regime, an unstable vapor
ﬁlm may exist between the droplet and the substrate
so that the bottom of the droplet can contact the
substrate locally.
At a small impact speed (for
example, We = 37 and T = 380◦C, Figure 2b), the
droplet will recoil, then bounce oﬀthe substrate with
spray-like ejection of tiny droplets (highlighted by
the red circle in Figure 2b). We name this mode of
droplet bouncing in which droplet retracts its shape
after the maximum spreading as retraction-bouncing
mode.
In contrast, at a large impact speed (for
example, We = 69 and T = 380◦C, Figure 2c1), the
droplet can bounce oﬀthe substrate without obvious

In this regime, the retraction-bouncing and the

of the tiny droplets is more uniform than that in
the transition boiling regime.
It can be explained
as that although there exists a stable vapor ﬁlm,
as the surface temperature increases, the growth
rate of the vapor bubbles becomes higher so that
it will be much easier for bubbles to rise through
the droplet and burst on the free surface. On the
other hand, with the impact speed increasing, the
liquid ﬁlm is thinner, and bubbles can rise to the free
surface and burst as well [33]. Then when the impact
speed or the surface temperature increases further
(for example, We = 60 and T = 440◦C, Figure 2e1),
the bouncing-with-spray mode can be seen in the ﬁlm
boiling regime. When We = 129 and T = 440◦C,
the splashing behavior and the bouncing-with-spray
mode still occur as shown in Figure 2e2.
The residence time in the bouncing-with-spray
mode is much smaller than that in the retraction-
bouncing mode in both transition and ﬁlm boiling
regimes. To understand the mechanism of the reduc-
tion of the droplet residence time, Figure 3 shows
a series of images of the bouncing-with-spray mode
from an aerial view.
During the impact process,
vapor bubbles burst at random sites of the liquid
ﬁlm, producing holes one by one in the liquid ﬁlm
accompanied by several tiny droplets.
The holes
expand rapidly, and the liquid ﬁlm recoils from these
holes to several fragments (indicated by the red
arrows) then bounces oﬀthe surface. The recoiling
distance is reduced and so is the coiling time. There-
fore, the residence time of the droplet is shortened
signiﬁcantly. This mechanism is similar to that of the
reduction in the residence time during the bouncing
of droplets on superhydrophobic surfaces with ridges
[22], where the ridges cause the fragmentation of
the droplet and decrease the recoiling distance, and
consequently reduce the residence time.
In this
study, the fragmentation of the droplet is induced
by the burst of the vapor bubbles generated in the
droplet ﬂuid.
Therefore, it is always accompanied
by the spray of tiny droplets during bubble bursting.
This mode of droplet bouncing and the consequent
reduction in the residence time were observed for
all kinds of liquids used in our experiments, and a
detailed analysis is provided in the next section 3.2.
To determine the key factors that aﬀect the
bouncing-with-spray mode and its residence time, we
varied the droplet viscosity by mixing glycerol with
water at diﬀerent concentrations. By using droplet
ﬂuids with diﬀerent viscosities while ﬁxing V and
D0, we ﬁnd that the residence time of the bouncing-
with-spray mode is independent of the viscosity (see
Figure 4). This indicates that the viscous force does
not play an important role in this process.
For droplet impact on superhydrophobic surfaces
or on superheated surface in the ﬁlm boiling regime,
the residence time in the retraction-bouncing mode
is aﬀected by the droplet radius, and scales with the
inertial and capillary timescale:

Conclusions
In summary, the impact of droplets on heated sur-
faces is studied, and a droplet bouncing mode caused
by the breakup of the liquid ﬁlm, i.e., bouncing-with-
spray mode, can contribute to a dramatic reduc-
tion of the droplet residence time compared to the
traditional bouncing mode, i.e., retraction-bouncing
mode.
Comparing with other strategies to reduce
the residence time, this approach induced by heat
is reliable by avoiding surface degradation and is
easy to achieve by avoiding complex fabrication of
the surface microstructures or surface modiﬁcation.
The residence time of the bouncing-with-spray mode
is independent of liquid’s viscosity, and the reduced
residence time compared with that of the retraction-
bouncing mode is about 40%.
The reduction in the residence time is due to the
burst of vapor bubbles formed in the liquid ﬁlm,
resulting in holes formation and recoiling of the liquid
ﬁlm from the holes. The reduction in the recoiling
distance leads to the reduction in the recoiling time.
We have investigated the residence time reduction
mechanism quantitatively by proposing a simpliﬁed
theoretical model considering the energy balance and
a critical condition of the bubble burst rv ∼bmin.
According to this theoretical model, a transition
boundary between the bouncing-with-spray mode
and the retraction-bouncing mode in the ﬁlm boiling
regime is proposed. For the same liquid and the same
initial droplet size, the transition between these two
modes in the transition boiling regime is discussed.
There are many open questions in this area of droplet
impact on heated surfaces and its residence time.
For example, detailed numerical simulations and
experimental measurements of the bursting bubbles
in the bouncing-with-spray mode will be helpful for
a better understanding of the impact process. This
study not only provides physical insight into the
mechanism of the impact dynamics but also can be
helpful in the optimization of this process in the
relevant applications.

Executive Summary
This study investigates the impact dynamics of droplets on heated surfaces, identifying a "bouncing-with-spray" mode that significantly reduces droplet residence time compared to the traditional "retraction-bouncing" mode. The reduction in residence time is attributed to the burst of vapor bubbles in the liquid film, leading to hole formation and subsequent recoiling of the film. Experiments were conducted using water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures impacting a heated silicon substrate. The residence time in the bouncing-with-spray mode was found to be independent of liquid viscosity. A theoretical model was developed to explain the transition between the two bouncing modes, proposing a scaling law for the transition boundary in the film boiling regime, which agreed with experimental data. The study demonstrates a 40% reduction in residence time in the bouncing-with-spray mode compared to the retraction-bouncing mode. The approach offers a simple and reliable method for reducing residence time, avoiding surface degradation and complex fabrication. Limitations include the need for further investigation through numerical simulations and experimental measurements of the bursting bubbles.

Research Context
Prior research on droplet impact on heated surfaces has focused on impact morphologies and the analysis of ejected secondary droplets. Studies have explored different impact regimes, including nucleate, transition, and film boiling. However, existing methods for reducing droplet residence time often involve surface modifications or complex fabrication techniques. This work addresses the need for a simple and reliable method to reduce residence time, particularly in applications like anti-icing and self-cleaning. The study differentiates itself by identifying and characterizing a bouncing mode induced by heat that achieves this reduction without surface alterations, offering a practical advantage over previous approaches.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to reduce the residence time of a droplet impacting a heated surface. The primary hypothesis is that a "bouncing-with-spray" mode, induced by the burst of vapor bubbles, will significantly reduce the residence time compared to the "retraction-bouncing" mode. This hypothesis is supported by the observation of different impact morphologies and the measurement of residence times in both modes. The study also investigates the factors influencing the transition between the two modes, specifically proposing a scaling law for the transition boundary in the film boiling regime. The alternative hypothesis is that factors like liquid viscosity will significantly impact the residence time in the bouncing-with-spray mode. This is refuted by the experimental results showing independence of residence time on viscosity.

Methodological Details
The study employed an experimental approach to investigate droplet impact dynamics. The experimental setup, shown in Figure 1, consisted of a syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus, Pump 11 elite Pico plus) to deliver droplets of varying liquids (water, ethanol, and water/glycerol mixtures) onto a heated silicon substrate (silicon wafers, roughness < 0.5 nm). The substrate was heated by a copper holder, with temperature controlled by a PID controller, and monitored by two K-type thermocouples. Side-view and aerial-view images of the impact process were captured using a high-speed camera (Photron Fastcam SA1.1) illuminated by an LED light source. Droplet size (D0), impact speed (V), and shape evolution were measured from high-speed images using a customized Matlab program. The Weber number (We = ρD0V^2/σ) and Jakob number (Ja = cp(Tw −Ts)/ℓ) were calculated to characterize the impact conditions. The residence time was defined as the interval between the moments that the droplet visually contacts the substrate and that it visually detaches the substrate. The impact process was analyzed across three boiling regimes: nucleate, transition, and film boiling. No mention of preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections was made. Ethical considerations were not explicitly addressed.

Procedures Architectures
The experimental procedure involved generating droplets of different liquids, controlling their impact velocity and size, and varying the substrate temperature. Droplets were formed at the tip of a blunt syringe needle and impacted a polished silicon substrate heated by a copper holder. The high-speed camera captured the impact process from side and aerial views. The images were processed using a custom Matlab program to measure droplet size, impact speed, and residence time. The key components of the experimental setup included a syringe pump, syringe needle, heated copper plate, silicon wafer, PID temperature controller, high-speed camera, LED light source, and a computer for data acquisition and analysis. The study focused on observing and quantifying the impact dynamics, specifically the residence time of the droplets under varying conditions. The novel aspect of the study is the identification and characterization of the bouncing-with-spray mode, which reduces residence time without requiring surface modifications. The study also proposed a theoretical model to explain the transition between the retraction-bouncing and bouncing-with-spray modes, which is a new contribution.

Key Results
The study identified two distinct droplet bouncing modes: retraction-bouncing and bouncing-with-spray. In the transition boiling regime, at We = 37 and T = 380°C, the retraction-bouncing mode was observed, with a residence time of 12.0 ms (Figure 2b). The bouncing-with-spray mode was observed at We = 69 and T = 380°C, with a residence time of 6.5 ms (Figure 2c1); and at We = 105 and T = 380°C, with a residence time of 6.3 ms (Figure 2c2). In the film boiling regime, the retraction-bouncing mode (We = 25, T = 400°C, Figure 2d1) showed ejection of tiny droplets (Figure 2d2, T=440°C), while the bouncing-with-spray mode (We = 60, T = 440°C, Figure 2e1) was observed. The residence time in the bouncing-with-spray mode was significantly smaller than in the retraction-bouncing mode. The residence time reduction in the bouncing-with-spray mode was about 40% compared to the retraction-bouncing mode (Figure 5). The residence time of the bouncing-with-spray mode was found to be independent of liquid viscosity (Figure 4). A scaling law, ∆T ∼ V^-1, was proposed for the transition boundary between the bouncing-with-spray mode and the retraction-bouncing mode in the film boiling regime, which agreed with the experimental data (Figure 6d).

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the bouncing-with-spray mode, induced by vapor bubble bursts, provides a mechanism for significantly reducing droplet residence time on heated surfaces. The independence of residence time on viscosity indicates that viscous forces play a minor role in this process. The theoretical model developed provides a framework for understanding the transition between the two bouncing modes, linking it to the energy balance and a critical condition of bubble burst. The study implies that by controlling the surface temperature and impact velocity, it is possible to tailor the droplet impact dynamics to achieve desired outcomes, such as faster evaporation or reduced contact time. The results shift the understanding of droplet impact by highlighting the importance of vapor bubble dynamics in controlling residence time and offering a new perspective on optimizing this process for various applications.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is the lack of detailed numerical simulations and experimental measurements of the bursting bubbles in the bouncing-with-spray mode, which could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the impact process. The study does not report the random seed used for the Matlab program or the train/test split. The external validity of the findings may be limited by the specific experimental conditions, such as the use of a polished silicon substrate. The study does not address the influence of surface roughness or other surface properties on the observed phenomena. The study does not explicitly discuss potential conflicts with prior literature, although it does position itself in the context of existing research on droplet impact.

(3) The primary limitation is the lack of detailed analysis of the bursting bubbles in the bouncing-with-spray mode, which suggests the need for future research involving numerical simulations and more detailed experimental measurements to further refine the understanding of the impact process.

Executive Summary
This paper investigates geometrically maximal abelian coverings of the modular curve $X_0(p)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that are unramified outside cusps, where $p$ is a prime number. Building upon Mazur's result, which identified the Shimura covering $X_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ as the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of $X_0(p)$, the authors demonstrate the existence of a geometrically maximal abelian covering $X'_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ that is cyclic of degree $2N_p$, where $N_p = (p-1)/\gcd(p-1, 12)$. The construction of $X'_2(p)$ relies on generalized Dedekind eta functions. The key finding is that the geometrically maximal abelian covering $X'_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ unramified outside cusps has a degree twice that of the Shimura covering. The approach involves constructing a quadratic extension of the function field $\mathbb{Q}(X_2(p))$ using a square root of a modular function. The result is significant because it provides a complete description of the geometrically maximal abelian covering of $X_0(p)$ unramified outside cusps. A key limitation is the reliance on the properties of generalized Dedekind eta functions, which restricts the analysis to modular curves. The work extends our understanding of the arithmetic of modular curves and their coverings.

Research Context
Mazur proved that the Shimura covering $X_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ is the geometrically maximal unramified abelian covering of $X_0(p)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. This paper addresses the gap in understanding the structure of geometrically maximal abelian coverings of modular curves, specifically focusing on those unramified outside cusps. Prior work, such as that of Mazur, established the foundation for understanding unramified coverings, but did not fully characterize the maximal abelian extensions. This work builds on Mazur's result by identifying a geometrically maximal covering with a degree twice that of the Shimura covering. The paper utilizes generalized Dedekind eta functions, which are related to Siegel functions, to construct the covering. The limitations of prior work include not fully characterizing the maximal abelian extensions and the lack of a construction method for the maximal covering. This paper addresses these limitations by providing a construction and characterization of a geometrically maximal abelian covering.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: What is the structure of the geometrically maximal abelian covering of the modular curve $X_0(p)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that is unramified outside cusps? The primary hypothesis is that a geometrically maximal abelian covering $X'_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ exists, is cyclic, and has a degree of $2N_p$. This is in contrast to Mazur's result, which identified the Shimura covering with degree $N_p$. The alternative hypothesis is that the maximal covering has a different degree or is not cyclic. The paper tests this hypothesis by constructing a covering $X'_2(p)$ and demonstrating its properties. The study's outcomes supporting the hypothesis include the construction of $X'_2(p)$ and the proof that it is a geometrically maximal abelian covering of degree $2N_p$. The approach differs from prior work by explicitly constructing the maximal covering and utilizing generalized Dedekind eta functions. The study's results would refute the hypothesis if the constructed covering did not satisfy the conditions of being geometrically maximal, abelian, or having the predicted degree.

Methodological Details
The paper employs a theoretical approach, focusing on the construction and analysis of modular curves and their coverings. The study considers the modular curves $X_0(p)$ and $X_1(p)$ as geometrically integral smooth proper curves over $\mathbb{Q}$. The authors choose a model of $X_1(p)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ such that the cusp at infinity splits completely in a finite cyclic covering $f_p: X_1(p) \to X_0(p)$ of degree $(p-1)/2$. The Shimura covering $f_p: X_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ is the unique subcovering of degree $N_p = (p-1)/\gcd(p-1, 12)$. The open subscheme $Y_0(p) \subset X_0(p)$ is defined such that $X_0(p) \setminus Y_0(p)$ consists of two cusps. The function field $\mathbb{Q}(X'_2(p))$ of $X'_2(p)$ is obtained as a quadratic extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_2(p))$ generated by a square root of an explicitly constructed rational function in $\mathbb{Q}(X_2(p))$. The key ingredient for this construction is the generalized Dedekind eta functions, defined as $E_g(\tau) = q^{NB(g/N)/2} \prod_{m=1}^{\infty} (1 - q^{N(m-1)+g})(1 - q^{Nm-g})$, where $B(x) = x^2 - x + 1/6$ is the second Bernoulli polynomial. The authors use properties of the generalized Dedekind eta functions, including their transformation properties under modular group actions, to construct modular functions on the curves. The proof involves analyzing the Galois module $M_{Tor}$ and its maximal $\mu$-type subgroup $M^{\mu}_{Tor}(-1)$. The analysis relies on the exact sequence $0 \to J^{\mu}_{Tor}(-1) \to M^{\mu}_{Tor}(-1) \to (L_D \otimes \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})^{\mu}(-1) \to H^1(\mathbb{Q}, J_{Tor}(-1))$. The paper uses the properties of the generalized Jacobian and the abelian fundamental group of a smooth curve. The study does not mention preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. Ethical considerations are not discussed.

Procedures Architectures
The paper constructs a geometrically maximal abelian covering $X'_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ of degree $2N_p$. The construction involves defining generalized Dedekind eta functions, denoted as $E_g(\tau)$, where $\tau$ is a complex variable. The functions are defined as $E_g(\tau) = q^{NB(g/N)/2} \prod_{m=1}^{\infty} (1 - q^{N(m-1)+g})(1 - q^{Nm-g})$. The authors then define modular functions $F_h(\tau)$ as products of the generalized Dedekind eta functions. Specifically, for an integer $h$ not congruent to 0 modulo $p$, $F_h(\tau) = \prod_{j=0}^{\ell-1} E_{g^{jk}h}(\tau)^{6/\ell}$, where $\ell = (p-1, 12)/2$. The function $F_h$ is shown to be a modular function on $X_2(p)$. The function field $\mathbb{Q}(X'_2(p))$ is obtained as a quadratic extension of $\mathbb{Q}(X_2(p))$ generated by the square root of $F_h^2$. The modular curve $X'_2(p)$ is associated with the group $\Gamma'_2(p)$, which is the kernel of a character on $\Gamma_2(p)$. The paper uses the properties of the modular group $\Gamma_0(p)$ and its subgroups, such as $\Gamma_1(p)$ and $\Gamma_2(p)$. The key components are the generalized Dedekind eta functions, the modular functions $F_h$, and the modular curves $X_0(p)$, $X_1(p)$, $X_2(p)$, and $X'_2(p)$. The novelty lies in the construction of the geometrically maximal abelian covering $X'_2(p)$ and the use of generalized Dedekind eta functions to achieve this.

Key Results
The paper demonstrates the existence of a geometrically maximal abelian covering $X'_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ of degree $2N_p$. Theorem 1.2.2 states that there exists a cyclic covering $f'_p: X'_2(p) \to X_0(p)$ of degree $2N_p$ such that (1) $f'_p|_{Y'_2(p)}: Y'_2(p) \to Y_0(p)$ is a geometrically maximal unramified covering of $Y_0(p)$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, where $Y'_2(p) := f'^{-1}_p(Y_0(p))$; and (2) $f'_p$ factors as $f'_p = f_p \circ \pi_p$, where $\pi_p: X'_2(p) \to X_2(p)$ is a degree two covering that is unramified outside cusps. The proof relies on the properties of the modular functions $F_h$. Lemma 3.3.4 shows that for $\gamma = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \ c & d \end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma_0(p)$, $F_h(\gamma\tau) = \psi(\gamma)F_{ah}(\tau)$, where $\psi$ is a character of order 2. Furthermore, for $\gamma \in \Gamma_2(p)$, $F_h(\gamma\tau) = \psi(\gamma)\chi(\gamma)F_h(\tau)$ if $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, and $F_h(\gamma\tau) = \psi(\gamma)F_h(\tau)$ if $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$. The order of $F^2_h$ at any cusp of $X_2(p)$ is odd. The order is zero elsewhere. The paper does not provide comparisons to baselines or state any effect sizes or confidence intervals. The results are primarily theoretical, with no negative results reported.

Interpretation Implications
The findings provide a complete description of the geometrically maximal abelian covering of $X_0(p)$ unramified outside cusps, showing that its degree is twice that of the Shimura covering. This result contributes to the understanding of the arithmetic of modular curves and their coverings. The construction of $X'_2(p)$ using generalized Dedekind eta functions highlights the importance of these functions in studying the structure of modular curves. The theoretical implications are that the study provides a deeper insight into the Galois theory of modular curves. The results suggest a mechanism where the structure of the maximal abelian extension is closely related to the properties of modular functions. The scope conditions are that the results apply to modular curves $X_0(p)$ and their coverings. The understanding shifts from knowing the existence of the Shimura covering to a complete characterization of the maximal abelian covering unramified outside cusps.

Contradictions Limitations
The paper relies on the properties of generalized Dedekind eta functions, limiting the analysis to modular curves. The study does not address the computational aspects of constructing the covering. The paper does not discuss the case when $p \equiv 11 \pmod{12}$ in detail. The lack of discussion on computational aspects and the specific properties of the generalized Dedekind eta functions are limitations. The paper does not provide any empirical validation or experimental results. The external validity is limited to the context of modular curves. The paper does not explicitly discuss any conflicts with prior literature, but it builds upon the work of Mazur. The key threat to inference is the reliance on the specific properties of the Dedekind eta functions, which may not generalize to other settings.

papers.fulltext:
Design of Real-time Semantic Segmentation Decoder
for Automated Driving
Arindam Das1, Saranya Kandan1, Senthil Yogamani2, Pavel Kˇr´ıˇzek3
1Detection Vision Systems, Valeo India
2Valeo Vision Systems, Valeo Ireland
3Valeo R&D DVS, Prague, Czech Republic
{arindam.das, saranya.kandan, senthil.yogamani, pavel.krizek}@valeo.com
Keywords:
Semantic Segmentation, Visual Perception, Efﬁcient Networks, Automated Driving.
Abstract:
Semantic segmentation remains a computationally intensive algorithm for embedded deployment even with
the rapid growth of computation power. Thus efﬁcient network design is a critical aspect especially for ap-
plications like automated driving which requires real-time performance. Recently, there has been a lot of
research on designing efﬁcient encoders that are mostly task agnostic. Unlike image classiﬁcation and bound-
ing box object detection tasks, decoders are computationally expensive as well for semantic segmentation
task. In this work, we focus on efﬁcient design of the segmentation decoder and assume that an efﬁcient
encoder is already designed to provide shared features for a multi-task learning system. We design a novel
efﬁcient non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoders which ﬁt into a small run-time budget using VGG10
as efﬁcient encoder. We demonstrate in our dataset that experimentation with various design choices led to an
improvement of 10% from a baseline performance.
1
Introduction
Semantic segmentation provides complete seman-
tic scene understanding wherein each pixel in an im-
age is assigned a class label. It has applications in var-
ious ﬁelds including automated driving, augmented
reality and medical image processing. The complex-
ity of Convolution Neural Networks (CNN) architec-
tures have been growing consistently. However for in-
dustrial applications, there is a computational bound
because of limited resources on embedded platforms.
It is essential to design efﬁcient models which ﬁt the
run-time budget of the system. There are many pa-
pers which demonstrate large run-time improvements
with minimal loss of accuracy by using various tech-
niques. An overview of efﬁcient CNN for semantic
segmentation is provided in (Briot et al., 2018).
Semantic segmentation architectures typically
have an encoder and a decoder as shown in Figure 1.
The encoder extracts features from the image which is
then decoded to produce semantic segmentation out-
put. ImageNet pre-trained networks are typically used
as encoder.
In early architectures (Badrinarayanan
et al., 2015) (Ronneberger et al., 2015), decoder was a
mirror image of encoder and had the same complex-
ity. Newer architectures use a relatively smaller de-
coder. There can also be additional connections from
encoder to decoder.
For example, SegNet (Badri-
narayanan et al., 2015) passes max-pooling indices
and Unet (Ronneberger et al., 2015) passes interme-
diate feature maps to decoder.
In this paper, we propose the design of a novel
non-bottleneck layer particularly to perform seman-
tic segmentation task where the encoder is task inde-
pendent unlike existing methods. Our non-bottleneck
layer based on residual learning, has been designed to
perform well for some classes that are not well repre-
sented in the dataset. Having cascaded skip connec-
tions make our non-bottleneck layer capable to han-
dle high gradient ﬂow and suitable for an embedded
platform to run on real time with lightweight encoder
model. Table 1 presents the efﬁcacy of the proposed
decoder architecture over many variants of the de-
coder model while maintaining the encoder to be task
independent and constant.
The rest of the paper is structured as follows. Sec-
tion 2 discusses the related work on semantic segmen-
tation. 3 explains the details of the proposed network.
Section 4 details the experimental setup and results.
Finally, section 5 summarizes the paper and provides
potential future directions.
arXiv:1901.06580v1  [cs.CV]  19 Jan 2019

2
Background
The main purpose of convolutional neural network
was to perform image classiﬁcation so that an object
of a particular category can be predicted irrespective
of its rotation, translation and scale. But Long et al.
(Long et al., 2015) considered the same concept as en-
coder and added fully convolutional upsampling layer
using the concept of unpooling to construct the out-
put. Later deconvolution technique was introduced
instead of unpooling in (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015)
along with considering skip connections to pull en-
coded feature maps. As part of the recent advance-
ment in semantic segmentation tasks, high usage of
dilated convolution is observed in many works (Chen
et al., 2018a) (Chen et al., 2018b) (Hamaguchi et al.,
2017) (Romera et al., 2017) (Wang et al., 2018) (Yu
and Koltun, 2015) (Zhao et al., 2017) (Yang et al.,
2018), this is because it helps to grow the receptive
ﬁeld exponentially without loss of resolution. As no-
table other works, DeepLab2 (Chen et al., 2018a)
uses spatial pyramid pooling in ResNet-101 and it
includes Conditional Random Fields (CRF) as well.
ReﬁneNet (Lin et al., 2017) proposed a multi-path
reﬁnement network that exploits information to per-
form better segmentation in higher resolution. It ba-
sically reﬁnes features from low resolution in recur-
sive manner to obtain better prediction in high res-
olution.
Though none of the methods use task in-
dependent lightweight encoder model as used in this
work. Pohlen et al. (Pohlen et al., 2017) proposed
a ResNet like architecture that considers multi-scale
input in two stream process. One stream extracts fea-
tures from full resolution to get knowledge about se-
mantic boundaries and the other one works on differ-
ent dimension as received from sequence of pooling
layers to extract robust local features. ENet (Paszke
et al., 2016) presented a network aimed for mobile
devices where ResNet like architecture is considered
as encoder and it contains dilated convolution to ex-
tract semantic features. Another realtime segmenta-
tion work, ICNet (Zhao et al., 2017) reported a multi-
branch architecture where inputs in different resolu-
tion are considered and it developed cascade feature
fusion unit across multiple branches. In one more re-
cent paper, ContextNet (Poudel et al., 2018) proposed
multi-column encoder architecture and later fusion at
decoder. A deep network as encoder is used to extract
contextual features from relatively smaller resolution
and another encoder that is shallow in nature is added
to extract global features.
The methods mentioned above do not use task in-
dependent lightweight encoder model as used in this
work and do not support multi task learning practice.
3
Proposed Method
3.1
Overview
The reported work is conceptualized for the embed-
ded platform where the entire system can run on real
time, thus priority is execution speed over accuracy.
Similar to existing neural network architectures such
as FCN (Long et al., 2015), SegNet (Badrinarayanan
et al., 2015), UNet (Ronneberger et al., 2015) for seg-
mentation, the proposed network has also two parts
which are encoder and decoder, which is furnished
in Figure 1. An encoder is basically a Convolutional
Neural Network (CNN) that helps to extract features
from various feature dimensions and thus reduces
the problem space as it becomes deeper. A decoder
does the opposite of encoder, it consumes the feature
maps from last layer as well as intermediate layers
of encoder and reconstructs the original input space.
For reconstruction we use deconvolution layer instead
max-unpooling as used in SegNet (Badrinarayanan
et al., 2015) and ENet (Paszke et al., 2016). Once
the reconstruction is done then the decoder generates
class prediction for each pixel in original input space.
3.2
Encoder
It is mentioned earlier that the intention of this study
is to develop a lightweight decoder for segmentation
task where the encoder is task independent. It means
that the features extracted by the single encoder will
be shared across all decoders to accomplish separate
tasks (segmentation, detection, classiﬁcation etc.). In
the context of our work, it is observed that the en-
coder design is mostly speciﬁc to the semantic seg-
mentation task such as (Badrinarayanan et al., 2015),
(Romera et al., 2017), (Treml et al., 2016), (Yu and
Koltun, 2015), thus these encoders had all necessary
components to extract semantic features and the de-
coder performs well with the readily available infor-
mation. However, our study is intended towards use
of a more generic encoder. So we designed a task
independent, designed a VGG (Simonyan and Zisser-
man, 2014) style classiﬁer of 10 layers as encoder and
no special attention given for semantic segmentation
such as heavy usage of dilated convolution as used in
(Chen et al., 2018a) (Chen et al., 2018b) (Hamaguchi
et al., 2017) (Romera et al., 2017) (Wang et al., 2018)
(Yu and Koltun, 2015) (Zhao et al., 2017) (Yang et al.,
2018) or information fusion at different resolution
(Lin et al., 2017) (Poudel et al., 2018) (Zhao et al.,
2017) (Zhang et al., 2018).
As per Figure 3, convolution with stride 2 fol-
lowed by max-pooling is used to reduce the problem

Figure 1: Typical encoder-decoder architecture of CNN based semantic segmentation network.
space, thus reducing the number of hyperparameters
and also the run-time. Obviously, this is a trade-off
for segmentation accuracy, but that is not the case for
other tasks like detection, classiﬁcation etc. Consider-
ing this encoder to be function independent, this gap
of spatial information exploration needs to be over-
come in the decoder side by learning semantic fea-
tures extensively. Convolution layers are added se-
quentially along with increasing width and decreas-
ing feature space in regular interval. All the convolu-
tion layers use kernel of size 5X5 followed by Batch-
Normalization (Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015) to speed up
the convergence and ReLU (Nair and Hinton, 2010) to
add non-linearity. The last layer of encoder produces
total 256 feature maps.
3.3
Decoder
The proposed architecture of decoder has been ob-
tained after redesigning the existing features of the
convolutional nets, such as residual learning (He
et al., 2016) and non-bottleneck layers (Romera et al.,
2017). In the recent past, learning through residual
blocks has shown breakthrough performance in many
vision related tasks and made it possible to make the
network grow more deeper very easily. This advance-
ment helped to outperform signiﬁcantly in many ob-
ject recognition tasks. Further the same learning strat-
egy has been also used for semantic segmentation as
in (Romera et al., 2017). However, in (Das and Yo-
gamani, 2018), it has been demonstrated that residual
learning for a network with lesser depth is not efﬁ-
cient.
This is because the network can not handle
high gradient ﬂow during back-propagation. To cir-
cumvent this issue, in this study, the original residual
learning (He et al., 2016) strategy has been modiﬁed
with an adequate arrangement to distribute the high
gradients through multiple skip connections.
As per our design of the encoder, it can be realized
that there has been no suitable mechanism employed
to extract semantic features. Now, following with the
recent trend, if the decoder is going to have only few
set of deconvolution layers to reconstruct the output
then the segmentation result will be deﬁnitely poor.
The reason is the performance of the decoder is lim-
ited to the knowledge shared by the encoder and as per
our design, the encoder is expected to share knowl-
edge that is non-semantic in nature. To address this
affair, there is a requisite to learn semantic informa-
tion from the encoded feature space in the decoder.
Hence, we need non-bottleneck blocks between two
deconvolution layers. In (Romera et al., 2017), the
authors have designed non-bottleneck layer which is
1D in nature and claimed to be a better regularizer and
also faster. The same non-bottleneck layer is used in
the encoder as well and most of the convolutions are
dilated.
The design of our non-bottleneck layer is shown
in Figure 2. It contains both 1D and 3D kernels. 1D
kernel is used to extract information mainly in one
direction at a time and 3D kernel is for gathering fea-
tures from bigger receptive area. Later we try to look
for dense information through multiple kernels with
different sizes for example 3X3, 5X5 and 1X1 respec-
tively. Following this, the features extracted using dif-
ferent kernels are fused. This method helps to sum-
marize the semantic features that are collected from
different receptive area.
The resultant features are
again fused with the input features to the same non-
bottleneck layer. The multiple skip connections to the
feature fusion blocks in the proposed non-bottleneck
layer help to handle high gradient ﬂow because dur-
ing back-propagation the incoming gradient gets dis-
tributed among all paths. As per Figure 2, our non-
bottleneck layer has two variants that are type-1 (left)
and type-2 (right). The only difference between two
variants is the block at the right uses dilated convo-
lution where the kernel size is 3X3 and 5X5.
Di-
lated convolution helps to extract spatial information
by expanding the ﬁeld-of-view as per the dilation fac-
tor while maintaining the same resolution. With in-
creasing dilation rate, receptive ﬁeld is also expanded
however, for the present work the dilation rate has
been kept constant and it is 1. It is possible to re-
ceive better accuracy with incremental dilation rate
but dilated convolution is computationally expensive
and it becomes more costlier as the dilation rate in-
creases. Considering the present study to be aimed
for embedded platform, usage of similar features need
to be employed carefully to meet the run-time. After
each convolution operation, ReLU (Nair and Hinton,
2010) is used as activation unit for better convergence

Figure 2: Illustration of non-bottleneck layers
(Krizhevsky et al., 2012).
3.4
Encoder-Decoder architecture
Figure 3 shows the encoder-decoder pair that is used
in this work. The encoder is a very generic one and
the decoder is our main proposal. The feature maps
passed from the encoder are downsampled from 256
to 4 as the present study concentrates on 4 classes.
One can argue that drastic change in the number of
feature maps such as this can impact on accuracy but
if we make the decoder wider that will shoot up the
runtime signiﬁcantly.
Thus decreasing the number
of feature maps in regular interval is not affordable
and out of our budget. After ﬁrst deconvolution layer,
non-bottleneck layer of type-1 is used two times. Fol-
lowing second and third deconvolution layers, non-
bottleneck layers of type-2 are used twice and once
respectively. There is no non-bottleneck layer used
after fourth deconvolution. The non-bottleneck layers
are designed in such a way that ﬁrst repetitive usage of
type-1 as intermediate block between two deconvolu-
tion layers and then having multiple type-2 especially
between the later deconvolution layers will help to re-
move the gap of learning semantic information that
we have seen in the encoder side. Hence, our pro-
posed non-bottleneck layer is generic and can be used
for any segmentation task. Also we pulled intermedi-
ate feature maps from the second and third last convo-
lution layers of the encoder. This has to be highlighted
that our encoder consumed most of the run time be-
cause it is much wider than the decoder. To circum-
vent this issue, we could use the concept of group con-
volution as proposed by Xie et al. (Xie et al., 2017)
but in (Das et al., 2018), it has been experimentally
demonstrated that aggregated residual transformation
shows adverse effect for lightweight networks such as
our encoder.
Details on how to train our proposed network end-
to-end, other training strategy and hyperparameter de-
tails, are discussed in the next section.
4
Experiments
We have performed thorough investigation to
show the efﬁcacy and robustness of our proposed net-
work.

Dataset
We have used dataset that is owned by our
organization. However, some samples of the dataset
are shown in Figure 4. In this dataset, dimension of
each image is 1280X384. Samples are highly var-
ied in nature and mostly urban scenes. Diverse light-
ing conditions and presence of dense shadow make

this dataset challenging. In the present study, to per-
form semantic segmentation, we concentrated only
on 4 critical classes that are lanes, curb, road and
void (everything else). The entire dataset is divided
into Training, Validation and Test set each containing
3016, 981 and 1002 images respectively. Correspond-
ing each sample image, single channel annotation was
developed where each pixel has only one class label.
Training
First we train our encoder from scratch on
ImageNet and then transfer the weights for the present
task.
This transfer learning will help to get better
initialization of the weights at the beginning of the
training for semantic segmentation. The pre-training
on a much larger dataset was required because our
model is quite shallow and the dataset used in this
work is very small in size. Consequently there is a
high chance that the network will suffer from over-
ﬁtting due to lack of training samples. We could fol-
low the concept of layer-wise training in a supervised
fashion to train the encoder to extract more robust fea-
tures as reported in (Roy et al., 2016) as the encoder
used in this work is quite lightweight. Implementation
of the proposed network and all experiments are ex-
ecuted using Keras (Chollet et al., 2015) framework.
We considered very popular Adam (Kingma and Ba,
2014) as optimizer. Regarding the other network con-
ﬁguration, weight decay and batch size were set to 0.9
and 4 respectively. Training was started with 0.0005
as initial learning rate including standard polynomial
decay strategy to decrease this value over 350K itera-
tions. Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) is not used in
our model. For all experiments, we used NVIDIA Ti-
tan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. No data augmen-
tation technique has been performed during training.
Experimental results and comparison study
The
hardware that we use is designed with automotive
power constraints in mind, thus having restricted
number of features for design of a convolutional neu-
ral network. Also we intend to utilize a generic en-
coder network that stays well within the budget.Thus
our main objective is to design an efﬁcient decoder
that satisﬁes both these constraints.
In the course
of design of an efﬁcient decoder, we have experi-
mented multiple versions of decoder all of which are
explained later in this section.
With all these de-
coders VGG10 pre-trained with Imagenet is used as
the encoder. This will help to have fair comparison of
the different variants of the decoder. The entire net-
work containing the encoder along with different de-
coders is trained end to end with the available pixel-
wise ground truth label. All these variants of decoder
reported in Table 1, ﬁts all our constraints. It is quite
general while capturing an urban scene, there will be
very limited region occupied by lanes, curbs but it is
exactly opposite for roads and void classes. So we
clearly see that for effective learning there is a huge
gap in problem space in these two classes while com-
paring with other. Without even attempting any data
augmentation and class weighing technique, our non-
bottleneck layers worked better for curb though there
is a slight deterioration for lanes. To evaluate the seg-
mentation performance on all the designed decoders,
widely used Intersection over Union (IoU) metric is
considered and details are furnished in Table 1.
As put forth earlier, we did experiments with sev-
eral combinations of Non-Bottleneck layers in the
network whose results are updated in Table 1. De-
coder D1 uses our proposed non-bottleneck layer
without 1X1 convolution after 3X3 and 5X5 convo-
lution. Decoder D2 is same as D1 but it does not
use second skip connection from encoder. Decoder
D3 shares the same conﬁguration as D2 but the batch
size during training was 8 whereas it was 4 for D2.
Decoder D4 is same as D3 but it does not use 1X1
convolution even before 3X3 and 5X5 convolution.
Decoder D5 is a bit different. After ﬁrst deconvolu-
tion layer two sets of 3X1, 1X3 convolutions followed
by ReLU is used. Also it uses skip connection to fuse
the resultant features with the input feature maps of
ﬁrst 3X1 convolution.
After second deconvolution
layer, one 3X3 dilated convolution with dilation rate
1 is used and then the same non-bottleneck as used
after ﬁrst deconvolution layer. Only 3X3 dilated con-
volution with dilation rate 1 is used after third and
fourth deconvolution layer. Decoder D6 is same as
D5 but it uses batch size as 4 where 8 was used in
D5. Decoder D7 is different in terms of kernel size
in deconvolution layers. It uses kernel of size 2X2
in ﬁrst and second, 3X3 in third and fourth, 5X5 in
ﬁfth upsampling layer. Decoder D8 uses same non-
bottleneck as D7 without 3X3 and 5X5 convolution.
In the pattern mNp in Table 1, m stands for number
of non-Bottleneck (N) layers, p stands for the type of

and ) stands for set of non-bottleneck layers after a

of our non-bottleneck layer from various aspects to
check what variant of change seems to work better.
Please note that the modiﬁed non-bottleneck layers
are non-repetitive between two deconvolution layers.
Of the different decoder variant, the best version is
the one put forth in Figure 3, which is obtained after
several optimization efforts and this network uses the
Non-bottleneck layers detailed in Figure 2. This net-

5
Conclusion
Design of efﬁcient encoders is a growing area of
research. In this work, we focused on design of efﬁ-
cient decoders. Firstly, we designed a novel efﬁcient
non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoders based
on this layer. We experimentally show that different
choice of decoder design had a large impact and the
optimal conﬁguration had 10% improvement of accu-
racy in terms of mean IoU over a baseline conﬁgu-
ration. In particular, for more difﬁcult segmentation
classes like lanes and curb, higher improvements of
12% and 18% were obtained. Thus we demonstrate
that the design of an efﬁcient decoder can play a crit-
ical role for segmentation tasks as it covers a signif-
icant portion of the overall computation of the net-
work. We hope that our preliminary study demon-
strates the need for further research on efﬁcient de-
coders. In future work, we build a systematic fam-
ily of meta-architectures with a ﬁxed run-time bud-
get and learn the optimal conﬁguration using meta-
learning techniques.
papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces an efficient decoder architecture for semantic segmentation in automated driving applications, focusing on real-time performance on embedded platforms. The study addresses the computational expense of decoders in semantic segmentation, particularly in contrast to the more task-agnostic nature of efficient encoders. The authors propose a novel non-bottleneck layer and a family of decoders designed to work with a VGG10 encoder, aiming to fit within a constrained run-time budget. The methodology involves designing and evaluating various decoder configurations using a custom dataset of urban scenes. The primary finding is that the optimal decoder configuration, incorporating the proposed non-bottleneck layer, achieves a 10% improvement in mean Intersection over Union (IoU) score compared to a baseline configuration. This improvement is more pronounced for challenging classes like lanes (+12% IoU) and curb (+18% IoU). The novelty lies in the design of an efficient decoder that can improve segmentation accuracy while maintaining real-time performance. The work is significant because it highlights the importance of decoder design in achieving efficient and accurate semantic segmentation for resource-constrained applications like automated driving. A key limitation is the use of a task-independent encoder, which may not fully exploit the potential of the overall architecture.

Research Context
Semantic segmentation, crucial for applications like automated driving, faces computational challenges, especially on embedded systems. Existing research has focused on efficient encoder design, but decoders are also computationally expensive. Prior methods include architectures like FCN, SegNet, and UNet, which often mirror the encoder's complexity in the decoder or use skip connections. These methods do not necessarily prioritize efficiency for real-time applications. This work addresses the gap by focusing on efficient decoder design, assuming a task-independent encoder, and aiming for real-time performance on embedded platforms. This contrasts with existing approaches that either focus on encoder efficiency or use computationally expensive decoders.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to design an efficient decoder for semantic segmentation that maintains accuracy while meeting real-time constraints in automated driving. The primary hypothesis is that a novel non-bottleneck layer, integrated into a family of decoder architectures, will improve segmentation performance compared to a baseline configuration, while remaining computationally efficient. The study predicts that the proposed decoder will achieve higher IoU scores, particularly for challenging classes like lanes and curb, without significantly increasing run-time. Alternative hypotheses could include that the proposed non-bottleneck layer does not improve performance, or that the performance gains are offset by increased computational cost. The research differs from prior work by prioritizing decoder efficiency and assuming a task-independent encoder. The study aims to demonstrate that a well-designed decoder can significantly impact segmentation accuracy, even with a fixed encoder, and that the proposed non-bottleneck layer can effectively handle the challenges of semantic segmentation in urban scenes.

Methodological Details
The study employs an empirical approach, evaluating different decoder architectures on a custom dataset. The dataset, owned by the authors' organization, comprises 1280x384 pixel images of urban scenes, including diverse lighting conditions and shadows. The dataset is divided into training (3016 images), validation (981 images), and test (1002 images) sets. The semantic segmentation task focuses on four classes: lanes, curb, road, and void. The encoder used is a VGG10-style classifier. The proposed decoder architectures are built using a novel non-bottleneck layer. The models are implemented using the Keras framework. The Adam optimizer is used, with a weight decay of 0.9 and a batch size of 4 (or 8, depending on the decoder variant). The initial learning rate is 0.0005, with a standard polynomial decay strategy over 350,000 iterations. Dropout is not used. Experiments are conducted on an NVIDIA Titan X 12G GPU with 24 GB RAM. No data augmentation is performed. The performance of different decoder variants is evaluated using the Intersection over Union (IoU) metric. The study compares the performance of the proposed decoder variants against a standard FCN decoder. The hardware used is designed with automotive power constraints in mind. The training process involves pre-training the encoder on ImageNet and then transferring the weights for the semantic segmentation task. The study does not mention the random seed used.

Procedures Architectures
The study focuses on designing an efficient decoder for semantic segmentation, assuming a task-independent encoder. The overall architecture follows an encoder-decoder structure. The encoder, a VGG10-style classifier, extracts features from the input images. The decoder reconstructs the original input space and generates class predictions for each pixel. The decoder uses deconvolution layers for reconstruction, instead of max-unpooling. The core innovation is the proposed non-bottleneck layer, which is designed to handle high gradient flow and learn semantic information from the encoded feature space. The non-bottleneck layer has two variants (Type-1 and Type-2). Type-1 uses 1D and 3D kernels, while Type-2 incorporates dilated convolutions. The architecture uses multiple skip connections to distribute gradients during backpropagation. The encoder-decoder architecture is illustrated in Figure 3. The encoder downsamples feature maps from 256 to 4. The decoder architecture consists of deconvolution layers and non-bottleneck layers. The optimal decoder configuration uses two non-bottleneck layers of Type-1, followed by two non-bottleneck layers of Type-2, and then one more non-bottleneck layer of Type-2. Intermediate feature maps from the second and third-to-last convolution layers of the encoder are also used. The encoder consumes most of the run-time. The design avoids the use of group convolution, as it was found to have adverse effects for lightweight networks. The architecture is designed for real-time performance on embedded platforms.

Key Results
The study evaluates the performance of different decoder variants using the IoU metric. Table 1 presents the results. The optimal decoder configuration, labeled as "Optimal" in Table 1, achieves a mean IoU score of 0.7441. The baseline configuration (not explicitly defined, but implied to be a less optimized decoder) is improved by 10% in mean IoU. The optimal decoder achieves an IoU of 0.5304 for lanes (+12% relative), 0.4696 for curb (+18% relative), and 0.9314 for road. The best performing decoder configuration is (2N1)(2N1)(2N2)(2N2). The standard FCN decoder is used for comparison, with the proposed decoder showing an improvement in IoU, especially for key classes, with less than 2ms increase in runtime. The results demonstrate that the design choices in the decoder architecture significantly impact segmentation performance. The study also shows that the proposed non-bottleneck layer is effective for handling class imbalance, particularly for lanes and curb. The best performing variant achieves a mean IoU of 0.7441, with the optimal configuration improving the IoU scores for lanes and curbs.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the design of the decoder plays a critical role in achieving accurate and efficient semantic segmentation, even with a task-independent encoder. The proposed non-bottleneck layer effectively learns semantic information from the encoded feature space, leading to improved performance, especially for challenging classes. The results support the idea that careful architectural design can overcome limitations in the encoder, particularly in resource-constrained environments. The study implies that the proposed decoder architecture can improve the performance of semantic segmentation tasks in automated driving applications. The improvement in IoU scores for lanes and curb suggests that the proposed method is particularly effective in handling classes with limited representation in the dataset. The results indicate that the proposed non-bottleneck layer is a suitable component for constructing efficient decoders. The study demonstrates that the design of an efficient decoder can play a critical role for segmentation tasks as it covers a significant portion of the overall computation of the network.

Contradictions Limitations
A key limitation is the use of a task-independent encoder, which may not fully exploit the potential of the overall architecture. The study does not explore the impact of different encoder choices on the performance of the proposed decoder. The dataset is limited to urban scenes, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to other environments. The study does not report the random seed used for training, which could affect reproducibility. The study does not use data augmentation techniques, which could potentially improve performance. The study does not perform a detailed ablation study to isolate the contribution of each component of the proposed decoder. The study does not provide details on the class weights used, if any, which could affect the results. The study does not provide a detailed analysis of the run-time performance of the different decoder variants. The study does not discuss the potential impact of the encoder's design on the overall performance.

Robustness Ablation Notes
The study evaluates multiple decoder variants with different configurations of the non-bottleneck layer (Table 1). The results show that the choice of decoder design has a large impact on performance. The study does not provide a detailed ablation study to isolate the contribution of each component of the proposed decoder.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the results of different decoder variants, showing the mean IoU scores for different classes and the overall mean IoU. This table is critical for comparing the performance of different decoder configurations and demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed non-bottleneck layer. Figure 4 provides a visual comparison of the segmentation outputs of the proposed optimal decoder and a standard FCN decoder, illustrating the improvements in segmentation quality.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the design of an efficient decoder architecture for semantic segmentation, featuring a novel non-bottleneck layer, that improves segmentation accuracy while maintaining real-time performance, particularly for automated driving applications. (2) The strongest evidence is the 10% improvement in mean IoU score, with significant gains in IoU for lanes and curb, as shown in Table 1, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed decoder design. (3) The primary limitation is the use of a task-independent encoder, which may not fully exploit the potential of the overall architecture, and the lack of a detailed ablation study. Future work could explore the impact of different encoder choices and conduct more detailed ablation studies to further refine the decoder design.

questions.question: Why does the proposed non-bottleneck block use multiple skip connections?

options.A: To eliminate batch normalization from all convolutional layers
options.B: To reduce the number of feature maps from 256 directly to four
options.C: To pass max-pooling indices from every encoder stage into the decoder
options.D: To distribute high gradients over multiple paths during back-propagation in a relatively shallow network

questions.formatted_question:
Why does the proposed non-bottleneck block use multiple skip connections?
A) To eliminate batch normalization from all convolutional layers
B) To reduce the number of feature maps from 256 directly to four
C) To pass max-pooling indices from every encoder stage into the decoder
D) To distribute high gradients over multiple paths during back-propagation in a relatively shallow network

options.C: Type-2 omits all skip connections and batch normalization

questions.rationale: The variant distinction is dilation in the block on the right; the paper holds dilation rate at one for this study.

questions.question: Why did the authors avoid increasing the decoder's width after the encoder reduces its feature maps from 256 to four?

options.D: Four channels are mathematically required for deconvolution

Executive Summary
This paper investigates the characterization of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators using Lusin area integrals. The Hermite operator, denoted as L, is defined as the negative Laplacian plus the squared Euclidean norm of the position vector. The study focuses on Hardy spaces, denoted as H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), with an index p in the range (0, 1], which are constructed using the maximal function of the semigroup generated by the Hermite operator. The central result, Theorem 1.1, establishes an equivalence between the Hardy space H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) and a space defined using Lusin integrals, denoted as H<sup>p</sup><sub>S</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). The Lusin integral is defined using derivatives of the form ∂<sub>j</sub> + x<sub>j</sub>, which are specific to Hermite operators. The paper also demonstrates the boundedness of Riesz transforms, denoted as R<sup>L</sup><sub>j</sub>, on H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) for all j (Theorem 1.2). The methodology involves defining intermediate spaces and utilizing atom decompositions to characterize the Hardy spaces. The findings provide a new characterization of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators, offering a deeper understanding of their structure and properties. A key limitation is the focus on a specific class of operators, which limits the scope of the results. The work is significant because it provides a novel characterization of Hardy spaces, which are fundamental in harmonic analysis, and extends existing results to a more general setting.

Research Context
Hardy spaces are fundamental in harmonic analysis, with well-established characterizations. Prior work has characterized Hardy spaces associated with various operators, including the Laplacian. The existing literature lacks a comprehensive characterization of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators using Lusin area integrals. The novelty of this work lies in the use of more general Lusin area integrals, defined using derivatives specific to Hermite operators, and the characterization of H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) in terms of these integrals. Previous studies, such as those by Stein, and others, have explored similar characterizations, but this work offers a different approach, particularly in the definition of the Lusin area integrals. The paper builds upon the work of Jiz12, which focused on Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators with index p=1.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: Can the Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators be characterized using Lusin area integrals? The primary hypothesis, supported by Theorem 1.1, is that the Hardy space H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) can be characterized in terms of Lusin integrals associated with the Hermite operator. An alternative hypothesis could be that such a characterization is not possible or that the Lusin integrals would need to be defined in a different manner. The study also investigates the boundedness of Riesz transforms on H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), with the hypothesis that these transforms are bounded (Theorem 1.2). The outcomes supporting the hypotheses would be the establishment of the equivalence between H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) and a space defined using Lusin integrals, and the proof of the boundedness of the Riesz transforms. This work differs from prior research by using a specific form of Lusin integrals tailored to the Hermite operator, providing a novel perspective on the characterization of Hardy spaces.

Methodological Details
The study employs a theoretical approach, focusing on mathematical analysis and proof. The core methodology involves defining the Hermite operator L = -Δ + |x|<sup>2</sup> on its maximal domain in L<sup>2</sup>(R<sup>d</sup>), where d ≥ 3 and p ∈ (0, 1]. The Hardy space H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) is defined as the completion of a set of functions in L<sup>2</sup>(R<sup>d</sup>) with respect to a quasi-norm based on the maximal function of the semigroup generated by L. The Lusin integral, denoted as Sf(x), is defined using the gradient of the Poisson semigroup associated with the Hermite operator. The paper defines intermediate spaces, such as H<sup>p</sup><sub>L,max</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) and H<sup>p</sup><sub>A</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), to facilitate the proof of the main theorem. Atom decompositions are used to characterize the Hardy spaces. The proof of Theorem 1.1 involves demonstrating the equivalence of the quasi-norms of H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) and H<sup>p</sup><sub>S</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). The boundedness of Riesz transforms is proved using the properties of the Hardy spaces and the Lusin integrals. The study relies on existing mathematical tools and techniques from harmonic analysis, functional analysis, and operator theory. The study does not involve any empirical data or experiments. The analysis relies on definitions, propositions, lemmas, and theorems. The paper cites several references, including [Tha93], [Ste95], [SY16], [JPY16], [Jiz12], [Kat80], [BDL18], [She95], [BDY12], [HLM+11], [AF03], [Rus07], and [CMS85]. No preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections are mentioned.

Procedures Architectures
The paper focuses on the mathematical properties of the Hermite operator and associated function spaces, rather than on specific architectures or procedures. The Hermite operator, L = -Δ + |x|<sup>2</sup>, is the central mathematical object. The Poisson semigroup, P<sub>t</sub> = e<sup>-tL<sup>1/2</sup></sup>, and the heat kernel, g<sub>t</sub>, of the semigroup T<sub>t</sub> = e<sup>-tL</sup>, are essential components in the definitions of the Hardy spaces and the Lusin integrals. The Lusin integral, Sf(x), is defined as an integral involving the gradient of the Poisson semigroup. The Riesz transforms, R<sup>L</sup><sub>j</sub> = (∂<sub>j</sub> + x<sub>j</sub>)L<sup>-1/2</sup>, are also key operators. The paper defines several function spaces: H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), H<sup>p</sup><sub>S</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), H<sup>p</sup><sub>L,max</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), H<sup>p</sup><sub>A</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>), and H<sup>p</sup><sub>L,at,M</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). The atom decomposition of H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) is a crucial technique. The paper utilizes the properties of these operators and function spaces to prove the main theorems. The approach involves the use of kernel estimates, atom decompositions, and the Calderon reproducing formula. The paper does not describe any specific software or hardware.

Key Results
The main result is Theorem 1.1, which establishes the equivalence of the Hardy space H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) and the space H<sup>p</sup><sub>S</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). The proof relies on the intermediate spaces and atom decompositions. The paper also proves Theorem 1.2, demonstrating that the Riesz transforms R<sup>L</sup><sub>j</sub> are bounded on H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). Proposition 2.1 provides estimates for the function ρ(x). Proposition 2.2 and 2.3 provide kernel estimates for the heat kernel and the Poisson semigroup, respectively. Proposition 2.5 describes the atom decomposition of the space H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). Proposition 3.1 demonstrates that H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) ⊂ H<sup>p</sup><sub>L,max</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>). Proposition 4.2 shows that the operator A is bounded on L<sup>2</sup>(R<sup>d</sup>). Proposition 4.11 establishes that H<sup>p</sup><sub>L</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) = H<sup>p</sup><sub>A</sub>(R<sup>d</sup>) ∩ L<sup>2</sup>(R<sup>d</sup>). Lemma 5.1 provides an estimate for S<sup>ε,R</sup><sub>α</sub>f(x). Lemma 5.2 provides an estimate for the measure of the set where eS<sup>ε,R</sup><sub>1/20</sub>f(x) > 2λ and f<sup>*</sup><sub>L</sub>(x) ≤ γλ. Lemma 5.3 shows the equivalence of the Lp norms of S<sup>ε,R</sup><sub>α</sub> and S<sup>ε,R</sup><sub>β</sub>. Proposition 5.4 establishes an inequality relating the Lp norm of Sf and the Lp norm of f<sup>*</sup><sub>L</sub>. The results are presented in the form of theorems, propositions, and lemmas, with proofs based on mathematical analysis and established results in harmonic analysis. No quantitative comparisons with baseline or SOTA methods are provided, as the work is theoretical. No effect sizes or confidence intervals are provided. P-values are not applicable.

Interpretation Implications
The findings provide a new characterization of Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators, offering a deeper understanding of their structure and properties. Theorem 1.1 provides an alternative way to define and study these spaces using Lusin area integrals. The boundedness of the Riesz transforms, as demonstrated in Theorem 1.2, is a fundamental property of these spaces. The results contribute to the broader theory of harmonic analysis by extending the existing characterizations of Hardy spaces to a specific class of operators. The paper suggests that the Lusin area integrals, defined using derivatives specific to the Hermite operator, are suitable tools for studying these spaces. The findings suggest that the techniques used in the paper can be applied to other similar problems in harmonic analysis, potentially providing new insights into the properties of other function spaces. The results do not directly propose a mechanism, but rather, they provide a new way to understand the relationships between different function spaces. The scope conditions are that the dimension d ≥ 3 and the index p ∈ (0, 1]. The understanding of the Hardy spaces is shifted by providing a new characterization.

Contradictions Limitations
The primary limitation is the focus on Hardy spaces associated with Hermite operators, which limits the scope of the results. The results are specific to the Hermite operator and may not generalize to other operators or function spaces. The theoretical nature of the work means that the results are not directly applicable to practical problems. The paper does not address the limitations of the atom decomposition or the choice of the intermediate spaces. The paper does not provide any empirical validation of the theoretical results. The paper does not discuss potential conflicts with prior literature, although it builds upon and extends previous work in the field. The study does not mention the random seed or train/test split, as it is a theoretical work. The external validity is limited by the specific choice of the Hermite operator. The study does not discuss any internal inconsistencies.

source.source_title: Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive MIMO for Hybrid Precoding

papers.fulltext:
1
Deep-Learning-based Millimeter-Wave Massive
MIMO for Hybrid Precoding
Hongji Huang, Member, IEEE, Yiwei Song, Jie Yang, Member, IEEE,
Guan Gui, Senior Member, IEEE, and Fumiyuki Adachi, Life Fellow, IEEE
Abstract—Millimeter wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input
multiple-output (MIMO) has been regarded to be an emerging so-
lution for the next generation of communications, in which hybrid
analog and digital precoding is an important method for reducing
the hardware complexity and energy consumption associated with
mixed signal components. However, the fundamental limitations
of the existing hybrid precoding schemes is that they have high
computational complexity and fail to fully exploit the spatial
information. To overcome these limitations, this paper proposes
a deep-learning-enabled mmWave massive MIMO framework
for effective hybrid precoding, in which each selection of the
precoders for obtaining the optimized decoder is regarded as a
mapping relation in the deep neural network (DNN). Speciﬁcally,
the hybrid precoder is selected through training based on the
DNN for optimizing precoding process of the mmWave massive
MIMO. Additionally, we present extensive simulation results
to validate the excellent performance of the proposed scheme.
The results exhibit that the DNN-based approach is capable of
minimizing the bit error ratio (BER) and enhancing spectrum
efﬁciency of the mmWave massive MIMO, which achieves better
performance in hybrid precoding compared with conventional
schemes while substantially reducing the required computational
complexity.
Index Terms—Millimeter wave (mmWave), massive multiple-
input multiple-output (MIMO), deep learning, hybrid precoding.
I. INTRODUCTION
W
IRELESS data trafﬁc is predicted to improve 1000-fold
by the year 2020 and may increase by over 10 000-fold
by the year 2030 [1], thus promoting the development of the
ﬁfth generation (5G) concept to cope with the explosive data
increase. As one of the most highly efﬁcient techniques to meet
the 5G requirements, the use of enormous chunks of under-
utilized spectrum in the ultra-high-frequency bands, such as
the millimeter-wave (mmWave) band, has recently attracted
considerable interest in the research community [2]. Compare
with current wireless systems, one evolutionary progress of
mmWave communications is that the ten-fold increase in
carrier frequency. In another words, mmWave signals bring an
orders-of-magnitude enhancement in free-space pathloss [3].
Inspired
by
massive
multiple-input
multiple-output
(MIMO), a mmWave massive MIMO system is considered
to be a potential technique for enhancing system throughput.
H. Huang, Y. Song, J. Yang, and G. Gui are with College of Telecommuni-
cation and Information Engineering, Nanjing University of Posts and Telecom-
munications, Nanjing 210003, P. R. China. (e-mail: b14111829@njupt.edu.cn,
b15080234@njupt.edu.cn, guiguan@njupt.edu.cn, hikmet@njupt.edu.cn)
F. Adachi is with Wireless Signal Processing Research Group, Research Or-
ganization of Electrical Communication (ROEC), Tohoku University, Sendai
980-8577, Japan. (e-mail: adachi@ecei.tohoku.ac.jp)
To multiplex a large amount of data streams and achieve
more accurate beamforming in mmWave massive MIMO,
hybrid precoding was proposed [1]. In [4], a successive
interference cancellation-based hybrid precoding that can
realize excellent performance with low complexity was
presented, in which the sum rate optimization problem with
non-convex constraints was divided into several sub-rate
optimization issues. Then, the authors in [5] designed a
low-complexity hybrid analog/digital precoding for multiuser
mmWave systems by conﬁguring a hybrid precoder. However,
these precoding schemes proposed in the previous works
have high commotional complexity and require a complicated
bit allocation strategy since the previously proposed hybrid
anlog/digital precoding schemes are based on singular value
decomposition (SVD). Additionally, the newly proposed
geometric mean decomposition (GMD)-based scheme [6]
can avoid the bit allocation issue, but it still brings great
challenges in addressing the non-convex constraint on the
analog precoder and in exploiting the structural characteristics
of the mmWave massive MIMO systems.
However, in the context of the mmWave massive MIMO
systems, though a quantity of researches have been devoted to
enhancing the hybrid precoding performance, there are still
a lot of problems remaining and two major challenge are
the extraordinarily high computational complexity and poor
system performance. In the past few years, many scholars have
realized this gap and they have provided different methods
for reducing the computational complexity or improving the
precoding performance, such as the (GMD)-based scheme
[6], the matrix factorization-based hybrid precoding mean
[7], a precoding method based on radio-frequency (RF) and
baseband signal processing [8], and hybrid spatial processing
architecture aided precoding approach [9], et al. Also, for the
sake of realizing high spectrum efﬁciency with low complex-
ity, an alternating minimization scheme for effectively design-
ing hybrid precoder was provided [10]. Then, by exploiting
low-dimensional beamspace channel state information (CSI)
processed by compressive sensing (CS) detectors, paper [11]
presented a beamspace-SVD based hybrid precoding method
for reducing complexity. In general, these works are based on
conventional mathematical means such as the SVD and the
GMD, which are too weak to exploit the sparsity statistics
of the mmWave massive MIMO. Simultaneously, since the
traditional methods are inadequate to leverage the structural
characteristics of such mmWave systems, traditional low-
complexity schemes are realized at the cost of degrading the
hybrid precoding of the systems. Therefore, previous works
arXiv:1901.06537v1  [eess.SP]  19 Jan 2019

2
fail to deal with these issues fundamentally and new methods
are urgent need to be put forward for enhancing the hybrid
precoding performance of the mmWave massive MIMO.
Recently, the emerging solution called deep learning [12]
is an extraordinarily remarkable technology for handling ex-
plosive data and addressing complicated nonlinear problems.
It has been proved that deep learning is an excellent tool to
deal with complex non-convex problems and high-computation
issues, which is dedicated by its super-excellent recognition
and representation abilities. Some previous works which in-
corporate deep learning into communications have been in-
vestigated, including beam selection, heterogeneous network,
non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), massive MIMO, and
heterogeneous network [13]–[18]. Additionally, deep learning
has been applied to intelligent trafﬁc control area [19]–[22],
showing great advancements resulting from the deep-learning-
based communication schemes.
Thus, this study investigates a framework which integrates
deep learning into hybrid precoding in mmWave MIMO sys-
tems. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as
follows.
1) First, this is the ﬁrst work to design a framework that
incorporates the deep learning technique into hybrid
precoding. Speciﬁcally, we regard a deep neural network
(DNN) as an autoencoder, and this model is regarded
as a black box, where activation functions optimize
multiple layers of the network and create corresponding
mapping relations.
2) In our work, a hybrid precoding scheme based on deep
learning is provided. Here, the DNN is capable of cap-
turing structural information of hybrid precoding scheme
through the training stage, contributing to lowering
the computational complexity. Additionally, simulation
results and comparisons have veriﬁed the superiority of
the proposed methods.
The rest of this paper is organized as follows. To begin
with, we establish a mmWave massive MIMO model, in which
many antennas are implemented at the base station (BS). Then,
in Section III, to achieve hybrid precoding with good perfor-
mance, we develop a DNN framework and provide a deep
learning-enabled scheme. Simulation results for assessing the
