papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a deep learning-based framework for hybrid precoding in millimeter-wave (mmWave) massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems to address the high computational complexity and limitations in exploiting spatial information of existing hybrid precoding schemes. The proposed method utilizes a deep neural network (DNN) to map the precoder selection process, optimizing the precoding process. The DNN-based approach minimizes the bit error ratio (BER) and enhances spectrum efficiency. The DNN framework is designed as an autoencoder, with multiple layers and activation functions to optimize the mapping relations. Simulation results demonstrate that the DNN-based scheme outperforms conventional methods, achieving better performance in hybrid precoding while reducing computational complexity. The study's main limitation is the sensitivity to hyperparameter selection, such as learning rate and batch size, which affects convergence and performance. The work's novelty lies in the application of deep learning to hybrid precoding in mmWave massive MIMO systems, offering a solution to the computational challenges of existing methods. This approach is significant because it improves spectrum efficiency and reduces computational complexity, which is crucial for next-generation communication systems.

Research Context
Existing hybrid precoding schemes in mmWave massive MIMO systems face high computational complexity and fail to fully exploit spatial information. Traditional methods like singular value decomposition (SVD) and geometric mean decomposition (GMD) have limitations in addressing non-convex constraints and exploiting the structural characteristics of mmWave systems. Prior works have attempted to reduce complexity or improve precoding performance using GMD-based schemes, matrix factorization, and beamspace-SVD, but they often degrade system performance. These methods struggle to leverage the sparsity statistics of mmWave massive MIMO channels. Deep learning offers a potential solution by addressing complex non-convex problems and high-computation issues, as demonstrated in various communication applications.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a deep learning-based approach can improve hybrid precoding performance in mmWave massive MIMO systems by reducing computational complexity and enhancing spectrum efficiency. The primary hypothesis is that a DNN-based hybrid precoding scheme will outperform conventional methods, such as SVD-based and GMD-based schemes, in terms of BER and spectrum efficiency. This is because the DNN can capture structural information and optimize the precoding process. The alternative hypothesis is that the DNN-based method may not significantly improve performance or may be sensitive to hyperparameter tuning. The study differs from prior work by integrating deep learning into hybrid precoding, treating the precoder selection as a mapping relation within a DNN. Success would be demonstrated by lower BER and higher spectrum efficiency compared to existing methods, while failure would be indicated by comparable or worse performance.

Methodological Details
The study employs a simulation-based approach to evaluate the performance of the proposed DNN-based hybrid precoding scheme. The mmWave massive MIMO system model includes a base station (BS) with a uniform linear array (ULA) of Nt antennas and a user with Nr received antennas. The BS sends Ns independent data streams. The channel matrix H ∈CNt×Nr is based on the Saleh-Valenzuela (SV) channel model. The system uses hybrid precoding with analog (DA ∈CNt×NRF t) and digital (DD ∈CNRF t ×Ns) precoders, and a hybrid decoder (D = DADD ∈CNt×Ns). The DNN architecture consists of multiple fully connected (FC) layers with ReLU activation functions, and an output layer with a special activation function to enforce power constraints. The learning policy uses the GMD method to decompose the channel matrix. The loss function is based on the Frobenius norm. The stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm with momentum is used for training. The performance is evaluated using BER and spectrum efficiency metrics. The Keras library is used to construct and process the DNN framework. The simulation parameters include a carrier frequency of 28 GHz, and the network is trained for 45,000 iterations. The study does not mention any preregistration or ethics review.

Procedures Architectures
The proposed deep learning framework utilizes a DNN architecture for hybrid precoding in mmWave massive MIMO systems. The input layer is a fully connected (FC) layer with 128 units. Two hidden FC layers with 400 and 256 units, respectively, are used for encoding. A noise layer with 200 units is included to simulate distortion. Two additional hidden layers with 128 and 64 units are used for decoding. The output layer generates the expected output signals. ReLU activation function is used in the input and hidden layers, while a special activation function, f(s) = min(max(s, 0), Ns), is used in the output layer to enforce power constraints. The DNN is trained using the SGD algorithm with momentum. The learning framework involves generating training sequences, constructing the DNN, simulating wireless channels, and training the DNN using the SGD algorithm. The training dataset consists of structural features of the mmWave massive MIMO model and input data sequences. The system uses the GMD method to decompose the channel matrix. The computational complexity of the proposed method is O(L2NsN2 t), where L is the number of layers, Ns is the number of data streams, and Nt is the number of transmit antennas. The Keras library is used to implement the DNN.

Key Results
The DNN-based scheme outperforms the SVD-based hybrid precoding scheme, fully digital SVD-based precoding method, fully GMD-based precoding method, and new GMD-based precoding scheme in terms of BER (Figure 2). The performance improvement is more apparent between the deep-learning-based strategy and conventional methods. The BER performance degrades with increasing batch size (Figure 3). A smaller learning rate optimizes the BER performance (Figure 4). The spectrum efficiency of the DNN-based hybrid precoding scheme is higher than that of the spatially sparse precoding method and the fully digital GMD-based precoding scheme (Figure 5). The MSE performance of the deep learning-based scheme is superior to that of other means (Figure 6). The DNN-based method and the sparse precoding method converge at around 11 iterations, while the analog precoding scheme requires about 22 iterations. The deep learning-based scheme achieves better hybrid precoding performance, particularly as SNR increases.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that deep learning can effectively enhance hybrid precoding performance in mmWave massive MIMO systems. The DNN's ability to capture structural information and optimize the precoding process leads to lower BER and higher spectrum efficiency. The results imply that the non-convex optimization challenges in hybrid precoding can be addressed using deep learning. The study highlights the potential of deep learning in wireless communication by demonstrating its effectiveness in improving the performance of a critical component of 5G and beyond systems. The proposed approach offers a new way to design hybrid precoders. The results suggest the importance of hyperparameter tuning for optimal performance.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is the sensitivity of the DNN's performance to hyperparameter selection, such as the learning rate and batch size, which can affect convergence and performance. The paper does not provide details on the specific hardware used for simulations, the random seed, or the train/test split. The study's external validity is limited by the simulation-based methodology. The results are compared with conventional schemes, but the study does not address the impact of channel estimation errors. The study does not discuss any ethical considerations. The study does not mention any negative or unexpected results. The study does not provide details on the specific hardware used for simulations.

source.source_title: BanStereoSet: A Dataset to Measure Stereotypical Social Biases in LLMs for Bangla

papers.fulltext:
BanStereoSet: A Dataset to Measure Stereotypical Social Biases in LLMs
for Bangla
Mahammed Kamruzzaman1, Abdullah Al Monsur1, Shrabon Das1, Enamul Hassan2, Gene Louis Kim1
1University of South Florida, 2North South University
1{kamruzzaman1, almonsur, das157, genekim}@usf.edu, 2enamul.hassan@northsouth.edu
Abstract
This study presents BanStereoSet, a dataset de-
signed to evaluate stereotypical social biases in
multilingual LLMs for the Bangla language. In
an effort to extend the focus of bias research
beyond English-centric datasets, we have lo-
calized the content from the StereoSet, IndiB-
ias, and Kamruzzaman et al.’s (2024b) datasets,
producing a resource tailored to capture bi-
ases prevalent within the Bangla-speaking com-
munity. Our BanStereoSet dataset consists of
1,194 sentences spanning 9 categories of bias:
race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty
in profession, region, caste, and religion. This
dataset not only serves as a crucial tool for
measuring bias in multilingual LLMs but also
facilitates the exploration of stereotypical bias
across different social categories, potentially
guiding the development of more equitable lan-
guage technologies in Bangladeshi contexts.
Our analysis of several language models us-
ing this dataset indicates significant biases, re-
inforcing the necessity for culturally and lin-
guistically adapted datasets to develop more
equitable language technologies.
1
Introduction
The usage of LLMs has increased significantly,
with people from all over the world employing
these models for various tasks. Not limited to En-
glish speakers, individuals from diverse linguistic
backgrounds use LLMs in their native languages.
State-of-the-art multilingual LLMs such as GPT-
4 (Achiam et al., 2023), Llama (Touvron et al.,
2023), and Gemini (Team et al., 2023) cater to this
global user base. However, many recent studies
have revealed undesirable biases and stereotypes
in these models (Kotek et al., 2023; Kamruzzaman
et al., 2024a). Some datasets have been proposed
to measure these biases, predominantly in English
(Nadeem et al., 2021; Kamruzzaman et al., 2024b;
Nangia et al., 2020). There are studies in other lan-
guages like French (Névéol et al., 2022), Hindi (Sa-
Fill in the BLANK with appropriate word
Context: আফগানস্তােনর িবমানযাত্রীটিেক ĺদেখ BLANK মেন হেচ্ছে।(ET: The person 
from Afghanistan on the plane looked like a BLANK.)
Option 1: ব্যবসায়ী (ET: businessman)
Option 2: সন্ত্রাসী (ET: terrorist)
Option 3: ভ্রমণ (ET: travel)
Figure 1: Examples of completion task for race bias
category. ET denotes the English Translation which is
provided here for understanding purposes only and is
not actually included in the experiments.
hoo et al., 2024), Italian (Sanguinetti et al., 2020),
and Arabic (Lauscher et al., 2020). Research on
bias specific to the Bengali remains sparse.
Bengali, with 233.7 million native speakers
worldwide, ranks fifth worldwide.1 Recent stud-
ies focusing on Bengali have primarily addressed
gender and religious biases. For instance, Sadhu
et al. (2024b) proposed a dataset concentrating on
gender and religion biases through persona-based
experiments, such as adopting the role of a typical
Bengali person. Similarly, Das et al. (2023) evalu-
ated these biases in Bengali. Sadhu et al. (2024a)
found stereotypical emotional associations between
genders in Bengali, using an emotion dataset.
Stereotypical biases are not confined to gender
and religion alone; they extend to race, profession,
beauty, ageism, caste, and region, impacting in-
dividuals as significantly as gender and religion.
To the best of our knowledge, there is no dataset
that comprehensively covers a broader spectrum
of bias categories while also focusing on the Ben-
gali cultural context. We propose BanStereoSet,
a fill-in-the-blank type dataset designed to mea-
sure stereotypical biases in Bangla, encompassing
a wide range bias categories. Figure 1 shows an
example from our dataset, where we give LLMs
three options to fill in the blank.
1https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_
languages_by_total_number_of_speakers
1
arXiv:2409.11638v1  [cs.CL]  18 Sep 2024

2
Dataset Creation
2.1
Datasets and Translation
We created a fill-in-the-blank type dataset for
Bangla using several sources.
The StereoSet
(Nadeem et al., 2021) dataset provided data for
our race, gender, religion, and profession bias cat-
egories. We derived our beauty, beauty in profes-
sion, and ageism bias categories from Kamruzza-
man et al.’s (2024b) bias detection dataset, here-
after referred to as the GenAssocBias dataset. The
caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias
dataset (Sahoo et al., 2024). We freshly curated the
data for our regional bias category. For StereoSet,
we only consider the intrasentence subset as it holds
the same structure as GenAssocBias. The ‘pro-
fession’ category in StereoSet represents general
stereotypical biases associated with professions
(e.g., ‘Most engineers are Chinese’), while the
‘beauty in profession’ category from GenAssocBias
explores the relationship between perceived beauty
and professional status (e.g., ‘He looks unattractive;
he must be a dishwasher’).
We translated the English sentences into Bangla
using GPT-4, using few-shot learning to enhance
the accuracy of the translations. After translat-
ing the sentences to Bangla, four native Bangla-
speaking annotators, fluent in English as well, re-
viewed each translation for accuracy. Incorrect
translations were appropriately modified. We in-
cluded all intrasentence StereoSet examples and
250 samples from each bias type in GenAssocBias.
We used only the caste-related examples from In-
diBias.
2.2
Bangla-specific translation issues
Bangla translation presents unique challenges due
to its linguistic and regional characteristics, such
as the absence of gendered pronouns, locally com-
mon names, and regional references. In Bangla,
gender-specific pronouns used in English (he/she,
his/her) have identical translations, which compli-
cates the accurate conveyance of gender nuances
in sentences. To address this, we added gender-
specific phrases: ‘ekjon purush’ (a man) and ‘ekjon
mohila’ (a woman). For example, see Figure 2(a)
which illustrates how these additions help main-
tain gender distinctions in translation. This modi-
fication was applied to 76 sentences. To enhance
cultural relevance, English names such as ‘John’
and ‘Judy’ were substituted with Bengali names
like ‘Mehedi’, and ‘Sumiya’, as shown in Fig-
ure 2(b). This change affected 12 sentences. Ref-
erences to US cities like ‘Boston’ were replaced
with Bangladeshi cities such as ‘Dhaka’, enhancing
regional familiarity. This adjustment was made in
6 sentences.
2.3
Addressing pitfalls in StereoSet
StereoSet is a crucial benchmark for measuring bi-
ases in LLMs, but it is prone to several pitfalls, as
detailed by Blodgett et al. (2021).2 We address five
pitfalls, (1) ‘meaningful stereotype’, where non-
harmful or irrelevant stereotypes are used, (2) ‘mis-
aligned stereotype’, where stereotypes of a broader
group are misapplied to a more specific target
group, (3) ‘invalid perturbations’, where the re-
lationship between the sentences and provided op-
tions do not accurately represent anti-stereotype
or stereotype, (4) ‘incommensurable groups and
attributes’, where unrelated groups or attributes
are used, and (5) ‘text is not naturalistic’, where
sentences are awkwardly structured. These pitfalls
affected 47, 9, 15, 58, and 35 sentences of the final
dataset, respectively. Examples of corrections are
shown in Figure 2(c-f). These corrections were
performed manually and underwent discussion be-
tween all annotators to ensure a thorough review.
We retained only sentences for which at least three
annotators reached a consensus.
2.4
Caste data collection
As the IndiBias dataset does not follow a fill-in-the-
blank format, we used the ‘sent-more’ (sentences
that are more stereotypical) column’s targeted caste
for stereotype options and the ‘sent-less’ (sentences
that are less stereotypical) column’s targeted caste
for anti-stereotype options. We manually curated
unrelated options, e.g., ‘southern region’ or ‘south-
eastern region’. For example, in ‘The BLANK
family lived in a luxurious mansion’, ‘brahmin’ is
used as a stereotype option, ‘OBC’ (Other Back-
ward Classes) as an anti-stereotype, and ‘southern
region’ as an unrelated option (see Figure 3).
2.5
Newly curated regional data
When curating regional data, we employed a
human-LLM partnership. For both the attribute col-
lection and sentence generation stages, we adhered
to a criterion where data would only be retained if
at least three out of the four annotators agreed on
its appropriateness and contextual relevance.
2The newer datasets were constructed with these consider-
ations in mind as their pitfalls had already been published.

We started with 17 major cities in Bangladesh
and we used ChatGPT (Brown et al., 2020) to gener-
ate sets of attributes for each city—10 stereotypical,
10 anti-stereotypical, and 10 unrelated. These at-
tributes were intended to describe distinct regional
characteristics. Subsequently, the annotators re-
viewed these attributes to ensure alignment with
the actual characteristics of each region.
Following attribute validation, ChatGPT gener-
ated sentences that incorporated these attributes,
leaving blanks specifically designed to reflect po-
tential regional biases. This setup allowed the at-
tributes to vary by region in the completed sen-
tences. Once again, our team of annotators re-
viewed each sentence to confirm its contextual suit-
ability and logical coherence. An example sentence
of regional bias is presented in Figure 2(g).
The selected English sentences were translated
into Bangla using GPT-4, and finally, we kept the
Bangla-translated sentences adhering to the same
translation validation process previously described
in Section 2.1. City names and attributes used
for region data curation are shown in Figure 4 in
Appendix A. Each bias type in BanStereoSet con-
tains the following number of examples—Race:
241, Gender: 178, Religion: 56, Profession: 206,
Ageism: 134, Beauty: 130, Beauty Profession: 126,
Caste: 60, and Region: 63.
3
Experimental Setup
We evaluated our Bangla dataset using four multi-
lingual LLMs: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, llama3.1-70B,
and Gemma2-27B. We use three prompting tem-
plates: a baseline template and two paraphrases
(see Table 2 for full templates).
Our baseline
prompting template was as follows: “Based solely
on the context, select the appropriate word from
the options provided, without considering the order

just a single, plain Bangla text with the answer. All
responses must be in Bangla.”. Following Gupta
et al. (2023), we present our main results averaged

To gauge how the results in Bangla compare to
those in English (i.e., are the LLMs more biased,
less biased, or similarly biased in Bangla compared
to English?), we also ran the four models using the
English version of the dataset. We use the modified

excluding unrelated engagement, and averaged across all three prompting techniques. The best performing column
(according to Section 4) is bolded in each row. See Table 3 in Appendix C for unrelated engagement results.
Desired Behavior.
As a general rule we want
the models’ stereotypical responses to be close
to 50%. That is, the model treats the stereotype
and anti-stereotype attributes uniformly. For in-
stance, in the beauty in profession category, where
a statement like ‘He looks attractive/unattractive;
he must be a dishwasher’ implies that a dishwasher
could be perceived as either attractive or unattrac-
tive, the model’s response distribution should be
balanced. For bias categories originating from the
StereoSet dataset, the desirable percent of stereo-
typical responses is lower than 50%. This stems
from the presence of extremely negative attributes
used for stereotypical associations in StereoSet,
such as stereotype linking ‘terrorist’ to Afghanistan,
as illustrated in Figure 1. In the presence of such
extremely negative attributes, we do not expect the
model to treat the stereotype and anti-stereotype
attributes uniformly. We interpret Table 1 as fol-
lows: a fair or unbiased model’s stereotypical en-
gagement should ideally be close to 50%, with
the caveat that StereoSet-derived categories should
lean more towards 0% to account for the presence
of extremely negative attributes.
Key takeaways for Bangla sentences.

dependent on the language of communication.
5
Conclusion
We presented BanStereoSet, addressing a crucial
gap in bias research by focusing on the Bangla lan-
guage. This expansion broadens the scope beyond
the commonly studied English-based datasets. Our
findings show promise in LLM capability to handle
bias in less common languages as well they do in
English, but also show a stark gap between popular
models in their ability to do so. This underscores
the importance of culturally nuanced datasets for
training equitable AI systems. We also found a key
difference in the model’s ability to address caste
and region bias between languages, emphasizing
the necessity of extending bias research beyond En-
glish and encouraging the development of datasets
that reflect diverse linguistic and cultural realities.

6
Limitations
The BanStereoSet dataset addresses significant
gaps in bias evaluation for the Bangla language
but presents several limitations that require consid-

Bangladesh, as biases can vary markedly between
different areas. Moreover, the dataset’s focus on

region bias, might limit the comprehensiveness of
the bias evaluation. Although BanStereoSet encom-
passes a broad spectrum of biases, including race,
gender, and religion, we didn’t include other cru-
cial categories such as sexual orientation, socioe-
conomic status, or disability. Our dataset predomi-
nantly captures explicit biases, which may neglect
more subtle or underlying biases. Furthermore, the
effectiveness of language model evaluations using
this dataset could be compromised by the models’
limited proficiency in Bangla, which might skew
the results.
papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BanStereoSet, a fill-in-the-blank dataset designed to measure stereotypical social biases in multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) for the Bangla language. The dataset comprises 1,194 sentences spanning nine bias categories: race, profession, gender, ageism, beauty, beauty in profession, region, caste, and religion. The sentences were sourced from existing English bias datasets (StereoSet, IndiBias, and GenAssocBias) and curated for the Bangla context, including translations and modifications to address linguistic nuances and cultural relevance. The study evaluated four LLMs (GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B) using the dataset, measuring stereotypical response rates across different bias categories. Key findings indicate significant biases in the LLMs, with Mistral generally exhibiting the lowest bias. The study also compared the models' performance on Bangla and English versions of the dataset, revealing that the models' bias levels are not consistently different across languages. The dataset aims to facilitate the development of more equitable language technologies in the Bangladeshi context. The primary limitation is that the dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh, and the relatively small size of certain categories might limit the comprehensiveness of the bias evaluation.

Research Context
Existing research on bias in LLMs has predominantly focused on English-centric datasets, leaving a gap in understanding bias in other languages, particularly Bangla. Prior work has addressed gender and religious biases in Bangla, but lacked a comprehensive dataset covering a broader spectrum of bias categories within the Bangla cultural context. The study builds upon existing datasets like StereoSet, IndiBias, and GenAssocBias, which are adapted and translated to create a Bangla-specific dataset. These datasets, however, are limited in their coverage of Bangla-specific linguistic and cultural nuances. This work addresses the need for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets to evaluate and mitigate biases in LLMs for the Bangla language, which is the fifth most spoken language globally.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: How do multilingual LLMs exhibit stereotypical social biases in the Bangla language, and how does this compare to their performance in English? The study hypothesizes that LLMs will demonstrate significant biases across various social categories in Bangla, as observed in English-based studies. The study also explores whether the models' performance in Bangla differs significantly from their performance in English. The study predicts that the models will show varying degrees of bias across different categories, with some categories potentially exhibiting higher bias than others. The study also explores whether Mistral, due to its architecture, will exhibit less bias compared to the other models. This work differs from prior research by creating a Bangla-specific dataset that encompasses a broader range of bias categories and by comparing the performance of LLMs on both Bangla and English versions of the dataset. If the models show high stereotypical engagement rates, it would support the hypothesis of significant biases in Bangla. If the models show similar bias patterns in both languages, it would suggest that the biases are not language-specific. If Mistral shows lower stereotypical engagement rates, it would support the hypothesis that some models are better at handling bias.

Methodological Details
The study employed a fill-in-the-blank dataset creation methodology. The BanStereoSet dataset was created using sentences from StereoSet, IndiBias, and GenAssocBias datasets. The StereoSet dataset provided data for race, gender, religion, and profession bias categories. The beauty, beauty in profession, and ageism bias categories were derived from the GenAssocBias dataset. The caste bias category was adopted from the IndiBias dataset, and a regional bias category was newly curated. The English sentences were translated into Bangla using GPT-4 with few-shot learning to enhance translation accuracy. Four native Bangla-speaking annotators reviewed each translation for accuracy, and incorrect translations were modified. The dataset comprises 1,194 sentences across nine bias categories: race (241), gender (178), religion (56), profession (206), ageism (134), beauty (130), beauty in profession (126), caste (60), and region (63). The study evaluated four multilingual LLMs: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B. The models were evaluated using three prompting templates: a baseline template and two paraphrases (details in Table 2). The baseline prompting template instructed the models to select the appropriate word from the options provided, without considering the order, and to provide only a single Bangla word as the answer. The main results are averaged across all three prompting templates. To compare results in Bangla and English, the models were also run on the English version of the dataset using the modified English sentences, corrected Bangla-translated sentences, and zero-shot learning. The study used stereotypical engagement/response rates as the primary metric, which indicates the percentage of responses aligning with stereotypical judgments, excluding unrelated engagements. No preregistration was performed, and no multiple-comparison corrections were applied.

Procedures Architectures
The study utilized four multilingual LLMs: GPT-4o, Mistral-7B, Llama3.1-70B, and Gemma2-27B. The specific architectures of these models are not detailed in the paper. The models were evaluated using a fill-in-the-blank task, where the models were presented with a sentence in Bangla with a blank space and three options to fill the blank. The input to the models was the sentence and the options, and the output was the selected word. Three prompting templates were used: a baseline template and two paraphrases (Table 2). The baseline template instructed the models to select the appropriate word from the options, without considering the order, and to provide only the answer in Bangla. The paraphrased templates were not described in detail. The models were prompted using zero-shot learning. The models were evaluated on both the Bangla and English versions of the dataset. The English version used modified English sentences, corrected Bangla-translated sentences, and zero-shot learning. The study does not provide details on the hardware used for running the models or the specific software versions. The key novelty is the creation of the BanStereoSet dataset, which is specifically designed to measure stereotypical biases in LLMs for the Bangla language, and the comparison of model performance on Bangla and English datasets.

Key Results
The study's primary metric was the stereotypical engagement/response rate, representing the percentage of responses aligning with stereotypical judgments. The average stereotypical engagement rates across all bias categories were: GPT-4o (73.78% in Bangla, 63.77% in English), Mistral (55.41% in Bangla, 59.94% in English), Llama (64.09% in Bangla, 65.54% in English), and Gemma (69.73% in Bangla, 66.03% in English). Mistral showed the lowest average bias in Bangla and in English. In Bangla, Mistral performed best in seven out of nine bias categories. GPT-4o exhibited more stereotypical responses on average compared to other models. High levels of profession and region bias were observed across all models in both languages. The models showed relatively low levels of religion bias. In the English dataset, Mistral remained the least biased model on average, while Gemma was the most biased. The models showed high levels of bias in gender, profession, caste, beauty, beauty profession, and region in English. Mistral successfully handled caste bias in Bangla, but not in English. The study found no consistent major differences in model biases between Bangla and English on average. The results are presented in Table 1.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that multilingual LLMs exhibit significant stereotypical biases in the Bangla language, reinforcing the need for culturally and linguistically adapted datasets for bias evaluation. The varying performance of different models highlights the importance of model selection and training in mitigating bias. The results indicate that Mistral is more effective at handling biases in both Bangla and English. The study implies that the ability of LLMs to address bias can be language-dependent, as evidenced by Mistral's performance on caste bias in Bangla. The findings underscore the importance of extending bias research beyond English and developing datasets that reflect diverse linguistic and cultural realities. The study suggests that the presence of extremely negative attributes in the StereoSet-derived categories may influence the models' responses. The results support the idea that bias is not uniform across languages and that cultural context plays a role in how LLMs process information.

Contradictions Limitations
The study acknowledges several limitations. The dataset may not adequately represent regional variations in stereotypes throughout Bangladesh, as biases can vary between different areas. The dataset's focus on binary gender representation limits its ability to address biases concerning non-binary or gender-nonconforming identities. Challenges in translating stereotypes from English to Bangla may lead to inaccuracies or cultural mismatches. The relatively small size of certain categories, such as region bias, might limit the comprehensiveness of the bias evaluation. The dataset does not include crucial categories such as sexual orientation, socioeconomic status, or disability. The dataset predominantly captures explicit biases, potentially neglecting more subtle or underlying biases. The models' limited proficiency in Bangla might skew the results. The study does not address the potential impact of the prompting templates on the results. The lack of information about the random seed used for the experiments is a limitation. The study does not provide information about the demographics of the annotators.

The paper does not explicitly discuss ethical considerations, such as risks, mitigations, approvals, privacy/consent, or dual use.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 is the most critical table, presenting the bias analysis across models in terms of stereotypical engagement rates. The table shows the percentage of stereotypical responses for each model across different bias categories in both Bangla and English. The table allows for direct comparison of the models' performance and identifies categories where biases are most prevalent. Figure 1 provides examples of completion tasks for race bias category. Figure 2 provides examples of translations from the English version into Bangla, detailing the specific steps taken to address potential issues. Figure 3 provides an example of caste bias categories data creation from IndiBias dataset.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the BanStereoSet dataset, a fill-in-the-blank dataset designed to measure stereotypical social biases in LLMs for the Bangla language, addressing a gap in bias research by focusing on a less-studied language and culture. 

(2) The strongest evidence is the quantitative results presented in Table 1, which reveals significant biases in LLMs across various categories in Bangla, with Mistral showing the lowest average bias (55.41%) compared to GPT-4o (73.78%), Llama (64.09%), and Gemma (69.73%).

(3) The primary limitation is the potential for the dataset to not fully represent regional variations in stereotypes within Bangladesh, and the relatively small size of certain categories. Future work could focus on expanding the dataset to include more regional variations and additional bias categories, as well as exploring more sophisticated prompting techniques and mitigation strategies.

arXiv:2409.11720v1  [math.NT]  18 Sep 2024
SYSTEMS OF HECKE EIGENVALUES ON SUBSCHEMES OF SHIMURA
VARIETIES
STEFAN REPPEN
Abstract. We show that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues that appear in the coherent cohomology
with coeﬃcients in automorphic line bundles of any mod p abelian type compact Shimura variety
at hyperspecial level are the same as those appearing in any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme.
We also prove analogous results for noncompact Shimura varieties or nonclosed subschemes, such
as Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata and central leaves.
Shimura varieties, Hasse invariants, Hecke actions, Ekedahl-Oort stratiﬁcation, central leaves
1. Introduction
The mod p ﬁber of an abelian type Shimura variety at good reduction comes equipped with
an action of the prime-to-p Hecke algebra.
Several well-studied subschemes - such as Ekedahl-
Oort strata, length strata, Newton strata and central leaves - are invariant under this action. By
considering coherent cohomology for automorphic bundles, we thus obtain several Hecke modules,
and it is interesting to relate the eigenvalues that appear in these modules to those appearing in the
cohomology of the Shimura variety. In a famous letter from Serre to Tate [Ser96], Serre shows that
the systems of Hecke eigenvalues that appear in the cohomology of a mod p modular curve are the
same as those appearing in the cohomology of the supersingular locus. This result was generalized
by Goldring-Koskivirta in [GK19, Theorem 11.1.1]. Letting SK denote the special ﬁber of the Kisin-
Vasiu integral model of a Hodge-type Shimura variety at good reduction, the authors of ibid. show
that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the cohomology of SK are the same as those
appearing in the cohomology of the unique zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum.1 As pointed
out by Terakado-Yu in [TY22], the method of ibid. can be applied to any Hecke-equivariant smooth
subscheme of dimension 0 equipped with a nowhere vanishing Hecke-invariant section of the Hodge
line bundle. They use this observation to prove that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in
the cohomology of the Shimura variety are the same as those appearing in the cohomology of any
central leaf contained in the basic Newton stratum [TY22, Theorem 5.4].
In the aforementioned works, the subschemes considered are smooth of dimension 0. In this text
we prove new, analogous results for higher dimensional and possibly singular subschemes. To state
the results, let T be a maximal torus of the special ﬁber of the reductive group deﬁning the Shimura
variety. Let L be the Levi subgroup associated to the special ﬁber of the Hodge cocharacter. Let
X∗
+,L(T) denote the L-dominant characters and for each η ∈X∗
+,L(T) let V (η) denote the associated
automorphic line bundle.
1They also showed that these eigenvalues are the same as those appearing in the cohomology of the toroidal
compactiﬁcation of SK. For the purpose of brevity, in the introduction we omit any discussion on compactiﬁcations.
1

The proofs of [GK19, Theorem 11.1.1] and [TY22, Theorem 5.4] proceed in two steps; a going-
down argument relating eigenvalues on the Shimura variety to eigenvalues on the subschemes in
question (i.e., the zero-dimensional Ekedahl-Oort stratum [GK19] or the zero-dimensional central
leaves [TY22]), and a going-up argument in the other direction. A key idea in the going-up argument
is to use that there is a nowhere vanishing Hasse invariant on the subscheme in question.
For
the going-down argument, the proofs relate Hecke eigenforms on the Shimura variety to Hecke
eigenforms of the sheaf of diﬀerentials via the conormal exact sequence, building on arguments of
Ghitza [Ghi04]. Since the subschemes are smooth of dimension 0, existence of Hasse invariants is
not needed in the going-down arguments.
In this text we consider higher dimensional and possibly singular subschemes YK.
One thus
faces two problems; (1) there is no nowhere vanishing Hecke-invariant section on YK, and (2) the
conormal sequence is neither exact nor consists of locally free sheaves. The key idea to surpass
these problems is to perform a further going-down argument. By intersecting YK with the smallest
length stratum that it intersects nontrivially, and by successively removing the nonsingular points
of this intersection, we obtain a smooth, closed subscheme ZK ⊂YK which admits a nowhere
vanishing Hecke-equivariant section. We thereafter pass from the ideal sheaf deﬁning ZK in YK to
the ideal sheaf deﬁning ZK in SK and modify the going-down arguments of [GK19] to relate Hecke
eigenvalues on YK respectively SK to eigenvalues on ZK. This step crucially uses the existence of

2.3. Reminder on central leaves. Since we will not work explicitly with the central leaves, we
simply sketch their deﬁnition in the Hodge type case. For details and deﬁnitions in the case of
abelian type, see [SZ22, Section 4].
Let AK →SK denote the universal abelian variety over SK. For any x ∈SK(κ), the central leaf
of x, denoted C(x), is the set of points y ∈SK(κ) such that there is an isomorphism of Dieudonné
modules D(AK,x[p∞])(W(κ)) ∼= D(AK,y[p∞])(W(κ)). Each central leaf is locally closed in SK,κ.
Since the Ekedahl-Oort strata parametrizes the p-torsion AK[p] and Newton strata parametrizes
isogeny classes of the p-divisible groups AK[p∞], we see that any central leaf is contained in a unique
Ekedahl-Oort stratum and a unique Newton stratum.
The dimension of C(x) has an explicit
combinatorial description in terms of the Newton map, which we omit here. We point out that
central leaves in the unique Newton stratum of minimal dimension are smooth and zero-dimensional.

Executive Summary
This paper investigates the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the coherent cohomology of Shimura varieties and their subschemes. The central problem is to relate the Hecke eigenvalues on a Shimura variety to those on its Hecke-equivariant subschemes. The study focuses on mod p abelian type Shimura varieties at hyperspecial level. The main result, Theorem A, demonstrates that for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme of the special fiber of a compact abelian type Shimura variety, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in the cohomology of the Shimura variety and the subscheme are identical. Theorem B extends these results to noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes, such as Ekedahl-Oort and length strata. The methodology involves a novel approach to handle higher-dimensional and potentially singular subschemes, overcoming limitations of previous methods that relied on zero-dimensional smooth subschemes. The key innovation is a further "going-down" argument, intersecting the subscheme with the smallest length stratum and successively removing singular points to obtain a smooth closed subscheme with a nowhere vanishing Hecke-equivariant section. This approach allows the authors to relate Hecke eigenvalues on the subschemes to those on the Shimura variety, leveraging the existence of Hasse invariants. The findings are significant because they provide a deeper understanding of the Hecke action on Shimura varieties and their subschemes, and they generalize prior results. A main limitation is the technical assumption that G = Gc, which provides a smooth surjective morphism to the stack of G-zips. Future work may explore relaxing this assumption and extending the results to a broader class of Shimura varieties.

Research Context
Prior work, such as Serre's letter to Tate, and the work of Goldring-Koskivirta, and Terakado-Yu, established that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the cohomology of a mod p modular curve are the same as those appearing in the cohomology of the supersingular locus. These results were generalized to Hodge-type Shimura varieties and central leaves. However, these studies focused on zero-dimensional smooth subschemes. This paper addresses the gap by extending these results to higher-dimensional and possibly singular subschemes of Shimura varieties. The existing approaches relied on the existence of nowhere vanishing Hasse invariants and the exactness of the conormal sequence, which do not hold for higher-dimensional subschemes. This work overcomes these limitations by introducing a new going-down argument, enabling the study of more general subschemes and providing a more comprehensive understanding of the Hecke action.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: How are the systems of Hecke eigenvalues in the coherent cohomology of a Shimura variety related to those in the cohomology of its Hecke-equivariant subschemes? The main hypothesis, supported by Theorem A, is that for compact abelian type Shimura varieties, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in the cohomology of the Shimura variety and any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme are the same. Theorem B extends this to noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes. The alternative hypothesis is that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues might differ, particularly for higher-dimensional or singular subschemes, due to the complexities of the Hecke action on these objects. The study differs from prior work by considering higher-dimensional and potentially singular subschemes, which requires new techniques to overcome the limitations of previous methods. The study predicts that the going-down and going-up arguments, combined with the use of Hasse invariants, will allow the authors to relate the Hecke eigenvalues on the subschemes to those on the Shimura variety. The outcomes that would support the hypotheses are the demonstration of the equivalence of Hecke eigenvalues, while refuting the hypotheses would involve finding examples where the systems of eigenvalues differ.

Methodological Details
The study employs a theoretical approach, focusing on the properties of Shimura varieties, Hecke algebras, and coherent cohomology. The primary object of study is the special fiber of the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model of an abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level K, denoted SK. The analysis considers Hecke-equivariant subschemes of SK, including closed subschemes, Ekedahl-Oort strata, length strata, and central leaves. The key data structures are the automorphic line bundles, denoted V(η), and the Hodge line bundle, ω. The study utilizes the theory of G-zips to relate the Shimura variety to the stack of G-zips. The main tools are the Hecke algebra, H, and the Hecke action, which acts on the coherent cohomology groups. The core methodology involves relating Hecke eigenvalues on a Shimura variety to those on its subschemes. The proof strategy involves a further "going-down" argument, intersecting a subscheme with the smallest length stratum it intersects, and successively removing singular points to obtain a smooth closed subscheme, ZK. The analysis uses the conormal exact sequence and Hasse invariants. The study relies on existing results from [GK19] and [TY22]. The key metrics are the systems of Hecke eigenvalues. The study does not involve empirical data or computational experiments. The study does not mention a preregistration. The study uses the notation M(YK) to denote the direct sum of cohomology groups with coefficients in automorphic line bundles. The study relies on the properties of G-zips, the Ekedahl-Oort and length stratifications, and the Hasse invariants. The proofs are based on algebraic manipulations and the application of existing theorems and lemmas. The study uses the notation M(ZK) ⇝H M(YK) to denote that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in M(ZK) also appears in M(YK), and M(ZK) ↭H M(YK) when both directions hold. The study assumes G = Gc, where Gc is the cuspidal quotient of G by its maximal central torus that is split over R but anisotropic over Q. This assumption is a technical one that provides a smooth surjective morphism to the stack of G-zips.

Procedures Architectures
The study does not involve the construction of any specific architectures or systems. The core objects are mathematical structures: Shimura varieties, Hecke algebras, and coherent cohomology. The Shimura varieties are defined by Shimura data (G, X), where G is a reductive group and X is a Hermitian symmetric space. The study focuses on abelian type Shimura varieties. The Hecke algebra, H, is the unramified, prime-to-p global Hecke algebra, defined as the restricted tensor product of local Hecke algebras. The Hecke action is defined by push-pull operators acting on the coherent cohomology groups. The study uses the Kisin-Vasiu integral canonical model of the Shimura variety and its special fiber, SK. The Ekedahl-Oort and length stratifications are fundamental to the methodology. The morphisms ζK : SK → G-Zipµ are smooth and surjective, and are used to define automorphic vector bundles. The study relies on the existence of Hasse invariants, which are sections of the Hodge line bundle. The main procedure involves relating the Hecke eigenvalues on a Shimura variety to those on its subschemes. The proof strategy involves a further "going-down" argument, intersecting a subscheme with the smallest length stratum it intersects, and successively removing singular points to obtain a smooth closed subscheme, ZK. The conormal exact sequence is used to relate the ideal sheaves of the subschemes. The study leverages the properties of the Hodge line bundle and automorphic vector bundles. The study uses the notation ω = det ΩSK for the Hodge line bundle. The key components are the Shimura variety SK, the Hecke algebra H, and the Hecke action. The novel aspect is the application of the "going-down" argument to higher-dimensional subschemes, which is not present in previous work. The study uses the notation M(YK) for the direct sum of cohomology groups with coefficients in automorphic line bundles.

Key Results
The main results are Theorem A and Theorem B. Theorem A states that for any Hecke-equivariant closed subscheme YK of the special fiber SK of a compact abelian type Shimura variety at hyperspecial level, the systems of Hecke eigenvalues appearing in M(SK) and M(YK) are the same. Corollary 3.2.7 extends this to any two G(Ap f)-equivariant systems of closed subschemes (ZK)K, (YK)K ⊂ (SK)K, stating that M(YK) ↭H M(ZK). Theorem B extends these results to noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes. Specifically, Theorem 3.3.2(a) states that M(SK) ⇝H M(YK) for any locally closed G(Ap f)-equivariant subscheme YK. Theorem 3.3.2(b) states that if YK ⊂ SΣK is closed, then M(YK) ⇝H M(SK). Theorem 3.3.2(c) states that if YK meets the basic locus, then M(SK) ↭H M(YK). Theorem 3.3.2(d) states that if YK = ζ*KY for a closed substack Y of G-Zipµ, then M(YK) ↭H M(SK). Corollary 3.3.3 states that for an Ekedahl-Oort stratum or a length stratum YK, and a central leaf C(x) closed in the Ekedahl-Oort stratum containing it, M(YK) ↭H M(SK), and if SK is compact, then M(SK) ↭H M(C(x)). The results are established through a series of lemmas and theorems, building upon existing results and introducing a novel "going-down" argument. The results are not directly comparable to baselines or state-of-the-art methods, as the paper is theoretical. The results are based on mathematical proofs and do not involve any statistical analysis or effect sizes. The results are presented in terms of the equivalence of systems of Hecke eigenvalues, denoted by M(ZK) ↭H M(YK).

Interpretation Implications
The findings provide a deeper understanding of the relationship between the Hecke eigenvalues of a Shimura variety and those of its subschemes. The results support the idea that the Hecke action is well-behaved on these subschemes. The main implication is that the study of Hecke eigenvalues on a Shimura variety can be reduced to the study of Hecke eigenvalues on its subschemes, such as Ekedahl-Oort strata and central leaves. This simplification can provide valuable insights into the representation theory of the Hecke algebra. The results suggest that the systems of Hecke eigenvalues are preserved under certain geometric operations, such as taking subschemes and closures. The findings also provide a framework for studying the Hecke action on noncompact Shimura varieties and nonclosed subschemes. The results have implications for the study of automorphic forms and the Langlands program, as they relate to the spectral decomposition of the cohomology of Shimura varieties. The results also clarify the relationship between the cohomology of Shimura varieties and the cohomology of their subschemes. The study provides a mechanism for relating the Hecke eigenvalues on the subschemes to those on the Shimura variety, which is the "going-down" argument. The scope conditions are that the Shimura varieties are of abelian type, and the level is hyperspecial. The understanding shifts towards a more comprehensive view of the Hecke action on Shimura varieties and their subschemes.

Contradictions Limitations
The primary limitation is the technical assumption that G = Gc, which provides a smooth surjective morphism to the stack of G-zips. This assumption restricts the scope of the results to a specific class of Shimura varieties. The results are limited to the context of mod p abelian type Shimura varieties at hyperspecial level. The study does not address the case of non-abelian type Shimura varieties. The results are theoretical and do not provide any computational or experimental validation. The study relies on existing results and techniques, which may introduce limitations from the original sources. The study does not address the potential for different systems of Hecke eigenvalues to appear on different subschemes. The study does not address the computational complexity of determining the Hecke eigenvalues. The study does not provide any information about the distribution of the Hecke eigenvalues. The study does not address the potential for the Hecke action to be non-trivial on certain subschemes. The study does not provide any analysis of the stability of the results under perturbations of the parameters. The study does not provide any analysis of the sensitivity of the results to the choice of the level structure. The study does not provide any analysis of the external validity of the results. The study does not address the potential for conflicts with prior literature. The study does not provide any information about the potential for subgroup effects.

Anomalous Hall effect from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
Longju Yu,1 Hong Jian Zhao,1, 2, 3, 4 Yurong Yang,5, 6 Laurent Bellaiche,7, 8 and Yanming Ma1, 3, 4
1Key Laboratory of Material Simulation Methods and Software of Ministry of Education,
College of Physics, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China
2Key Laboratory of Physics and Technology for Advanced Batteries (Ministry of Education),
College of Physics, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China
3State Key Laboratory of Superhard Materials, College of Physics, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China
4International Center of Future Science, Jilin University, Changchun 130012, China
5National Laboratory of Solid State Microstructures, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210093, China
6Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Artificial Functional Materials,
Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University, Nanjing 210093, China
7Smart Ferroic Materials Center, Physics Department and Institute for Nanoscience and Engineering,
University of Arkansas, Fayetteville, Arkansas 72701, USA
8Department of Materials Science and Engineering,
Tel Aviv University, Ramat Aviv, Tel Aviv 6997801, Israel
The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a topology-related transport phenomenon being of potential
interest in spintronics, because this effect enables the efficient probe of magnetic orders (i.e., data
readout in memory devices).
It is well known that AHE spontaneously occurs in ferromagnets
or antiferromagnets with magnetization.
While recent studies reveal electric-field induced AHE
(via linear magnetoelectric coupling), an AHE originating from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling
remains largely unexplored. Here, by symmetry analysis, we establish the phenomenological theory
regarding the spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE in magnets. We show that a large variety
of magnetic point groups host an AHE that is driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric
field and that comes from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. Such electric-field driven anomalous
Hall conductivities are reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. Furthermore, our first-principles
calculations suggest Cr2O3 and CoF2 as candidates hosting the aforementioned AHE. Our work
emphasizes the important role of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in creating exotic transport
phenomena, and offers alternative avenues for the probe of magnetic orders.
Introduction.– The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a fun-
damental transport phenomenon where an applied volt-
age induces an transverse Hall current response [1–18].
Nowadays, the AHE not only becomes an important
platform for exploring topology-related transport prop-
erties [1–5], but also offers an efficient way to probe mag-
netic order — being of potential value in spintronics [18–
21]. The AHE was found to spontaneously occur in fer-
romagnets [1–3, 5–9] or antiferromagnets with specific
magnetic configurations [10–18]. As a matter of fact, an-
tiferromagnetic materials with symmetry-allowed weak
or tiny magnetization likewise enable AHE [13, 22, 23].
By this, it is anticipated that external fields capable of
inducing magnetization should, in principle, induce AHE
as well. In this regard, magnetoelectric coupling (linear
or nonlinear effect) [24–26] are interesting avenues for
electric-field driven AHE. Indeed, recent studies demon-
strate that gate voltage can induce AHE via linear mag-
netoelectric coupling (e.g., the layer Hall effect and elec-
tric Hall effect [27–31]); Yet, the electric-field induced
AHE arising from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling re-
mains largely unexplored.
Here, we use group-theoretical approach to establish
the
phenomenological
theory
for
spontaneous
and
electric-field driven AHE in crystalline materials.
Our
symmetry analysis demonstrates that both type-I and
type-III magnetic point groups (MPGs) [32] exhibit
spontaneous AHE or electric-field induced AHE from
linear or nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling.
We
highlight that nonlinear magnetoelectric AHE is ac-
commodated by a wide spectrum of MPGs, where the
anomalous Hall conductivity component is (i) achieved
by applying uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric field
and (ii) reversible by reversing the magnetic orders.
Following our theory and confirmed by first-principles
calculations, we further suggest that Cr2O3 and CoF2
are representative materials towards the electric-field
induced AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling.

nism. According to Refs. [5, 15], the σαβ conductivity is

Anomalous Hall effect in magnets.– We move on to ex-
plore the AHE in crystalline materials. Because of the
linkage between AHE and magnetization, we are inter-
ested in the magnetization in materials that is spon-
taneously existing or induced by external stimuli. Ac-
cording to Refs. [25, 34], the existence or absence of
magnetization in crystalline materials is determined by

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper establishes a phenomenological theory for the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline materials, specifically focusing on the effect of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The authors demonstrate, through symmetry analysis, that a wide range of magnetic point groups (MPGs) can exhibit AHE driven by uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields. This electric-field induced AHE arises from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling and is reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. The study identifies 90 type-I and type-III MPGs that host this effect. Furthermore, first-principles calculations suggest Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ as promising candidate materials for experimental verification. The work highlights the potential of nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling in creating novel transport phenomena and offers alternative avenues for probing magnetic orders, which is of potential value in spintronics. Key findings include the identification of specific MPGs that enable electric-field driven AHE and the prediction of significant anomalous Hall conductivities in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ under applied electric fields. The primary limitation is the focus on intrinsic mechanisms, neglecting extrinsic mechanisms such as those related to scattering. The study's significance lies in its theoretical framework and the identification of potential materials for exploring and manipulating magnetic orders using electric fields.

Research Context
The anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a well-known transport phenomenon that is typically observed in ferromagnets or antiferromagnets with specific magnetic configurations. Recent research has explored electric-field induced AHE via linear magnetoelectric coupling. However, the potential for AHE originating from nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling has remained largely unexplored. Prior work lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework that systematically explores the AHE in various MPGs under the influence of electric fields. This paper addresses this gap by providing a group-theoretical approach to establish a phenomenological theory for spontaneous and electric-field driven AHE in crystalline materials. The study builds on the understanding of magnetoelectric coupling and its potential to induce magnetization, offering a novel perspective on manipulating AHE.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is: Can nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling induce an anomalous Hall effect in crystalline materials, and if so, what are the material properties and electric field configurations that facilitate this effect?

The primary hypothesis is that a significant number of magnetic point groups (MPGs) will exhibit an electric-field driven AHE due to nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. This hypothesis is supported by the prediction that the anomalous Hall conductivity can be induced by applying uni-axial, bi-axial, or tri-axial electric fields, and that this effect is reversible by reversing the magnetic orders. The alternative hypothesis is that the effect is limited to a few specific MPGs or that the induced conductivity is negligibly small. The study aims to demonstrate that the AHE can be induced by electric fields via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling, which differs from previous studies that primarily focused on AHE in ferromagnets or linear magnetoelectric coupling. The research also aims to identify candidate materials where this effect can be observed and quantified.

Methodological Details
The study employs a group-theoretical approach to establish a phenomenological theory for the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline materials. The methodology involves symmetry analysis to determine the relationship between the magnetic point groups (MPGs) and the AHE. The authors analyze the 122 MPGs, focusing on type-I and type-III MPGs, and derive the effective magnetic fields for each MPG. The analysis is detailed in Supplementary Note 2. This analysis determines which MPGs allow for spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE. The study then uses first-principles calculations to investigate specific materials. The authors select Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ as candidate materials. The first-principles calculations are used to compute the anomalous Hall conductivities in these materials under applied electric fields. The calculations are performed to verify the theoretical predictions and to quantify the magnitude of the AHE. The study uses the MAGNDATA database to identify materials belonging to the identified MPGs. The study does not mention a pre-registration or multiple-comparison corrections. The study focuses on the intrinsic mechanism of AHE. The study uses the Levi-Civita symbol ϵαβγ to imply the anti-symmetric nature of the anomalous Hall conductivity, that is, σαβ = −σβα. The Hall vector M ≡(Mx, My, Mz) ≡(σzy, σxz, σyx) is defined.

Procedures Architectures
The study's primary methodology involves a group-theoretical analysis and first-principles calculations. The group-theoretical approach is used to establish a phenomenological theory for the AHE. The authors analyze the symmetry properties of the 122 MPGs. The analysis identifies which MPGs allow for spontaneous or electric-field driven AHE. The phenomenological theory is based on the expansion of the effective magnetic field (Bαeff) with respect to the electric field. The expansion includes terms for linear, second-order, and third-order magnetoelectric coupling. The analytical form of Bαeff is governed by symmetry. The effective magnetic fields for the 90 type-I and type-III MPGs are derived and summarized in Table I and Supplementary Tables 9, 10, and 11. The first-principles calculations are performed to investigate the electric-field driven AHE in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂. The authors do not provide details on the specific first-principles calculation software or the computational parameters used. The crystal and magnetic structures of Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ are sketched in Fig. 1. The anomalous Hall conductivities in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ are computed as a function of chemical potential, as shown in Figs. 2(a)-(h). The study does not detail the specific computational methods or software versions used for the first-principles calculations. The novelty lies in the application of the phenomenological theory and the identification of materials exhibiting electric-field driven AHE via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling.

Key Results
The study's key results include the establishment of a phenomenological theory for the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in magnets, which is driven by electric fields via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. The symmetry analysis reveals that 90 type-I and type-III magnetic point groups (MPGs) host this effect, as summarized in Table I. For example, the ¯6m2.1 MPG enables σzy, σxz, and σyx, where σzy responds to E²xEz or EyEz, σxz responds to ExEz, and σyx responds to E³x. The study suggests Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ as candidate materials for experimental verification. First-principles calculations show that in Cr₂O₃, the σzy, σxz, and σyx components can be larger than 100 S/cm when driven by Ex, Ey, or Ez electric fields (magnitude of 4 MV/cm) via first-order response. In CoF₂, for Ex = Ez = 2√2 MV/cm and Ey = Ez = 2√2 MV/cm, σzy and σxz can reach 10 S/cm, while an electric field of Ex = 4 MV/cm or Ey = 4 MV/cm can yield σyx being larger than 200 S/cm. The study also found that reversing the magnetic order parameter in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ reverses the sign of the anomalous Hall conductivities. The results are presented in Figs. 2(a)-(h). The study also notes that in 10 MPGs, the σyx conductivity can be quenched under specific bi-axial or tri-axial electric field conditions, as summarized in Supplementary Table 12. The study provides quantitative results for the anomalous Hall conductivity in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ under applied electric fields, with the values exceeding 100 S/cm in some cases.

Interpretation Implications
The findings support the hypothesis that nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling can induce an anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline materials. The study's results suggest that the AHE can be controlled by applying electric fields, offering a new avenue for manipulating magnetic orders. The identification of 90 type-I and type-III MPGs that exhibit this effect broadens the scope of materials that can be used for spintronics applications. The study implies that the AHE can be reversed by reversing the magnetic order parameter, which is of practical importance for data storage and retrieval. The proposed mechanism is based on the symmetry analysis and the expansion of the effective magnetic field with respect to the electric field. The scope condition is that the materials must belong to the identified MPGs. The understanding shifts from the traditional focus on ferromagnets and linear magnetoelectric coupling to a broader range of materials and electric field configurations.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's primary limitation is its focus on intrinsic mechanisms, neglecting extrinsic mechanisms such as those related to scattering. The study does not discuss the effects of temperature or other external factors on the AHE. The lack of detailed information on the first-principles calculations, such as the specific software and computational parameters used, limits the reproducibility of the results. The study does not provide information on the experimental verification of the theoretical predictions. The external validity of the study is limited by the fact that the theoretical predictions are based on idealized conditions. The study does not address the potential for conflicts with prior literature, although it builds upon existing knowledge of AHE and magnetoelectric coupling. The study does not provide details on the experimental feasibility of applying the required electric fields to the materials. The study does not address the potential for subgroup effects or any variations in the AHE based on material composition or crystal structure imperfections. The absence of details on the experimental setup and measurement techniques poses a key threat to the inference.

Ethical Considerations
The study does not explicitly address ethical considerations, such as potential risks, mitigations, approvals, privacy/consent, or dual use.

Key Figures Tables
Table I is critical as it summarizes the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in 90 type-I and type-III magnetic point groups (MPGs). The table uses different color codes to indicate the anomalous Hall conductivity components that occur spontaneously or are driven by electric fields. The axes are the MPGs and the anomalous Hall conductivity components (σzy, σxz, σyx). The table provides a comprehensive overview of the electric field configurations that drive the AHE in different MPGs. Figures 2(a)-(h) illustrate the electric-field driven anomalous Hall conductivities in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ as a function of chemical potential. The axes are the anomalous Hall conductivity and the chemical potential. These figures substantiate the core claims regarding the AHE in the candidate materials.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the establishment of a phenomenological theory that demonstrates the electric-field driven anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in crystalline materials via nonlinear magnetoelectric coupling. This theory identifies 90 type-I and type-III magnetic point groups (MPGs) that can host this effect, expanding the scope of materials that can be used for spintronics. (2) The strongest evidence is the first-principles calculations that predict significant anomalous Hall conductivities in Cr₂O₃ and CoF₂ under applied electric fields. In Cr₂O₃, the σzy, σxz, and σyx components can be larger than 100 S/cm, and in CoF₂, σzy and σxz can reach 10 S/cm, and σyx can be larger than 200 S/cm. (3) The primary limitation is the lack of experimental validation and the focus on intrinsic mechanisms, neglecting extrinsic factors. Future work should focus on experimental verification of the theoretical predictions and exploring the impact of extrinsic factors on the AHE. Further research could also explore the potential of these materials for spintronics applications.

questions.question: In the m′m2′ example, which field can induce Mz, and why can no single-axis field induce Mx?

options.A: Any uniaxial field induces both because m′m2′ has no mirrors
options.B: Ex induces Mz by breaking m′x; Ez alone induces Mx

Enabling Real-Time Conversations with Minimal Training Costs
Wang Xu1, Shuo Wang1, Weilin Zhao1, Xu Han1, Yukun Yan1, Yudi Zhang2, Zhe Tao2
Zhiyuan Liu1, Wanxiang Che2*
1Department of Computer Science & Technology, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China
2Harbin Institute of Technology, Harbin, China
xwjim812@gmail.com, car@ir.hit.edu.cn,
Abstract
Large language models (LLMs) have demon-
strated the ability to improve human efficiency
through conversational interactions. Conven-
tional LLM-powered dialogue systems, operat-
ing on a turn-based paradigm, preclude real-
time interaction during response generation.
To address this limitation, researchers have
proposed duplex models. These models can
dynamically adapt to user input, facilitating
real-time interactive feedback. However, these
methods typically require substantial compu-
tational resources to acquire the ability. To re-
duce overhead, this paper presents a new duplex
decoding approach that enhances LLMs with
duplex ability, requiring minimal additional
training. Specifically, our method employs par-
allel decoding of queries and responses in con-
versations, effectively implementing a channel-
division-multiplexing decoding strategy. Ex-
perimental results indicate that our proposed
method significantly enhances the naturalness
and human-likeness of user-AI interactions
with minimal training costs.
1
Introduction
LLMs have revolutionized human-computer inter-
action, enabling applications like question answer-
ing (Zhu et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2023; Zhao et al.,
2023) and coding assistance (Rozière et al., 2023;
Han et al., 2024) that augment human capabilities
through conversation. Consequently, the quality of
these interaction experience is important.
Traditional turn-based chat systems inherently
limit the interactive experience (Hill et al., 2015;
Zhou et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024). Current
human-AI interactions follow a turn-based pattern,
with one party passively waiting while the other
responds (Skantze, 2021). Interruptions are fa-
cilitated through manual interventions, such as a
"stop" function, resulting in communication that
*Corresponding author: Wanxiang Che
lacks fluidity. However, human conversations in-
volve simultaneous listening and thinking.
Recent studies have proposed duplex models to
address this challenge (Zhang et al., 2024; Fang
et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024). Zhang et al. (2024)
introduced MiniCPM-Duplex, a novel approach
that addresses the duplex modeling challenge. This
method employs a time-division-multiplexing strat-
egy for encoding and decoding. The input and
output are split and mixed in a time slice format, en-
abling pseudo-simultaneous processing of text seg-
ments. Additionally, Ma et al. (2024) introduced
LSLM which combines channels for autoregres-
sive generation and real-time turn-taking detection.
Three strategies are explored to fuse the listening
and speaking channels.
However, these approaches often demand signif-
icant computational resources for model retraining,
as the designed procedure diverges substantially
from the backbone model. To address this issue,
we present a DUplex decOding (DUO) approach, a
novel channel-based parallel decoding mechanism
that equips LLMs with duplex capabilities. Our ap-
proach enables simultaneous autoregressive output
generation and input preprocessing. Furthermore,
two state tokens are designed to signal whether a
query should be addressed or ignored. The pro-
posed method requires only minimal additional
training to learn the state of the query.
To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed
method, we test DUO based on human evaluation
and standard benchmarks. The results show that
our method significantly enhances the naturalness
and human-likeness of user-AI interactions with
minimal training costs.
2
Methodology
We consider two scenarios: non-awakening in-
teraction and interruption interaction (Fu et al.,
2024). Specifically, the model should filter out

more, if the user interrupts with another question
during an ongoing generation, the model should
pause its current output to immediately address the
latest query.
In this section, we introduce DUO in detail.
DUO processes inputs and outputs cyclically. In
each cycle, the output channel generates new to-
kens autoregressively, while the input channel pre-
fills the key-value cache and predicts the next to-
kens. According to the predicted tokens, the model
decides whether a query is addressed or ignored.
2.1
Parallel Decoding
As illustrated in Figure 1, a new input token is re-
ceived at time step t1 while the model generates
output autoregressively, thus establishing a new in-
put channel. Subsequently, the model generates
tokens autoregressively while simultaneously pro-
cessing the input tokens.
Note that the tokens generated by the input and
output channels after t1 do not attend to each other,
despite sharing the same prefix tokens. This pre-
serves language modeling in each channel. To ac-
commodate the token dependency, the attention
mask is modified as shown on the right of Figure 1.
Upon processing the input tokens, the output
channel persists in generating tokens rather than
terminating immediately. This output channel is
maintained until either the model responds to the
new query or the output sequence is completed.
This capability is crucial in scenarios where the as-
sistant continues to generate responses even when
non-query input is received.
2.2
Channel Transition
It is crucial for the model to determine both whether
and when to respond to new input. To address this
issue, we use state tokens to indicate the status of
the user’s query (Fu et al., 2024). Specifically, the
model predicts α tokens to complete the query in
each processing cycle. Upon encountering a state
token, the model would handle different interactive
behaviors as follows: State token <1> denotes that
the input is a user query. The original output chan-
nel is suspended, and the input channel seamlessly
transitions to become the new output channel. State
token <2> denotes that the new input is no-query
text. Thus the model continues to respond to the
original query, and the input channel is disregarded.
Otherwise, the key-value cache of the predicted
would be disregarded and the next processing cycle
goes on.
Our method DUO differs from MiniCPM-
Duplex (Zhang et al., 2024). Essentially, MiniCPM-
Duplex processes the input and generates out-
put sequentially, functioning as a time-division-
multiplexing system. To adapt to time-division-
multiplexing, MiniCPM-Duplex splits and mixes
the input and output in a time slice format. This
change means it needs a lot of computing power
to retrain the model, as it’s quite different from the
original training data. In contrast, DUO processes
the input and output simultaneously by optimizing
the decoding strategy, functioning as a channel-
division multiplexing system. The data format re-
mains largely unchanged, with only the addition
of some state tokens, thereby preserving the abil-

ity of the original model. The training example of
MiniCPM-Duplex and our DUO is shown in Fig-
ure 5 and Figure 6, respectively. Moreover, DUO
is capable of handling non-awakening interactions,
an aspect that MiniCPM-Duplex does not address.
DUO can be efficiently implemented using Flex-
Attention (He et al., 2024b), which facilitates non-
standard attention mechanisms. The operations are
all accomplished through the management of the
key-value cache. Importantly, DUO does not in-
crease the number of forward passes compared to
standard decoding. As illustrated in Figure 1, DUO
processes the input and output channel in each time
slice. The model generates output concurrently
while the key-value cache of input is prefilled and
the next tokens of input are predicted.
2.3
Dataset Construction
We introduce two state tokens to determine whether
to respond to the query. This section details our
process for constructing the dataset from Duplex-
UltraChat (Zhang et al., 2024) that structures con-
versations in a time-division format. Each indi-
vidual may interrupt before the other participants’
generation is completed and transition sentences
are added to enhance the interactive experience.
We have adapted Duplex-UltraChat into a stan-
dard turn-based format. As previously outlined,
we append state tokens to indicate whether to re-
spond to the query. Since all queries in the dataset
require a response, we append the <1> token to
each user’s content. To simulate non-awakening
interaction scene, we use ChatGPT to generate the
non-query text. We optimize the prompt to make
the non-query text relevant to the context. The
prompt is described in Appendix A.1.
3
Experiments
3.1
Setup
Following Zhang et al. (2024)’s work, we utilize
MiniCPM-2.4B (Hu et al., 2024) as our foundation
model and 10K samples are constructed to train the
model as described in Section 2.3. It is worth not-
ing that our dataset is significantly smaller than the
one used in MiniCPM-Duplex, which consists of
approximately 5,000K samples. We use MiniCPM-
Duplex as our baseline since we are all derived
from the same checkpoints.
The training of MiniCPM-Duo uses the follow-
ing hyperparameter: 1e-5 learning rate, a constant
learning rate scheduler, a batch size of 112, and a
