CONCLUSIONS
This study presents an innovative method that effectively
merges the computational efficiency of recurrent neural net-
works with the high-quality probabilistic modeling of the
diffusion model, specifically applied to probabilistic time se-
ries forecasting. Grounded in stochastic interpolants and an
expanded conditional generation framework featuring con-
trol features, the method undergoes empirical evaluation on
both synthetic and real datasets, showcasing its compelling
performance.
papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces a novel method for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting that combines the efficiency of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with the probabilistic modeling capabilities of diffusion models. The approach, termed Recurrent Interpolants (SI), leverages stochastic interpolants and conditional generation with control features. The motivation stems from the limitations of existing methods, such as RNNs and transformers, in capturing complex, high-dimensional distributions and cross-feature dependencies, and the scalability challenges of generative models like diffusion and flow-based models. The SI model uses an RNN to encode a context window of past time series observations into a history prompt. This prompt is then used by a conditional stochastic interpolant module to generate the distribution of future time points. The method was evaluated on synthetic datasets and real-world time series forecasting tasks, including Solar, Exchange, Traffic, and Wiki datasets. The results, as measured by the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS-sum), demonstrate that SI achieves competitive or superior performance compared to baseline models, including Vec-LSTM, DDPM, SGM, and FM. For example, on the Exchange rate dataset, SI achieved a CRPS-sum of 0.007 ± 0.001, outperforming Vec-LSTM (0.008 ± 0.001), DDPM (0.009 ± 0.004), FM (0.009 ± 0.001), and SGM (0.008 ± 0.002). The study's novelty lies in the application of stochastic interpolants within a conditional generation framework for time series prediction, offering a computationally efficient approach to modeling complex distributions. A primary limitation is the performance on the Traffic dataset, where FM achieved better results. The authors suggest that stochastic interpolants are a strong candidate for conditional generation, particularly for multivariate probabilistic forecasting.

Research Context
Autoregressive models, including RNNs and transformers, are standard for time series forecasting, but struggle with high-dimensional distributions and cross-feature dependencies. Generative models, such as diffusion and flow-based models, offer improved probabilistic modeling, yet face scalability issues. Prior work has explored latent neural SDEs and extensions of state space models using deterministic and stochastic transformation plans. These methods often require learning a mapping from noise to data distributions, which can be computationally intensive. The proposed work addresses the need for a computationally friendly framework for large-scale generative model-based time series prediction by blending the efficiency of RNNs with the probabilistic modeling of diffusion models. This is achieved by using stochastic interpolants within a conditional generation framework.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to develop a computationally efficient generative model for probabilistic multivariate time series forecasting that can capture complex distributions and cross-feature dependencies. The primary hypothesis is that a model combining the efficiency of RNNs with the probabilistic modeling of diffusion models, specifically using stochastic interpolants in a conditional generation framework, will achieve competitive or superior performance compared to existing methods. The alternative hypothesis is that the proposed method will not outperform existing methods, such as DDPM, SGM, FM, and Vec-LSTM, on standard time series forecasting benchmarks. The study aims to demonstrate that the proposed SI model can effectively learn the joint distribution of consecutive time steps conditioned on a context window, enabling accurate and reliable probabilistic forecasts. The research differs from prior work by integrating stochastic interpolants into a conditional generation framework, using an RNN to encode the context window, and applying this approach to time series forecasting.

Methodological Details
The study employs a methodological approach, introducing a novel model called Recurrent Interpolants (SI) for probabilistic time series forecasting. The study uses both synthetic and real-world datasets for evaluation. The synthetic datasets, including Circles, Moons, etc., are two-dimensional datasets with regular patterns. The real-world datasets include Solar, Exchange, Traffic, and Wiki, which are commonly used for probabilistic forecasting tasks. The preprocessing steps follow [Salinas et al., 2019]. The SI model is trained using a loss function based on the mean squared error, with importance sampling using a Beta distribution to stabilize training, particularly when the diffusion time is close to the ends. The model's architecture involves an RNN to encode the context window and a conditional stochastic interpolant module. The RNN encodes the context window xt−P:t−1 into a history prompt ht. The SI module then transports the context vector xt to the target distribution with the condition ht, following the forward SDE. The baseline models include DDPM, SGM, and FM-based generative models. The probabilistic forecasting is evaluated using CRPS-sum, normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), and normalized deviance (ND). The CRPS-sum metric is used to compare the performance of different models, with smaller values indicating better performance. The code will be publicly available. The training algorithm (Algorithm 1) takes as input sample 3-tuples (xti+1, xti, xti−P:ti−1), interpolant schedules α(s), β(s), γ(s), and models velocity ˆb, score ˆs, and RNN. The inference algorithm (Algorithm 2) takes as input sample 2-tuples (xt, xt−P:t−1), trained models velocity ˆb, score ˆs, RNN, and diffusion variance ϵ. The model diagram is illustrated in Figure 2.

Procedures Architectures
The core of the proposed method is the Recurrent Interpolants (SI) model, which combines an RNN with a conditional stochastic interpolant module. The RNN encodes the context window, xt−P:t−1, into a history prompt, ht. The stochastic interpolant module then performs conditional generation, diffusing from xt with the condition ht. The SI model is based on stochastic interpolants, which model the dependent couplings between (x0, x1) with their joint density ρ(x0, x1). The stochastic interpolant is defined as xs = α(s)x0 + β(s)x1 + γ(s)z, where z ∼ N(0, I). The model is trained to match the equality by minimizing the mean squared error loss functions Lb and Ls (Equations 15 and 16). For the time series prediction task, the model learns the joint distribution p(xt+1, xt|xt−P:t−1) of the pair (xt+1, xt) given the past observations xt−P:t−1. The baseline models, including DDPM, SGM, and FM, are adapted for step-by-step prediction. The key innovation is the use of the RNN to encode the context window and the application of stochastic interpolants within a conditional generation framework. The model uses the same neural networks for the baseline models to make a fair comparison. The model diagram is illustrated in Figure 2 and the modified framework is shown in Figure 5. The model uses a Beta distribution for importance sampling.

Key Results
The SI model was evaluated on both synthetic and real-world datasets. On synthetic datasets, the model generated samples comparable to baseline models (DDPM, SGM, FM) as measured by the Wasserstein distance (Table 1). For example, on the Circles dataset, the Wasserstein distance was 0.52 for SI (quad, linear), 0.59 for SI (sqrt, linear), 0.75 for SI (sqrt, trig), 0.52 for SI (trig, linear), 2.58 for DDPM (cosine), 0.70 for DDPM (linear), 1.10 for SGM, and 0.58 for FM. On the real-world time series forecasting tasks, the SI model achieved competitive performance. The CRPS-sum results (Table 2) show that SI outperformed or matched other models on three out of four datasets. For example, on the Exchange rate dataset, SI achieved a CRPS-sum of 0.007 ± 0.001, outperforming Vec-LSTM (0.008 ± 0.001), DDPM (0.009 ± 0.004), FM (0.009 ± 0.001), and SGM (0.008 ± 0.002). On the Solar dataset, SI achieved a CRPS-sum of 0.359 ± 0.06, which was better than Vec-LSTM (0.391 ± 0.017), SGM (0.364 ± 0.029), and DDPM (0.359 ± 0.061). On the Wiki dataset, SI achieved a CRPS-sum of 0.080 ± 0.007, which was better than Vec-LSTM (0.133 ± 0.002), DDPM (0.084 ± 0.023), and SGM (0.108 ± 0.026). However, on the Traffic dataset, FM achieved a better CRPS-sum of 0.038 ± 0.002, while SI achieved 0.083 ± 0.005. Figure 4 demonstrates the quality of the forecast on the Solar dataset, showing precise predictions and uncertainty quantification.

Interpretation Implications
The results suggest that the proposed SI model effectively combines the strengths of RNNs and diffusion models for probabilistic time series forecasting. The competitive performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicates that the stochastic interpolants framework is a viable approach for modeling complex distributions and capturing cross-feature dependencies in time series data. The success of SI, compared to other baselines, implies that carefully modeling the probability distribution is critical for large-dimension time series prediction. The findings support the theoretical extension of stochastic interpolants to a more general conditional generation framework, as described in Theorem 1. The results suggest that the proposed method offers a computationally efficient approach to modeling complex distributions in time series data.

Contradictions Limitations
A key limitation is the performance on the Traffic dataset, where FM achieved better results than SI. The authors note that they were unable to achieve satisfying results with flow matching hyperparameters on the Wiki dataset. The study does not provide details on the specific architectures of the RNNs or the hyperparameters used for the stochastic interpolant module, which could impact reproducibility. The study does not provide an error analysis to investigate the sources of errors in the predictions. The external validity of the results is limited by the specific datasets used. The paper does not discuss the computational cost of training and inference for the SI model compared to the baseline models. The model's performance may be sensitive to the choice of interpolant schedules and the design of the RNN encoder. The study does not address the potential for overfitting or the impact of different data preprocessing techniques.

The code will be publicly available (github_place_holder).

The paper tests different schedulers for the stochastic interpolant model. For example, “SI (sqrt, linear)” means we use square root gamma-function γ(s) = sqrt(2s(1 −s)) and a linear interpolant. Other gamma-functions that we consider are quad: γ(s) = t(1 −s), and trig: γ(s) = sin(πt)2. We show that most of the gamma-interpolant function combinations achieve good results modeling the target distribution.

Key Figures Tables
Table 2 presents the CRPS-sum results for the different models on the four real-world datasets. The table shows the performance of SI compared to the baseline models. Figure 4 demonstrates the quality of the forecast on the Solar dataset, showing median prediction, 50th and 90th confidence intervals. Figure 3 shows examples of model generated samples for synthetic two-dimensional datasets. The axes are not explicitly defined, but the figure visually compares the generated samples from different models.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the development of the Recurrent Interpolants (SI) model, which combines the efficiency of RNNs with the probabilistic modeling of diffusion models for time series forecasting, using stochastic interpolants within a conditional generation framework. (2) The strongest evidence is the competitive performance of SI on real-world datasets, as measured by CRPS-sum, outperforming or matching baseline models on three out of four datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. For example, on the Exchange rate dataset, SI achieved a CRPS-sum of 0.007 ± 0.001. (3) The primary limitation is the performance on the Traffic dataset, where FM achieved better results. Future work could focus on improving the performance of SI on all datasets and exploring different architectures and hyperparameter settings.

Title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH 3 COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
Authors: Shahid Khalid (University of Milan-Bicocca); Nicolò Pianta (University of Milan-Bicocca); Simone Bonizzoni (University of Milan-Bicocca); Piercarlo Mustarelli (University of Milan-Bicocca); Riccardo Ruffo (University of Milan-Bicocca)

Abstract:
Highly concentrated aqueous binary solutions of acetate salts are emerging as promising systems for advanced energy storage applications. Together with superior solubility of CH3COOK helpful in achieving water-in-salt electrolyte concentrations, the presence of CH3COOLi or CH3COONa permits intercalation of desired cations in electrode crystalline phases. Although these systems 2 have captured profound scientific attention in recent years, a fundamental understanding of their physicochemical properties is still lacking. In this work, the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties for a series of solutions comprising of 20 mol kg -1 of CH3COOK with different concentrations of CH3COONa are reported and discussed. The most concentrated solution, i.e., 20 mol kg -1 of CH3COOK with 7 mol kg -1 of CH3COONa came out to be the best in terms of a compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability window. Such a solution has a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25°C and shows a stability window up to 3 V in "ideal" conditions, i.e., using small surface area and highly electrocatalytic electrode in a flooded cell. As a proof of concept of using this solution in sodium-ion batteries, carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) demonstrated the ability to reversibly insert and de-insert Na + ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE with a first cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g -1 , average charge efficiency of 96% at low current and a 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The very good kinetic properties of the interface are also demonstrated by the low value of activation energy for the charge transfer process (0.12 eV).


## Introduction
Driven by the unique benefits of inherent safety, low cost, electrochemical stability, high ionic conductivity and environmental friendliness, super-concentrated aqueous electrolytes are receiving great interest in defining new chemistries for batteries 1 . Although conventional lithiumion batteries (LIBs) employing organic electrolytes have reached an acceptable performance limit, they still suffer of serious issues, such as safety and cost. The non-aqueous organic carbonate electrolytes used in conventional Li-ion batteries, indeed, have low flashpoints, high melting points and high viscosities rendering them useless at lower temperatures 2 . Moreover, conventional Liion batteries mostly rely on thermally unstable LiPF6 which, in the presence of moisture, can undergo degradation, giving HF and causing corrosion of battery components 3 . To alleviate these challenges, several strategies were proposed, including the use of non-flammable, less toxic and cost-effective aqueous electrolytes. However, a major limitation in the use of aqueous electrolytes is the extremely narrow thermodynamic electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V). Though the ESW can be kinetically extended up to 1.5 V using diluted salt solutions, such aqueous systems cannot yet compete with their organic counterparts, which translates into poor energy density 4 .
To widen the ESW of aqueous electrolytes, researchers ventured into high concentration regimes, that were first discouraged by increased ion coupling and rheological limitations. As early as in 1985, McKinnon and Dahn reported a saturated LiAsF6 solution in propylene carbonate (PC) demonstrating an unusual intercalation behavior that could not be possible in ordinary 1 M electrolyte 5 . Curiously, the earlier attempts to breach the concentration restraint were performed with polymer electrolytes, giving origin to the "Polymer-in-Salt" concept 6 . The extreme extension of super-concentration is the so-called "Water-in-Salt" electrolyte (WISE) developed by Suo et al., by dissolving LiTFSI in water up to 21 mol kg -1 , enabling a voltage window of 3 V 1, 7 . The reason for this enhanced ESW stems from the low activity of water molecules at such a high concentration, where the ions outnumber the water molecules which are incorporated into the solvation shells 8 . In the high concentrated scenario, water molecules form clusters, in the subnanometer range, strongly interacting with one or more ions, resulting in large kinetic overpotentials for the electrolysis of water 9 . Wider ESW electrolytes employ per-fluorinated sulfonyl imide salts such as lithium (fluorosulfonyl)(trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide (FTFSI) 10 , lithium (pentafluoroethane sulfonyl)(trifluoromethane sulfonyl)imide (PTFSI), lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) 11 , sodium trifluoromethanesulfonate (NaOTF) 12 , sodium bis(fluorosulfonyl)imide (NaFSI) 13 and potassium trifluoromethanesulfonate (KOTF) 14 .
Despite the outstanding improvements in the ESW, the environmental and economic concerns related to the use of fluorinated salts remain unresolved. In particular, LiTFSI, which is widely used in LIBs, exhibits severe oral and dermal toxicity, skin issues and can cause chronic aquatic toxicity 8 . Furthermore, the limited availability and very high cost of these fluorinated salts practically nullify the advantages brought by super-concentration, making the practical implementation of WISE in energy storage very challenging 15, 16 . Conversely, the main problem in selecting new formulations for WISE is the lack of suitable salts with enough solubility to satisfy the WISE condition. Examples of cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available salts are LiCl, CH3COONa (NaAc), and CH3COOK (KAc). In particular, KAc has been recently investigated by our group 17 , proposed in potassium ion batteries (KIBs), and employed in supercapacitors 18 . Moreover, KAc can be coupled with Li, Na and Zn salts to achieve binary electrolytes with concentrations above 20 mol kg -1 19 . For instance, S.G. Chen et al. reported a mixed-cation electrolyte composed of 32 mol kg -1 KAc and 1 mol kg -1 (CH3COO)2Zn allowing a (2.0 V) Zn-MnO2 aqueous rechargeable cell 20 . Another interesting report features a 32 mol kg -1 KAc with 7 mol kg -1 CH3COOLi electrolyte utilizing C-TiO2 an anode and LiMnO4 as a cathode 8 .
In the design of secondary batteries, a critical issue is the choice of electrode materials to be used in such a highly concentrated environment. In this framework, NASICON compounds offer significant advantages owing to their stable structure and large ionic channels with accessible sites for highly efficient ions insertion-extraction 21 . Moreover, the very low solubility and the possibility to modify the intercalation potential by tuning the chemical composition, so matching the cell voltage with the electrolyte ESW, make NASICON compounds an ideal choice as electrode materials 18 .
Taking advantage of the high solubility of KAc, we investigated a binary system comprised of KAc and NaAc, by keeping the KAc concentration constant at 20 mol kg -1 , and increasing NaAc up to 7 mol kg -1 . A single composition (32 mol kg -1 KAc with 8 mol kg -1 NaAc) was recently investigated as far as the electrochemical applications were concerned 22 . In this paper, we performed a careful study on the physico-chemical properties of the binary system, which are crucial to correctly address its application in batteries. To prove the advantages of using the most concentrated solution i.e., 7 mol kg -1 NaAc with 20 mol kg -1 KAc as a WISE electrolyte, we studied the intercalation process of alkaline ions (Na, K) using carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON as an electrode material. Such a material has already been used as the negative electrode with aqueous electrolytes 23 . The electrochemical measurements include a kinetic analysis trough impedance spectroscopy as a function of the temperature.

## Electrolyte preparation
Appropriate amounts of NaAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) and KAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) were dissolved in high-quality Milli-Q water ( = 6.7 S cm -1 ) under sonication. Keeping KAc constant at 20 mol kg -1 and varying the concentration of NaAc, four different electrolytes were prepared, namely 1 mol kg -1 NaAc with 20 mol kg -1 KAc (1N20K), 2.5 mol kg -1 NaAc with 20 mol kg -1 KAc (2.5N20K), 5 mol kg -1 NaAc with 20 mol kg -1 KAc (5N20K), and 7 mol kg -1 NaAc with 20 mol kg -1 KAc (7N20K). 1 M NaAc solution was also prepared for comparison. All the electrolytes were stored and used at room conditions. The investigated samples are listed in Table 1 with the corresponding compositional parameters.

## Synthesis of CLTP
Carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 NASICON, (CLTP) phase was synthesized using a facile one-pot synthesis route. Firstly, 1.78 g of NH4H2(PO4)3 as a phosphate precursor were dissolved in 40 ml of ethanol via stirring, then 3.51 g of Ti(OC4H9)4 as a Ti source were added until complete dissolution. As lithium and carbon sources, CH3COOLi2H2O, 0.52 g and C6H12O6, 0.58 g were added, respectively. The mixture was stirred for 4 h at 55 C in a sealed container. The system was then opened, and the temperature was raised to 80 C to get rid of ethanol and obtain a gel. The precursor was dried under vacuum at 100 C and finely grinded with mortar and pestle. The obtained powdered precursor was calcined at 800 C for 6 h under argon flux in a tubular furnace.
The ramp rate was set to 5 C min -1 and the gas flow was adjusted to 50 ml min -1 . Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized via the same route, without using C6H12O6 in the synthesis steps. .05 n= ratio of the number of water molecules to the salt molecules X-Rays Diffraction analysis was carried out using Rigaku Miniflex 600 equipped with a Cu cathode. The analysis was performed in a 2 range from 10 to 80 degrees with a step size of 0.02 and scan speed of 1 deg min -1 . Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was done using Zeiss® Gemini SEM 450.

## Viscosity Measurements
Viscosity measurements were done with MCR Rheometer 102 (Anthon Paar). A parallel plate (50 mm) setup was used to perform shear tests with shear rates in the range 10-300 s -1 with steadystate settings. The measurements were carried out at 10 C, 20 C, 30 C and 40 C.

## Thermal Studies
Thermal analysis was performed with Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) using DSC 1Star ® (Mettler Toledo). STARe ® software was used for the evaluation of the data. The samples were analyzed in a temperature range from -120 C to 90 C. The following protocol was used: cooling from 30 C to -120 C at a rate of 1 C min -1 , followed by a 5 min isotherm at -120 C, and finally by a heating step from -120 C to 90 C at a ramp rate of 1 C min -1 . Initially, all the samples were equilibrated at 30 C for 30 minutes to ensure a completely liquid state. The heating/cooling rate of 1 C min was chosen to allow the system to undergo structural relaxation without sacrificing sensitivity. Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA) was carried out using Mettler Toledo TGA/DSC-1.

## Conductivity measurements
The conductivity measurements were performed using Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) employing a dip probe cell with two platinum foils in a glass casing, with a cell factor of 1.04 cm -1 . Impedance spectra were recorded in a frequency range of 1 Hz to 200 kHz with an amplitude of 25 mV. All the samples were first degassed with nitrogen flux and the measurement was done under N2 flux in a temperature range from 5 C to 70 C in a climatic chamber (Angelantoni). For all the samples, the bulk ohmic resistance was recorded via the x-axis intercept of high frequency side in the Nyquist plots.

## Electrode/Cell Preparation
Prior to the use with aqueous electrolytes, the electrode materials (CLTP/LTP) were characterized in benchmark organic electrolytes. Slurries of active materials, PVDF (6020 by Solvay) binder and carbon black (Super P from Erachem Comilog, Inc.) in weight ratio 8:1:1 were prepared using anhydrous N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone (Merck) as the solvent. For the measurements in organic electrolytes, the slurries were casted on metal foils (Al) and R2032 coin cells were assembled in an argon-filled glovebox ([O2] < 0.1 ppm, [H2O] < 0.1 ppm) using alkaline metal foils (Li, Na, K) as the counter electrodes. The active material loads were 2.4 mg cm -2 , 2.7 mg cm -2 and 1.7 mg cm -2 for Li, Na and K based cells, respectively. The cells were equipped with commercially available 1.0 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC (LP30, Merck), 1 M NaClO4 (Merck) in PC/FEC and 0.8 M KPF6 (Merck) in EC/DEC to test the Li + , Na + and K + intercalation, respectively. To avoid possible corrosion problems, the NASICON-based electrodes for aqueous electrolytes were prepared by dip-coating carbon cloth current collectors in the slurries of the active materials. In this case, the active material load was 6 mg cm -2 .

## Electrochemical Measurements
The ESW was estimated in flooded three-electrode cells equipped with glassy carbon as working, platinum mesh as counter and double junction SCE as reference electrode, respectively. Galvanostatic Charge-Discharge with Potential Limitation (GCPL) technique was used in the proper potential range at different current rates for the investigation of the performance of the NASICON/electrolytes interfaces. In the case of aqueous electrolytes, the GCPL measurement was done using a flooded three-electrodes cell with a double junction SCE and a Pt foil as reference and counter electrodes, respectively.
All the GCPL measurements have been conducted at different current rates using the same protocol to compare the different interfaces, i.e. starting with 10 cycles at 0.1 C, then increasing the current every 10 cycles to 0.5 C, 1 C, 5C, and 10 C, and finally reducing the current again at 0.1 C for the last 10 cycles. In the C-rate calculation, 1C value corresponds to 136 mA g -1 , considering the insertion and de-insertion of two alkaline ions into the structure. To characterize the electrode electrolyte interface, EIS measurements were conducted in temperature range of 20 °C to 70 °C inside the climatic chamber. EIS spectra were recorded in a frequency range of 1 kHz to 100 KHz using a sinusoidal voltage of 50 mV under N2 in a flooded cell, using three-electrode configuration. To avoid any interference from the surrounding, all the impedance measurements were carried out in a Faraday cage inside the climatic chamber.

## Results and Discussion
Figure 1 reports the DSC thermograms of the electrolyte solutions. The samples show distinct thermal features which include the glass transition temperature (Tg) below -70 C, exotherms of cold crystallization (Tc) below -20 C, and finally the melting endotherms (Tm) around 0 C°. It can be observed that increasing the salt concentration result in the shifting of Tg to higher temperatures (see Table 2 ) which is correlated to a growing interaction among the solution species. Such increase in the Tg with concentration accounts for the transition of the solution characteristics from salt-in-water to water-in-salt as already reported for KAc solutions 17 and LiTFSI 24 . The Tg of all the samples showed an overshot which can be ascribed to structural relation 25 . Interestingly, 1N20K and 2.5N20K did not show any cold crystallization, or melting endotherm, meaning that they were frozen in the glassy state with the employed thermal protocol. In the case of 5N20K and 7N20K, single cold crystallization events occurred at -28.06 C and -33.70 C, respectively, while melting endotherms were recorded for both these samples at around 0 C. However, the shape of the endotherms suggests that the melting process started well below the room temperature. Reber et al. 26 reported liquidus temperatures for similar electrolytes such as 35 mol kg -1 NaFSI, 30 mol kg -1 NaFSI with 5 mol kg -1 NaFTFSI, 25 mol kg -1 NaFSI with 10 mol kg -1 NaFTFSI, and 19.5 mol kg -1 LiTFSI with 8.3 mol kg -1 LiBETI, equal to 50 C, 44 C, 38 C and 28 C, respectively.
They also reported liquidus temperatures of 28 C and 22 C for 35 mol kg -1 LiFSI and for 25 mol kg -1 LiFSI with 10 mol kg -1 LiFTFSI, respectively 26 . It is thus evident that even using different anions by mixing FSI and FTFSI didn't influence the liquidus temperature to a great extent. In this scenario, our electrolyte 7N20K will provide a significant advantage by preventing premature cell failure caused by salt crystallization in long-term cycling.

The ionic conductivity decreases with increasing the electrolyte concentration (Figure 2b ), as expected in highly concentrated electrolytes. All the sodium containing samples, indeed, show values lower or nearly equal to that of 20 m CH3COOK 17 , however the 7N20K concentration still exhibits a good value of conductivity i.e., 21.2 mS cm -1 at 25°C (see Table 2 ). The decrease in ionic conductivities with increasing salt concentration is related to the Tg shift to higher temperatures, which determines the increase of viscosity resulting in increased resistance to the shear flow 27, 28 . The values of T are in good agreement with values of T g from DSC measurements (see Table 2 ) and the two temperatures have the same dependence on concentration. An increase in concentration is associated with high T values as a result of a higher activation barrier to the movement of ions 29 . This dependence of TO on concentration is attributed to the strong interaction between the ions and water molecules suggesting the formation of an internal liquid structure. The considerable levels of conductivity at high concentration strongly suggest the possibility of the formation of water-salt structures 27 . Here, the available water molecules cannot effectively shell the respective cations, promoting the interaction of anions (CH3COO -in our case) with the cations without causing any significant reassociation resulting in the modification of the local hydrogen bonding 30 . The molar conductivities (m), activation energies (Ea), ionic conductivities (), T and Tg values are reported in Table 2 . The results on the charge transport are supported also by the viscosity measurements vs. the temperatures, which follow an Arrhenius behavior (Figure 3a ) for all the electrolyte samples. As expected, the viscosities increase as a function of concentration, however, the trend does not vary linearly as it is in the case of diluted solutions (Stokes-Einstein equation) due to complex ion interactions at elevated concentrations 31 . In the case of salts having a similar anion (as in our case) the change in viscosity is predominantly caused by the cations 32 . Moreover, the behavior of aqueous concentrated acetates renders them as the so-called "structure-making salts'', because none of the samples show any decrease in viscosity with increasing salt concentration.
Furthermore, this behavior signifies the reduced activity of water molecules, since the cations and acetate anions being strongly hydrated are contributing to some fashion of molecular ordering 33 .

## Figure 5. Electrochemical stability window of water vs SHE
The cathodic and anodic decomposition potentials for all the samples obtained in these conditions are summarized in Table 3 . The noticeable increase in the stability on the cathodic side with increasing salt concentration confirms an obvious suppression of the hydrogen evolution. This is a confirmation for the reduced activity of water in agreement with the rheological and thermal analysis. The ESW expansion on the anodic side is not as significant as it is on the cathodic one, in agreement with previously reported results on acetate-based electrolytes 17 . Thanks to the good conductivity, broad ESW of WISE, and the large concentration of alkaline cations, the 7N20K was coupled with a NASICON LiTi2(PO4)3 based electrode to study an anodic interface for alkaline ion battery. As already demonstrated in the literature, the low electrical conductivity of this NASICON phase requires a carbon shell around the active material particles to enable good electrochemical performances 23 . Following this approach, the coated NASICON (CLTP) was produced by one pot sol gel route in presence of a carbonaceous precursor (glucose).
For sake of comparison, the same synthesis was repeated in absence of glucose, obtaining the pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 material (LTP).
The XRD patterns of the LTP and CLTP samples are reported in Supporting Information (Figure S5 ) and show the phase purity without crystalline secondary phases. All the peaks are indeed in good agreement with the rhombohedral NASICON type crystal structure (R-3c space group, JCPDS: 35-0754) 38 . The peak positions in both samples are the same, signifying that the carbon content present in the coated sample does not affect the crystal structure, which consists of because of the higher energy required to introduce and accommodate the larger K + ion into the crystalline structure. This suggest that in a Na + /K + mixed electrolyte, the Na + ions will be preferentially introduced in the anode. The performance of CLTP was then evaluated in the 7N20K solution, for sake of comparison and to highlight the beneficial effect of the WISE approach, we have also tested the same electrode in 1 M NaAc aqueous electrolyte (Figure 7a and 7b). The potential profiles reported in Figure 7a show the preferential insertion of sodium cation as expected, despite its concentration being 2.85 times lower than that of potassium for 7N20K. Furthermore, Figure 7 also demonstrates that the performances in the WISE electrolyte are clearly better than those in the diluted solution in terms of specific capacity and efficiency. In particular, the cathodic and anodic capacities are 104 and 84 mAh g -1 , (80% charge efficiency) at the first cycle in 7N20K, while in the diluted solution the values decrease to 96 and 36 mAh g -1 (40% efficiency), respectively. Moreover, when cycled in the WISE electrolyte at 1C (136 mA g -1 ) the CLTP is capable to provide an average anodic specific capacity of 68 mAh g -1 with an average charge efficiency of 99.0%. Finally, at the end of the test (60 cycles), the CLTP/WISE interface shows a capacity retention of 90%.
To better understand the electrode/electrolyte interface, the kinetics of the mechanism of charge transfer, and the diffusion of alkaline ions inside the electrode structure, EIS analysis was performed on a partially sodiated CLTP electrode. To do so CLTP was first sodiated while during the de-sodiation the measurement interrupted in the middle of the first plateau and EIS spectra were collected at every 10 °C steps from 20 °C to 70 °C. Moreover, the low activation energy value (0.48 eV) suggests that the diffusion can be easily improved by increasing the temperature.

## Conclusions
In this work, the physico-chemical properties of a series of binary aqueous acetate salts solutions are thoroughly investigated via DSC, rheological, electrical, and electrochemical measurements.
Four different solutions are prepared by dissolving 20 mol kg -1 of CH3COOK, with different amounts of CH3COONa, ranging from 1 to 7 mol kg -1 . DSC analysis carried out in a temperature range of -120 C to 90 C revealed that the glass transition temperature Tg increases with increasing the salt concentration. Moreover, the DSC also confirms the low liquidus temperature for the 7N20K sample. Viscosity measurements carried out as a function of temperature classified the acetate salts to be the so-called ''structure making salts''. The ionic conductivity decreased by increasing the salt concentration, however, it remained comparable to the organic counterparts even for the highest concentration (21.2 mS cm -1 at 25C for 7N20K). Electrochemical measurements carried out in ideal conditions showed that the electrochemical stability window increased by increasing the CH3CCONa concentration. To test the possible use in alkaline ion batteries, a carbon-coated NASICON based electrode was used as an anode. The performances were quite promising, with a first cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g -1 , an average charge efficiency of 96% and 99% at low and high currents, respectively, and a 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. Moreover, the impedance spectroscopy measurements performed as a function of the temperature highlighted the very good kinetic properties of the NASICON/7N20K interface.
These results demonstrated the possibility to design electrode interfaces for the successful development of alkaline ion rechargeable batteries in the context of the water-in-salt approach.

papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the physicochemical properties of highly concentrated aqueous binary solutions of potassium acetate (CH3COOK) and sodium acetate (CH3COONa) as potential electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The research focuses on solutions with a constant CH3COOK concentration of 20 mol kg-1 and varying CH3COONa concentrations. The most promising electrolyte, 7 mol kg-1 CH3COONa with 20 mol kg-1 CH3COOK, demonstrated a good balance between transport properties and electrochemical stability. This solution exhibited a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm-1 at 25°C and an electrochemical stability window (ESW) of up to 3 V. As a proof of concept, carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) was used as an electrode material in a sodium-ion battery using the 7N20K electrolyte. The CLTP electrode showed reversible Na+ ion insertion/de-insertion at approximately -0.7 V vs. SHE, with an initial anodic capacity of 85 mAh g-1, an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low activation energy for the charge transfer process (0.12 eV) indicated favorable kinetic properties at the electrode/electrolyte interface. The study's novelty lies in the use of a binary acetate salt system as a water-in-salt electrolyte, offering a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to fluorinated salts. A primary limitation is the use of a small surface area and highly electrocatalytic electrode in a flooded cell for ESW measurements. The findings suggest the potential for developing safe and efficient sodium-ion batteries using concentrated aqueous electrolytes.

Research Context
Conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) face challenges related to safety and cost due to the use of organic electrolytes. Aqueous electrolytes offer advantages like inherent safety and environmental friendliness but suffer from a narrow electrochemical stability window (ESW). Prior work has explored the use of high-concentration electrolytes, including water-in-salt electrolytes (WISE), to broaden the ESW. However, the use of fluorinated salts in WISE raises environmental and economic concerns. This study addresses the need for cost-effective and sustainable alternatives by investigating binary acetate salt solutions as WISE electrolytes, which have not been extensively studied in this context. The study builds on the concept of WISE, but focuses on more sustainable and cost-effective salts.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a highly concentrated aqueous binary solution of CH3COOK and CH3COONa can serve as a viable electrolyte for sodium-ion batteries, offering a balance of electrochemical stability and transport properties. The study hypothesizes that a specific concentration of CH3COONa in CH3COOK will yield an electrolyte with a wider ESW and improved ionic conductivity compared to diluted aqueous solutions. It is predicted that the 7N20K electrolyte will exhibit a wider ESW and improved ionic conductivity. The study also hypothesizes that a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) electrode will demonstrate reversible Na+ ion insertion/de-insertion in the 7N20K electrolyte, with good capacity retention and charge efficiency. These hypotheses are tested by measuring the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of the electrolyte solutions. The study differs from prior work by focusing on a binary acetate salt system, which is cost-effective and environmentally friendly, as a WISE electrolyte and testing its performance in a sodium-ion battery.

Methodological Details
The study employed an empirical approach to investigate the properties of aqueous acetate salt solutions. Four electrolyte solutions were prepared by dissolving NaAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) and KAc (99%, Alfa Aesar) in Milli-Q water. The KAc concentration was kept constant at 20 mol kg-1, while the NaAc concentration varied: 1 mol kg-1 NaAc with 20 mol kg-1 KAc (1N20K), 2.5 mol kg-1 NaAc with 20 mol kg-1 KAc (2.5N20K), 5 mol kg-1 NaAc with 20 mol kg-1 KAc (5N20K), and 7 mol kg-1 NaAc with 20 mol kg-1 KAc (7N20K). A 1 M NaAc solution was also prepared for comparison. Carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route. The CLTP was synthesized by dissolving NH4H2(PO4)3, Ti(OC4H9)4, CH3COOLi·2H2O, and C6H12O6 in ethanol, followed by stirring, drying, and calcination at 800 °C under argon. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized using the same route without C6H12O6. Viscosity measurements were conducted using an MCR Rheometer 102 (Anton Paar) with a parallel plate setup, shear rates from 10-300 s-1, and temperatures of 10°C, 20°C, 30°C, and 40°C. Thermal analysis was performed using Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) with a temperature range from -120°C to 90°C and Thermal Gravimetric Analysis (TGA). Conductivity measurements were performed using Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) with a dip probe cell in a frequency range of 1 Hz to 200 kHz. The ESW was estimated in flooded three-electrode cells using a glassy carbon working electrode, a platinum mesh counter electrode, and a double junction SCE reference electrode. Galvanostatic Charge-Discharge with Potential Limitation (GCPL) was used to investigate the performance of the NASICON/electrolyte interfaces. EIS measurements were conducted in a temperature range of 20°C to 70°C. The study did not mention preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections.

Procedures Architectures
The study investigated the impact of varying NaAc concentrations on the properties of 20 mol kg-1 CH3COOK solutions. The synthesis of carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (CLTP) involved a one-pot sol-gel method. The process began with dissolving NH4H2(PO4)3, Ti(OC4H9)4, CH3COOLi·2H2O, and C6H12O6 in ethanol. The mixture was stirred, then dried under vacuum at 100 °C, and calcined at 800 °C under argon. Pristine LiTi2(PO4)3 (LTP) was synthesized similarly, but without C6H12O6. The CLTP was then used as an electrode material in a sodium-ion battery. The electrochemical measurements were conducted in a flooded three-electrode cell configuration. The ESW was determined using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), with a threshold of 0.1 mA cm-2 on a glassy carbon electrode. Galvanostatic Charge-Discharge with Potential Limitation (GCPL) was used to evaluate the performance of the CLTP electrode in the 7N20K electrolyte. EIS measurements were performed to analyze the electrode/electrolyte interface kinetics. The study employed a variety of analytical techniques, including DSC, rheometry, EIS, and GCPL, to characterize the electrolyte and electrode materials. The novelty lies in the use of a binary acetate salt system as a WISE electrolyte and its application in a sodium-ion battery, along with the use of carbon-coated NASICON as an electrode material in this context. The study used standard laboratory equipment and techniques for materials synthesis and electrochemical characterization.

Key Results
The DSC analysis revealed that the glass transition temperature (Tg) increased with increasing salt concentration. The 7N20K sample showed a low liquidus temperature. Viscosity measurements classified the acetate salts as "structure-making salts." The ionic conductivity decreased with increasing salt concentration, but remained comparable to organic counterparts, with 7N20K exhibiting 21.2 mS cm-1 at 25°C. Electrochemical measurements showed the ESW increased with increasing CH3COONa concentration. The CLTP electrode in the 7N20K electrolyte showed an initial anodic capacity of 85 mAh g-1, an average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. At 1C, the CLTP provided an average anodic specific capacity of 68 mAh g-1 with a 99.0% charge efficiency. The activation energy for the charge transfer process at the CLTP/7N20K interface was 0.12 eV. The diffusion coefficient was around 10-13 cm2 s-1 at room temperature. The 7N20K electrolyte exhibited an ESW of up to 3 V. The first cycle cathodic and anodic capacities in the 7N20K electrolyte were 104 and 84 mAh g-1, respectively, with an 80% charge efficiency. In the diluted solution, the values decreased to 96 and 36 mAh g-1, respectively, with a 40% efficiency. The molar conductivity at 25°C for the 7N20K solution was 52.90 ohm-1 cm2 mol-1. The study did not provide any baseline or SOTA comparisons with absolute/relative deltas.

Interpretation Implications
The findings suggest that the binary acetate salt system can be successfully employed as a WISE electrolyte for sodium-ion batteries. The increased Tg with concentration indicates a transition from a salt-in-water to a water-in-salt behavior. The good ionic conductivity and broad ESW of the 7N20K electrolyte, coupled with the performance of the CLTP electrode, support the potential of this system for energy storage applications. The low activation energy for charge transfer at the CLTP/7N20K interface suggests fast kinetics. The study implies that the strong interactions between ions and water molecules in the concentrated electrolyte contribute to the formation of water-salt structures, which enhance the ESW. The results demonstrate the possibility of designing electrode interfaces for the successful development of alkaline ion rechargeable batteries using the water-in-salt approach.

Contradictions Limitations
The study's ESW measurements were conducted using a small surface area and a highly electrocatalytic electrode in a flooded cell, which may lead to an overestimation of the decomposition limits. The study did not report the random seed used for any of the experiments. The study did not report the demographics of the materials. The study does not provide a detailed discussion of the potential degradation mechanisms of the electrolyte or the electrode materials during cycling. The study does not provide a detailed comparison with other WISE electrolytes, limiting the assessment of the relative performance of the binary acetate system. The study does not address the long-term cycling stability of the battery cells. The study does not discuss the potential environmental impact of the acetate salts.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 presents DSC curves showing the glass transition temperature (Tg) shifting to higher temperatures with increasing salt concentration. Figure 2a shows the dependence of ionic conductivity on temperature, and Figure 2b shows the ionic conductivity decreasing with increasing electrolyte concentration. Figure 3a shows the viscosity measurements vs. the temperatures, which follow an Arrhenius behavior for all the electrolyte samples, while Figure 3b shows the evolution of viscosity as a function of temperature. Figure 4a shows the molar/conductivities vs. the fluidity at different temperatures, and Figure 4b shows the Kohlrausch's law for the 7N20K solution. Figure 5 shows the linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) profiles vs standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) for the electrolyte samples. Figure 7a and 7b show the potential profiles and the performances in the WISE electrolyte. Figure 8 shows the EIS spectra. Figure 9 shows the Arrhenius plot of the charge transfer resistance. Table 2 reports the molar conductivities, activation energies, ionic conductivities, T and Tg values. These figures and tables are critical for understanding the thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties of the electrolyte solutions and the performance of the CLTP electrode.

Three Takeaways
(1) The core novel contribution is the demonstration of a binary acetate salt system as a water-in-salt electrolyte for sodium-ion batteries, offering a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative to fluorinated salts. (2) The strongest evidence is the performance of the 7N20K electrolyte, which exhibited a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm-1 at 25°C, an ESW of up to 3 V, and a CLTP electrode with a first cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g-1, an average charge efficiency of 96%, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. (3) The primary limitation is the use of a small surface area and highly electrocatalytic electrode in a flooded cell for ESW measurements, which may lead to an overestimation of the decomposition limits. A forward path would be to conduct a more detailed comparison with other WISE electrolytes and to investigate the long-term cycling stability and degradation mechanisms of the battery cells.

Title: Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation
Authors: Yuki Kamijo (The University of Tokyo); Ratmir Derda (University of Alberta)

Abstract:
In this publication, we developed the high throughput screening implementation of freeze-float selection platform system we established in the previous publication. The goal of this publication is to expand the system to higher throughput and accuracy. In the following sections, we describe the steps for automated droplets generations, adaptation of freeze-float selection using controlled and uniform temperature cooling system, and semi-automated droplets detection program. We aimed to improve previously published system to add functional advantages, such as; a) increased efficiency of the screening with fewer manipulation steps; b) increased accuracy of measurement due to the increased sample size; c) increased uniformity of temperature distribution by incorporating the controlled-rate freezer. In the following sections, we describe the steps for automated droplets generations, freeze-float system adaptations using controlled and uniform temperature cooling system, and semi-automated droplets detection program.


## Introduction
In the previous publication, we reported a first proof-of-concept implementation of freezefloat selection system, 1 which was able to identify the ice-nucleation event in droplets that contained ice-nucleating entities. 1 cm 2 geometry cuvette system successfully accommodated up to 50  1 L droplets at once and separated the samples that have ice-nucleating activity from those do not. However, due to the low thermal conductivity of the silicone oil, it was not possible to increase the footprint of the container and accommodate a larger number of droplets without introducing a significant thermal lag. The throughput could be increased by setting up multiple cuvettes in parallel, but setting up more than 5-10 cuvettes in the same freezer system was difficult, and again, resulted in non-uniform results; for example, in setting up 10 cuvettes at the same time, we observed a difference of a few degrees' between cuvettes. To improve the uniformity of the temperature among multiple cuvettes, the system requires the good heat conductor between cuvettes.
High throughput screening (HTS) in multi-well plates miniaturization and automation of biochemical assays is well-established method to enable a large number of parallel measurements. HTS has been developed originally for drug discovery in the laboratory or pharmaceutical industry to screen the increasing number of potential targets and therapeutic compound libraries. [2] [3] [4] [5] The transition from the low-throughput assay to the HTS results in highly efficient and integrated system, which includes the shortened screening time, reduced amount of sample and reagent, and lower costs of the overall process. Miniaturization using 3456-well microtiter plate made it possible to carry out more than 100,000 assays per day and volume of less than 5 L. 6, 7 Combination of the automated liquid dispensing and plate handling robotics enabled even higher throughput and reproducibility while the increasing number of assays. 8, 9 To process the large data sets associated with the HTS, robust signal detection and statistical analysis systems have also been developed. 10 Droplets-based assays represent another form of high-throughput assay. It offers the advantage of chemical and physical compartmentalization to avoid cross-contamination of the samples by segmenting the uniform droplets by the immiscible carrier fluid. Successful examples of the droplet microfluidic assays such as crystallization study 11 or single cell screening of enzyme production 12, 13 reported a million fold reduction of reagent consumption and 300-folds increase in throughput when compared to the HTS-multiwell assays. Droplet-based assays have also been employed to measure tens of thousands ice nucleation events at one experiment. 12, 14 Microfluidic droplet based cell and virion counting techniques are also reported. 15 Droplet based analysis became a commercial success in digital polymerase chain reaction (dPCR) 16 and single-cell genomics. 17, 18 This technology successfully increased the sensitivity of the absolute nucleic acid quantification by compartmentalizing the individual DNA molecule into uniform droplets. When compared to HTS plate-based assays, the drawback of droplet systems is difficult in measuring a large number of droplets of arbitrary compositions.
Preparation of polydisperse silicone oil emulsions by simple mixing have been used in biochemical applications. 19 Despite the ease of manufacturing, polydispersity is detrimental in icenucleation studies because the freezing temperature is directly proportional to the logarithm of droplets diameter. 20 The polydispersity of the droplets can directly influence the accuracy of the freezing measurement. Swanson and co-worker observed that the droplet diameter and homogeneous freezing temperature can be expressed as
𝑦 = ln(𝑥) -26.8
where 𝑦 is nucleation temperature and 𝑥 is droplet radius. 21 This approximation will lead to 2.3 °C difference of mean freezing temperature between the 1 mm diameter and 0.1 mm diameter droplets.
Microfluidics can produce uniform droplets but interfacing of microfluidics and microtiter well plates used in HTS is not obvious and not trivial. Based on this knowledge, we produced uniform size droplets via the commercially available automated pipetting system and confirmed the monodispersity by image analysis.
To obtain the reliable freezing temperature, sample number is also important. Confidence interval of the freezing temperature of droplets was calculated via the formula:
𝑛 ≈ (2𝑘 𝐶𝐼 ⁄ ) 2 𝑠 2
𝑛 is the sample number, 𝑘 is the value for desired confidence level (1.96 for 95% confidence), 𝐶𝐼 is the confidence interval, and 𝑠 is the standard deviation of the outcome of interest. From the obtained value, we concluded that more than 30 droplets sample is sufficient to observe the reliable freezing temperature.
We introduced the robotic liquid transfer system Biomek® 3000 (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) to enable the automated parallel generation of droplets in wells of a multi-well plate. Biomek 3000 replaced manual generation of droplets by repeat pipetting employed in our previous report. This robotic system provides liquid handling operations with a spatial positioning ability compatible with many multi-well plate geometries. Simple modification to the Biomek program allowed changing the parameters of droplets generation including droplets number or droplets size.
From the prior study, the droplet freezing is hypothesized to be a random nucleation process which can be accelerated in the presence of ice nucleators. Due to the stochastic freezing behavior, the freezing spectra in droplet freezing assays usually shows inherent distributions, which results in a spread of the freezing temperature among droplets even when all the droplets have identical size and contain the same number of the INA species. 22 This dispersion makes it difficult to determine the ice nucleating temperature from a small number of samples. By expanding the size of the assay vessel from a 1 cm 2 footprint cuvette that contains up to 50 droplets to the 48 cryovials that can contain up to 40 droplets (40 droplets × 48 vials = 1920 droplets), the throughput can be increased by the factor of 38. The cooling setup employed the metal cooling plate and sample holder to achieve the homogeneous cooling through the vial to vial.
Wills and co-workers have reported that the droplet freezing assays with cooling rates from 0.8 to 10 K/min produced nucleation rates fit in a single line, 23 which suggested that the difference in cooling rate had minimum effect on the nucleation rate coefficients. However linear cooling rate is important for the droplet freezing assay in the stochastic model of heterogeneous nucleation measurement. 23 Based on this report, we conducted the freeze-float experiment incorporating a constant rate freezer Asymptote VIA freezer. This commercially available instrument affords a constant rate cooling with high precision down to -0.5 °C/min. We equipped this bench-top instrument with custom-made glass lid to enable automated image recording by generic digital camera.

## Automated droplets generation
To implement the freeze-float selection at the higher throughput scale, we first tested the 96 deep well plate which is compatible with the robotic liquid handling machine Biomek 3000
(Figure 1 A-B ). We used the same silicone oil buoyant layer with 1% silicone surfactant system and HFE-7500 cushion layer as we used in the previous publication.
We dispensed 30  1 L droplets into the silicone oil layer of 96 deep well plate using Biomek 3000. At a standard dispensing rate 1 droplet per 2 seconds, a pipetting arm successfully generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells (up to ~3800 droplets at once) in ~15 minutes. The rate can be further accelerated by using a multi-head dispenser.
Uniform volume is the key for quantitative detection of ice-nucleation events. To assess the droplets dispersity, we prepared the 60 1 L droplets with fluorescein dye by the Biomek 3000 in the silicone oil in the 12 well plate filled with silicone oil and acquired the fluorescent image by ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, CA) (Figure 1C ). The droplet diameters were measured by using Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m (Source Code S1). This program detects the circles in image in an automated manner and analyze the diameter of each droplets. The polydispersity of the 60 droplets defined as standard deviation of the radii of the droplets (here 2.8610 -5 ) divided by the mean radius (here 3.1010 -4 m) was 9.2%, which indicated that the droplets generated by the robotic system have sufficiently uniform volume (Figure 1 D-E ).
Swanson and co-worker observed that the droplet diameter and homogeneous freezing temperature can be expressed as
𝑦 = ln(𝑥) -26.8
where 𝑦 is nucleation temperature and 𝑥 is droplet radius. 21 Based on the standard deviation of the radii of the droplets, we expected no more than 0.09 °C dispersion in the measurement of the nucleation temperature.
We took several precautions to eliminate droplets coalescence. To avoid contact with the plastic wall which can cause the droplets destabilization, the HFE-7500 was always placed at the bottom of the system as a cushion layer. The static electricity of the Biomek 3000 which could cause coalescence of the droplets was removed by using Auto-set Ion Pump (#19500, Charles Water, MA). This machine is bench-top equipment that discharges static potential accumulation caused by the Biomek 3000 operation. Also when we move the droplet system, wet filter paper was placed below the plastic plate to minimize the accumulation of static electricity.
We conducted freeze-float validation experiment of the system implementing Biomek 3000. The Biomek 3000 successfully prepared 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein dye in a 96 deep well system. We placed this system in the commodity freezer employed in the previous publication, and recorded the droplets freezing and floating behaviour (Figure 2 ). The INA droplets showed droplet freezing behaviour with a good agreement with the previous report.
We used Python script KStest.ipynb (Source Code S3) to compare the freezing temperature distribution of droplets from two different samples. Briefly, this script compares cumulative distributions of the freezing temperature from two samples and calculate the p-value using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to show if the freezing temperature profile of the two samples are drawn from the same distributions.
To achieve the high throughput screening, it is necessary to establish the multi-well platform that can give uniform cooling through all wells in a plate. However, due to the low thermal conductivity of the silicone oil and geometry of the 96 deep well plate, it was difficult to avoid the cell to cell thermal gradient. The freezing temperature in cells in the same deep well plate showed p-value of 4.410 -7 at constant temperature -28 °C generic freezer (Figure 3 ). The thermal gradient was decreased (p = 0.31) with linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) compared to the constant temperature cooling, however it significantly increased the range of freezing time, and mean freezing time between the cells were different (47.4 and 50.6 min). We concluded that using these

## Asymptote VIA freezer
To achieve the constant rate cooling of the freeze-float system and better uniformity of the cell to cell temperature, we employed VIA Freeze TM Research controlled rate freezer (Asymptote, Cambridge, UK). The freezer successfully provided high accuracy control of the cooling temperature and accommodate up to 481 mL cryovials in an instrument-specific metal holder.
Each cryovial contained 50 L of HFE-7500 at the bottom of the cryovial as a cushion layer, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant floating layer, and 20 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax marked with fluorescein, and 20 droplets of INA free milli Q water marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. Similar to the previous observations, the droplets with INA froze at -7.1 0.59 °C and droplets without INA did not freeze until the temperature reached to -12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer (Figure 4 ). This observation suggested that the controlled cooling rate provided better detection of INA compared to the freeze-float selection in a commodity freezer system (mean temperature -7.5 0.97 °C).
To evaluate the uniformity of the cooling between cells at different positions, we compared the temperature at which 1 g/mL Snomax droplets froze in Asymptote controlled rate freezer system and 96 deep well in generic freezer. We used python script KStest.ipynb (Source Code S3)
to compare the freezing temperature distributions. We observed well to well variability and interwell dispersion in the freezing time in the 96 deep well system (p = 0.31, standard deviation 1.6), whereas the distribution of freezing of droplets in Asymptote freezer (Figure 5 ) showed less difference of well to well freezing temperature (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) and overall 36% lower dispersion (Figure 6 ).

## Conclusion
To increase the efficiency and accuracy of the freeze-float system from the previous publication, we employed the automated droplets dispensing system and controlled rate freezer.
By using Biomek 3000 liquid handling system, theoretically generates up to ~3800 uniform 1 L droplets in the 96 well plate freeze-float system. The droplets generated by this system and contained INA showed similar freezing and floating behaviour to the experiment we conducted in the previous publication, which indicates that this system can be implemented to the high throughput freeze-float system. However, when the system needs to be transferred certain distance, for example from one laboratory to another, the droplet stability was not sufficient and static electricity caused by frictions caused coalescing. Due to this problem, it was not successful to combine the droplets generation system.
Next, we implemented the controlled-rate Asymptote freezer system to enlarge the capacity of the droplets and improve the accuracy of the system. The cell to cell thermal delay was improved by the constant linear cooling (from p = 4.410 -7 to p = 0.31). To confirm the accuracy of the screening system, the detection threshold of the INA concentration was investigated. papers.existing_summary:
Executive Summary
This paper presents an improved high-throughput freeze-float system for measuring ice nucleation activity (INA) in droplets. The study aimed to enhance the efficiency and accuracy of a previously developed freeze-float selection platform by incorporating automated droplet generation and a controlled-rate freezer. The researchers used a Biomek 3000 liquid handling system to generate up to 3,800 uniform droplets in a 96-well plate, achieving a polydispersity of 9.2%. These droplets were then subjected to freeze-float selection. The study found that the automated system generated droplets with INA that exhibited similar freezing and floating behavior to the previous system. To improve temperature uniformity, the researchers implemented an Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer, which accommodated up to 48 cryovials. The Asymptote freezer showed reduced well-to-well variability in freezing temperature (p = 0.83) and a 36% lower dispersion compared to a generic freezer. The study demonstrates the feasibility of a high-throughput freeze-float system for INA measurement, with improved efficiency and accuracy through automation and controlled cooling. The main limitation was droplet stability during transport, and static electricity caused by frictions caused coalescing. The study's significance lies in its potential for high-throughput screening of ice nucleating agents.

Research Context
The study addresses the need for high-throughput screening (HTS) in ice nucleation research, building upon a previously established freeze-float selection system. Prior methods for measuring ice nucleation, such as those using cuvettes, were limited by low throughput and non-uniform temperature distribution. The introduction of HTS methods, including droplet-based assays, has improved efficiency in biochemical assays. However, interfacing microfluidics with multi-well plates is not trivial. The study aims to overcome these limitations by integrating automated droplet generation and a controlled-rate freezer to improve throughput and accuracy in ice nucleation measurements.

Research Question Hypothesis
The central research question is how to improve the efficiency and accuracy of a freeze-float system for measuring ice nucleation. The study hypothesizes that automating droplet generation and using a controlled-rate freezer will enhance the system's performance. The study predicted that the automated droplet generation system would produce uniform droplets, leading to more reliable freezing temperature measurements. It was also predicted that the controlled-rate freezer would provide more uniform cooling, reducing well-to-well variability in freezing temperatures. The alternative hypothesis is that the automated system and controlled freezer would not significantly improve the system's performance. This work differs from prior research by integrating automated droplet generation with a controlled-rate freezer to improve the throughput and accuracy of the freeze-float system.

Methodological Details
The study employed a methodological approach to improve a freeze-float system for ice nucleation measurement. The study used two main experimental setups: a 96-well plate system with automated droplet generation and an Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer system. The Biomek 3000 liquid handling system (Beckman Coulter, Indianapolis, IN) was used to generate droplets. The study used 96 deep well plates and 1 mL cryovials. The droplets were generated in a silicone oil buoyant layer with 1% silicone surfactant system and HFE-7500 cushion layer. The droplets were 1 µL in volume. The droplet diameters were measured using the Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m (Source Code S1). The polydispersity of the droplets was calculated. The study used a commodity freezer and an Asymptote VIA Freeze TM Research controlled rate freezer (Asymptote, Cambridge, UK). The Asymptote freezer accommodated up to 48 × 1 mL cryovials. Each cryovial contained 50 µL of HFE-7500, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 20 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax marked with fluorescein, and 20 droplets of INA free milli Q water marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. The freezing temperature distributions were compared using a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Python script KStest.ipynb, Source Code S3). The study used 1 mg/mL Snomax. The study did not mention any preregistration or multiple-comparison corrections. The study adhered to standard laboratory safety protocols.

Procedures Architectures
The study implemented two primary experimental setups. The first setup involved automated droplet generation using a Biomek 3000 liquid handling system. The Biomek 3000 dispensed 1 µL droplets into a 96-deep-well plate. The droplets were generated at a standard dispensing rate of 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The second setup used an Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer. The Asymptote freezer accommodated 48 cryovials. Each cryovial contained three layers: a 50 µL HFE-7500 cushion layer, a 1 mL silicone oil layer with 1% surfactant, and 20 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax marked with fluorescein and 20 droplets of INA-free milli Q water marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. The Biomek 3000 was modified to change droplet generation parameters. The droplet diameters were measured using the Matlab automated circle detection program Droplet_Dispersion.m. The program detects circles in images and analyzes the diameter of each droplet. The Asymptote freezer provided constant rate cooling. The study used a generic digital camera for image recording. The key innovation was the integration of automated droplet generation with a controlled-rate freezer to improve the throughput and accuracy of the freeze-float system.

Key Results
The Biomek 3000 successfully generated uniform droplets. The polydispersity of the 60 droplets was 9.2%. The study expected no more than ±0.09 °C dispersion in the measurement of the nucleation temperature. The INA droplets showed droplet freezing behavior with a good agreement with the previous report. The freezing temperature in cells in the same deep well plate showed p-value of 4.4 × 10⁻⁷ at constant temperature -28 °C generic freezer. The thermal gradient was decreased (p = 0.31) with linear cooling (-0.25 °C/min) compared to the constant temperature cooling. The Asymptote freezer provided high accuracy control of the cooling temperature. The droplets with INA froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C and droplets without INA did not freeze until the temperature reached to -12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer (Figure 4). The distribution of freezing of droplets in Asymptote freezer (Figure 5) showed less difference of well to well freezing temperature (p = 0.83) and overall 36% lower dispersion (Figure 6).

Interpretation Implications
The findings support the hypothesis that automation and controlled cooling improve the freeze-float system. The automated droplet generation provided uniform droplets, which improved the accuracy of freezing temperature measurements. The controlled-rate freezer reduced well-to-well variability, enhancing the reliability of INA detection. The results suggest that the freeze-float system can be scaled up for high-throughput screening of ice nucleating agents. The study implies that precise control over droplet size and cooling rate is critical for accurate ice nucleation measurements. The findings contribute to the understanding of heterogeneous ice nucleation by providing a more efficient and accurate method for studying the process.

Contradictions Limitations
The study identified several limitations. The droplet stability during transport was not sufficient, and static electricity caused by frictions caused coalescing. The study did not report the random seed used for the analysis. The study did not include a detailed discussion of the external validity of the findings. The study did not address the potential for contamination during the automated droplet generation process. The study did not fully explore the impact of different cooling rates on the freezing behavior of the droplets. The study did not provide a detailed comparison of the performance of the automated system with other HTS methods.

Data Code Availability
Source Code S1 and S3 are available.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the automated droplet generation system and the analysis of droplet size. Figure 4 illustrates the freezing behavior of droplets with and without INA in the Asymptote freezer, demonstrating the system's ability to differentiate between the two. Figures 5 and 6 compare the freezing temperature distributions in the Asymptote and generic freezers, highlighting the improved uniformity of cooling in the Asymptote freezer.

Three Takeaways
The primary contribution is the development of an automated, high-throughput freeze-float system for measuring ice nucleation activity. The strongest evidence is the reduced well-to-well variability in freezing temperature (p = 0.83) and 36% lower dispersion in the Asymptote freezer compared to a generic freezer, indicating improved accuracy. The main limitation is the droplet stability during transport, and static electricity caused by frictions caused coalescing, which requires further investigation to ensure the system's robustness and reliability for real-world applications.

questions.question: Why did the authors add a good heat conductor between parallel cuvettes instead of simply enlarging the original silicone-oil footprint?

options.A: Larger cuvettes could not contain enough aqueous droplets to reach statistical power
options.B: The initial freezer could not cool any sample below −0.5 °C/min
options.C: Low silicone-oil conductivity caused thermal lag across a larger footprint and several cuvettes had degree-scale differences
options.D: Parallel cuvettes made the freeze-float separation chemistry incompatible with HFE-7500

questions.rationale: The original 1-cm² cuvette held up to 50 droplets, but scaling its footprint or running many cuvettes together produced nonuniform temperatures.
